timeline.status: subdivision application submitted; applicant asked to produce an alternative townhouse layout and 3D visualizations before further review
timeline.summary: Application to subdivide a ~32-acre parcel (previously the subject of a 4-year Town Board rezoning/EIS process and a $1.5 million community benefits agreement) into a 10.6-acre hotel lot (115-key hotel) and a 21.8-acre, 72-unit townhouse lot, essentially unchanged from the plan the board gave a positive recommendation on in April 2021. The Town Planner and Chair pushed back hard on the townhouse layout — straight, tightly-spaced 'stadium seating' rows of paired units running down the slope from the IBM property line toward the hotel — calling it poor site planning driven purely by fitting 72 units within Town-Board-imposed constraints (30-ft unit separation, no more than two units per block); the applicant's team countered that the 72-unit count and those spacing constraints were locked in through the Town Board's finding statement and that any unit reduction would jeopardize project economics and potentially the community benefits payment. After a pointed back-and-forth about whether 'good site planning' could ever justify fewer than 72 units, the board asked the applicant to produce at least one genuine alternative layout and 3D renderings/elevations (rather than a flat 2D plan) to better evaluate the design, and separately flagged the unresolved question of how residents would safely cross Route 22 to reach the adjacent community park, noting NYSDOT has been unresponsive to the applicant directly and wants to deal only with the town.

timeline.status: referred — positive recommendations to Town Board (4 stories, 124 keys) and to ZBA for the story variance; ARB referral deferred pending building elevations/cross-section
timeline.summary: The applicant returned with a revised landscape plan (500+ new, largely native trees, dark-sky-compliant lighting, and an internal trail network) developed with input from Toll Brothers as the eventual builder. The board discussed increasing the hotel from 3 to 4 stories (staying within the existing 45-foot height limit) and from 115 to 124 keys, both requested because hotel operators would not commit to a 3-story building; the board voted positive recommendations to the Town Board on both changes and a positive referral to the ZBA for the story variance. A proposed pedestrian sidewalk connection across Route 22 into town was discussed and judged impractical without NYSDOT participation. The board referred the project to the Conservation Board but held the ARB referral until building elevations and a cross-section (to assess view impacts from the hotel roofline) are submitted.

timeline.status: referred to ARB; public hearing scheduled for December (submission deadline November 28)
timeline.summary: The board reviewed cross-sections showing the hotel's relationship to the townhouse rows, extensively debated whether to require internal sidewalks (ultimately asking the applicant to study a one-sided, curb-adjacent 4-foot sidewalk that would push the back-to-back townhouse yards roughly seven feet closer together and closer to 12-foot retaining walls) versus land-banking a future connector sidewalk toward Business Park Drive that the board acknowledged wasn't practical to build now given a dangerous Route 22 crossing. The board also discussed relocating the amenities building toward the site's interior, screening a hillside meadow near the hotel parking lot with native evergreens (e.g., red cedar) rather than converting it entirely, and pushed back on a Town Planner comment that the two-bedroom townhouse units were oversized, accepting the applicant's argument that the unit size matched market demand for 55+ housing. The board agreed to refer the project to the ARB and to schedule a public hearing for the December 12 meeting.

timeline.status: public hearing kept open, no date certain — applicant to revise and resubmit
timeline.summary: The board pressed hard on whether to require internal sidewalks along at least one side of each street, learning that doing so would push townhouse backyards roughly four feet closer to already-tall retaining walls and that the end-user (Toll Brothers) opposed sidewalks as an HOA maintenance burden with little real use; the applicant also revealed that a New York State fire code update may require 26-foot-wide roadway sections near fire hydrants (versus the planned 24 feet), which would compound the sidewalk-driven space crunch on the dead-end road. Michael Pollack and James Jensen argued walkability was effectively promised during the environmental review and findings-statement process for this age-restricted community and pushed back on the applicant's claim it was merely 'encouraged'; Steven Sauro was reluctant to force a decision without seeing a fully engineered alternative. The board also discussed relocating the pool/amenities building to a more central, less roadside location (leaving the choice to the applicant) and confirmed the applicant had separately obtained a ZBA variance for the fourth hotel story and a Town Board hearing on the amended findings statement. No sidewalk decision was reached; the hearing was kept open pending revised plans.

timeline.status: board gave direction to proceed without internal sidewalks (26-foot roads instead); public hearing adjourned pending final plans
timeline.summary: In the meeting's central and most extended debate, the applicant argued that internal sidewalks are incompatible with the site's tight townhouse layout and topography — requiring roughly seven feet of additional width per road that would push units closer to already-tall retaining walls — and offered 26-foot-wide roads (versus a 24-foot minimum) throughout as a walkability compromise instead of sidewalks. The board reviewed a Westchester County Planning Board advisory memo (which raised age-restriction and regional-connectivity concerns the board found largely outside its jurisdiction, since those parameters were fixed by the Town Board's zoning and findings statement) and debated at length whether the project's environmental findings statement effectively committed the applicant to sidewalks, with Michael Pollack and James Jensen arguing the board had never been shown a quantified trade-off (e.g., smaller units freeing room for sidewalks) while Steven Sauro, Lawrence Ruisi, and Chairman Carthy concluded sidewalks were impractical here and that requiring them risked killing project viability. The Chairman summarized a 3-2 board lean toward moving forward without sidewalks and directed the applicant to finalize plans on that basis; the hearing was adjourned without a date certain.

Town Board referral on an amended rezoning petition to reclassify the full roughly 32-acre site (previously split between OB-H hotel zoning and RMF-SCH age-restricted senior zoning) to RMFA multifamily, proposing 83 fee-simple townhouse units (market-rate plus affordable) with a clubhouse, pool, and trails, entirely eliminating the previously controversial hotel component. Board members welcomed the hotel's removal but raised concerns about amenity adequacy for a now car-dependent, potentially family-oriented (not age-restricted) community, and about whether the layout still leveraged the site's topography for views as an earlier iteration had. The Board voted unanimously to send a letter endorsing removal of the hotel and an all-residential, non-age-restricted concept with a maximum unit cap, while reserving site plan-level issues (internal circulation, sidewalks, unit design) for later review.

timeline.status: referred — town board to consider rezoning; hearing tentatively scheduled July 10
timeline.summary: Applicant presented a redesigned 88-unit, fee-simple townhouse project (80 market-rate, 8 affordable) proposed for rezoning to RMFA ahead of a Town Board hearing, eliminating the prior hotel (OBH) zoning designation. Board discussion covered whether affordable units should be spread throughout the project versus concentrated near the pool/clubhouse, a large rock-processing/cut-and-fill operation (~100,000+ cubic yards) not yet fully engineered, a possible DOT-funded roadway/turn-lane improvement near Route 22, and whether the project's community benefit agreement funds (currently earmarked broadly, with $500,000 for parking/circulation) could be directed toward that roadway project. The board referred the matter to the Conservation Board and County Planning and tentatively set a July 10 public hearing pending Wednesday's Town Board rezoning action.

timeline.status: public hearing opened and kept open (adjourned) pending outstanding details
timeline.summary: Public hearing opened on the 88-townhouse (91-lot) subdivision/site plan following the town's RMFA rezoning; the applicant presented landscaping (500+ trees, dark-sky lighting, pollinator meadow), a proposed woodland walking trail whose extent was still under internal debate, and floor plans showing flex-room/loft spaces the board flagged as potential de facto bedrooms that could exceed the environmental review's assumed unit-bedroom counts. Lawrence Ruisi pressed on clubhouse programming, parking adequacy, a roughly 55-foot site slope's cut-and-fill implications, and requested full building elevations (having received only one page). No members of the public spoke; the board adjourned (kept open) the hearing to allow the applicant to work directly with planning/engineering staff on these details.

timeline.status: public hearing reconvened, kept open — continuing design refinement
timeline.summary: Applicant reported completed ARB (model/color approval) and Conservation Board recommendations, shifted several units (81-88 and 49-52) for more separation from the entrance drive aisle and added a retaining wall creating flatter backyards, relocated a water main to avoid steep slopes, and — in response to a Conservation Board/town engineering concern about concentrating stormwater discharge onto adjacent park athletic fields sitting partly in a floodplain — agreed to pipe runoff through an upsized existing park pipe rather than using a hillside level spreader. The landscape plan now proposes over 460 new trees, tree-themed street "neighborhoods," and a roughly 1.5-acre central passive-recreation open space with rustic seating/art. Two items remained open: defining room/bedroom counts for zoning-calculation purposes, and confirming whether the built design still satisfies specific site-design commitments (pavers, stone walls, cottage gardens evoking the site's farm history) made in the DEIS.

timeline.status: approved (SEQRA findings adopted; preliminary and final subdivision resolutions adopted as amended)
timeline.summary: Finalization of the residential subdivision (now all-residential after the hotel component was dropped) following an earlier environmental impact statement. The board adopted the SEQRA findings statement (updated primarily to reflect removal of the hotel), closed the hearing, and adopted both preliminary and final subdivision resolutions as amended to require native/drought-tolerant plantings, clarification of community/open-space acreage credit, and later confirmation that AFFH-unit patio space matches market-rate units - deferring detailed site plan issues (fuel source for heating, generator siting, patio/fence details) to individual lot site plan review.

Approval of a master site plan for the townhome subdivision, with individual lot-level site plans (chosen from three pre-approved unit models) delegated to the RPRC rather than returning to the full board, and the future clubhouse to come back as its own separate site plan. Board members new to this style of phased, menu-based approval (as opposed to a traditional subdivision-then-individual-RPRC-review process) questioned how the mechanism would work in practice, drawing a comparison to the prior Shoemaker Lane subdivision; staff explained the site's tight lot constraints leave little room for RPRC-level deviation. The board adopted the master site plan resolution.
The board granted an extension of time for Eagle Ridge on a quick motion with no substantive discussion.
Procedural item: the board granted an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge application with no discussion.
The board granted an extension of time for Eagle Ridge, which is working through a brownfield designation for orchard-related soil before potentially advancing a different development.
The board approved an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge final subdivision.

The board granted an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge subdivision, which is awaiting Department of Health sign-off (verbal approval received) before final condition checks with the town's consultants.

The board discussed the pesticide/herbicide soil contamination on the site being handled through the DEC Brownfield/BCP program, the roughly 30,000 cubic yards of soil to be trucked out, phasing, and buyer disclosure, then granted a 90-day extension of time.

Request for an extension of time on the Eagle Ridge subdivision. The applicant reported the Mylar had been submitted to the County Health Department but review had stalled because the reviewing staffer was out for about a month with no clear hand-off. The board granted the extension of time.

The applicant's attorney requested an extension of time for the Eagle Ridge subdivision and site plan. The subdivision plat is still with the county Department of Health for execution, but all other outstanding items (easements, etc.) have been completed, with the DOH being the only hold-up; completion is hoped for by spring 2026. The board had no questions and approved both the subdivision extension and the site plan extension.

As a condition of the 2024 master site plan approval, the applicant returned for site plan approval of a two-story, ~5,100 sq ft clubhouse with pool, bocce, pickleball, and an event lawn. Parking was short - 56 spaces required versus 26 provided at the building plus dispersed visitor spaces - and the board declined to let visitor parking be double-counted, voting to refer the applicant to the ZBA for a parking variance. The dominant concern was tall tiered retaining walls (12 to 13.5 feet) facing the community park, which the board found too industrial; the applicant offered landscaping screening, stamped/colored concrete, and staking. The board scheduled a site visit for the following Wednesday and acknowledged receipt of the town engineer's bond memo.

The board handled a routine request for an extension of time for Eagle Ridge. A member reported an update from Corey indicating the applicant is able to move forward and obtain the final sign-off, so this should be the last extension needed. The chair made a motion to grant the extension and it passed. Brief confirmation was given that the DEP paperwork was in order.

timeline.status: tabled; new site walk to be scheduled, immediate drainage fix directed
timeline.summary: Long-running (over a year, since April 2021) dispute over a roughly 9-foot retaining wall built without a permit at the property line, now proposed to remain as-is on the strength of a post-hoc engineer certification, plus a PVC drainage pipe discharging driveway runoff directly onto the adjacent neighbor's property. The neighbor testified to repeated basement flooding and objected strongly to legitimizing the unpermitted wall via landscaping mitigation alone. A board member (likely Michael Pollack) challenged the board for treating the illegally-built wall as a fixed 'given' rather than asking what proper planning would have produced from scratch; the chair agreed the board needed to revisit the matter in the field rather than continue accepting the status quo, citing the year-long delay's ongoing harm to the neighbor. The board directed the applicant to plug/disconnect the offending point-discharge pipe immediately (ahead of the rainy season) while scheduling a fresh site visit to reconsider the wall itself.

Long-running violation case (wall built 5-8 years ago without required permits, now up to roughly 7.5 feet tall) with a newly introduced HES soil report finding non-residential-level contaminants and recommending a demarcation layer and additional fill — a remedy the applicant's soil consultant sharply disputed as using the wrong DEC standard. Board members voiced strong, consistent criticism that the resulting wall severely and permanently harmed the neighboring property's quality of life, sunlight, drainage, and value, and stated they would never have approved the wall as built. No vote was taken; the Board directed the applicant to prepare a cut-and-fill topography comparison and coordinate a site meeting between the Town Engineer, HES, and the applicant's team before returning.

The applicant presented three alternative wall-reduction concepts (a new lower wall filled/terraced in front of the existing 7.8-foot wall; a shorter modified section preserving certain trees; and a no-new-wall grading/boulder option preserving existing vegetation), all keeping the existing wall largely intact while reducing its effective height to roughly six feet through combinations of new walls, fill, and plantings. After extensive back-and-forth on each option's tradeoffs (proximity to the neighbor, tree preservation, material selection), the Board gave the applicant conceptual direction — favoring moving the wall closer to the soil stockpile, preserving a substantial landscape buffer, reconsidering wall material (skepticism toward a "Unilock" modular option in favor of natural stone), and reviewing whether certain pine trees should come out to enable better landscaping — while still awaiting official fill-quantity data needed for HES to set a soil testing protocol. The exchange ended cordially, a marked shift from the sharply critical March 27 session.

timeline.status: tabled — additional soil testing and revised cross-section plans required
timeline.summary: Continuation of a contentious matter to legalize an unpermitted retaining wall and roughly 650 cubic yards of imported fill near a property line; a neighbor (Corey, representing the abutting owner) objected strongly that the applicant's newest "double wall" proposal did not address the board's prior direction to set walls back from the property line and that the wall remained overbearing. After extended technical debate on wall heights/setbacks, septic and drainage implications, and site history (with a neighbor asserting fill was trucked in as early as 2000), the board recessed into executive session with counsel and, on returning, directed the applicant to develop a soil-testing protocol with HES and prepare two alternative wall/cross-section plans (a stepped/lowered-wall option and a set-back-new-wall option) for a future meeting.

timeline.status: tabled — dispute over soil testing protocol unresolved, continued to July 10
timeline.summary: Continued dispute over whether imported fill (contested as either under or over 1,000 cubic yards) must meet the town consultant HES's more stringent "unrestricted use" soil testing standard versus the "restricted use" general-fill standard the applicant's completed testing already satisfied under DEC Part 360. The applicant's attorney argued the fill's provenance being unknown (because it was never permitted in advance) justified the town's tougher standard, while the visibly frustrated property owner argued he had already spent roughly $11,000 on testing that showed compliance and that the town had let the unpermitted wall construction proceed for years without objection. The board tabled the matter again, directing the applicant to work quickly with HES and asking that HES attend the July 10 meeting.

timeline.status: pulled from calendar — building inspector cited continued noncompliance
timeline.summary: The board briefly noted this long-running matter had been removed from the agenda by the building inspector pending the applicant coming into compliance with outstanding violations; no substantive discussion occurred.

Discussion item where the board acts in an advisory capacity to the building department over fill imported without a permit. The applicant's attorney and consultant argued prior testing (with slightly elevated but acceptable lead) was sufficient, while the town's HES consultant recommended a more rigorous DEC Part 360 sampling protocol. The board directed the applicant to comply with the HES testing protocol before the fill could be allowed to remain.

Continued discussion of a stone retaining wall built without a permit (~150 ft long, a section over 6 ft, up to ~9 ft near the street). The board reiterated its 18-month-old April 2023 direction to step the existing wall back and cap it at four feet with a tiered second wall and plantings, while the applicant pushed a grade-and-bury alternative and ultimately declined to prepare new plans, asking the board to deny the six submitted plans. The board declined to issue denials (which would force fill removal) and left it at an impasse, with soil-contamination testing still outstanding.
Item was removed from tonight's agenda; the board hopes to take it up at a future meeting.

Public hearing on legalizing an existing ~7-year-old unpermitted wall, fill, grading, tree removal and shed; the applicant proposed adding ~8 cubic yards of fill and four trees to lower the wall exposure below six feet rather than tiering it. The board rejected this, found itself at an impasse because the applicant refused to tier/reduce the wall as previously directed, closed the public hearing, and directed staff to prepare a resolution of denial for the next meeting.
With the public hearing previously closed, the board adopted the draft resolution after amending the language of a passage quoting a board member.

timeline.summary: The prior owners of a 5.8-acre parcel, who retained subdivision rights when they sold the existing house and lot to the current owner, proposed splitting off a 3.4-acre undeveloped lot. The board found the submitted plans inadequate (missing wetland boundary and buffer delineation) and directed the applicant to have a wetland scientist flag and survey the wetlands and confirm septic area location before the application could meaningfully proceed to the Conservation Board, cautioning that the buffer alone might leave little room for development.

timeline.status: discussion only; site walk to be scheduled, public hearing to follow
timeline.summary: Follow-up on a two-lot subdivision simplified by the town's determination that a stream along the High Street frontage is an unregulated drainage channel rather than a wetland. The board asked the applicant to show a more realistic future house footprint/disturbance area (rather than an undersized placeholder) so future buyers aren't constrained, to resolve stormwater discharge routing near the drainage ditch/wetland boundary to avoid triggering a wetland permit, and confirmed the New York City aqueduct easement crossing the property would not be disturbed. The board agreed to schedule a site walk ahead of a public hearing.

Public hearing on a two-lot subdivision of a ~5.8-acre R-1A parcel (lots of 1.25 and 4.59 acres); after confirming the frontage area is a drainage ditch rather than regulated wetland and reviewing stormwater and septic, the board closed the hearing, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the preliminary and final subdivision plats as amended, with a note added that future homes return to the Planning Board.

timeline.summary: Extension granted due to COVID-related construction cost increases and supply-chain delays; the site has already been stabilized and seeded pending resumption of work.

timeline.status: board declared intent to be lead agency; referrals deemed premature
timeline.summary: Initial presentation of a new owner's amended site plan for a previously-approved (2021) 74,850 sq ft warehouse building, now proposed as a 146,000 sq ft building with the identical footprint but three self-storage stories (~92,000 sq ft) alongside a smaller warehouse component (~53,000 sq ft) for existing tenant Jan Tile, who will remain under a 10-year lease. The redesign requires a parking variance (220 spaces provided vs. 277 required) and an FAR variance (0.43 proposed vs. 0.3 permitted). The applicant intends to retain Jan Tile's existing approved outdoor storage in its current, more limited footprint and relocate front-facing loading docks given the building's new public-facing self-storage use. The board declared its intent to act as lead agency for SEQRA review but declined to make county/ZBA/ARB referrals yet as premature.

timeline.status: continued — to return to the Planning Board in December before a January ZBA referral for FAR and parking variances
timeline.summary: The applicant presented a revised plan flipping the proposed warehouse and self-storage uses to separate their circulation, plus added screening for loading docks and outdoor storage areas. The bulk of the discussion concerned the existing Jantile stone-fabrication tenant's history of expanding outdoor storage well beyond what was previously approved; the board explicitly cast this application as an opportunity to correct that prior 'mistake' by requiring all loading/unloading and storage to occur within building footprints and enforceable striped limits, while acknowledging the tenant's stated need for some outdoor staging. The board also flagged an incomplete site plan that omits overnight commercial-vehicle parking (which would worsen an already roughly 50-space parking shortfall) and unresolved truck-turning movements around the new building, directing the applicant to resolve both before returning in December ahead of a January ZBA referral for FAR and parking variances.

timeline.status: referred to ZBA without a board recommendation, 3-1 (a prior motion for a positive recommendation failed for lack of majority support)
timeline.summary: The board debated at length whether to support roughly a 50% FAR variance (0.30 to 0.43) driven by a proposed three-level self-storage component, alongside a 57-space parking variance. Current tenant Jantile's owner testified that all loading/unloading occurs at interior loading docks and none outdoors, and that any additional storage needs would go into the new building rather than expand outdoor storage; Steven Sauro supported keeping outdoor storage within previously approved limits, while Michael Pollack argued forcefully that granting such a large FAR variance for converted interior volume set a troubling precedent ('opens the floodgates') that any warehouse tenant could exploit, and Christopher Carthy voiced similar concerns about departing from the district's 0.3 FAR policy judgment. A motion for a positive ZBA recommendation failed to pass; the board then, after waiting for Lawrence Ruisi to return, passed a motion (3-1) to refer the application to the ZBA without any recommendation, leaving the variance merits for the ZBA to weigh independently.

Applicant sought after-the-fact approval for removal of 38 town-regulated trees beyond the roughly 200-plus previously approved, attributed to a large silver maple falling the wrong way during construction and damaging surrounding trees, which the applicant said prompted a broader (uncoordinated) cleanup. A mitigation plan proposing 87 new trees, mostly evergreen screening, was presented informally. After debate over whether to condition approval on an already-accepted mitigation plan versus a future one, the Board adopted a SEQRA negative declaration and an amended resolution removing the tree-removal violation, requiring that any future mitigation plan and bonding amount be reviewed and approved by the Planning Board (not staff). The vote passed 4-1.
Routine extension of time granted for the approved site plan at 100 Business Park Drive, with no discussion of substance.

Applicant presented a revised plan reducing the requested FAR variance from .13 to .07 and eliminating the previously-needed 57-83 space parking variance by adding parking (317 spaces total) through a reconfigured self-storage/warehouse building plus an 11-court pickleball/recreation facility with locker rooms and a mezzanine party space. Board members pressed hard on whether the original variance justification ("benign," low-traffic self-storage/warehouse use) still holds given the recreation use's much higher intensity, on pedestrian safety from parking to the facility, and on what happens if the use later converts to office. With a ZBA hearing set for June 1, the board concluded it had no further substantive input before that hearing and let the applicant proceed to the ZBA.

timeline.status: negative declaration adopted; positive recommendation sent to Town Board for special use permit
timeline.summary: Applicant sought a Town Board special use permit for recreational uses — 11 pickleball courts and legalizing roughly 1,700 sf of an existing personal gym inside an existing building — noting the Town Board had added a rec-center special use requirement in this zone within the past couple of years where it was previously a permitted use. The board adopted a negative declaration and voted a positive recommendation sending the applicant to the Town Board for the special use permit; the amended site plan itself (including reworked, centralized parking near the pickleball courts) remains before the planning board and is targeted for the September 28 meeting once the Town Board acts.

timeline.status: advancing toward public hearing, scheduled for October 28
timeline.summary: Following the Town Board's grant of the special use permit for the recreation uses, the board worked through remaining minor site plan conditions (outdoor storage restricted to the Jantile tenant only, with permission expiring; an overnight-truck-parking note to be added) and discussed traffic-flow/signage separation between truck traffic, the Jantile business, and pickleball-court visitors. The board scheduled the public hearing for the October 28 meeting.

timeline.summary: Ahead of redeveloping the site, the applicant sought to crush existing building foundations and concrete features in place (separating out rebar) to backfill basement voids and create a level, structurally engineered pad rather than hauling material off-site, with a nearby crusher location chosen for being relatively removed from residential receptors. Board members probed whether importing fill to supplement the crushed material and whether stockpiling near the site's two water courses would require additional safeguards, and whether reusing on-site debris constituted a landfill/construction-demolition-debris situation requiring separate permitting (staff did not believe so, since material stays on-site). The board approved the permit with added conditions requiring a sediment/erosion control plan reviewed by the Town Engineer, a defined limited-disturbance work-area boundary, a stop-work condition if the dust-suppression system fails, and a daily street-sweeping requirement.

timeline.status: referred (town board holds public hearing June 14)
timeline.summary: Extensive review of a revised 34-unit townhouse concept (down from 43) ahead of the Town Board's June 14 special-use-permit hearing, with the applicant reorienting buildings to eliminate a loop road along Maple, splitting four-unit buildings into pairs to look like single-family homes, and citing a roughly $1-1.25 million cumulative community benefit agreement (CBA) with the town. The board pushed hard on front/back orientation so backyards wouldn't face Maple Avenue at the town's "gateway," screening while preserving the church view, whether open (uncounted-FAR) carport parking versus town-board-requested fully enclosed garages would require a new FAR variance or a code amendment, a 10% fair-and-affordable housing component, traffic/turning-lane and fire-truck circulation concerns, and a requested pedestrian crosswalk to the shopping center. The board agreed to send the Town Board a recommendation rather than requiring new renderings first, given the June 12/14 deadlines.

timeline.status: referred / deferred — board declined to vote on a recommendation this meeting
timeline.summary: Applicant presented a revised layout (loop road along Maple eliminated, buildings split into two-four-two unit groupings, all units facing one direction) and pushed for a same-night board recommendation ahead of a Wednesday Town Board special-permit hearing. Several board members, led by Lawrence Ruisi, objected strongly to reviewing a just-submitted plan "on the fly" and setting a precedent for rushed reviews, while also debating whether enclosed garages (versus open carports) would require a zoning text amendment or an area variance given FAR limits. The board ultimately asked the applicant to formally submit plans and return in two weeks rather than issuing an immediate recommendation, over the applicant's objection about deadline pressure.

timeline.status: referred — board voted to send Town Board a positive recommendation with conditions
timeline.summary: After extensive review of the revised plan (loop road removed, units regrouped into two-four-two clusters facing away from Maple, back facades redesigned to look front-like), the board formally endorsed the design and voted to send the Town Board a special-use-permit recommendation. Conditions/asks included: pursuing enclosed garages via a ZBA variance or code text change to resolve the FAR conflict, upgraded landscaping/screening of backyard vistas along Maple, an easement for a future right-turn lane and sidewalk to the bus stop plus a crosswalk toward Armonk Square, coordinating the unit bedroom count (flagging a den/office with a full bath as a de facto bedroom against the environmental review's unit-count benchmark), and support for a roughly 3.7%-over building/lot coverage variance. James Jensen separately cautioned that unresolved floodplain/compensatory-storage engineering could force the applicant to materially alter the layout after Town Board approval, which the applicant and Town Attorney Roland agreed would be handled at site plan review.

timeline.status: board voted to refer applicant to ZBA for FAR and building-coverage variances
timeline.summary: Applicant finalized the garage-enclosure design the board had previously requested: fully enclosing parking garages on all five affected buildings, raising FAR from 0.40 to 0.477 and building coverage from a 20% code maximum to 23.7% (both requiring ZBA variances). In exchange, the "tucked-under-car" open-garage look is eliminated town-wide across the project, with field-stone and clapboard detailing to break up massing. The board discussed redirecting community-benefit funds (potentially $100,000+) toward a sidewalk/crosswalk connection to the county bus stop across Bedford Road, and agreed the dense evergreen screening along the shared boundary with the adjacent town-owned parcel could be relaxed now that the site is being redeveloped from a construction/storage use into a residential community (no longer needing to be hidden). The board voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the two variances, with next steps including the ARB, a Conservation Board wetland-buffer-impact review, and a targeted return by the September 28 meeting.

timeline.status: discussion only; working toward a public hearing
timeline.summary: Continued site plan review of this gateway-to-town townhouse project, following resolution of an earlier floor-area-ratio issue via ZBA variance. Roughly 20 mostly stormwater-related engineering comments from the town's consultant were largely deemed resolvable, including upsizing a sewer line and floodplain-related adjustments. The dominant concern was aesthetic: a large stormwater detention area integrated along the Maple Avenue-facing frontage and behind unit patios was described by board members as resembling a dry "moat," a significant departure from the park-like open space originally envisioned, prompting suggestions of a landscaped wall to soften the appearance; a proposed $100,000 pledge from the applicant (made during the earlier town board rezoning) toward Bedford Road sidewalks/crosswalk was also discussed as needing to be finalized. No vote was taken; the applicant continues revising plans toward a public hearing.

timeline.status: referred to ZBA with a positive recommendation
timeline.summary: Continued review of the gateway-to-town townhouse project, with the board clarifying the approval sequence needed: ZBA variance first, then Town Board special use permit, then a return to the Planning Board. The board voted to send the applicant to the ZBA with a positive recommendation.

Applicant reported completing the required off-site mitigation (Town Board license along Maple/municipal lot, modified deed and CBA); board resolved the affordable-unit count (30 market-rate plus 4 affordable of 34 total), reviewed stormwater/floodplain and wetland-mitigation conditions, then closed the hearing and approved the site plan and wetlands permit.

The board granted a site-plan extension of time to August 11, 2025, mirroring the town board's special-use-permit extension. Discussion centered on the town's dissatisfaction with the property's appearance ('an eyesore' at the town entrance) and a 'gentleman's agreement' for the applicant to clean up the site; the board also pressed on why the permitted on-site rock crushing hadn't occurred (the crushed material is intended for reuse in the project).

cases.name: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road
cases.address: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Jerry Tortarella (Hocherman Tortorella & Wexler), attorney; Tim Allen (Bibbo Associates)

trajectory.status: public hearing continued/adjourned to first September meeting
public hearing continued | adjourned to Nov 10

timeline.summary: Introductory review of two related wetland applications: shifting/reworking golf putting greens and access paths on 92 (originally permitted administratively in 1999) and remediation of path work behind a pool on 94 that had drawn a building-department violation resolved by plea; treated as a Type II action, the board directed a site walk and referral to the Conservation Board, with a functional wetland analysis to follow.

Discussion of after-the-fact wetlands/buffer disturbance (a reconstructed golf hole on 92 and unpermitted pool work on 94) with a conservation-board-endorsed 2-to-1 mitigation and 5-year monitoring plan; the board wanted the debris/shed and stored fuels cleaned up and a site walk done before voting, and scheduled a public hearing for the second February meeting.

Combined public hearing on site plan, wetlands, and tree-removal permits for a golf green/tees on 92 and a pool renovation and access path on 94, following a building-department violation for pool work and path creation without permits; multiple neighbors and two attorneys objected on safety, wetlands, tree-clearing, and commercial-use grounds, and after an executive session the board kept the hearing open and asked staff to research the approval history while the applicant addresses neighbor concerns.

The reopened public hearing proceeded even though the applicant's representative failed to appear and the application had not changed since the last meeting; neighbors reiterated safety and wetland concerns and the board discussed how to constrain the greens and tees before adjourning the hearing.

timeline.status: public hearing continued/adjourned to first September meeting
timeline.summary: Continuation of the hearing on after-the-fact wetlands and site-plan approval for golf features on two adjoining wetland-buffer properties: one retained (unfinished) green, two sand traps, a constructed tee box (T1) and three additional turf tee positions (T2-T4), plus paths and a shed. The applicant argued the tees are de minimis, non-structural, that no golf-ball incidents have occurred in 26 years, and that setbacks for pools/tennis courts do not apply. Neighbor Barry Edelman (88 Round Hill Road) opposed through counsel, stressing safety of children/grandchildren, the green sitting only 8-16 feet from the shared line, trajectories aimed at his glass-walled house, intensification from two to four tees, and requesting a 30-foot setback, DEC review, and stronger screening. After an executive session with counsel, the board indicated it favors retaining the green with a robust landscape and net mitigation plan along the 88 line but wants T3 and T4 eliminated, and directed the applicant to pursue DEC and a building-inspector determination. Adjourned to the first September meeting.

Reopened (re-noticed) public hearing on renovation/expansion of existing golf greens and tees, plus wetlands and tree-removal permits. The applicant removed two proposed tees, submitted a buffer/screening landscape plan (12 trees, 54 shrubs), and brought a golf pro to argue the short hole poses little errant-ball risk. Neighbors (Kalindi Bhat at 98, and Barry Edelman at 88 via counsel) pressed safety concerns about golf balls crossing property lines. The Board debated whether the 1998 legalization (via the Conservation Board's wetlands permit) binds this review, and discussed adding a low deflector screen/netting near the tees. No vote due to the short board; hearing left open and adjourned to Oct 27, with the applicant to show the screening on the plan.

timeline.status: public hearing continued | adjourned to Nov 10
timeline.summary: Continued wetlands-permit hearing for an existing golf putting green and two tee boxes. The applicant proposed a localized 10-ft-wide by 6-ft-high net above the upper tee plus deflectors to protect the neighbor. Chairman Carthy floated conceptual town legislation to regulate putting greens (treat greens as structures respecting side-yard setbacks, and limit tee distance to 3x the setback), while stressing it would not govern this application. The board pressed the applicant to pull the tees closer to the green so only chip/pitch shots are used, add netting at the road-side tee, and add evergreen screening near the OWTS; the applicant argued a 25-year no-incident history. The hearing was adjourned to Nov 10 for a revised plan and a resolution vote.

The chair announced at the outset that the public hearing for 92 & 94 Round Hill Road had been moved off the agenda for the evening and would be covered on another night. No substantive discussion occurred. The board confirmed whether anyone in the audience was present for the item before moving on.

The applicant's attorney appeared without the applicant, who was unavailable, and asked to carry the continued hearing to the second January meeting to allow time to review draft approval documents with the client over the holidays. He reported the client elected to remove retaining-wall segment 'T1' entirely and submitted revised plans reflecting that. The neighbor's counsel spoke constructively, praising progress and raising administrative cleanups (drawing revision dates, papering the T1 removal, an as-built condition, a null-and-void-on-alteration clause, and whether the T2 netting should also be netted on top). The board reopened, took the neighbor's comments, and re-adjourned to January 26, 2026.

cases.name: 47 Windmill Road — House Addition & Retaining Walls
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by engineer Thomas Carrigan and architect Dan Simone)

trajectory.status: negative referral leaning; applicant asked to redesign to avoid variances

timeline.status: negative referral leaning; applicant asked to redesign to avoid variances
timeline.summary: Proposed addition, driveway/motor-court expansion, and tiered retaining walls near a rear-yard wetland/pond required front-yard setback variances for the motor court (which the town's motor-court law was specifically written to prevent so close to the road), plus a gross-land-coverage variance and floodplain/wetland permits. The Chair told the applicant the plan did not respect 'the spirit of the zoning laws' and urged a redesign within code (e.g., a smaller apron or a second curb cut rather than a full motor court) before returning; the applicant's team explained the real need was simply drop-off access at the front door given the site's constrained, wedge-shaped topography between the road and the lake. A joint site walk was scheduled.

Extensive design workshop on a revised plan for a house addition, garage, and tiered retaining walls near a lake/wetland buffer and steep slopes. The planner found the plan still 'aggressive,' flagging that a proposed motor court and second curb cut sited within the wetland buffer are not permitted by code. The board negotiated design mitigations (natural boulder walls instead of faced walls, pulling the garage back a bay, softening the rear wall curve, green-screening exposed foundations) and directed the applicant to engage the Conservation Board and return with a finalized plan and landscaping/mitigation details; the applicant confirmed the reduced plan would fall under the gross land coverage threshold, avoiding a ZBA referral.

After planning staff recapped the prior meeting's concerns (motor court and second curb cut sited within the wetland buffer), the applicant's team presented a new conceptual alternative eliminating the second curb cut in favor of a single combined curb cut and turnaround, still within the buffer but reduced in footprint, along with continued discussion of retaining-wall heights on the southwest side.

Applicant finalized the alternate plan floated at the prior work session: single curb cut (removing the second), one fewer garage bay, a redesigned front turnaround, and a single (rather than double-tiered) retaining wall on the garage's western corner with an exposed, screened foundation footing, plus added wall screening throughout to reduce visual impact.

Continued review of a house addition with tiered retaining walls (roughly six and a half feet at the highest point, tapering to zero) facing Long Pond, following a positive Conservation Board recommendation. The Board discussed visibility of the exposed garage foundation from a neighboring property and from across the pond, concluding a large tree canopy and rock outcropping would largely screen the walls, which will be finished in natural rubble stone rather than mortared masonry. The Board directed the applicant to schedule a public hearing with a draft resolution.

Continuation following prior conservation and ARB approvals; the applicant requested the draft resolution's extensive conditions be trimmed since they left too much open-ended follow-up to the Town Engineer. The Board closed the public hearing (no members of the public appeared) and directed staff to prepare a streamlined resolution for adoption at the next meeting.

Review of the updated draft resolution; the applicant asked to soften language regarding the existing septic expansion area given the system's age. Larry Ruisi pressed pointedly on why numerous straightforward open items (gross land coverage, floor area, elevations) remained unresolved after months of review despite the applicant's belief they had already been submitted, questioning whether a miscommunication with staff was to blame. The Board declined to adopt the resolution as-is and directed the applicant to close out the remaining items before the next meeting.

Final resolution adoption for the site plan, steep-slope wetland permit, and tree removal permit, after the Board's earlier insistence on trimming the resolution's conditions was satisfied. Very few conditions remained. The Board approved the resolution unanimously, closing out an application reviewed across multiple meetings since February.

cases.name: Summit Golf Club
cases.address: Summit Golf Club, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Represented by Janet Keras (Del Bello, Donnellan) and architect Ken Anderson

trajectory.status: positive recommendation to Town Board to amend the special use permit
positive recommendations to Town Board on two of three requests; permanent special use permit deferred pending more information
public hearing reconvened and kept open pending final resolution language
extensions of time granted (site plan and 8th/final subdivision 90-day)

timeline.status: positive recommendation to Town Board to amend the special use permit
timeline.summary: The applicant presented a new roughly 6,000-square-foot, two-story golf-course maintenance building to replace the existing facility, which sits in the way of active construction on the residential component and cannot practically coexist with ongoing golf operations. Because tying the maintenance building to the golf course's special use permit (rather than the residential site plan) requires Town Board action, the board voted a positive recommendation referring the special use permit amendment to the Town Board.

timeline.status: positive recommendations to Town Board on two of three requests; permanent special use permit deferred pending more information
timeline.summary: Responding to a Town Board referral, the board recommended a six-month extension of the golf course's expired temporary special use permit and endorsed a request to allow public (non-member) golf bookings during the residential construction period to help the club's finances, while asking the Town Board to have counsel review the specific zoning code amendment language needed. The board also endorsed, in concept, locating a new maintenance and storage building on the golf course lot (relocating it out of the path of residential construction) as part of the eventual special use permit, but declined to recommend the permanent special use permit itself, since Town Planner Kauffman's memo still had open questions about club operations, membership caps, and chemical storage that the applicant agreed to address promptly.

Reopened public hearing on a permanent special use permit for club operations (membership caps, golf outings, social events, day camp for members' children, guest cottages, surface water sampling). The Board extensively negotiated operational parameters — a 500-member cap, member-sponsored golf outings, undefined "social events" left uncodified at the applicant's request, and a 100-child day camp — before voting to positively refer the permit to the Town Board, which holds final approval authority.

timeline.status: public hearing reconvened and kept open pending final resolution language
timeline.summary: Applicant summarized roughly two years of design changes made in response to board and public comment (eliminating a seventh building and its access road, relocating tennis courts and parking outside the 100-foot buffer, dropping the standalone clubhouse in favor of the amenities building) and presented final engineering changes tied to the six-building layout. The board discussed clarifying resolution language distinguishing between on-site recreational amenities and a recreation fee payment tied to any recreational programming deficiency, then adjourned (kept open) the hearing to finalize that language rather than close it that night.

The board considered two extensions of time for the Summit Club: one for the final subdivision plat approval and one for the site plan (with steep slopes and tree-removal permit approvals). Staff explained the applicant is working through the approval process and is reportedly taking deposits/listing units for sale, with the county Board of Health notoriously slow on the substantial infrastructure (including a sewage treatment plant). The board granted both extensions of time.

timeline.status: extensions of time granted (site plan and 8th/final subdivision 90-day)
timeline.summary: The project is awaiting Westchester County Health Department approval for a pump station, tank and water/sewer system, expected to be approved together. The board granted an extension of time on the site plan approval and the eighth (final) 90-day extension on the final subdivision plat.

No representative was present. The chair and planner gave an update noting background activity on water infrastructure: a water-line extension easement is already in place, but the timeline may accelerate so that water could be brought through the club and interconnected (potentially reaching Windmill), rather than the development operating as its own on-site water district. The board granted an extension of time.

Routine extension request for the ongoing Summit Club subdivision: the original approval carried a 180-day window, followed by a first 90-day extension, and this was a second 90-day extension (third overall grant). Staff reported the applicant is still working with the Westchester County Department of Health on wastewater and well-system technical submissions and is making diligent progress. The board granted the extension with brief discussion and no objection.

cases.name: 113 King Street (RCLA Enclave at Armonk / Toll)
cases.applicant: Developer (represented by attorney "Anthony")

trajectory.status: discussion only; initial referrals (ARB, engineering) to begin
discussion only; public hearing to be scheduled for January 2024

timeline.summary: Advisory referral from the Town Board on a proposal to rezone a roughly 38-acre site (includes converting a 100,000-sq-ft office building to RMF-SCH senior housing and rezoning the remainder to RMFA multifamily) for approximately 125 units including 18 affordable units, tied to a related tax-grievance settlement and a town water-infrastructure agreement. The Board discussed traffic circulation, school bus access, FAA/airport-approach height considerations, and amenity adequacy, and voted to send a revised advisory letter to the Town Board raising density/economics balance, traffic-consultant review, noise mitigation, and infrastructure cost-sharing clarity, while explicitly leaving the ultimate density decision to the Town Board.

timeline.status: discussion only; initial referrals (ARB, engineering) to begin
timeline.summary: First Planning Board presentation of the integrated redevelopment following town board rezoning and SEQRA approval: 125 age-targeted townhomes (Toll Brothers) plus repurposing an office building into 43 age-restricted senior apartments (Airport Campus), on a site vacant for eight years amid a regional office-space glut. The applicant emphasized community-benefit elements: Byron Hill School District's support, an NRDC/Riverkeeper water-quality agreement, an expanded conservation easement (over 9 acres), extension of public water to the site (aiding a future water district), affordable-housing compliance, roughly 900 new trees and a half-mile of walking trails, and net-positive tax revenue after municipal/school costs. The board raised the still-unresolved recreation-fee calculation (a potentially large per-unit fee the applicant argued their amenity package should offset) and construction phasing between the two co-applicants; no formal action was taken, with next steps being ARB and engineering referrals.

timeline.status: discussion only; public hearing to be scheduled for January 2024
timeline.summary: Continued design review, with the applicant pressing to keep the process moving toward a public hearing even with open items - notably centerline/curb radii adjustments on internal roads that could shift some unit locations, and a request that staggered units be pushed back slightly to widen driveways from 20 to roughly 22 feet. The board agreed public input at this stage would be valuable and authorized scheduling a public hearing for January.

Wrap-up discussion of a multifamily townhouse project with a clubhouse; the board reviewed draft findings statement and site plan/subdivision resolutions, resolved engineering/water-sewer conditions, discussed adding first-floor-bedroom and 45 dBA noise conditions, and flagged a school-bus routing/sight-line concern on Cooney Hill Road, aiming for final action on the 11th pending ARB approval.

The board adopted the SEQRA findings statement (consistent with the town board's) and approved the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions as amended, dated March 11, 2024; site plan approval was withheld because the applicant has not yet obtained ARB approval. Members debated the roughly 70 conditions but staff confirmed most were routine engineering items.
The board granted a routine extension of time; the applicant reported substantial progress on conditions but still needs DEP/SWPPP approval and county health department sign-off.

The applicant appealed an RPRC decision that referred it back to the ARB to finalize color-scheme distribution and per-lot landscaping across the 125-unit development. The applicant argued the ARB approval already provided for randomly distributed one-third/one-third/one-third color schemes and that reappearing was unnecessary and conflicting. After discussion, the Board granted the appeal but secured a commitment that the applicant will provide a progress report to the planner (Adam) at the one-third construction mark to give the ARB oversight of the distribution. Motion to grant the appeal passed.

A field-change request after a CAD software error caused the water-tank foundation, pumping station, and generator to be built roughly 10 feet north of the approved location, with minor adjustments to spacing between the components; the generator remains six feet from the property line and everything stays zoning-compliant. With no board questions, the resolution was adopted.

cases.name: 94 Business Park Drive — Loading Ramp Widening (Field Change)
cases.applicant: 94 Business Park Drive applicant
cases.lastStatus: approved — public hearing closed and resolution adopted as amended

trajectory.status: under design review; public hearing to be scheduled alongside continued information requests
public hearing continued (tabled pending revised application)
not approved as proposed — public hearing reopened and re-adjourned; applicant directed to return with a revised, enclosed-loading solution
approved — public hearing closed and resolution adopted as amended

timeline.summary: New York State DEC required additional stormwater treatment/a landscaped 'rain garden' along the northern parking-lot property line because regrading work didn't meet the redevelopment exemption; separately, the applicant value-engineered the roof-runoff storage from 60-inch storage pipes to StormTech chamber units (same storage volume, different material) due to cost/availability. Because construction was still early, the board treated this as a re-signed construction-plan revision rather than a minor field change and approved it after the Town Engineer explained why an infiltration design wasn't feasible (insufficient separation to the water table) and that irrigation reuse of the detained water wasn't practical given the short (multi-day) retention time.

timeline.status: under design review; public hearing to be scheduled alongside continued information requests
timeline.summary: Applicant proposes converting part of an existing warehouse building to portable-storage (POD) operations, with up to ~108 outdoor container storage spaces (three-high stacking) in the rear yard, serviced by a single forklift and roughly four to five delivery trucks. Board members probed the operational logistics (loading/unloading location, forklift movements, container cleaning happening off-site, seasonal storage utilization swings, truck routing), pressed for clarification on conflicting container-count figures in the application, and raised planning-level concerns about the ratio of outdoor storage to the site's already-maxed floor area ratio/building coverage and potential noise impact on neighbors. The board requested photos and site-utilization data from the company's existing Valley Cottage facility, a closer look at the approved landscaping plan (requested by a board member), and directed the applicant to submit outstanding information while scheduling the public hearing in parallel to avoid delay.

timeline.status: public hearing continued (tabled pending revised application)
timeline.summary: Continuation of a public hearing on an amended site plan to allow outdoor storage of up to 108-180 storage containers behind an existing warehouse building. The board pressed on inconsistent container counts between the application, staff report, and a draft resolution (108 vs. 180 vs. 858 interior units), questioned whether removing all 16 required loading docks would shift all pod loading/unloading activity outdoors, and raised noise, visual/leakage, and 'material supply yard' use concerns. The hearing was kept open with the applicant directed to return with clarified logistics, a defined storage volume/footprint, and screening details.

Reopened hearing at which the applicant presented an acoustical expert's testimony (projecting 30-35 dB noise levels across the street) and clarified operational details, but sustained, detailed opposition from adjacent owner Ed Lashes and a nearby business-park property representative (citing lack of tax benefit, precedent for outdoor storage along the whole park, and loss of enjoyment for Bristol assisted-living residents) dominated the hearing. The board pressed hard on whether the site plan, as originally approved, actually permits any outdoor forklift/loading activity at all (concluding it does not — only interior loading docks were approved) and directed the applicant to consider redesigning loading so trucks are effectively 'parallel parked' against the building (functioning like a loading dock) rather than staging pods outdoors, eliminating the outdoor-operation objection. The hearing was adjourned without a vote.

timeline.status: not approved as proposed — public hearing reopened and re-adjourned; applicant directed to return with a revised, enclosed-loading solution
timeline.summary: The applicant sought to widen two rear loading ramps from 16 to 20 feet, framed as a safety improvement for forklifts in winter conditions, but neighboring property owners (adjacent to an assisted-living facility) argued the real purpose was to enable outdoor loading/unloading of PODS storage containers by a prospective tenant, which the board had already precluded via a no-outdoor-storage condition in a prior hearing. After extensive debate over whether outdoor loading/unloading was an as-of-right accessory use of a PLI-zoned warehouse absent an explicit site-plan restriction, the board declined to approve the wider ramps as presented, citing the inability to police how frequently they would be used, and adjourned the hearing again so the applicant could return with a design (e.g., a fully enclosed drive-through loading configuration, as used at a prior Stop & Shop application) that keeps all loading and forklift activity inside the building.

Work session in which the applicant's team and a PODS representative explained the operation and proposed two options (pass-through loading on the far south side vs. rear loading with a sound wall) to keep noise and loading away from the adjacent assisted-living facility. The board asked for a schematic showing interior staging and capacity and felt the meeting made progress.

timeline.status: approved — public hearing closed and resolution adopted as amended
timeline.summary: The applicant returned with a significantly revised approach: PODS containers would be driven through the building on a ramp rather than loaded outdoors, with a small designated area on the building's south side (acting as a sound barrier toward sensitive receptors) reserved only for multi-container trailer trucks. A PODS representative walked the board through how internal staging would work even with the warehouse full, without ever needing to store or stage containers outdoors. After extensive line-by-line resolution editing — clarifying that all staging must occur indoors while only loading/unloading of multi-pod trucks may occur in the designated exterior area, prohibiting container storage anywhere outside the building, limiting overnight truck parking to a depicted rear area, restricting use to a single (southern) dumpster to protect neighbors from early-morning noise, and requiring additional street-facing landscaping/evergreen screening — the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended.

cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue (restaurant)
cases.applicant: Tony Viniziano; Stefan (developer, Remix Properties); Roxanne (chef); John Canning (Kimley-Horn, traffic engineer)

trajectory.status: referred — traffic study to Town's consultant, then ZBA variance hearing (targeting September 7)
discussion only; applicant to return to ZBA (adjourned to November 2) and Planning Board scheduling own public hearing for November 13, 2023
discussion only; applicant directed to return and defend valet/parking plan and explore a parking district
extension of time granted, then flagged; variance validity referred to town attorney and ZBA

timeline.status: referred — traffic study to Town's consultant, then ZBA variance hearing (targeting September 7)
timeline.summary: New farm-to-table restaurant proposed for a long-vacant 1820s building adjacent to CVS in Armonk Square, expanding from roughly 900 to 3,400 sf (144 seats) with a rooftop terrace, greenhouse dining addition, and facade preservation. The code requires 48 parking spaces against only 15 on-site, so the applicant proposed valet parking plus a secured 20 Maple Avenue lot arrangement (up to 22 self-park or 32 valet-stacked spaces) and stalled informal talks for overflow use of the adjacent CVS lot, backed by the town's 2020 parking study and a cell-phone mobility study showing complementary (lunch-vs-dinner) peak demand patterns among nearby businesses. The applicant cited substantial community support (400+ responses in a local Facebook thread), 20 new jobs, increased tax assessment, and commitments to unified downtown wayfinding signage and reviving the Armonk community lunch/events tradition as community benefits. The board directed the applicant to submit to the town's traffic consultant (H2M) for a report, then proceed to the ZBA for the parking variance (targeting a September 7 ZBA hearing off an August 15 submission), holding off on ARB submission for now, and to consult the town engineer on water/sewer capacity given the use change.

timeline.status: discussion only; applicant to return to ZBA (adjourned to November 2) and Planning Board scheduling own public hearing for November 13, 2023
timeline.summary: Extensive discussion of parking for the proposed 141-144 seat restaurant. The site has 15 on-site spaces against a 48-space code requirement; the applicant's plan combines valet service (providing 56 spaces total), a proposed long-term lease for 22 spaces at neighboring 20 Maple Avenue (evenings/weekends), and efforts to secure additional off-site employee parking (American Legion, other Main Street lots). The town's traffic consultant found the valet-based plan sufficient, especially given restaurant-industry data showing only ~20% of business occurs at lunch. Board members pushed back hard: skepticism that valet parking is a strong planning argument post-COVID, concern that the 20 Maple lease could unravel if that property sells (the applicant countered the lease would be structured to survive a sale/financing default), doubt about employee-parking enforcement (docking pay was raised and questioned as possibly illegal), and explicit statements that the board should not consider informal overflow parking at CVS as part of the calculus even though everyone acknowledged it would happen in practice. The applicant leaned on the project's economic/community case ($4 million investment, tax revenue, job creation, ~950 petition signatures of community support, filling a decade-vacant building) as justification for the scale of the parking ask. The board ultimately deferred to the applicant's procedural right to pursue the ZBA variance and did not send an additional recommendation, while scheduling its own site plan public hearing for November 13.

timeline.status: discussion only; applicant directed to return and defend valet/parking plan and explore a parking district
timeline.summary: Discussion-only review of a proposed 141-seat fine-dining restaurant with a kitchen addition. The site can only provide about 15 on-site spaces against a roughly 43-45 space need, which the ZBA already granted a large parking variance to cover; the plan relies on valet service, evening off-site spaces leased across the driveway at 20 Maple Avenue (assumed 100% cleared out at night), and 9 staff spaces leased at the American Legion (subject to the town's right of first refusal and not a guaranteed long-term solution). A board member voiced strong reservations: the daytime/lunch parking model (assuming only ~20% lunch occupancy) seemed unrealistic, the single shared in/out driveway allows queuing for only about 3 vehicles, and the practical reality is overflow parking into the nearby CVS lot - which the board explicitly said it has no authority to rely on or facilitate. The discussion pivoted to reviving a long-dormant idea (previously explored around when Mark Miller was practicing) of forming a formal parking district for that stretch of Maple Avenue, which under the town code would durably satisfy off-street parking requirements without relying on terminable private agreements; a prior attempt by the 12 Maple Avenue owner to organize neighboring property owners (including a resistant adjacent owner, "Trulis"/spelling uncertain) had failed for lack of participation, though a district could be imposed on non-participants representing less than 51% of assessed value. The board asked the applicant team to return prepared to defend the valet operations plan in detail and to explore parking-district feasibility with the town before scheduling a public hearing.

Continued public hearing on a restaurant with an off-street parking variance relying on valet and shared/leased parking at 12 and 20 Maple plus the American Legion; the board closed the hearing and approved the site plan 4-1, adding conditions requiring a town-board community benefits agreement and incorporating the H&H traffic-consultant letter.

The board granted an extension of time together with a field-change notification for a facade modification (fewer windows, metal roof extended to the building edge, and photochromatic skylights) that had already been reviewed by the ARB.

timeline.status: extension of time granted, then flagged; variance validity referred to town attorney and ZBA
timeline.summary: The applicant sought an extension of time on a previously approved restaurant site plan, reporting secured funding, an ARB-approved revised exterior, and a request tied to the new town employee parking lot. The board granted the extension, but Michael Pollack then raised Town Code Section 355-77, arguing that the ZBA parking variance (issued Dec 7, 2023) had expired after two years because no building permit or CO had been issued, and that without a valid variance there is no site plan to extend. Town attorney 'Mary' agreed there is a two-year limit and would investigate, and planner Adam Kaufman noted variances can be extended by the ZBA. The board concluded the applicant likely must return to the ZBA for a variance extension and then get re-approved by the Planning Board.

At the prior meeting the board had approved an extension of time for 12 April Avenue, but it emerged that the applicant's ZBA variance had already expired and no extension was sought before it lapsed, rendering the variance and therefore the site plan null and void. The board voted to rescind its prior approval of the extension of time.

cases.name: 76 Virginia Road (National Fire Sprinklers)
cases.address: 76 Virginia Road, North White Plains, NY
cases.applicant: John Luciano / National Lawn Sprinklers (reps. Tony Vinesiana, Ron, engineer Franz Lackey/SESI)

timeline.summary: First review of a ~24,000 sf flex warehouse requiring roughly 70 feet of rock cut, a retaining-wall system up to ~50-71 ft, ~40,000 yards of material and ~2,000 truck trips, plus a green/blue roof and stormwater vaults; the board discussed the applicant's as-of-right, lot-coverage relief (47% vs 40%), blasting vs chipping, and truck traffic, then declared itself lead agency and directed referrals to the county and emergency services.

Discussion of a new warehouse/office complex on a vacant rock-outcrop lot requiring a large rock cut (~30,000+ cubic yards), anchored/gunite-stabilized walls up to 60 feet, and stormwater detention. The board raised concerns about FAR (interior warehouse parking counting as floor area), the scale and duration of excavation, blasting vs chipping, and mid-job stoppage risk; it referred the FAR variance to the Zoning Board of Appeals and asked for a full construction/excavation/geotechnical package.

Non-hearing discussion of a warehouse-and-office proposal requiring a large rock cut and slope stabilization; the applicant's geotechnical engineer walked through the soil-nail and controlled rock-removal method, and the board decided the town must hire its own geotechnical engineer, with an FAR variance still pending at the ZBA and a public hearing still to come.

Discussion of a substantial rock-excavation and retaining-wall project. Following a prior board directive, a town geotechnical engineer (Carlin Simpson) reviewed the applicant's plans and, after 21 test pits and eight borings with geophysical scanning, reported that roughly 99% of requested data had been provided, with only anchor pull-out loads still to be translated onto the plans. The engineer described a controlled, no-blasting method (line drilling, chopping/feather splitting in 10-foot lifts, draped ring-net systems with rock anchors, vibration monitoring, existing-condition surveys within 500 feet) over a three-to-four-month timeframe. The board pressed on safety and what happens if something is 'missed,' and agreed to schedule a public hearing (targeted for December 8) with the geotechnical engineer present. Counsel raised SEQRA: the action is unlisted, a full EAF was requested, and the ZBA variance may need to be revisited because SEQRA was not completed before it.

The applicant presented a reduced 15,000 sq ft flex warehouse/office (FAR variance already granted) requiring a large six-on-one rock cut with soil nails, rock anchors, and steel mesh netting on a steep slope 12-15 feet from Miller Hill Park, a Revolutionary War battlefield. The applicant's geotechnical team and the town-retained peer reviewer, Bob Simpson (Carlin Simpson Associates), testified the design is achievable with only minor open technical items and confirmed no blasting is proposed. Extensive public comment opposed or questioned the project on catastrophic-slope-failure risk, historic preservation, water/sewer capacity, dust, truck logistics, and long-term (50+ year) maintenance liability, and Open Space chair Carrie Kayza detailed alleged misrepresentations in the applicant's environmental assessment form (SHPO consultation, air pollutants, critical environmental area). The board secured the applicant's consent to a no-blasting condition on the site plan and adjourned the hearing to gather more on the EAF, construction oversight, and a maintenance covenant/deed restriction.

Reopened hearing on a project involving a substantial rock cut stabilized by an anchored netting system, tied to bringing the applicant's nearby office property into conformance. The applicant reported a completed Phase 1A archaeological study (no/low sensitivity, submitted to and accepted by SHPO) and the board adopted an amended negative declaration removing a mischaracterized historical-society letter reference. Major unresolved items kept the hearing open: a written seismic/vibration monitoring plan for the town engineer to review, a deeded perpetual maintenance obligation plus bonding, whether a maintenance bond also covers repair/re-pinning after a rock dislodgement, and a truck-staging/queuing plan for a project projecting ~20 trucks a day for months. Public speakers raised the NEG DEC wording and challenged anchor lengths, safety, and whether an alternate design was considered.

After roughly six weeks of work, the board closed the public hearing and adopted a conditioned site-plan resolution for a landscaping-business building requiring a large rock cut (up to ~70 feet, chipping not blasting, no on-site crushing) with a soil-nailed/netted retaining wall. Extensive discussion covered a seismic/vibration/air/noise monitoring plan with stop-work exceedance thresholds and town notifications, a truck-routing safety plan queuing trucks off-site, an annual operating permit and wall-maintenance manual traveling with the deed, and a Phase 1B archaeological survey (nothing on site; high Revolutionary-War sensitivity next door at Miller Hill). A long exchange on insurance and catastrophic-failure risk resolved into a condition requiring the owner to maintain reasonable liability/property insurance to the satisfaction of the town attorney.

cases.name: 23 Bedford-Banksville Road (special use permit and site-plan extension)
cases.applicant: Property owner/contractor (represented by Tony Veneziano)

trajectory.status: negative recommendation on the proposed sunset provision; board asked for more information before further action
continued — resolution not ready for adoption; public hearing adjourned to a future meeting

timeline.status: negative recommendation on the proposed sunset provision; board asked for more information before further action
timeline.summary: The Town Board sought feedback on (1) a zoning text amendment to permit masonry/stone sales in the town's only GB district and (2) a special use permit to legalize an existing, long-illegal contractors yard on the same site, under a proposed multi-year 'sunset' framework where the illegal yard would gradually be replaced by a conforming masonry business. After extensive discussion of wetland-buffer impacts, whether the use might already be covered under the existing 'building materials storage and sales' permitted use, and enforcement risk, the board declined to support a sunset arrangement — reasoning that a performance bond adequate to guarantee cleanup would likely be prohibitively expensive/impractical given unknown soil contamination risk, and that approving a site plan around a currently-illegal use set a bad precedent — and instead recommended the applicant present a plan showing only permitted uses, with existing violations cleaned up before site plan approval. The board directed staff to check with the building inspector on the 'building materials' classification question and report back.

timeline.status: continued — resolution not ready for adoption; public hearing adjourned to a future meeting
timeline.summary: The applicant is working to occupy a 15,500-square-foot multi-tenant office/storage building and establish a building-materials storage and sales yard at the rear, while relocating several existing tenants operating out of a former contractor's yard under court-supervised stipulations. Roughly 1.78 acres of wetland and wetland buffer previously used as a contractor's yard would be restored and re-naturalized.
