The board directed the applicant to the ARB for exterior repainting/roof work, discussed waiving construction of up to 50% of required parking as 'land banked' green space (with a requirement that any currently-paved land-banked area be ripped out and re-vegetated rather than left as unstriped asphalt), and noted Westchester County Health Department septic constraints capping occupancy at 16 people. The resolution remains open with many unresolved conditions.

A previously opened hearing that the applicant requested to adjourn again to the February 12 meeting. A board member pushed back on simply carrying the item forward without re-noticing neighbors, given that several members of the public were concerned about the application; staff agreed to re-notice neighbors for the February hearing date.

Continued public hearing to legalize a rehabbed formerly-vacant building whose uses straddle two zoning districts; the board closed the hearing, adopted a negative declaration, and approved the site plan and wetlands permit as amended, resolving how contaminated fill removal would be tested/monitored (DEC and/or town).

The board reviewed a petition, referred by the town board, to rezone the split-zoned parcel entirely into CBB and add a special-use permit allowing existing wood-processing and pre-cut metal/aluminum assemblage uses; the board voted to recommend adoption with added limits (use confined to roughly the rear 50% of the building not fronting the road, ground floor only, with a separate entrance).

Now that the whole parcel is in the CBB district and code was amended to permit the rear special-permit uses, the board made a positive recommendation to the town board on the special use permit and, after amending its agenda, granted a one-year extension of time on the previously approved site plan.

cases.name: 655 Bedford Road — Mittman Two-Lot Subdivision (Reapproval)
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by Tony Veneziano and engineer Ralph Fonzetti; contractor Vann DiZemo Construction) for Deborah James (daughter of the neighboring Mittelman family)

trajectory.status: lead agency intent declared; referral to ZBA to follow once a SEQRA negative declaration issues
negative declaration adopted; hearing pending ZBA variance

timeline.status: lead agency intent declared; referral to ZBA to follow once a SEQRA negative declaration issues
timeline.summary: A 28-acre R2A lot with one existing (non-conforming, undocumented) house would be split into two lots — the new lot for a house for the owners' daughter, accessed via a 50-foot easement rather than direct road frontage — with a conservation easement placed over the remainder. Because the new lot lacks frontage, the applicant will need either a ZBA frontage-variance or a Town Board open-development-area designation; the applicant and board planner agreed the ZBA route was preferable. Since SEQRA review can't segment a phased subdivision, the board must evaluate potential impacts as if up to six lots (the applicant's larger, unused development-rights study) could eventually be created, even though only two lots are actually proposed; the applicant will submit an impacts matrix. The board declared its intent to be lead agency (required before a negative declaration can issue and before the ZBA can act) and will refer the frontage variance to the ZBA once ready, noting Conservation Board interest given the parcel's size and no proposed wetland disturbance.

Workshop review of a bifurcated two-lot subdivision plan (with a 14-acre conservation easement) benchmarked against a hypothetical six-lot 'phantom' subdivision to demonstrate reduced environmental impact. The board discussed stormwater/percolation testing, road/driveway geometry, and confirmed the resolution would describe but not approve the six-lot alternative. The applicant reported a pending July 7 ZBA application for a front-yard/access variance needed before returning for a formal subdivision public hearing.

timeline.status: negative declaration adopted; hearing pending ZBA variance
timeline.summary: Applicant presented revised, more realistic septic and stormwater mitigation areas (softening overly conservative percolation assumptions) and a wetland-buffer mitigation tabulation (2:1 ratio) addressing the town engineer's prior memo, benchmarked again against the six-lot 'phantom' subdivision to demonstrate the two-lot plan's reduced impact. The board adopted a negative declaration but declined to set the public hearing date immediately, wanting to wait until the applicant secures a required frontage variance from the ZBA (scheduled for August 4) so the hearing isn't presupposing that outcome; a September 12 hearing was anticipated.

The applicant revised the approach from a conservation easement to an outright donation of the non-building 14-acre remainder lot to the Town, prompting board questions about whether this reconfiguration affects the front-yard/frontage variance already granted by the ZBA in August. The town planner had not yet reviewed the newly-submitted plan (received the day of the meeting) and recommended against approving it without review; the board agreed and adjourned the hearing to September 29 rather than approve subject to review, with the chair noting it would be improper to approve a same-day submission.

After the town planner reviewed the applicant's revised plan (donating two non-building/open-space lots to the Town rather than the earlier conservation-easement approach, without changing the number of building lots or density), the board resolved a resolution typo (misidentifying which lot had the front-yard setback issue), closed the public hearing, and adopted both the preliminary and final subdivision plan approvals as amended — concluding a matter that had run since at least June.

Reapproval of a previously-approved-but-expired two-lot subdivision preserving most of the estate parcel as open space with one new building lot; the county could not sign the final plat because the resolution had lapsed. No neighbors appeared. The board closed the public hearing and re-adopted the negative declaration, preliminary resolution, and final resolution unchanged in substance.

cases.name: 23 Bedford Banksville Road zoning text amendment
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by Tony Vinesiano and engineer Peter Gregory)

trajectory.status: discussion — referred to ARB and Conservation Board
board voted to refer applicant to ZBA for a reduced variance (third story within 30 ft height)
referred to ZBA (referral already made); board reviewed follow-up elevations and expressed disappointment

timeline.summary: Continuation of a public hearing to legalize an existing warehouse/office building split between CBB and GB zoning districts, following removal of prior tenants' outdoor storage and receipt of ARB and Conservation Board approvals. The applicant needed to demonstrate that a large rear storage/warehouse use was legally accessory to office use (not the reverse) to avoid a use variance or rezoning, but had not yet provided that analysis; the Board found the draft resolution presented far too many open items to consider approval and adjourned the hearing, suggesting the applicant may need to pursue a Town Board rezoning instead.

timeline.status: discussion — referred to ARB and Conservation Board
timeline.summary: Long-running, repeatedly-revised application (previously involving an outdoor building-materials storage/sales use and an unpermitted fill operation with evicted tenants) pivoted to a self-storage warehouse use, now proposed after the applicant agreed to remove roughly 10-12 feet of illegally imported fill down to grade and to replace a dilapidated building at the building inspector's request rather than simply demolish it. Board members questioned anticipated traffic flow/circulation for the self-storage use and FAR compliance for both buildings combined; the applicant was directed to the ARB (for building design) and Conservation Board (for the fill-removal mitigation plan) while site details were refined.

timeline.status: board voted to refer applicant to ZBA for a reduced variance (third story within 30 ft height)
timeline.summary: After Town Planner comments flagged that the applicant's self-storage building calculation improperly used gross rather than net lot area, the applicant revised the proposal from a 90,000 sf, four-story, 38-foot building down to a 68,000 sf, three-story building held within the code's 30-foot height maximum — needing only a single story-count variance (two permitted, three requested) rather than both height and story variances. The board also worked through floodplain compliance (flood-proofing versus a two-foot freeboard elevation requirement, with compensatory storage available from fill removal elsewhere on site) before voting to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the reduced story variance, with elevations to be presented at the September 28 meeting.

timeline.status: referred to ZBA (referral already made); board reviewed follow-up elevations and expressed disappointment
timeline.summary: As a courtesy the board had requested, the applicant returned to show the elevations submitted with the ZBA referral for the reduced (68,000 sf, three-story, 30-foot) self-storage building. Board members found the submitted drawings to be a bare, minimally-detailed sketch (unclear whether depicted openings were real or decorative windows, no proper rendering, no view showing the building's relationship to the street or existing neighboring building) and expressed regret at having referred the matter to the ZBA before seeing better documentation, while noting the board retains full site plan approval authority regardless of the ZBA's story-variance decision and will likely require a more refined design at that stage.

Public hearing on a site plan for occupancy of an existing ~15,500 sq ft multi-tenant office/storage building plus removal of the existing contractors' yard, with the previously proposed self-storage building now withdrawn from this application; the board declined to vote, citing possibly non-permitted storage/woodworking-metalworks uses and requiring a building-inspector opinion, and kept the hearing open.

The town board sent back draft language to rezone the property to CBB instead of GB (to bar the more intensive warehouse/self-storage use), and the Planning Board discussed whether narrowing permitted uses could have unintended consequences before making a positive referral back to the town board, 3-0.

cases.name: 154 Lafayette Avenue (Mistis Transport)
cases.applicant: Michael Miele
cases.lastStatus: public hearing opened and closed; approved with conditions

trajectory.status: public hearing opened and closed; approved with conditions

timeline.summary: First introduction of a proposal to legalize unpermitted work by converting a nonconforming single-family house in the industrial (INDA) district to office/storage use; the board asked the applicant to clean up the plan, consider consolidating the three lots he controls, address off-street parking (possibly via ZBA), and deal with the outstanding violations.

Discussion of converting a house to office use; the board pressed the applicant to address parking deficiencies comprehensively across three commonly owned Lafayette Avenue parcels rather than piecemeal, and to resolve multiple building-department notices of violation, directing a meeting with the chair and building inspector.

The board reviewed a revised plan to remove a lot line and combine two of three properties, keep an existing non-conforming residence, convert a building to an office, store 16 commercial vehicles, and add parking, then referred the applicant to the ZBA and Town Board for the necessary variances and license.

Discussion of a site plan for a business relying on outdoor truck storage (19 truck spaces in back). The Police Department objected to proposed front parking spaces that would sit partly in the right-of-way and require vehicles to back into the road, calling it a new hazardous condition rather than a memorialized existing one. The board explored alternatives at length: parallel parking in front, angle parking, stacking trucks, and having drivers park cars in the truck spaces they vacate, plus relocating ADA spaces nearer the accessible ramp. No decision was made; the applicant was asked to prepare a parallel-parking layout and a narrative (with distances to the pavement) to bring back, potentially for the Police, Zoning Board of Appeals, and Town Board.

Discussion of a plan to establish an office, merge lots/move a lot line, and store US-mail delivery trucks. The applicant originally proposed perpendicular parking partly in the right-of-way, but the police department recommended against it and the town code prohibits it; the applicant returned with six parallel spaces. The board debated at length whether parallel (respecting the police) or perpendicular (which neighbors do under grandfathered variances) better serves the site, given early-morning (3-5am) truck turnover and a possible 'demolition derby' of drivers arriving at once. The owner spoke passionately, feeling singled out relative to neighbors who park outside. The board ultimately directed the applicant to move forward with the parallel-parking plan as presented and scheduled a public hearing, reasoning that pursuing perpendicular would require ZBA/town-board approvals and delay.

timeline.status: public hearing opened and closed; approved with conditions
timeline.summary: Change of use of a legal non-conforming home to office use, treating three existing non-conforming parcels together by moving a property line, removing one dwelling and converting another to an office, plus commercial truck storage. The long-standing sticking point was parking; the board reaffirmed acceptance of six parallel spaces in front and required the plan to clearly show the nine off-street spaces needed for the office kept truck-free, with the balance available for overnight truck storage. It was determined ARB review was unnecessary (no exterior changes) and that whether ZBA approval is needed turns on a building-inspector determination of whether the nonconformity is increased. The board struck a condition, adopted the NegDec, the site-plan resolution, and the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.

cases.name: 26 Chestnut Ridge Road — Fill Import Violation & Soil Remediation
cases.applicant: Anthony Marino (represented by engineer Rick Bolander, JMC)
cases.lastStatus: board directed staff to prepare a resolution denying the fill permit and requiring removal of the imported soil; public hearing adjourned to January 23

trajectory.status: under review; soil testing required before further action
ongoing; remediation plan accepted, neighbor notification deferred one meeting
under review — proceeding to neighbor notification
continued — public hearing adjourned again pending two alternative grading plans and a full board
board directed staff to prepare a resolution denying the fill permit and requiring removal of the imported soil; public hearing adjourned to January 23

timeline.status: under review; soil testing required before further action
timeline.summary: Fill was brought in without permits to level a steep, rocky backyard and prepare for a patio (work stopped when violations were issued in November 2021). The Town Engineer's central concern was the quality/safety of roughly 1,500 cubic yards (150-200 truckloads) of imported fill, since lab tests on stockpiled material showed detectable heavy metals and semi-volatile compounds; he questioned whether those tested stockpiles actually matched what was placed on site and recommended on-site test holes plus review by the town's environmental consultant (paid via applicant escrow). A site walk was agreed to.

timeline.status: ongoing; remediation plan accepted, neighbor notification deferred one meeting
timeline.summary: Follow-up (after being pulled from the June 27 agenda) on soil contamination concerns from imported fill. Soil testing found lead levels exceeding unrestricted-use cleanup objectives but within acceptable limits for restricted residential use, so the fill can remain in place; the soil scientist recommended a demarcation layer (orange construction fencing over the fill, capped with 6 inches of topsoil), which the applicant agreed to install. The board deferred scheduling neighbor notification for one more meeting so the applicant could meet with the town's consultant to finalize details.

timeline.status: under review — proceeding to neighbor notification
timeline.summary: The applicant imported roughly 1,500 yards of fill without a permit, which was later found to slightly exceed the unrestricted-use residential soil cleanup objective for nickel (a memo error had initially misidentified the metal as lead). The applicant's environmental consultant recommended leaving the fill in place under a demarcation layer with a clean topsoil cap (originally proposed at 6 inches, versus a state standard the board understood to be up to 18 inches) rather than exporting it, since levels remained well under the restricted-use and groundwater-protection thresholds. The board debated at length whether a deed covenant/disclosure was needed to protect future buyers and whether the six-inch cap was adequate, ultimately voting to proceed to neighbor notification while leaving the exact cap depth and covenant mechanism to be finalized with a revised consultant memo.

timeline.status: continued — public hearing adjourned again pending two alternative grading plans and a full board
timeline.summary: The applicant's engineer revealed that simply capping the contaminated (nickel-elevated) fill in place with 24 inches of clean soil, as previously discussed, would not work with existing site grading without spreading the fill outward roughly 10-15% beyond the current disturbance area. The town's geologist, Bill Canavan, reaffirmed that DEC had endorsed a 24-inch cap and demarcation layer as adequate and that nickel at the levels found poses no meaningful health or groundwater risk, while the Town Attorney cautioned that a deed covenant might be unwarranted overkill given the soil scientist's findings. The board asked the applicant to prepare two alternatives — spreading the fill farther out with a wider cap, versus regrading to keep the disturbance within the previously discussed limits — and adjourned to allow a full complement of the board to weigh in.

timeline.status: board directed staff to prepare a resolution denying the fill permit and requiring removal of the imported soil; public hearing adjourned to January 23
timeline.summary: The applicant's engineer confirmed that capping the fill in place with two feet of clean soil is not gradeable without either expanding the disturbed area by about 15% or removing roughly 1,000 cubic yards of the existing restricted-use soil — there is no option that avoids one or the other. After private legal counsel, the board concluded it could not in good conscience allow the soil to remain without a deed covenant, but also did not want to burden the property with a covenant given the soil scientist's view that the nickel levels were not seriously hazardous; a brief discussion of commissioning new, independent (town-selected and town-paid) soil testing was raised but judged likely to be expensive and to lead back to the same conclusion. The board settled on directing staff to prepare a resolution denying the fill permit and requiring the improperly imported soil be removed, effectively restoring the site to its pre-violation condition, after which the applicant could file a new fill permit application with a clean grading plan.

cases.name: 78 Lafayette Avenue
cases.applicant: Maria Martins
cases.lastStatus: public hearing continued to January 10, 2024 (board declined to adopt resolution)

trajectory.status: pending — applicant to submit updated/expanded building plans before referral to ARB
continued — floor plans/elevations submitted; heading to ARB
public hearing opened, kept open pending ARB review
public hearing continued to January 10, 2024 (board declined to adopt resolution)

timeline.summary: Initial introduction of a new ~4,900 sq ft warehouse/office building on a vacant half-acre lot for an infrastructure/water-main contracting business, with rear-yard outdoor storage of equipment (hydrants, valves) behind retaining walls for aesthetic screening. The applicant indicated the code's 15%-of-lot outdoor storage allowance may be insufficient and is considering a ZBA variance; the board asked for more detailed plans showing exactly what would be stored before it could weigh in on a ZBA referral, and directed a site walk before further review.

timeline.status: pending — applicant to submit updated/expanded building plans before referral to ARB
timeline.summary: The applicant no longer needs a zoning variance for extra outdoor storage because the building itself will be enlarged instead, reducing the outdoor storage need. The board discussed retaining-wall material (large 'ready rock' blocks), a buffer of trees plus a fence at the top of the walls to screen adjacent residential uses, and a circular internal drive avoiding a zero-lot-line build-out. The board informally agreed the applicant can go straight to the ARB once updated plans reflecting the larger building are submitted.

timeline.status: continued — floor plans/elevations submitted; heading to ARB
timeline.summary: With elevations now submitted, the board focused on a tight roughly 12-13-foot secondary driveway pinch point, retaining walls up to about 40 feet high requiring temporary construction easements onto a neighbor's property (with the neighbor's informal consent), and screening for the wall facing residential properties below — questioning whether Norway spruce trees are appropriate or safe to maintain on such a steep drop and suggesting lower shrubs instead. The board indicated it was comfortable sending the application to the ARB once floor plans and elevations are finalized.

timeline.status: public hearing opened, kept open pending ARB review
timeline.summary: Public hearing opened on a revised office/warehouse building (relocated per prior board direction to go to the ARB, not yet submitted); tenants include a children's clothing distributor (van pick-up/drop-off only, no tractor-trailers) and a winter/summer storage operator with minimal traffic. The board could not adopt a resolution absent ARB approval, so it took public comment (none offered) and recommended curbing and parallel parking along the Lafayette Avenue frontage as a streetscape model for future redevelopment on that street, and discussed reusing large existing granite roadside blocks as a landscape feature. Hearing adjourned (kept open) pending ARB submission.

timeline.status: public hearing continued to January 10, 2024 (board declined to adopt resolution)
timeline.summary: A reopened public hearing that the board had previously declined to close because the draft resolution carried roughly 20 unresolved conditions. The applicant's team brought updated engineering plans but, by their own admission, had not resubmitted current architectural elevations to the board (only the original ARB submission), and had not brought details of a proposed roughly 20-foot "ReadyRock" retaining wall - including a needed temporary construction easement from a neighbor, top-of-wall fencing, a guide rail to stop vehicles, drainage/regrading behind the wall, and tree-health/removal near the wall - despite these being flagged as outstanding in staff review memos. After extended, increasingly frustrated back-and-forth about which plan versions had actually been submitted, the board concluded it was not comfortable adopting a resolution with this many open technical items and continued the public hearing to the January 10, 2024 meeting, directing the applicant to meet directly with the town engineer beforehand.

cases.name: 263 Bedford-Banksville Road (equestrian property)
cases.applicant: Michael & Chloe Gasserowski / Merengo Farms (represented by Jerry Torrella, Torrella & Wexstein; site plan by 'Jay')
cases.lastStatus: approved (field change amendment; pergola and fence changes to return as amended planning board approval)

trajectory.status: positive recommendation to Town Board; referred to ARB and Conservation Board; board declared itself SEQRA lead agency
approved (field change amendment; pergola and fence changes to return as amended planning board approval)

timeline.summary: Introductory presentation on converting a long-vacant, historically-equestrian property (indoor riding ring dating to a 1974 Town Board approval) into the family's primary residence with up to 20 horses — within the zoning ordinance's non-commercial accessory-horse formula and consistent with the previously-approved 20 stalls. Counsel pre-emptively argued against characterizing the use as commercial (no boarding of others' horses, no for-profit shows) and flagged open questions about whether existing paddocks encroaching on wetland buffers can continue as a legal non-conforming use or need variances. The applicant reached out to roughly 21 neighbors ahead of the meeting. No site plan detail was finalized; next step is Town Board special-permit review and further referrals.

timeline.status: positive recommendation to Town Board; referred to ARB and Conservation Board; board declared itself SEQRA lead agency
timeline.summary: The applicant negotiated extensively with neighbors before and after filing, agreeing to conditions including capping the horse count at 20 (with room to accommodate up to 23 including foals), maintaining strictly residential (non-commercial) equestrian use with no rentals or shows, a 150-foot landscape buffer, and a mechanism binding future property owners to the same conditions on transfer of title. A neighbor spoke strongly in favor, describing the roughly 70-acre property's role as a wildlife corridor connecting the Mianus River to Butler Sanctuary. The board voted a positive recommendation to the Town Board on the special use permit change, referred the applicant to the ARB and Conservation Board, and declared itself lead agency for SEQRA review.

Revised horse-facility expansion (indoor riding arena, ten-stall stable, garage with grooms' quarters) that eliminated a caretaker's cottage, reduced the main house from roughly 10,000 to 7,500 square feet, and reduced CEA disturbance, following positive referrals from the Architectural Review Board and Conservation Board. Existing paddocks and buildings require variances for wetland-buffer setbacks and double agricultural setback requirements from residential neighbors, and accessory structures now exceed the 25% floor-area limit due to the smaller main house. The Board adopted a SEQRA negative declaration and voted to refer the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals for the necessary variances before proceeding to the Town Board for the special permit.

An extension-of-time request for a large equestrian property with a new residence, pool/pool house, renovated exercise barn, second stable, and garage with room quarters above. Counsel explained construction is proceeding in good faith without compliance issues but cannot finish within the original 18-month window, and sought clarification that the completion deadline runs co-terminus with the building permit. The board granted a one-year extension.

timeline.status: approved (field change amendment; pergola and fence changes to return as amended planning board approval)
timeline.summary: A new landscape architect proposed relatively minor tweaks to the previously approved plan on this former horse-farm property: shifting the pool closer to the house, reducing patio and retaining-wall extents, adding planting to manage runoff, minor driveway curve/gate changes, and asking to use asphalt instead of gravel on a steep driveway segment. Drainage remains as previously engineered. The board treated most items as a field change but determined the pergola and fence changes require returning to the Planning Board (rather than being handled by the RPRC) since new structures can't be approved as a field change. Conservation liaison input was sought given the site's wetland-buffer history. The board adopted the field-change amendment resolution.

cases.name: 32 Orchard Drive subdivision (re-approval)
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by engineer Dan[ny] RCA, CRC Engineering)

trajectory.status: discussion — applicant to pursue ZBA frontage variances; not yet ready for hearing

timeline.summary: First presentation of a preliminary seven-lot subdivision on a roughly 13-acre estate with an existing single-family home, tennis courts, a barn, and an abandoned, unowned cemetery parcel requiring preserved public access. The applicant is exploring extending town water and possibly sewer service, and proposed rock-face cuts rather than retaining walls where feasible given road grading. Staff flagged that zoning-conforming lot yield (whether the site supports seven, six, or fewer lots) still needs to be established through slope, wetland, and net-lot-area analysis, and that clearing/grading limits should account for amenities beyond the houses themselves. The Board deferred declaring SEQRA lead agency until the zoning metrics are clarified in a future submission.

timeline.status: discussion — applicant to pursue ZBA frontage variances; not yet ready for hearing
timeline.summary: Revised four-lot subdivision minimizing disturbance versus an earlier iteration; the central issue was how a rear lot (Lot 3) obtains legally sufficient road frontage from a cul-de-sac — via either an awkward contrived frontage measurement along an easement or a cleaner ZBA-variance path providing a straight easement instead. The applicant favored seeking two area variances (frontage and, potentially, others) rather than the "contrivance," a path the board indicated the ZBA would likely find reasonable. Separately, the board raised whether/how continued public access to an existing cemetery on a neighboring parcel (referenced in a same-day email from the Town Supervisor's office) could be preserved via a small easement, which the applicant agreed to pursue with the affected property owner.

Public hearing on a five-lot (four new) subdivision of a ~13-acre R-1A parcel; extensive neighbor concern about steep slopes, stormwater, septic and well/aquifer impacts led the board to keep the hearing open, engage the town's hydrogeologist, and keep the lots under Planning Board (not RPRC) jurisdiction so each future house gets a public hearing.

The board reopened and closed the public hearing and adopted a negative declaration plus preliminary and final subdivision plat approvals with steep-slope and tree-removal permits, after an extended discussion of well/groundwater adequacy on the bedrock aquifer and of tightening the clearing-and-grading limit line to protect a steep slope.

Because the prior approval had expired, the five-lot subdivision of the 12.9-acre R1A parcel returned unchanged; the board opened and closed the hearing and adopted the negative declaration plus preliminary and final subdivision approvals.

cases.name: 12 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: John Jay Scarla Jr. (architect)

timeline.summary: Review of a plan to renovate a historic structure into a law office in the front and residential duplex in the rear, remove the barn/shed, and build a rear parking lot; the board worked through driveway width, buffer/screening and clearance so delivery vehicles won't hit the building, and directed the applicant to LPC (certificate of appropriateness), ARB, and possibly the ZBA before scheduling a public hearing.

With the applicant absent, the board referred the application to the ZBA for an off-street parking variance (seven spaces shown, nine required) and a variance for the sub-20-foot driveway width along the house.

Public hearing opened for converting a historic house into a front office plus rear apartment; a neighbor voiced extensive opposition and the applicant's plans lacked current engineering, an updated eight-space parking layout, and landscape/lighting details, so the board kept the hearing open pending revised submissions.

The board reopened and closed the hearing on converting the house to an office with one residential unit, reviewing the landscape/screening plan, parking (eight spaces incl. one handicap), lighting, stormwater, and ARB/historic-preservation approvals, then adopted the site-plan approval.

A brief extension-of-time request for a project involving a driveway to reach the rear of the property, described as very close to final approval with the applicant anxious to proceed. The board granted the extension, then closed the Planning Board for 2025.

trajectory.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions

timeline.summary: The board reviewed a detached garage over 800 sq ft (requiring a special use permit), a new pool and cabana, retaining walls and a formal lawn; no objection in principle, but floor plans and elevations are needed and the engineer must confirm stormwater/drainage given prior water issues at the site.

Discussion of a pool, cabana and detached three-car garage (garage exceeds 800 sq ft accessory-structure threshold; land coverage roughly 900 sq ft over the allowable). The board scheduled a site walk and voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the gross land-coverage variance so the ZBA and site work could proceed concurrently, with ARB and a public hearing to follow.

Post-site-walk discussion of a garage addition and rear pool complex; the board had no substantive objections and directed the applicant to obtain a GLA (floor-area) variance from the ZBA before scheduling the public hearing at a July meeting.

Opened public hearing for new pool, spa, patios, an open covered cabana, and a detached carport over 800 sq ft (special use permit); a variance for gross land coverage and accessory-structure FAR was already granted by the ZBA. Discussion centered almost entirely on drainage: the neighborhood has significant runoff draining to the cul-de-sac, and the town engineer wanted the applicant to verify the existing infiltration system/swale is working and to consider diverting proposed stormwater to the rear toward Tripling Lane rather than adding cul-tec units to a failing system. Neighbor Brian Kaminer testified to worsening street flooding. The Board scheduled a site walk (next Wednesday) and kept the hearing open.

timeline.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions
timeline.summary: Reopened hearing focused on cul-de-sac drainage. Following a site walk with town engineer John Kellard, the applicant split the drainage systems so the new garage has its own dedicated infiltration system (both designed to hold up to a 100-year storm with zero discharge), added a trench drain at the driveway bottom tied to the town culvert, converted lawn to planted meadow, and will confirm/repair the existing overflow pipe to the town system. The board closed the hearing and adopted the (date-amended) resolution, with the standing stormwater-mitigation condition delegated to the town engineer administratively.

cases.name: 100 Buckout Road
cases.applicant: Malik Samad, owner/applicant; Nicholas Shariah, Hudson Engineering; John Scarlato, architect

timeline.summary: Discussion of a proposed 3,700 sq ft new house replacing an existing dwelling on a lot with a cottage that will remain, referred by the RPRC to both the Planning Board and Conservation Board for steep-slope, wetland-buffer and grading impacts. The engineer corrected the plan to show two trees removed (not seven), described disturbing roughly 10,830 sq ft of steep slopes (largely bare rock outcroppings) and noted nearly all work sits within the wetland buffer, with the septic location constrained by the health department. To reduce impact, the applicant offered to eliminate a walk-out basement door and cut rock removal from about 12 feet to 4-5 feet near the wetlands. The board scheduled a joint site walk for November 19 at 8:30am and referred the application to the Conservation Board for concurrent review.

The board discussed 100 Buckout Road following a site walk, where the town engineer (John Kellard) suggested revisions to handle grading changes and the applicant's engineer Nick prepared a revised plan the board had not yet seen. The main procedural question was whether the wetland permit could be handled administratively as a minor permit rather than requiring Conservation Board review; the Conservation Board chair (George) confirmed by text that the sidewalk work is very minor with no need for board review. The board debated timing for a December versus January public hearing and agreed to move toward a public hearing, with a draft resolution finding the wetland permit minor and processing it administratively with town engineer input.

The applicant sought site plan, wetlands permit, and tree removal approvals for a new house. Because the engineer's review memo was far from resolved, the chair opened and adjourned the hearing. The applicant's engineer flagged disagreements on whether an NOI is required (under an acre of disturbance, not in the East-of-Hudson watershed), driveway drainage constraints between existing and proposed septic systems, staying under the one-acre wetland-buffer disturbance threshold, and rock removal on the south side for the sunroom/walkout. Missing ARB approval was also noted. The board directed the applicant to tighten the plans and reconcile the memo before returning.

Reopened continued public hearing on a new residence involving steep-slope and wetland-buffer disturbance. The applicant argued that many draft resolution conditions (retaining wall, tree count, earthwork, soil testing/infiltration, silt fence) were repeat comments already addressed, and asked to be voted on tonight. The board would not approve: an SHPO/historic-cemetery notification and a tax-map-versus-survey boundary discrepancy remained open, and, most significantly, roughly an acre of wetland mitigation for about a half acre of buffer disturbance had been steered toward administrative handling by the town wetland consultant rather than the Conservation Board. The board concluded that no site directive could authorize skipping the Conservation Board, directed the applicant to prepare a full mitigation plan and route it through the Conservation Board, and to re-notice the public hearing, targeting the May meeting.

This was a continuation of a public hearing on a wetlands permit that the board had previously declined to treat as a minor permit, sending the applicant back to the Conservation Board. The Conservation Board reviewed the home mitigation plan, found the structure could not be moved out of the buffer, judged the mitigation (slightly more than 2:1) adequate, and recommended approval. The applicant also confirmed via SHIPO that the project would not impact the African American historic cemetery across the street, and a previously missing page of engineering conditions was now reflected in the draft resolution. The board closed the public hearing and approved the resolution.

Public hearing on rebuilding a house that had been condemned and fully demolished due to powder-post beetle damage; the new structure keeps the identical footprint but is three feet taller (still within height limits) with three added windows. Hearing closed and resolution approved.

timeline.summary: Proposal to replace aging underground storage tanks and rehabilitate the convenience store interior within the existing footprint. The board's primary concern was vehicle circulation — the single aisle between pump islands is too narrow for two-way travel — prompting discussion of removing a pump near the store, relocating a utility pole, or shifting the oversized canopy to create proper travel lanes; the board also suggested the applicant consider aesthetic upgrades (the canopy was called disproportionately large) and repair of badly deteriorated sidewalks, and noted stormwater quality improvements (not otherwise required) were welcome, given the significant investment already planned. Board recommended the applicant coordinate design details with staff and, if exterior changes result, with the Architectural Review Board.

The board reviewed the revised gas-station plan covering pump circulation, removal of car-washing stations, stormwater infiltration, canopy size, landscaping and streetscape/sidewalk upgrades, and directed the applicant to the Architectural Review Board before returning for a hearing.

Public hearing on a site-plan application to renovate the interior, replace fuel pumps and underground storage tanks, rebuild the convenience store with a gable roof, and improve circulation, lighting, retaining walls and stormwater. No members of the public appeared. The board focused on a pump-queuing/circulation problem (cars stacking at the three in-line pumps blocking one another) and whether a 'pull forward' sign or full-service operation could mitigate it; the applicant agreed to raise full service with the owner. Rather than adopt the draft resolution, the board closed the hearing and sent the applicant home to satisfy the many open conditions (stormwater calcs for the 25-year event, upsized pipes to 8-inch minimum, ARB stone-pillar condition) and return with a tightened, near-final resolution before the building department stage.

Status update only on the 825 North Broadway gas station. Staff reported the board had previously been comfortable with the plan and requested a draft resolution, but outstanding comments remained, so the applicant made a further submission that addressed many but not all conditions. The town engineer still could not recommend adoption, so the applicant will make another submission. No action was taken.

The board debated how specifically to designate outdoor equipment-storage areas on the plan and whether the (long-standing but never-approved) site plan needed Architectural Review Board referral, concluding ARB referral was discretionary and not warranted for legalizing existing conditions. The applicant is amending its Town Board special-permit application (for July 13) and submitting to the Conservation Board for a retroactive wetlands permit.

timeline.status: negative declaration adopted (lead agency); hearing closed
timeline.summary: With the Planning Board acting as lead agency, the applicant confirmed a positive Conservation Board referral for the wetland-adjacent berm design and that the Town Board would hold its own special-permit hearings (nursery and contractor's-yard) in September. A board member asked how the equipment-storage dividing line between the two zoning districts would be physically identified in the field on an unpaved/gravel surface; the group settled on keeping a reference plan on-site rather than a physical marking. The board then adopted two separate positive recommendations to the Town Board — one for the nursery special permit, one for the contractor's-yard special permit — clearing the way for the Town Board's own hearings.

Board members caught several minor resolution typos (a zoning-district reference and a wetland seed-mix wording error) and confirmed the LOMA/floodplain letter was on file with the building department before adopting the final resolution granting site plan and wetland permit approvals — concluding a multi-meeting process that began in June.

The board needs the building/lot coverage figures to refer the matter to the ZBA for a variance and needs the corrected parking chart to confirm the roughly 100 required spaces are actually available, including whether some spaces near an adjacent gas station are properly available for the office building's exclusive use under the town's shared-parking rule. Board members expressed visible frustration at the repeated, incomplete submissions and offered to meet directly with the architect to walk through exactly what is needed.

The Town Board was slated to refer the matter to the ZBA for a building/lot coverage variance the same week, after which the Town Board could issue the special permit and the planning board could hold its hearing and adopt a resolution.

The Board raised process concerns about approving the change of use and legalizing pre-existing parking arrangements in the same resolution, but concluded the parking counts had been analyzed and were resolved. Referral from the Town Board for the Board's input on a special permit to allow outdoor display and sales at a gas station, consistent with a similar approval previously granted across the street. The board asked about the sidewalk's effect on pump access and confirmed additional landscaping (wood barrels, plantings) as previously requested, then adopted the draft resolution.

timeline.status: continued — awaiting soil testing report, wetland connectivity analysis, and Conservation Board referral
timeline.summary: The applicant is attempting to legalize roughly 2,600 cubic yards of unpermitted fill and the removal of an estimated 171 trees. Soil testing found elevated lead, copper, and pesticide residues (DDE/dieldrin), for which the town's geologist recommended a similar demarcation-and-cap approach as at 26 Chestnut Ridge Road, though board members noted this site appears more contaminated and the disturbance far larger. The board also questioned whether the fill disturbed a wetland connection between neighboring properties, requiring further investigation before a Conservation Board referral. Frustrated that the violation dated back roughly two years with slow progress, Christopher Carthy raised a broader concern — beyond this board's authority — that the town lacks a system to incentivize applicants to correct zoning violations promptly rather than benefiting from delay, and asked staff to relay that concern to the Town Board liaison.

timeline.status: continued — joint site visit planned; consultant to revisit demarcation-layer recommendation before next meeting
timeline.summary: The applicant's engineer presented an initial 2:1 wetland/tree mitigation plan based on wetland flagging from a neighboring parcel (2 Tripp Lane), but town consultants questioned whether a natural drainage swale historically connected wetlands between 2 Tripp and 6 Tripp Lane before the fill was placed, requiring further investigation (including site access through the 6 Tripp Lane neighbor). The board pushed back on the soil consultant's existing memo recommending only a 6-inch clean-soil cap over lead- and pesticide-contaminated fill, recalling that a comparable 26 Chestnut Ridge Road case ultimately required a much thicker cap (up to 24 inches); Christopher Carthy also questioned whether the town should be independently administering DEC-style soil remediation standards at all, but was told DEC declines to get involved in individual-lot matters, leaving enforcement with the town. The board asked the consultant (Bill Canavan) to attend the next meeting to clarify the memo and directed further coordination on the wetland connectivity question before deciding on the fill permit.

timeline.status: denied proposed remedy — board directed export of contaminated fill and a revised site plan
timeline.summary: Follow-up soil testing (with HES present) confirmed that native, undisturbed soil on the property tested clean while the previously imported fill (roughly 2,600+ cubic yards) had elevated impurities. The applicant proposed capping two feet of contaminated fill with a demarcation layer and clean topsoil under a deed covenant; the board rejected this outright, stating North Castle does not want contamination covenants or demarcation layers running with deeds, and directed the applicant to export the contaminated fill and return with a revised site plan reflecting the removal (with a wetlands consultant review also needed given an altered watercourse).

timeline.status: deferred — combined tree/wetland mitigation and fill-removal plan required before a removal permit issues
timeline.summary: Refined test-pit data (versus outdated historical topography) reduced the estimated imported-fill volume from roughly 2,600 to about 700 cubic yards; the town's hydrogeologist reviewed the methodology and requested a field report documenting actual removal limits. The applicant, under a court stipulation to resolve the violation, asked to begin fill removal immediately ahead of winter while mitigation planning continued, but the board declined to bifurcate the process, directing the applicant to finalize a combined tree-restoration/wetland-mitigation plan (addressing a severed hydraulic connection between wetlands on either side of the property) before any removal permit is issued.

timeline.summary: Petition to add car washes as a permitted use in the PLI (business park) zoning district for a proposed 6,900 sf single-lane, high-end, recycled-water car wash with four vacuum stations on a vacant 3.7-acre parcel (previously approved for office/warehouse use). The board was split: one member argued a car wash is incompatible with the business park's increasingly "stately," recreation/service-oriented character (citing the adjacent pickleball/gym use across the street) and that the town deliberately limited gas-station conforming zoning to Kensico Place years ago; Michael Pollack and others argued it was a compatible, low-traffic service amenity comparable to other non-industrial uses (assisted living) already allowed in the park. Given the split and two board members' absence, the board declined to finalize its recommendation and asked to revisit the item with fuller board input before responding to the Town Board's October 12 petition hearing.

timeline.summary: Discussion of a proposed zoning text change to permit car washes (here, a high-end single-lane tunnel wash with retail and 100%-recycled-water operations) in the PLI district, replacing a previously approved 9,300 sq ft office/warehouse building. Board members voiced significant reservations: that the use is a poor fit for the district's character, that permitting one automotive-adjacent use invites a slippery slope toward oil-change or collision-repair uses, and that a car wash would foreclose the site (the last substantially undeveloped PLI parcel in town) from other uses the comprehensive plan envisions for the corridor's evolution. A notified neighbor who disclosed a potential business interest in the venture spoke strongly in favor, calling it a valuable community amenity and noting the site's proximity to the sensitive water-supply watershed would require careful pollutant/wastewater mitigation. Rather than a formal recommendation, the board voted to forward the town planner's list of roughly eight discussion topics (compatibility, additional automotive uses, PFAS/environmental impacts, outdoor activity noise, screening, hours of operation, setbacks, and traffic intensity) to the Town Board for its consideration.
