The board and applicant treated the matter as straightforward with no public comment. The hearing was closed and the resolution adopted.

cases.name: 448 Bedford Road (church nursery-school)
cases.applicant: Steve Veneruso (Veneruso, Curto, Schwartz & Curto), attorney; Tom Curto/Carroll, architect

timeline.summary: Introductory review of a request to amend a 1983 special use permit (which allowed two classrooms) to legalize the six classrooms the ~30-year-old nursery school actually operates, with added egress; the board explained the parallel special-permit track through the Town Board and directed the applicant to compile the outstanding items from staff comments before referral.

The board reviewed a special use permit amendment to legalize the nursery school's long-standing expansion from two to six classrooms; it recommended the town board issue the permit and referred the applicant to the zoning board for an outdoor-recreation-space variance.

Having secured its amended special use permit and a ZBA variance to expand from two to six classrooms, the applicant sought site plan approval; two open items remained (delineating/striping the required parking spaces and demonstrating adequate parking-lot lighting), which the board asked to be resolved before a public hearing is scheduled.
Routine extension of time for a church's previously approved additional classrooms for its nursery school. Granted without discussion.

cases.name: 16 Davis Drive - three-car garage, driveway and fill (Paul Goudis)
cases.applicant: Paul Goudis (rep. Rick Bollinger, engineer)

timeline.summary: Early review of driveway repaving/widening, a three-car garage extension, driveway piers, a six-foot deer fence and screening, requiring a large coverage variance; the board raised the unpermitted fill already placed, driveway access depth, reducing impervious area, and possible wetland/hydric-soil impacts, and scheduled a site walk.

Imported fill tested clean; the application involves a covered parking area, driveway work near a federally-regulated (Army Corps class II) wetland buffer, land-coverage exceedance, and ~11,000 sq ft of steep-slope disturbance. The board referred it to the ZBA for coverage and noted conservation board (wetlands permit) and ARB steps remain.

The board reviewed an update on a garage/patio addition and driveway work; the applicant is pursuing a gross land coverage variance at the ZBA and has resolved conservation and stormwater concerns, with the board agreeing to send a favorable communication to the ZBA and schedule a public hearing pending soil test results and the conservation memo.

Public hearing on a site plan with tree-removal, steep-slope and wetlands permits for an attached three-car garage, driveway improvements and fill/regrading with a new stormwater/infiltration system; approved as amended with a condition to add seven arborvitae for neighbor screening.

cases.name: Seminary / St. Nurses addition, 46 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: Saint Nersess Armenian Seminary (Robert Sarafian, architect)

timeline.summary: The board reviewed a proposed two-story addition for guest lecturers and a small detached residence for the retiring dean, then referred the applicant to the ZBA for an area variance from the doubled front/side-yard setback required for churches in a residential district; stormwater on Seymour to be walked with the town engineer.

The applicant combined a previously two-building proposal into a single addition to the married-students building to solve sanitary-line elevation problems, having secured a side-yard variance and ARB approval; the board reviewed grading, septic/well capacity, runoff and a proposed rain garden and agreed to schedule a public hearing (targeting the second September meeting) once the SWPPP is submitted.
The board opened the public hearing, found no neighbors present, and adjourned the hearing to the next meeting.

Continuation of the public hearing for a two-story addition creating married-student quarters and a retired-dean residence at the rear of a former barn; with no public present the board closed the hearing and adopted a resolution approving the site plan.

cases.name: 1613 Old Orchard Street
cases.address: 1613 Old Orchard Street, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Marlene Doran
cases.lastStatus: public hearing closed | approved with conditions

trajectory.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions

timeline.summary: Discussion of a new house on a vacant Quarry Heights lot where the driveway cannot meet the 200-foot sight distance requirement, requiring a ZBA variance. The board questioned the claimed clear sight line to the east and asked the applicant to return with a sight-distance profile and dimensions before being referred to the ZBA.

The board reviewed a reduced-footprint single-family house within a wetland buffer and referred the driveway sight-distance variance (164 feet looking left vs. 200 required) to the ZBA, declining to attach a positive recommendation per its practice for individual residences.

Counsel gave a full status recap of this long-running application (since January 2023) for a single-family residence on a vacant lot largely within the regulated wetland buffer. The footprint was reduced ~500 sq ft per Conservation Board conditions, and superimposed aerial coverage analysis showed building and impervious coverage fall within the range of surrounding lots. A driveway location with adequate site distances was designed with traffic engineers and a ZBA variance was granted in June. Engineer John Kellard raised remaining comments on basement elevation/drainage and unclear tree-removal designation; the board directed the applicant toward noticing a public hearing at the next meeting.

timeline.status: public hearing closed | approved with conditions
timeline.summary: The applicant proposed a new two-story, four-bedroom colonial (~3,000 sq ft living area, ~4,000 sq ft gross) on a vacant lot, with nearly all disturbance in the wetland buffer, municipal sewer connection, and a mitigation plan the Conservation Board had recommended (conditioned on footprint reduction and a DEC wetland permit). A neighbor's engineer (Chris Morezello, for 1615 Old Orchard) raised three concerns: whether stormwater design accounted for climate change per the 2024 DEC manual, that the house remains among the largest by building coverage in the neighborhood, and driveway sight-distance/blind-spot safety. Jane Black reiterated the Conservation Board's view that the house should be smaller and in keeping with neighbors. The board defended the plan: the driveway conforms (200-foot sight line one way plus a variance), new construction is reasonably larger, footprint/impervious coverage sit within the neighborhood range, and the ten Cultec infiltrators exceed neighboring older homes' stormwater handling. The board declined to hold the applicant to a stricter-than-code future climate standard, closed the hearing, and approved the resolution as technically amended (septic reference corrected to sewer; DEC/NYC-DEP and plan-sheet conditions added).

cases.name: 111 Round Hill Road - rock crushing permit
cases.applicant: Robert Hoberman

timeline.summary: A lot-line realignment (no new lots, type-II SEQRA) combined with site plan and a special permit for an over-800-sq-ft accessory apartment; the applicant showed reduced clearing/grading, 108 proposed trees, and requested amending the 2002 clearing-and-grading limit line. The board agreed to a replanted buffer near property lines, voted to remove the required cistern (fire department won't maintain it) in favor of bedroom sprinklers, and set a public hearing for September 9.

The board held the public hearing and adopted preliminary and final subdivision/lot-line-change resolutions for 10 and 20 Round Hill Way, treating it as a SEQRA Type 2 action since no new lots are created, and amended the resolutions so the applicant's offered fire sprinklers apply only to second-floor bedrooms in lieu of the eliminated cisterns.
The board amended the extension resolution to reference the applicant's March 5, 2025 request for a 90-day extension and then approved the extension of time as amended.

Application to add rock crushing/processing to a previously approved site with rock chipping. The board debated noise, duration (about 30 crushing days, ~4,000 yards of rock), proximity to homes, and the fact that the more disruptive chipping/hammering is permitted separately by the building department without a hearing. It approved a crushing permit with a 10-week window at code hours; the motion carried with one dissent, and the board flagged wanting future coordination of chipping/hammering with crushing approvals.

cases.name: 22 Whippoorwill Road East
cases.address: 22 Whippoorwill Road East, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: owner/builder (Vladimir Levin, architect)
cases.lastStatus: public hearing closed; re-approved for 60 days with conditions

trajectory.status: public hearing closed; re-approved for 60 days with conditions

timeline.summary: Review of a front-yard retaining wall and regrading that the owner had already begun building; the board was uneasy about the wall being constructed before approval but agreed it was likely the right solution and asked the applicant to return with site and landscape plans for a public hearing.

Public hearing on revisions to an as-built house that was constructed taller and with a foundation wall instead of porch piers; the board approved a mitigation plan using a tiered retaining wall with heavy plantings, adding two conditions (additional rear-yard evergreen screening and memorializing the neighbor-side/easement planting).

Request to extend a site plan approval whose conditions (an easement to the town attorney's satisfaction and a revised evergreen-screening landscaping plan) remain unfulfilled. A neighbor's attorney letter recited a history of stop-work orders and non-compliance and asked the board to hold the applicant's feet to the fire. Rather than the default one-year extension, the board granted a shorter extension to Feb 7, 2026, to require the applicant to submit the easement and landscaping paperwork; planting itself is enforced later by the building department at CO.

timeline.status: public hearing closed; re-approved for 60 days with conditions
timeline.summary: The applicant sought re-approval of a previously approved (and twice-expired) house project, now controlled by a bank after the developer defaulted. Members and the direct neighbor were frustrated that the front yard remains dirt, the railing is damaged, landscaping is unfinished, and the required easement for screening on the neighbor's property was never executed. The board debated how to protect the neighbor without making the house unsellable, ultimately granting only a 60-day approval (rather than a year) with conditions requiring execution of the easement, irrigation of the plantings on the neighbor's property for two years, and a maintenance bond for the planting plan. The hearing was closed and the amended resolution adopted.

cases.name: 130 Old Mount Kisco Road
cases.address: 130 Old Mount Kisco Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Frank Madonna (rep. Corey Salmer, Zarin & Steinman; engineer Ralph Alfonso)

timeline.summary: The board revisited this 3.2-acre two-lot conservation subdivision (last seen in 2021), discussed an unresolved code interpretation on whether one-acre frontage/lot-width standards apply, and moved to refer the applicant to the ZBA with a positive recommendation if the building inspector's ruling requires variances, while signaling intent to retain site plan jurisdiction.

Public hearing on a conservation subdivision of an oversized, steep mountainside lot with a conservation easement placed over the mountainside; a neighbor raised drought and well-water concerns, and the board directed the applicant to revise the conservation-easement line (to let a future buyer add a pool) and resubmit, keeping the hearing open.

Continued public hearing on a two-lot conservation subdivision revised to create a separate non-buildable conservation lot owned by both lots; the board closed the hearing and adopted a negative declaration plus preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.

Amendment to a previously approved three-lot conservation subdivision. While preparing the Mylar, a roughly 900-square-foot overlap with a neighboring property's deed was discovered; the applicant shifted the lot/reliance lines to comply, keeping Lots 1 and 2 the same size and reducing the conservation area by about 900 sq ft. Counsel advised no new hearing was needed since the plat was in substantial conformance with the preliminary. The board found conformance and adopted the amended final plat; a related time extension was also granted.

cases.name: 73 Whippoorwill Road Subdivision
cases.applicant: Wellness Estates LLC / Alice Gasky (engineer Louis de Marzo)

timeline.summary: Preliminary two-lot subdivision of an 8.8-acre parcel (Lot A 5.5 ac keeping the existing house, Lot B 3.3 ac conceptual new home); soils passed for septic and drainage. The board asked the applicant to either deed-restrict/conservation-easement Lot A or demonstrate a third lot isn't feasible given frontage/pond/steep slopes, and to detail any tree removal needed for the 200-ft sight line.

Public hearing on subdividing an 8.8-acre lot into a 5.5-acre Lot A and a 3.3-acre Lot B; the applicant's engineer addressed the 11 staff comments (school-bus pickup area, road-widening reservation, no-further-subdivision note, archaeological survey), the board kept site-plan jurisdiction over future development, and it asked the applicant to tighten the 21-condition resolution for later administrative approval.

Conditions-review for a subdivision where the hearing had been closed but too many conditions remained. Working with the engineering department, the applicant reduced the preliminary plat conditions from 15 to 3 and the final subdivision conditions from 21 to 10, all remaining items being tasks to complete rather than plan changes. The board adopted the NEG DEC and both the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions.
Request for an extension of time on the subdivision, with the applicant dealing primarily with the Board of Health. The board granted the extension of time.

cases.name: 700 Bedford Road (new house)
cases.applicant: Joseph Casiotas (owner), represented by Elvis of Delhi Engineering

timeline.summary: First appearance before the Planning Board for a vertical and horizontal expansion (about 5,000 sq ft) of an existing single-family house plus a carriage house; the board reviewed site-plan, drainage/curb-cut and landscaping comments and referred the applicant to the ZBA (setback variance for the carriage house) and the ARB before returning.

Discussion of a site plan where the existing house has now been demolished and will be rebuilt on the existing foundation with a drive-through garage addition and improved gravel driveway. The board and engineer directed updated plans reflecting the fully new house, an expanded stormwater system designed for the 100-year storm, a more robust landscape/lighting plan, and confirmation of septic and DOT curb-cut items before scheduling the required public hearing.

The applicant seeks approval for a new house, with open issues on whether the county health department will accept the existing septic, NYSDOT right-of-way/curb-cut requirements, and whether the board will allow two curb cuts where code prefers one. The board was skeptical of retaining two curb cuts and pressed the applicant to document line-of-sight from each and consider a single reconfigured curb cut. Members debated a conditional approval tied to a health-department 'no objection' letter for the septic. The board scheduled a site walk for the following week and clarified that a noticed public hearing still must be conducted before any approval.

The board reviewed a recent site walk though no one appeared for the applicant. The property was described as effectively a blank slate showing existing conditions, and the board recommended the applicant hire a landscape architect to dial in the plan. The applicant is developing plans behind the scenes per prior feedback and is expected to return.

cases.name: Whippoorwill Club amended site plan and tree removal, 148 Whippoorwill Road
cases.applicant: Whippoorwill Club, represented by Jim Ryan (formerly JMC) and superintendent Paul Gonzalez

timeline.summary: The club sought approval to remove 54 trees (37 near holes 15 and 16) as part of a course restoration, plus removal of two trees within a man-made pond's wetland buffer. The board asked to see the site before deciding, scheduled a Wednesday site visit and set a public hearing for the March 24 meeting; the two buffer trees could be handled administratively if deemed minor wetlands.

The club presented revised plans to remove trees and add a raised 16th tee box, sand trap and screening plantings, but the board directed it to submit a comprehensive amended site plan (with elevations and fill quantities) before approval and adjourned the hearing held open.

Continued public hearing on an amended site plan and tree-removal permit for golf course changes at the 15th and 16th holes (tee boxes, a restored sand trap, grading and removal of roughly 54 trees); neighbors and the Conservation Board pushed back hard on tree loss and mitigation, and the hearing was kept open for further engineering review and another site walk.

Amended site plan and tree-removal permit for relocating the 16th tee box (~24 ft north, ~18 ft east) with adjusted grading and added screening plantings; 34 new plantings against 39 trees removed, most work outside the NYC DEP conservation easement (DEP permits removal of healthy trees within the easement). Added plan notes commit the club to coordinate final plantings with the neighbor/town and to remedy any future stormwater/drainage impacts on abutting properties, with disputes returning to the planning board. The public hearing was reopened and closed and the application approved.

cases.name: 7 Hollow Ridge Road (Wood Hollow Estates)
cases.address: 7 Hollow Ridge Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: owner/builder John Nickett; represented by Ralph Alpinsetti

trajectory.status: discussion only (public hearing to be scheduled; referral to ARB/RPRC)

timeline.status: discussion only (public hearing to be scheduled; referral to ARB/RPRC)
timeline.summary: A working discussion on developing a vacant 2.5-acre subdivision lot (no wetlands, sewer in the road) with a ~7,500-8,000 sq ft house comparable to neighbors, involving substantial cut and fill between a high and low grade. The planner suggested retaining walls to reduce cut, and the board explored slope steepness, a rock outcrop, and whether the design could include a walk-out basement under the current 30/38-foot height rules. The builder cited a nearly identical prior house he built on Terrace Circle; the board directed responses to the engineer's and planner's memos, a possible pre-submission meeting, and then a public hearing.

Continuation of a hearing on a single-family house with pool, patio, driveway and stormwater capture. The applicant reported reducing the disturbance area (from ~71,700 to ~62,000 sf) and tree removal (from 134 to 99). Much of the discussion centered on the town engineer's (John Kellard) memo, which had arrived late and which the applicant team had not yet seen: knoll grading, ~10-foot driveway cuts on a 14% grade, rock outcroppings, the need for a temporary sediment trap rather than just silt fence, and trench drains for driveway runoff. The board declined to adopt the resolution until the applicant reviews and addresses the memo, keeping the hearing open and adjourning. Landscaping (six white pines for rear screening) was also debated.

The resumed hearing covered erosion control, grading and drainage worked out that afternoon with town engineer John Kellard, including trench-drain sump structures, two temporary sediment basins, construction ditch relocation to the toe of slope, and possibly removing a rear retaining wall so drainage could be consolidated to the front. Roughly 22 trees may be removed and the drip-line grading impacts remain undefined. A neighbor's letter about screening was addressed via a resolution condition adding 20 green-giant arborvitae. The chair concluded the plans were too incomplete to approve and sent the applicant back to finalize drawings with the engineer before returning.

Continued public hearing on a residential site plan. The landscaping plan had been enhanced, with 21 green giant arborvitae shown in the rear versus the 20 requested, and a well permit from the Health Department was in hand. The town engineer noted that drip lines showed the tree-removal count increasing from 99 to 131 and required the site to be stabilized before framing, with those revisions on the plan. Board members had no further questions; the board closed the public hearing and adopted the site plan resolution.

cases.name: 65 Bedford-Banksville Road (Buck's Flower Garden)
cases.applicant: P. Daniel Hollis (attorney) and Joseph Rina (engineer) for the property owner

trajectory.status: discussion only; April 8 site walk scheduled

timeline.summary: Applicant sought amendment of a 1980 special permit for a nursery operation, adding a small retail farm stand, a rebuilt family residence, two horses/barn, expanded garage with offices, and planting areas, with the matter to be referred back to the town board as lead agency. The board discussed conflicts with the old permit (planting near wetlands/wells, building heights, retail prohibition) and traffic-safety concerns at the entrance, and agreed to schedule a joint work session with the conservation board rather than act tonight.

timeline.status: discussion only; April 8 site walk scheduled
timeline.summary: A ~46-year family wholesale nursery with a single-family home that accrued building-department violations, chiefly an unpermitted fill/boulder retaining area (~700+ cubic yards) with no fill certification, plus an unpermitted loop road, expired sign permit and other cleanup items. The applicant seeks to legalize the site while reducing nursery intensity (abandoning retail) and building a new home and barn/garage. Staff's memo argued the town board must re-approve the special use permit due to increased intensity of use (office and equipment garage space); the board wants a narrative of operations. Concerns focused on possible contamination in the undocumented fill (soil/core sampling via HES to be initiated) and tree removal for a proposed third horse paddock. The board scheduled a site walk for April 8 at 8:30 AM, partly so new member Thomas Crispi could see the property, and left the item open for further discussion in April.

This was a continuation discussing the board's recent site walk of the former nursery site. The key open items were verifying imported fill/soils (an HES sampling protocol is being prepared and HES will visit the site), unpermitted retaining walls the owner created, and a possibly relocated gravel road. Town counsel (Mary) clarified the board cannot itself decide whether an amended special-use permit is needed - that determination rests with the building inspector (Rob) - while the applicant argued they are reducing the level of activity. The applicant is under court-deadline pressure (adjourned to May 29) to move quickly. A curb-cut discrepancy in the memos was clarified as an existing display area, not a new curb cut.

cases.name: 428-436 Main Street
cases.applicant: P. Daniel Hollis (attorney) for the property owner

trajectory.status: unresolved — Town Attorney to confer with the Building Inspector; public hearing tentatively targeted for January

timeline.summary: Discussion of whether a 1996 ZBA parking variance for this pre-existing nonconforming mixed-use building was a blanket approval covering any future use. Counsel Baroni and staff disagreed with the blanket reading, advising the applicant either to return to the ZBA for any additional variance or to show that the currently proposed all-retail mix is no more intense than the 1996 uses (supported by a 1996 appraisal). The board agreed the appraisal plus resolution gives a benchmark to move forward.

timeline.status: unresolved — Town Attorney to confer with the Building Inspector; public hearing tentatively targeted for January
timeline.summary: The applicant's attorney argued at length that a 1996 zoning board variance finding 'no parking on premises' runs with the land and covers the building's long history of successive retail tenants (a prospective baseball-card shop was the immediate trigger), such that the Building Inspector's refusal to issue permits absent a formal site plan was legally improper (citing Esposito Builders v. Kauffman and related case law). The Town Attorney countered that the planning board lacks authority to overrule the Building Inspector's zoning interpretation and that any challenge belongs before the ZBA. The board could not resolve the underlying legal dispute, declined to recommend a temporary certificate of occupancy over the Town Attorney's objection, and asked the Town Attorney to discuss the matter directly with the Building Inspector, tentatively targeting a January public hearing on a formal site plan if the dispute isn't resolved first.

Largely procedural update to a site plan approved in January 2025. The prior approval was conditioned on providing parking for an accessory apartment; the ZBA later granted a variance for 22 parking spaces, so the site plan must be updated to match. The board declined to skip the required (now-expired) public hearing and scheduled a new hearing, with a resolution expected at the next meeting.

cases.name: 215 Business Park Drive extension (former CarQuest warehouse)
cases.applicant: 215 Business Park Drive property owner

timeline.summary: Routine third extension of time granted without discussion; no one appeared for the applicant.
Routine extension of time granted for the previously approved site plan at the former CarQuest building, with no substantive discussion.

The board granted a routine one-year extension of time for a previously approved ~45,000 sq ft warehouse/office addition (original 2017 approval), noting the approval has now been extended for roughly six years and that new DEC stormwater work will be required.

cases.name: 162 Bedford Road — Extension of Time
cases.applicant: 162 Bedford Road applicant

timeline.summary: Routine extension granted so the applicant could complete plat-filing requirements; the related site plan at E. Cole Drive was noted as having already been finalized and no longer needing its own extension.
Board granted a routine extension of time, noting the project was being delayed by outstanding Westchester County Health Department issues.
Board approved a fourth extension of time, with the project still awaiting final approval from the Westchester County Board of Health.

cases.name: 176 Virginia Road - extension of time
cases.applicant: Mister Properties Inc.

trajectory.status: approved (public hearing closed, resolution readopted largely unchanged)

timeline.status: approved (public hearing closed, resolution readopted largely unchanged)
timeline.summary: Public hearing to re-approve a previously-approved (now expired) site plan for two ~5,000 sq ft metal prefab buildings used as parking/wash bays for private contract mail trucks, near the historic, recently-restored Miller House. At an earlier meeting the board had asked the applicant to reconsider the buildings' height/appearance for better compatibility with Miller House; the applicant's architect reported the client opted to keep the design as originally approved, and the Architectural Review Board (whose approvals the town treats as non-expiring) had already re-approved it unchanged. The Chair expressed frustration at effectively 'changing the game in the middle of the game' against an already-approved design, and after discussion the board declined to press further, closed the hearing (no public comment), removed resolution language referencing a possible design change, and re-adopted the resolution as amended.

Continuation from the prior meeting's inquiry into unpermitted excavation/site work; staff confirmed the building department found some violations but no active summons, and that work is proceeding through the normal permitting process. With that clarified, the board closed the hearing and approved the draft resolution.

Instead of a one-year extension, the board granted only a three-month extension of time at the building inspector's recommendation, because the mail-delivery property owner is storing trucks and excavated without a permit, not in conformance with the approved site plan; the short window is meant to pressure compliance.

cases.name: 88 Byron Ridge Road
cases.address: 88 Byron Ridge Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Property owner (site-walk stage)

trajectory.status: site walk completed; board directed applicant to revise driveway buffer and house siting

timeline.status: site walk completed; board directed applicant to revise driveway buffer and house siting
timeline.summary: Site walk debrief: the board found the proposed driveway sited directly on the adjoining lot line without the expected buffer, and was concerned the house sat closer to Byron Lake than desired, exceeding the property's established building envelope. The applicant indicated a recent Westchester County septic regulation change could allow shrinking the septic field and shifting the house forward roughly 15 feet to address both concerns.

Applicant seeks a wetlands permit for a fence along the clearing/grading limit line and a propane tank; the board accepted the explanation that soil washed under the silt fence rather than being imported fill, and referred the buffer mitigation to the conservation board while encouraging a building-department permit for the LP tank.

This was an after-the-fact wetlands matter: additional disturbance occurred in the regulated wetland buffer during construction, drawing a notice of violation, and the originally approved 2022 mitigation plan had not been implemented for years. A proposed fence and 7,600 sq ft of 'no-mow' lawn had drifted into the record but were removed; the mitigation plan and fill removal have now been completed and observed by the town wetlands consultant, and the Conservation Board recommended approval. The board adopted the resolution as amended, adding a clarifying 'whereas' that the fence was removed and the placed fill was removed, with five-year monitoring beginning.

cases.name: Shell gas station, 375 Main Street extension of time
cases.applicant: 375 Main Street applicant

timeline.summary: Routine extension of time granted without discussion.
Routine extension of time granted; the applicant was reportedly ready to begin construction within days.
The board granted an extension of time for the Shell gas station; the applicant is still awaiting DOT permits for work in the state right-of-way and reconsidering scope amid an ownership change.

cases.name: Trip Lane — Unpermitted Fill / Contaminated Soil Remediation
cases.applicant: Homeowner

timeline.summary: The applicant's wetland consultant and the town engineer's office disagreed on the location of a flagged wetland line (town engineer's office believes it extends further south). The board directed the applicant's consultant to meet with the town engineer's office in the field to reconcile the flagging before applying to the Conservation Board for a retroactive wetlands permit covering a patio built without a permit. Separately, the board and applicant resolved a decades-old question about historically-approved fill on the property, locating old inspection/compliance records confirming it had been properly approved and inspected in the 1990s.

Continued discussion of unpermitted fill (up to seven feet in places) brought onto the property without required testing, resulting in numerous building department violations and removal of 171 trees plus construction of retaining walls and a basketball court. Soil sampling found lead and pesticide (DDD/DDE) concentrations exceeding the state's unrestricted-use soil cleanup objective, though within restricted-use limits. The Board firmly rejected the option of allowing the fill to remain under a demarcation layer/covenant, citing concerns about setting a dangerous precedent, and directed the applicant to return with a revised site plan proposing removal of the fill; no resolution was adopted at this meeting.

Follow-up from the February 13 meeting: the applicant submitted a revised site plan showing removal of the contaminated fill and a proposed patio. The Board added a condition requiring town inspection during fill removal and discussed whether replacement topsoil could itself trigger a new fill permit. The public hearing was closed and the amended resolution was adopted.

cases.name: Ledgewood — House & Pool Site Plan
cases.applicant: Not specified (no representative present at this appearance)
cases.lastStatus: referred to Conservation Board and ARB

trajectory.status: workshop discussion; site walk and applicant follow-up needed
referred to Conservation Board and ARB

timeline.status: workshop discussion; site walk and applicant follow-up needed
timeline.summary: Initial board discussion (applicant not present) of a new house replacing a demolished, dilapidated residence on a wetland/pond-constrained lot near Wokamo, where much of the proposed work (including a pool) falls within the wetland buffer requiring Conservation Board review. Plan shows 44 trees to be removed against roughly 20,000 sq ft of wetland buffer disturbance, mitigated by 40,000 sq ft of plantings. The board asked staff to confirm the house and pool are staked in the field before conducting a site visit and inviting the applicant back.

Follow-up appearance (after the August 1 initial board discussion) confirming the project — a 2.5-story dwelling on the existing footprint near three recognized wetlands, with roughly 20,000 sq ft of buffer disturbance offset by over 40,000 sq ft of mitigation planting — was properly referred to Planning first before the Conservation Board's review, as directed.

timeline.status: referred to Conservation Board and ARB
timeline.summary: On a previously developed and disturbed site surrounded by multiple overlapping wetland buffers, the applicant is rebuilding a house near the footprint of a prior structure with an adjacent pool roughly 10 feet off the back of the house. The Town Engineer's stormwater comments for the pool were incorporated into updated drawings. The board referred the application to the Conservation Board for wetland/buffer review and to the ARB for architectural review.

cases.name: Rosenthal residence expansion, 10 Creamer Road
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Tom Carrigan)

trajectory.status: discussion only; awaiting Conservation Board memo before scheduling a hearing

timeline.summary: Applicant seeks approval for a single-family home addition plus an interior-area (not footprint) expansion of an existing accessory cottage, requiring a special use permit, Westchester County Health Department septic approval, and a local wetland permit for a newly-flagged wetland/buffer and stormwater mitigation system. The board noted substantial outstanding work (updated architectural plans were omitted from the submission in error) and directed the applicant to go to the Conservation Board directly without a formal referral, and to resolve open questions about a possible pre-1984 certificate of occupancy for the cottage directly with the building inspector.

timeline.status: discussion only; awaiting Conservation Board memo before scheduling a hearing
timeline.summary: Special use permit for an accessory apartment expansion (confirmed permissible by the building department) plus a local wetland permit, delayed by a lengthy DEC wetland-jurisdiction review that has now concluded. About 14 trees would need removal and the proposed accessory structure height (about 16+ feet) falls within the code's allowable range (up to 22 feet). No fundamental board concerns were raised; the Conservation Board's recommendation memo will trigger scheduling of the public hearing.

Public hearing on expansion of a main residence and accessory guest cottage on a 5.6-acre wetland/pond property, seeking an accessory-apartment special use permit (a lapsed 1986 permit), wetlands permit, and tree removal permit; with DEC permits and Conservation Board recommendation in hand, the board closed the hearing and approved all permits subject to an engineering condition on rain-garden sizing.

cases.name: 10 New King Street — Landscaping & Parking Lot Revisions
cases.applicant: Navara Landscaping (tenant), represented by Martin Deano (H2M architects/engineers)

trajectory.status: continued — board to conduct a site walk before further review
referred to ZBA with a positive recommendation for the 8-foot fence variance; contingent on continued tenancy

timeline.status: continued — board to conduct a site walk before further review
timeline.summary: A landscaping company already permitted to store equipment as a use customarily incident to its office tenancy sought to expand its fenced storage area further into an adjacent overflow parking lot. Board members expressed concern that the landscape business appeared to be overtaking what was originally approved as an office use, questioned the poor physical condition of the existing overflow lot, and were uncertain whether the expansion was reasonable without seeing the site firsthand; the board opted to schedule a site walk and have the applicant return with more information rather than decide that night.

timeline.status: referred to ZBA with a positive recommendation for the 8-foot fence variance; contingent on continued tenancy
timeline.summary: After a site visit, the board revisited concerns that a landscaping tenant's storage yard had expanded well beyond the vehicle-parking use originally approved years earlier, now including stockpiles, equipment, and a stump grinder in an unpaved, poorly maintained overflow lot. James Jensen pressed on whether this was drifting into an inappropriate 'contractor's yard,' but ultimately the board found the roughly 1,000-square-foot expansion nominal and appropriate given the site's industrial, airport-adjacent location, asked for a few evergreens to soften the area, and voted to refer the application to the ZBA with a positive recommendation for the required 8-foot fence height variance, with the resolution to make clear the use expires if Navara's tenancy ends.

Final revisions to a landscaping plan, parking lot repaving, and an equipment enclosure expansion. The applicant confirmed acceptance of prior performance conditions (pavement repair, relocated sand storage). The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the draft resolution without amendment.

cases.name: 3 Maple Way — Single-Family Home Site Plan (Draft Resolution)
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by architect Wally Tuscano)

timeline.summary: Continued site plan review involving parking-area revisions and screening between neighboring properties, complicated by a dispute over whether an off-site wetland/watercourse buffer on an adjacent parcel (also owned by the applicant) extends onto the subject property, and by the applicant's frustration that the Town Engineer's comment memo was only posted online rather than directly emailed. The Board directed the applicant's wetland consultant (Beth Evans) to coordinate directly with the Town's wetland consultant (Dave Sessions) to reconcile the buffer question, and to resubmit missing plan sheets, before scheduling a public hearing. Michael Pollack recused himself from this matter.

Public hearing held on the pool/addition project first reviewed in March; remaining items were narrow engineering and pool-code technicalities (pool fence height compliance, drainage treatment, septic relocation confirming no wetland permit needed). No neighbors spoke at the hearing. The Board closed the hearing and directed the applicant to resolve the remaining engineering checklist items with the Town Engineer so the resolution could be kept brief rather than adopted with numerous open conditions.

Board reviewed and adopted a draft resolution for a single-family home, working through a minor driveway grading/drainage issue (a long, nearly flat 150-foot driveway needing pitch to avoid ponding and ice) that engineering staff indicated would only require a fractional grading adjustment and would not require the board to revisit the approval if changes stayed minor. Christopher Carthy recused himself from this application and did not participate.

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road condition amendment
cases.applicant: Daniel Hollis (Hollis Leland Simon, counsel); Mr. Rina (engineer); Brenda McKenny (property manager)

trajectory.status: advanced — board declared intent to be SEQRA lead agency; referred to Conservation Board and ARB
advancing — targeting a November 13 hearing/negative declaration, Town Board final vote targeted November 29

timeline.status: advanced — board declared intent to be SEQRA lead agency; referred to Conservation Board and ARB
timeline.summary: New owners of a 40+ acre equestrian property with a 2008 special permit for 10 horses sought to amend it for up to 26 competitive/show horses (rarely all present at once given a competition circuit that keeps them elsewhere much of the year), plus a barn addition and a new second barn, with no new paddock disturbance proposed. The board confirmed fire alarm/monitoring and rodent-control conditions from the original permit would carry over, clarified no broader "animal husbandry" use (e.g., livestock/poultry) was being sought, declared its intent to serve as SEQRA lead agency, and directed referrals to the Conservation Board (whose next meeting isn't until September 19) and the ARB, tentatively targeting a September 11 or 28 public hearing alongside the Town Board's own special permit hearing.

timeline.status: advancing — targeting a November 13 hearing/negative declaration, Town Board final vote targeted November 29
timeline.summary: Continued progress on the horse-count expansion (as-of-right is 2 horses; the code allows requesting up to 40+ via special permit, well above the 26 requested); ARB approved September 20, and the applicant held a neighbor picnic and door-to-door outreach ahead of the Town Board's still-open public hearing. The board debated whether a Conservation Board referral was even necessary given no floodplain or wetland-adjacent disturbance in the working area, ultimately deciding to wait for that input anyway "out of courtesy" before adopting a negative declaration, targeting the planning board's own hearing and negative declaration for November 13 so the Town Board could close its hearing and vote November 29.

Applicant requested moving three conditions to be satisfied prior to the certificate of occupancy so the building permit could issue and construction proceed; with the building inspector's concurrence the board granted the change.

cases.name: Two Trip Lane (extension of time)
cases.applicant: Represented by Michael Surin on behalf of the homeowner

trajectory.status: discussion only; routed to Conservation Board (wetland flow verification)

timeline.status: discussion only; routed to Conservation Board (wetland flow verification)
timeline.summary: Update on remediating unpermitted imported fill, now understood to be concentrated along the western boundary line rather than site-wide; the applicant confirmed the fill will be removed. A wetland flow feature at the rear of the property still needs conservation board review before the application can proceed further.

Board discussed a requested extension of time tied to a prior notice of violation; the building inspector felt a year was unnecessary, and after discussion the board granted a three-month extension, mainly to allow the required Town Board submission.
The board granted an additional three-month extension of time at the request of the building inspector, noting the applicant is due before the town board Wednesday.

cases.name: 60 Cox Avenue (Breezemont Day Camp)
cases.applicant: Breezemont day camp (Walter, with engineer Dan Holt)

timeline.summary: Referred back from the Town Board, the board discussed legalizing the existing day camp via site plan, focusing on the required 15-foot landscaped screening buffer adjacent to residences and summer vehicle parking/traffic; no approval tonight, and a site walk was scheduled (the 18th) before setting a public hearing.

Public hearing held on a site plan memorializing the existing day camp (now a permitted special-use); the only new construction is a front parking lot with a pervious paver section for drainage. After discussion of a discretionary conservation-board referral for parcels over 10 acres (deemed inapplicable since this is not a new subdivision/development), the hearing was closed and the resolution approved.

The board discussed a proposed site plan amendment to formalize on-site overflow parking for special events and staff training days at the Breezemont camp, prompted by the building department. The applicant emphasized nothing changes for the regular camp season, when hundreds of attendees are still shuttled in by bus, and the extra spaces would be used only a few days a year. Members raised concerns about spaces directly on Cox Avenue being visible and unscreened, and asked that the newly added spaces be clearly marked in color on a revised map so they can be distinguished from previously approved spaces. The matter will proceed to a noticed public hearing.

cases.name: Kent Place / Verizon Parking (23 Whippoorwill Road East)
cases.address: 23 Whippoorwill Road East, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Verizon

trajectory.status: approved (negative declaration, site plan, preliminary and final subdivision resolutions adopted)

timeline.summary: The board adopted the draft resolution granting an extension of time for the Ken Place Verizon parking plan as procedural closing business.

timeline.status: approved (negative declaration, site plan, preliminary and final subdivision resolutions adopted)
timeline.summary: A re-approval of an already-built parking expansion whose original approvals expired because Verizon never signed the plat map; no changes to what was built. A long-time abutting neighbor (Suzanne) testified at length about Verizon's chronic lack of maintenance, tree removal without replacement, an unstabilized dirt frontage with U-turns and a porta-potty, a downed fence, and unfinished screening she paid ~$40,000 to remedy herself. The board acknowledged those are largely building-department property-maintenance matters, advised her to write the building department, and re-adopted all resolutions so the plat can be filed with the health department.

The board granted an extension of time for the Ken Place Verizon parking plan. Staff reported the required Verizon signatures had finally been obtained and the matter now rests with the department of health, and that the applicant's variance had been renewed about a year ago so there is no variance concern.

cases.name: 18 Long Pond Road
cases.address: 18 Long Pond Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Daniel and Joanna Novick (landscape architect Dean Portula)

timeline.summary: Introduction of a swimming pool proposal entirely within a 100-foot wetland buffer on a constrained, sloping lot; the board referred it to the Conservation Board and scheduled a joint site visit, with stormwater and mitigation plans still being engineered.

Referral back from the Conservation Board (which was split, with only four of seven members present) on a pool, spa, and patio within a wetland buffer. The applicant reduced the pool and patio (~25-50%), increased the wetland setback from about 12 to 19-20 feet, and raised mitigation planting to three-to-one to convert a low-functioning wetland to higher-functioning. Conservation liaison Jane Black explained the split: two members found the property would be improved by the mitigation, while dissenters objected over a culvert/former stream location and the small backyard size. The Board was favorable, viewing it as a net positive for the wetland and a reasonable suburban amenity, and directed that a public hearing be scheduled (in November).

The board opened and closed a public hearing on a swimming pool, patio, deck modification, tree removal and landscaping within a regulated wetland buffer, ultimately approving the site plan, wetlands permit and tree removal permit. The landscape architect described a stormwater plan storing pool drawdown with slow release, an extensive planting plan providing 3x mitigation, elimination of pesticides, and habitat features; diseased beech trees would be removed. The Conservation Board deadlocked 2-2, with the town engineer explaining both sides: some members opposed 'rewarding' new disturbance on a site with a decades-old buried water course, while others saw the mitigation as a net improvement to a low-functioning wetland. The board examined topography, whether the existing 60+ year-old pipe still functions, and read a neighbor's email opposing the project despite the mitigation explanation.

cases.name: 167 Mianus River Road (Mianus River Gorge)
cases.address: 167 Mianus River Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Mianus River Gorge Inc.

trajectory.status: public hearing opened and adjourned without date

timeline.status: public hearing opened and adjourned without date
timeline.summary: Public hearing to construct an office addition and a gravel parking lot on the 960-acre preserve property in the R4A zone. Steven Sauro read the public hearing notice. The town planner advised that the applicant must first obtain an amended special use permit from the Town Board before the Planning Board can proceed. With no neighbors present, the board opened and immediately adjourned the hearing without a date.

The applicant sought site plan approval for a science-education office addition and a gravel parking lot (reduced from 10 to 8 spaces), with variances already granted by the ZBA and stormwater handled via infiltration trenches on a low-sensitivity, non-watershed site. A revised plan had been submitted only the prior week, after the deadline, and the applicant had not yet obtained Architectural Review Board approval, which the resolution would have made a post-approval condition. The chair objected on process grounds, preferring the applicant obtain ARB approval first and return with a clean submission rather than set a precedent. The board carried the matter over, placing the applicant on the September 25 agenda after the ARB's September 17 meeting; the applicant can begin assembling building-permit materials in the meantime.

Continuation of a public hearing on an addition to the non-profit nature center, including a building expansion for office space, a new septic system, an overflow parking area, and stormwater management. The only change from the prior meeting was a reduction of two parking spaces, revising the layout from stacked to directly accessed spaces, and leaving the existing paved driveway as-is. No members of the public spoke; the board closed the hearing and approved the site plan. The board praised the applicant's engineering work.

cases.name: 258 East Middle Patent Road (Matthews accessory barn)
cases.address: 258 East Middle Patent Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Chris Salabarria & Carol Matthews (engineer Allen Pilch, ALP Engineering)

trajectory.status: referred (to ZBA; also ARB and Conservation Board)

timeline.status: referred (to ZBA; also ARB and Conservation Board)
timeline.summary: Initial concept presentation to replace a 100-plus-year-old dilapidated barn/garage with a combined garage and accessory apartment, intended primarily to give the owners' wheelchair-using adult son accessible visits since the existing home has interior steps. The structure is beyond saving (crumbling foundation), so the project needs several variances and touches the wetland buffer with a small portion of an ADA ramp and stormwater mitigation, requiring Conservation Board review. The chair suggested the applicants consider whether the existing footprint is truly the best location. The board referred the applicant to the ZBA and agreed to refer to the Conservation Board.

Discussion of an accessory dwelling unit in a barn/garage building, before the board for a wetland permit, scenic-road frontage and a special permit. The applicant reported that after an October site walk and a follow-up meeting the Conservation Board was satisfied with the wetland permit and mitigation, with buffer impacts reduced from over 2,400 sq ft to 1,514 sq ft (about 70 sq ft for a handicap ramp plus stormwater and a relocated rain garden). Invasive species (Oriental bittersweet, mugwort, multiflora rose) would be removed and a mitigation planting plan provided; percolation testing was to be witnessed by the town engineer. The board found the application strong and scheduled the public hearing (targeted for the December meeting, ultimately the 24th) with a draft resolution to follow.

The board opened and closed a public hearing and approved the site plan for a detached accessory apartment (over 800 sq ft) in a renovated garage/barn to accommodate an owner's mobility needs, including a wheelchair-accessible ramp, new septic for the barn, and stormwater/rain garden improvements. The engineer reported no direct wetland impacts, minor wetland-buffer impacts offset by invasive removal and native plantings, and successful percolation testing. Members debated resolution conditions at length: whether the building-permit trigger tied to Department of Health approval should be relaxed given DOH delays, the redundant existing-septic review condition, and a weekly stormwater-inspection reporting requirement (condition 10) the applicant felt was onerous. The board kept the DOH condition intact but clarified the septic language applies to the barn, and approved the site plan.

cases.name: 250 East Middle Patent Road
cases.address: 250 East Middle Patent Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Neil and Vanessa Lucy (owners); attorney Michael Sirignano; Jerry Barrett (landscape architect) and Nicholas of Hudson Engineering

timeline.summary: A pool application first seen ~5 years ago under prior owners (the Benises) returned with the Lucy family. After a site conversation with the chair, the team presented a sketch moving the pool 16 feet back and about 4 feet lower so it sits in the side yard rather than the front yard, eliminating the zoning setback variance but still implicating the scenic road overlay, a conservation buffer, and 25% slopes. The revised concept would tie the pool to the existing bluestone patio via a retaining/engineered wall (est. 6-8 ft) with a forward sitting wall. The board strongly endorsed the new direction and asked the applicant to formalize plans with landscape and wetland mitigation plans and return.

Following a site walk the prior week, the board reviewed a revised plan that pulls the structure a full 16 feet further from the road and roughly 18 feet lower in elevation, making it essentially not visible. Members found it favorably sited and no longer in the front yard. A wetland permit is triggered because the work is within 150 feet of the wetland, and discussion clarified the steep-slope (25%) regulation, with engineer John Kellard noting the rear yard is under 25% which narrows the review. The board voted to refer the applicant to the Conservation Board, targeting a September public hearing on return.

The applicant sought to install a swimming pool on a property fronting scenic East Middle Patent Road. After a prior version needed a variance, the board's site-walk feedback led the applicant to move the pool back 16 feet and 4 feet lower in elevation, eliminating the front-yard setback variance (edge of water ~79 feet versus 75-foot setback). Sections were cut to show minimal visibility from the road, aided by existing vegetation, rock forms, and proposed landscaping, with an engineered rear wall not visible from the road. The board praised the collaborative result, closed the hearing, and approved the site plan.

cases.name: 2 Israel Townsend Hill (Lot 1, 32 Orchard Drive subdivision)
cases.address: 2 Israel Townsend Hill, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: 32 Orto Drive LLC; Andrew Vaccarello, B&J Engineering; colleague Matt (architect)

trajectory.status: public hearing opened | public hearing continued

timeline.summary: Site plan for a single-family dwelling on Lot 1 of a recorded subdivision over which the board retained jurisdiction. The ~2,900 sq ft footprint is fully zoning compliant with generous setbacks; it is about 700 sq ft larger than previously depicted with a slightly enlarged driveway in the same location, an on-site septic and well, a rain garden for the slight impervious overage, reduced downstream peak flows, and about 24 trees removed. Members discussed the landscaping/replanting plan and tree preservation, and the board directed the applicant to the ARB, asking that a landscape plan be brought along.

timeline.status: public hearing opened | public hearing continued
timeline.summary: New four-bedroom single-family dwelling with three-car garage on a subdivision lot, replacing an existing tennis court, with septic, well, driveway and stormwater (shared BMP plus a rain garden); 24 trees to be removed. Neighbors Darren and Susan Lampert (24 Orchard Drive, 25-year residents directly behind the lot) objected that shrubbery is inadequate and asked for tall staggered evergreen screening along the driveway and rear, citing loss of privacy, headlight glare, and the home's height. The applicant agreed to add staggered evergreens of mixed species and proposed eliminating the rear rain garden to save trees and redirect flow to the shared BMP. The board kept the public hearing open pending a revised landscape plan, targeting the next meeting (Oct 16) alongside another subdivision lot.

Continued public hearing on new house construction with a tree-removal permit. In response to prior direction for a 'robust planting plan,' the applicant added 12 trees (8 Arborvitae, 4 Eastern Hemlock) integrated with existing vegetation along the neighbor's property line for headlight/visual screening, and removed a rain garden to save trees. The neighbor (Darren Lampert) objected that the proposed 4-foot trees were insufficient. The Board closed the hearing and approved the site development plan and tree-removal permit, conditioned on noting the prior-day ARB approval and revising the planting schedule to 8-10 foot trees.

cases.name: 4 Vincent Lane (wetland restoration)
cases.applicant: Lewis Fusco, landscape architect, for owners Tom and Sarah DeSwart

trajectory.status: public hearing closed; decision adjourned pending ARB approval of existing sheds/barn

timeline.summary: New owners seek to modify the existing driveway (new circular drive) and re-wild the property with native plantings while memorializing prior work done without Planning Board approval (a pool built under a building permit, several sheds, and turf/paved areas in wetland buffers). The plan reduces land coverage from over 23,000 sq ft to under the approved 19,000 and removes turf/paving from wetland buffers; wetlands were flagged by a specialist and invasives are being removed. The board viewed the request as largely procedural memorialization and directed coordination with the Conservation Board, which will do a site visit before sending a memo back to the Planning Board.

timeline.status: public hearing closed; decision adjourned pending ARB approval of existing sheds/barn
timeline.summary: A wetlands/site-plan application to modify a driveway and front walkway, remove astroturf golf areas and invasive wetland plants, and install native plantings, removing roughly 25,000 sq ft of lawn/hardscape and providing 40,000 sq ft of wetland mitigation. The Conservation Board had commended the project and the applicant addressed the town engineer's comments. The board closed the public hearing but could not adopt the resolution because two sheds and a barn built under earlier building permits never received Planning Board/ARB sign-off (a town-side glitch); it opted to send the applicant to the ARB and adopt at a later meeting without requiring the applicant to reappear.

The board had previously closed the public hearing and instructed the applicant to obtain ARB approval before returning for adoption. With ARB approval now in hand, the board adopted the draft resolution without the applicant needing to appear.

cases.name: 2 & 4 Massaro Court (two-family residences)
cases.applicant: Nicholas Shari, Hudson Engineering & Consulting
cases.lastStatus: discussion only (to ARB, then public hearing)

trajectory.status: discussion only (to ARB, then public hearing)

timeline.summary: Two proposed two-family dwellings on the first two lots of a recently approved three-lot subdivision. Much of the driveway, utilities and stormwater remain unchanged from the subdivision plans; updates add the buildings and elevated decks (at-grade rear terraces to be removed). Outstanding items include structural plans and protective barriers for tall retaining walls, a driveway revision to add a required parking space per unit, and a possible gross land coverage variance the applicant expects to avoid by converting a turnaround area to parking. Chairman Carthy strongly pressed for tiered, more attractive retaining walls (some near 10-11 ft) rather than a single tall wall. No hearing yet; revised plans to follow.

The applicant presented revised site/steep-slope plans for two two-family residences, addressing prior comments by adding a terraced retaining wall to soften the driveway wall's appearance, providing two dedicated parking spaces per unit, reworking side/rear grading, and clarifying overland footing-drain discharge. Outstanding engineering memo items (landscape plan revisions, planting detail, drain pipe sizes/inverts, peak flows) were deemed handleable administratively. The board approved the resolution for 4 Massaro Court that night; since the buildings are identical, 2 Massaro Court would be approved administratively at a future meeting once the applicant obtains ARB approval, without needing to return. The board flagged that any rock encountered on the up-hill site would require checking back.

timeline.status: discussion only (to ARB, then public hearing)
timeline.summary: This is the last of a previously approved three-lot, two-family subdivision, with the first two lots already built. The town engineer raised concerns about the proposed house footprint's proximity and view-shed impact on the adjacent home, plus an exposed-foundation/grade drop-off at the rear northwest corner. The applicant's engineer agreed to regrade that corner (up to about 372) and consider shifting the house, while noting retaining walls are less substantial than the prior lots and structural wall designs are under town review. The board was generally comfortable and directed the project to the ARB and a revised grading plan before a public hearing.

cases.name: 4 Kensico Court (Awesome Landscaping)
cases.applicant: John G. Scarlett Jr. for Awesome Landscaping

timeline.summary: Proposed reuse of an existing building for a small (~150 sq ft) office plus truck parking and outdoor storage for a landscaping business. Review letter issues include lighting, some existing parking spaces sitting on town property, and 20-ft aisles that fall short of the 24-ft standard. The board discussed reworking the ~51-space lot to become code-compliant (or seeking targeted ZBA variances) while preserving impervious coverage and truck turnaround. The chair was supportive of the concept and directed the applicant to produce the best compliant site plan possible before any variance request.

The board reviewed a revised plan for a parking lot where some spaces had encroached on town/road right-of-way. The applicant eliminated the off-property spaces (they cannot be counted and may need physical removal if the highway department requires it) and restriped the existing lot, converting some aisles to one-way angled parking, yielding 41 spaces against a 30-space requirement. One outstanding item is a lighting plan for the area, which the applicant has engaged someone to prepare. The board praised the 'clever design' and will schedule a public hearing once the paperwork and notice are ready.

The applicant sought an amended site plan to add a second tenant (a landscaping equipment/vehicle storage use) to a warehouse building that had never received formal site plan approval. Changes included reworking parking to a one-way in/out layout with spaces designated for the principal building versus the tenant, and a new lighting design brought up to current dark-sky code. No members of the public appeared. The board closed the hearing and approved the amended site plan, with the lighting review satisfying condition number two.

cases.name: 909 North Broadway Cigar / Membership Club (Sir John's Plaza)
cases.applicant: James Montelione (representing the membership club)

timeline.summary: A town-board special-use-permit application for a membership club at Sir John's Plaza was referred to the Planning Board for comment. The chair questioned how the code's required 25-foot-deep planting buffer would be satisfied given the site's history and rock conditions, and the planner explained the buffer requirement is aimed at screening golf-course-type clubs, not two converted storefronts. The board had no substantive objections. It voted to send a positive referral back to the town board.

A cigar membership club (special permit already granted by the Town Board, now in the site-plan phase) faced a parking question in the Surjon's Plaza strip mall. Adam Kaufman explained the membership-club parking code offers three standards and recommended the one-space-per-200-square-feet floor-area standard (about nine spaces), which likely avoids a variance, noting the shared lot and evening-only use. Members debated whether to use the more conservative fire-code/occupancy figure (about 17-18 spaces) as a more defensible, realistic number. The board agreed to cite a standard, made a referral to the ZBA for a parking variance if necessary, and Adam agreed to run the numbers; the submitted plan already showed 18 spaces.

The board took up the change-of-use site plan for the Social Life members club and cigar lounge. The planner explained the applicant already obtained its special use permit and, because the prior use was a bakery, the off-street parking calculation for the shopping center showed no parking variance was needed (17 spaces under the one-space-per-three-seats standard). With no physical changes to the site, this was a simple change of use. Members joked about the concept, asked about liquor licensing and membership tiers, then closed the hearing and approved the change-of-use site development plan.

cases.name: 11 New King Street — Parking Garage (Extension of Time)
cases.applicant: Applicant not named in transcript (represented by engineer Justin Ciney of AKRF and architect Chris Fisher)

trajectory.status: public hearing opened, then adjourned (not closed)

timeline.status: public hearing opened, then adjourned (not closed)
timeline.summary: Continued public hearing on an automated parking garage facility. The applicant reported completed Conservation Board (with a ~$136,000 wetland-bank contribution), ARB, and Town Board special-permit approvals, but said the state DOT had not yet approved the required traffic-mitigation plan from the environmental review, with a DOT meeting scheduled for August 9. The board (citing its lead-agency responsibility) declined to close the hearing so the public could weigh in once DOT's position on mitigation is known, while allowing the applicant to keep refining site-plan details (including a reversed, left-side vehicle/bus circulation pattern at the entrance) in the interim.

Routine extension of time for the previously-approved automated parking garage project (last discussed in 2018), pending installation of a new water line on New King Street before construction can begin. No board discussion beyond confirming no outstanding questions; approved without dissent.

cases.name: Residential Driveway Relocation & Fill (Off Davis Road area)
cases.address: Address unclear in ASR transcript (referenced as near "Davis" road/drive)
cases.applicationType: site plan / wetlands permit (driveway relocation, fill)
cases.applicant: Joe Daniel
cases.lastStatus: referred to Conservation Board (not yet approved)

trajectory.status: referred to Conservation Board (not yet approved)

timeline.summary: Brief presentation of a landscape plan (previously approved by the ARB with 15 added trees) tied to removal of roughly eight to ten trees in the rear yard to create a lawn, with septic/well/percolation details reviewed. The board indicated comfort with the proposed rear tree removal; a public hearing had already been noticed for the following Monday, August 6, 2018.

timeline.status: referred to Conservation Board (not yet approved)
timeline.summary: Follow-up to a January 13 site walk on a driveway relocation requiring imported fill (either natural material or manufactured geofoam/cellular fill blocks) to cross a ravine/water course; an alternative backyard-expansion layout suggested at the site walk was rejected by the applicant's team as more impactful (more fill, more retaining walls) than the original plan. The board pushed to minimize truck trips and wetland-buffer disturbance by exploring natural fill sourced on-site (potentially combined with excavation from a separately-planned playroom/gymnasium addition) rather than importing geofoam, and one member floated designing small bridge-like structures over the water course (echoing an existing pair of crossings) to reduce both fill volume and water-course impact. The applicant pressed for the board's support before investing further engineering effort; the board declined to commit and instead voted to refer the matter to the Conservation Board for further review, cautioning the applicant that, as with any application, the ultimate outcome remains undecided until a vote.

cases.name: Extensions of Time — Procedure Discussion
cases.applicant: Applicant names ASR-garbled/unclear ("Dr. Tourette"/East Lane matter; a second "dam" matter)

timeline.summary: The board granted two routine extensions of time: one for a property on East Lane where the applicant was reported to be nearly finished with final conditions, and a second six-month extension for an unrelated dam-related approval nearing expiration. Both were approved without discussion or dissent.

Adam Kaufman opened a policy discussion on how the board handles extensions of time. The board agreed to place extensions at the top of future meetings so professionals can dispatch them quickly, while a participating professional argued the published agenda order should not bind the chair (comparing it to a courtroom). Adam also proposed adding whereas clauses to extension resolutions stating whether another board (e.g., the ZBA) had a required approval and its status, so lapses are clearly documented. The board and staff endorsed the changes.

cases.name: Summit Club — Temporary Golf Clubhouse Facilities (2021-2022 Seasons)
cases.address: Brynwood/Summit Club, Bedford Road (Route 22), Armonk, NY
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners LLC (represented by attorney Mark Winegarten, principal Jeff Mendel, architects Rich Granoff and Ken Anderson of Granoff Architects, and engineer Paul Cisak of JMC)

trajectory.status: informational joint work session — no board action

timeline.status: informational joint work session — no board action
timeline.summary: Following roughly a decade of process (2011 zoning text amendment creating a golf course community overlay district, 2016-2020 approvals for the golf course and subdivision into a 130-acre golf parcel and 26-acre residential parcel), the applicant presented the residential component's design directly to a joint Planning Board/ARB session: 73 luxury one-floor-living condominium units across seven buildings (six along the golf course, one set higher to the east), an amenities building (bar/grill, pool, fitness center, spa) doubling as an initial sales center, and four tennis courts set back roughly 100 feet from Bedford Road. Discussion covered building height relative to road grade, unit parking (two indoor spaces plus a golf-cart space per unit), massing/staggering to manage perceived height and buffer views from Route 22, and general architectural character (modern theme, described by the applicant as unusual for the town but intended to appeal to an empty-nester/second-home buyer market). The chair confirmed the boards were largely finished offering initial comments and that the applicant would continue refining the plan with staff (Town Planner Adam Kaufman and Town Engineer John Kellard) ahead of a future submission; no vote was taken.

Public hearing on a special permit for temporary golf-season facilities (limited operation for up to 300 members, a repurposed construction trailer serving as clubhouse/pro shop/offices, a bathroom trailer, a prefabricated wooden bar structure, and a food truck) while the permanent residential/amenity buildings remain in process, for the 2021 and 2022 golf seasons. Board members pressed on Health Department approval timelines for food service and septic/sanitary operations (with the applicant citing a 21-day notice requirement) and scrutinized draft-resolution conditions, including a noise-chapter compliance reference. A related procedural dispute arose over whether the trailers required formal ARB review or could be waived to the building inspector's discretion; the Town Attorney advised the ARB has independent jurisdiction the planning board cannot waive on its own, so the board directed the applicant to work with the building inspector or seek an ARB slot. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended (striking an as-built-survey condition given the facilities' temporary nature).

cases.name: 50 East Middle Patent Road — Two-Lot Subdivision
cases.address: 50 East Middle Patent Road, Armonk, NY
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by architect Craig Tenerelli, landscape architect Glenn Tysers, and engineer Matt Jiranda of Bibo Associates)

The board voted to positively refer the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals for a front-yard-setback variance (needed for a nonconforming addition, unrelated to the subdivision itself) so that process could run in parallel while the applicant finalizes updated subdivision/FAR/lot-coverage calculations and prepares for a scheduled subdivision public hearing, after which separate special use permits for an oversized garage and pool house would follow.

timeline.status: subdivision approved; associated site plan sent back to staff, resolution not yet adopted
timeline.summary: Building on the ZBA referral discussed at the August 9 meeting, the applicant presented a ~29-acre, two-lot subdivision (a 23.8-acre lot retaining the existing house, pool house, and detached garage, and a new 5.28-acre building lot) that had since received ARB, Conservation Board, and ZBA (front-yard setback) approvals. A notice neighbor asked clarifying questions about future subdivision potential and lot lines, which the board and applicant answered without objection. The board closed the hearing and adopted a negative declaration and the amended preliminary and final subdivision plans (adding a two-year, from-plat-filing deadline for the new lot's principal residence to reach certificate of occupancy, ensuring the accessory structures don't become the sole use). However, when the discussion turned to the associated site plan for the lots (garage, pool house, and driveway-grade details), a board member pushed back on adopting a resolution with roughly 40 still-open engineering conditions; the board closed that portion of the hearing but declined to adopt the site plan resolution, instead directing the applicant's team to work with Town Engineer John Kellard to resolve outstanding items and return with a tightened resolution.

cases.name: 73 North Broadway — Restaurant/Taproom

trajectory.status: continued — ZBA referral deferred pending a reconciled parking plan

timeline.status: continued — ZBA referral deferred pending a reconciled parking plan
timeline.summary: The applicant proposed mitigating a parking shortfall via a valet program (fitting 27 vehicles on site) plus a pending off-site lease for 5-7 additional spaces from an adjacent property owner, and brought in a new traffic/parking engineer to respond to the town's parking consultant (Michael Galante), whose memo (received just days earlier) raised concerns about peak parking demand (up to 58 vehicles under a worst-case restaurant benchmark) and limited on-street parking capacity near a busy, narrow-access intersection. Jim Jensen voiced a specific access/circulation concern about the site's constrained side-street entrance potentially creating a traffic "quagmire," while acknowledging support for the restaurant concept generally. Rather than send a still-unreconciled plan to the ZBA with a lukewarm recommendation, the board opted to let the applicant's engineer work directly with the town's consultant to tighten the parking plan and return in two weeks so the board could make a stronger, better-informed referral.

The applicant team returned after the ZBA granted a 26-space parking area variance on a second attempt, reporting no remaining major site-plan issues and requesting the board move to a public hearing. The board discussed how the traffic study and ZBA parking/circulation commitments would be incorporated into the site-plan resolution, revisited (without resolving) whether to remove a no-left-turn sign at the driveway exit to help patrons head north on Route 22 versus keeping commercial trucks out of the residential street (deferred to public comment), and confirmed the applicant was ready to notice a public hearing for March 14, 2022 pending final ARB approval running on a similar timeline.

The board voted unanimously to send the positive recommendation, including the expanded definition, to the Town Board.

cases.name: 873 North Broadway — Restaurant & Accessory Brewing Adaptive Reuse
