timeline.status: public hearing closed; decision pending (applicant still awaiting ABC/liquor authority approval)
timeline.summary: Adaptive reuse of a ~3,435 sq ft commercial building into a 45-seat fine-dining restaurant with a small accessory brewing operation, offsite parking arrangements, and an 18-seat rear outdoor dining area; the applicant had already obtained a ZBA parking variance for 26 spaces. The owner of the adjacent non-conforming two-family residential rental (877 North Broadway) vehemently objected, citing traffic, noise, parking spillover onto tenant amenity, and incompatibility of a brewery/restaurant use next to a pre-1923 residence. After extended negotiation over outdoor-seating hours, screening/fencing/planters behind the patio, and location of outdoor dining (front vs. rear), the board and applicant agreed to last outdoor seating at 8 p.m. Monday-Thursday and 9 p.m. Friday-Sunday, no live music, and evergreen/planter screening; the public hearing was then closed but a vote was deferred because the applicant had not yet secured required ABC (liquor authority) approval.

The board finalized and adopted the site plan resolution. Key negotiated points: because the required NYSDOT highway work permit/easement (a multi-year Attorney General review process) could delay the sidewalk/frontage work well past occupancy, the board substituted a performance bond (new bond in the new owner's name, amount set by the Town Engineer, work completed within one year of DOT permit issuance) for a strict pre-CO completion requirement, with proof of a submitted DOT application required before CO issuance; condition 12 was revised to track whatever on-site inspection frequency DOT's permit actually requires; a prior no-left-turn restriction onto Washington Place was removed at the applicant's request (already reflected on the site plan); and the outdoor dining hours were locked in at last seating 8 p.m. Monday-Thursday and 9 p.m. Friday-Sunday, with a landscaping/planter screening commitment toward the rear-yard neighbor.

No wetlands were found on site (confirmed by the town's consultant), but nearly the entire buildable area falls within a 100-foot buffer of an adjacent watercourse, so the applicant proposed over 2:1 plant-material mitigation. Board members pushed back on whether the hardship justified variances given the buffer impact, questioned whether the septic field could instead be partially relocated to bring the pool closer to the house (engineers said soil/ledge conditions and current stricter Health Department separation regulations make that difficult), and asked for better mapping of a nearby vacant Connecticut-adjacent parcel's development potential to confirm no future neighboring house would be affected. Because the ZBA referral is a 'gating' issue for the applicant (who wants to avoid further engineering cost before knowing if variances are viable), the board opted to hold the item two more weeks for additional data rather than send it to the ZBA immediately.

timeline.summary: The applicant is transferring development potential from a non-contiguous four-acre vacant parcel (to be deed-restricted against further development) onto the developed six-acre parcel, requiring eight ZBA variances for coverage and height. Chairman Carthy pressed the architect on how many fewer variances would be needed if the two lots were legally contiguous, drawing out the mathematical point that combining two separately-calculated allowances (X and X) yields more total permitted coverage than treating the combined area as one lot (X+Y) — an argument the applicant plans to make to the ZBA. The board also confirmed a pre-existing garden shed on the vacant parcel would be treated as a legal nonconforming structure from the 1993 subdivision rather than requiring a separate use variance, and noted that removing a previously-discussed connector between the main house and guest house to reduce coverage inadvertently made the detached garage exceed height/size limits, adding to the variance count. The board voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA.

cases.name: 25 North Broadway
cases.applicant: Not named in the recording (represented by project engineer)

trajectory.status: continued — applicant to revise plans addressing circulation, canopy, facade, landscaping, and lighting

timeline.status: continued — applicant to revise plans addressing circulation, canopy, facade, landscaping, and lighting
timeline.summary: The applicant proposed new gas pumps and eliminating one of two pumps positioned against the convenience store building, but the board found the resulting on-site circulation still too tight — a car at the remaining building-adjacent pump could trap other vehicles from reaching the convenience store or exiting. The Town Engineer suggested shifting the site's south exit further south to fit a third pump in-line and improve circulation, which the applicant agreed to explore alongside a request from the board for a canopy trim-back to the building edge, sidewalk/drainage repairs, a detailed landscaping plan for the Route 22 median island, a lighting plan, and consideration of facade improvements (e.g., a gable roofline) to modernize the building's appearance.

A previously-negotiated draft resolution that had been left unadopted because of numerous conditions, whittled down over several meetings. The chair questioned aloud whether the board's practice of sending such applicants away rather than finishing on the spot was wise, but confirmed the conditions had been addressed. The board adopted the resolution as drafted.

cases.name: 188 King Street — Rear Awning Installation
cases.applicant: Represented by project architect and project manager Kelly McRae

timeline.summary: The applicant proposed covering an existing non-enclosable patio with a fixed operable awning as part of minor interior renovations; because the structure cannot be enclosed, the board agreed it does not trigger additional floor-area or parking review, provided the applicant documents that non-enclosure capability in writing. The board directed staff to schedule a public hearing and prepare a resolution.

Simple commercial application to add an awning over an existing rear patio. The applicant did not attend due to weather but had discussed the matter with staff beforehand. The Board proceeded with the noticed public hearing, closed it, and adopted the resolution.

cases.name: 38 Creamer Road — Accessory Apartment Special Use Permit (Reissuance)
cases.applicant: Property owners (represented by attorney Taylor Palmer, Cuddy & Feder; contractor Pallotta/THP Consulting)

timeline.summary: A roughly 300-year-old barn containing an existing accessory apartment was substantially rebuilt under a valid building and floodplain permit, but the building inspector determined the extent of replacement made it "new construction," triggering the need for a variance (since detached accessory structures built after 1984 require ZBA relief) and a new special use permit. The Board found the applicant's presentation thorough, praised the preservation effort, and voted to refer the matter to the Zoning Board of Appeals for the necessary variances, without a positive or negative recommendation.

A 1996 accessory-apartment special use permit needed reissuance after extensive structural rehabilitation (including physically moving the historic building to a new foundation to save it from sinking) led the building department to deem the structure "new," also requiring and obtaining a ZBA variance. A neighbor and longtime area resident spoke in support, recounting the barn/structure's history as part of the historic Green Valley Farm. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution with minor wording amendments and an added condition for additional landscaping to the planning department's satisfaction.

cases.name: Single-family residence & pool (Angela) - cut/fill grading
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by design professional "Wally")
cases.lastStatus: discussion only (direction given to respond to memos and schedule a public hearing)

trajectory.status: discussion only (direction given to respond to memos and schedule a public hearing)

timeline.summary: A new single-family residence referred to the Planning Board from the Residential Project Review Committee (RPRC) for review of driveway/property-line screening adequacy and the proposed house's alignment relative to neighboring homes. The Board requested revised plans clearly showing property lines, proposed setbacks, and the driveway, and did not take a final vote at this meeting.

timeline.status: discussion only (direction given to respond to memos and schedule a public hearing)
timeline.summary: A working discussion on a hillside single-family home with a pool, garage, and retaining walls where the applicant had already reduced imported fill and wall heights and relocated the pool per prior board feedback. New wetland flagging in the rear was coordinated between the applicant's wetlands engineer and the town's consultant (Dave). The planner questioned whether setting the first floor at 473 (vs. ~470.5 garage) could be lowered to reduce cut/fill and wall grading; the board directed the applicant's professionals to answer the planner's and town engineer's memos and then set a public hearing.

cases.name: Harris pool and patio, 9 Sterling Road North
cases.applicant: Homeowner Mr. Harris (with landscape architect Andrew Monaco of Yost Landscape Architecture)

timeline.summary: Long-running, contentious application (four prior Conservation Board denials over roughly two and a half years) for a revised pool/septic/stormwater plan with a new wetland mitigation plan and functional analysis. The Town's wetland consultant found the applicant's functional analysis adequate but noted the mitigation plan had not yet been reviewed, and flagged a discrepancy between the Westchester County Health Department-approved septic plan and the infiltration area shown on the current site plan. The Board directed the visibly frustrated applicant back to the Conservation Board with the completed functional analysis and mitigation plan, working concurrently with the Health Department to resolve the septic/infiltration discrepancy; no vote was taken.

Public hearing on a new pool and patio in a town-regulated wetland buffer; with Conservation Board recommendation and only technical engineering items remaining, the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution approving it after roughly six years of review.

cases.name: Subdivision Extension of Time — Second Matter
cases.applicant: Subdivision applicant (represented by Mr. McKenna)

timeline.summary: Fourth extension of time granted for an approved subdivision, with the applicant paying the standard extension fee (up to $1,000/year) while finalizing outstanding items; the Board raised no substantive objection. (Note: the property name is garbled in the ASR transcript as "124-year-old Monteusco Road" and could not be confirmed precisely.)
A second, separate subdivision extension-of-time resolution was granted in brief with no discussion of substance. (Subdivision name is garbled in the ASR transcript and could not be confirmed.)

cases.name: 601 Bedford Road (Embassy Club / old country club)
cases.applicant: Nick Waller (property owner)

timeline.summary: Proposal to rebuild the fire-gutted 1959 ruins of the former Signal Hill Country Club mansion (stone exterior walls intact since the fire) into a single-family home for the applicant's extended family, converting the existing smaller cottage (currently his residence) to an accessory structure requiring a special permit. The roughly 18,000+ square foot restoration will need variances (likely rear-yard setback for a water tank buffer) but relies on existing nonconforming coverage predating current zoning. The applicant plans a taller roofline/cupola partly to screen a neighboring water tower, coordinated informally with adjacent neighbors. The Board found the concept appealing and directed the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals and Architectural Review Board.

The applicant is restoring a fire-damaged former club building back into a house (with the existing house to become an accessory apartment) and reported the ARB required a strict restoration to the original appearance (cupola removed, six-over-six windows); unresolved septic and roof-stormwater questions remain because the existing leaching field cannot be located, and zoning variances are still to be defined, so the board asked the applicant to address staff comments before any ZBA referral.

cases.name: 845 North Broadway — Rooftop Solar Array (Westchester Jewish Community Services)
cases.applicant: Westchester Reform Temple (represented by Jamie Glover, Green Hybrid Energy Solutions)

timeline.summary: Proposal for an 86 kW community-solar rooftop array at the former North White Plains Elementary School, now the Westchester Reform Temple, with panels set roughly 9.5 inches off the roof deck behind a parapet wall to minimize street visibility. A resident's letter raised concern about visibility from elevated homes on Nethermont and Roberta Place looking down onto the roof; the applicant clarified that only one lower-roof array (of four) would be partially visible from those homes, at a shallow 5-degree tilt. The Board discussed temporary safety railing color/permanence and requested a board site visit to view the roof before scheduling the public hearing.

Public hearing on the 86 kW rooftop solar array first reviewed in April, following a board site visit. The applicant detailed panel height (4 to 8.9 inches above roof grade), a 10-year operation and maintenance commitment to the nonprofit (double the standard term, offered given the applicant's own adjacent building and neighborly relationship), and grant funding covering the full project cost while saving the nonprofit roughly $25,000/year. A neighbor and local historian spoke supportively while reiterating that some panels would be visible from elevated homes; Michael Pollack asked about screening exposed mounting hardware, which the applicant addressed by showing cross-sections confirming minimal visible hardware. The Board closed the hearing and adopted a negative declaration and resolution.

cases.name: 2 Massaro Court lot line change
cases.applicant: Subdivision applicant

timeline.summary: Reconfiguration of a previously approved three-lot subdivision (in a two-family zoning district) to increase spacing between houses, with no new building lots created. The Board retained site plan jurisdiction over future house construction on each lot. The Board closed the hearing and adopted a negative declaration, preliminary resolution, and final resolution.

Public hearing on a previously approved lot line change (no new lots) whose approvals had twice expired; the board held the hearing with no public present and re-approved it a third time, passing the negative declaration, preliminary and final subdivision plat resolutions so the plat can be signed and two-family houses built.

cases.name: 11 New King Street — Extension of Time
cases.applicant: Dennis Knoskin (architect) for New King Street Associates

trajectory.status: discussion — hearing to be scheduled pending further review

timeline.status: discussion — hearing to be scheduled pending further review
timeline.summary: Applicant sought to legalize overnight outdoor storage of an electrical contractor's service vans and a landscaping tenant's equipment on a gravel pad, framed as an accessory use to office tenants in the building. Board members debated at length whether this was truly "incidental" to permitted office use or was effectively converting the site into a contractor's/landscaping yard use not otherwise permitted in the IND-A zone, and questioned the adequacy of screening toward nearby residential lots. No formal action was taken; the matter was to be refined and scheduled for a hearing.
Two-year extension granted for a 2018-approved automated parking structure while the applicant awaits county water-line installation on New King Street before filing to move the project forward.

cases.name: 15 Old Route 22 - Gavi restaurant improvement / mixed-use building
cases.applicant: David Gussle (engineer); Frank Diodati; Joseph and Chris Procco (architects)
cases.lastStatus: discussion only; applicant to revisit FAR calculation and site design before returning

trajectory.status: discussion — proceeding to Architectural Review Board
discussion only; applicant to revisit FAR calculation and site design before returning

timeline.status: discussion — proceeding to Architectural Review Board
timeline.summary: Applicant proposed demolishing an existing 1,240 sf retail building and constructing a new 2,500 sf mixed retail/carry-out-restaurant building with two apartments above, paving an existing gravel lot with a modular retaining wall to add parking (roughly 35 existing spaces increasing to 52-55), and adding municipal sidewalk/streetscape improvements; the adjacent Gavi restaurant building itself would not be altered. Board reaction was generally positive; members asked about building elevations, retail-versus-carryout-restaurant use classification, and whether additional spaces could be fit along the street frontage. No hearing was opened; next step is the Architectural Review Board and addressing staff review comments.

timeline.status: discussion only; applicant to revisit FAR calculation and site design before returning
timeline.summary: Follow-up review of an expanded restaurant (Gavi) renovation plus a new mixed-use building with basement parking, two upper-floor apartments, and flexible "vanilla box" ground-floor retail space. The board questioned whether the two speculative retail spaces made sense functionally next to a restaurant, whether a fully residential building might fit the site better, and - the central issue - whether the basement parking area should be excluded from the FAR calculation; if it were, the project would need a variance from the 0.3 FAR max (currently ~0.4). The applicant agreed to revisit the FAR calculation and consider board feedback on site layout (e.g., relocating parking away from the restaurant patio) before deciding whether to proceed to the ZBA.

cases.name: 11 Whippoorwill Lane
cases.applicant: represented by project counsel (unnamed)

trajectory.status: appeal granted — remanded to RPRC for administrative review conditioned on road-access improvements

timeline.status: appeal granted — remanded to RPRC for administrative review conditioned on road-access improvements
timeline.summary: A new owner sought to appeal an RPRC referral to the full planning board, arguing the redesigned house (same size, location, driveway, septic, and stormwater system as a prior approved plan under the previous owner, which had not required planning board review) should be handled administratively like its predecessor. The RPRC had referred it up specifically over access-safety concerns on narrow, driveway-like Whippoorwill Lane, prompting debate over whether the new applicant should bear the cost/burden of road improvements never required of prior approvals. The board granted the appeal and sent the house portion back to the RPRC for administrative review/approval conditioned on a hammerhead turnaround and town-engineer/emergency-services sign-off on road access; the accompanying pool (which needs a retaining wall over six feet, requiring planning board review) was paused to resume once the house obtains its building permit.

Continued public hearing on a single-family house reverted to the originally-reviewed design; the board kept the hearing open pending resolution of a shared-lane turnaround/hammerhead on a neighbor's easement, tree-removal counts, a retaining-wall treatment, and minor lane improvements.

cases.name: Maraki Tavarna restaurant, 450 Main Street (CVS shopping center)
cases.applicant: Chris Crocco (representing the salon tenant)

trajectory.status: referred to ZBA to address parking deficiency

timeline.status: referred to ZBA to address parking deficiency
timeline.summary: A long-standing local hair salon sought to relocate within Armonk Square to a larger space carved out of a former A&P/CVS-anchored retail building; because retail and salon uses carry different (roughly double) parking requirements, the change of use created an estimated 12-13 space parking deficiency that the planning board cannot waive by code once a shortfall exists. The applicant's representative cited a self-conducted parking survey showing the lot never exceeded 68 occupied spaces across multiple days/times, intending to make that case to the ZBA; the board voted to refer the application to the ZBA to address the parking deficiency, with sign-related approvals handled as separate applications.

Change of use for a restaurant space at the CVS center; the applicant was not present so the item was adjourned, but the board held a long policy discussion about the cumulative parking-variance requests in the Armonk hamlet and whether the property should join or form a parking district rather than seek repeated variances.

cases.name: 28 Kensico Court — Wetlands Permit (Administrative Determination)
cases.applicant: unnamed engineer, on behalf of the property owner

trajectory.status: approved — deemed a minor administrative wetlands matter

timeline.status: approved — deemed a minor administrative wetlands matter
timeline.summary: Applicant sought to reconfigure a pathway over a wetland/stream into a loading area and walkway near an existing culvert/bridge, asking the board to deem the wetlands permit "minor" so it could bypass a Conservation Board referral (which does not meet in August, adding a month's delay). The board's engineer, having recused his firm from formal review due to a client relationship, noted the disturbed area was already degraded and the driveway turnaround work was minimal and above (not within) the culvert itself. The board voted to process the wetlands application administratively rather than refer to the Conservation Board, with a resolution expected the following meeting.

Public hearing on expanding an existing stone pathway into an access driveway/loading area over a culvert within a Delaware Aqueduct DEP easement. After incorporating late engineering comments (confirming HS-20 loading capacity for the culvert, DEP easement sign-off, no-parking signage near the wetland, and bollards/chain in place of a sidewalk as previously discussed), the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended, with the wetland mitigation/restoration plan left to the satisfaction of the acting town engineer.

cases.name: 4 Ledgewood Place - re-approval of expired residence site plan
cases.applicant: unnamed applicant team

timeline.summary: New four-bedroom home and pool on a lot whose prior house had been demolished, largely reusing the previous building envelope; included a re-vegetation plan addressing earlier tree removal around an on-site pond and ARB-approved elevations. Hearing closed with no substantive opposition and the site plan/wetlands/tree-removal resolution was adopted.

Public hearing for re-approval of an expired site plan, wetlands permit, and tree removal approvals for a new four-bedroom residence; with no public present the board declined to vote on the resolution because 17 conditions remain unsatisfied, opting instead to have the applicant address them with staff and return for administrative approval.

cases.name: 1 Guion Lane — New 8,525 SF Home
cases.applicant: engineer/surveyor team (unnamed) for a new owner of a previously-reviewed lot

trajectory.status: hearing adjourned (kept open) — resolution not adopted, sent back for staff coordination

timeline.status: hearing adjourned (kept open) — resolution not adopted, sent back for staff coordination
timeline.summary: New owner proposing a new 8,525 sf home on a lot with access off Guion Lane (frontage technically on Gyon Curry) via a shared driveway easement; septic expansion-area timing, road-profile/vertical-curve (K-value) grading details, and roughly 18 open resolution items remained unresolved. The applicant's engineer grew visibly frustrated at the pace of staff review (citing an August 8 submission with limited response from the town's consulting engineer), and the Chair firmly declined to work through the resolution line-by-line at the dais, directing the applicant's team, Town Planner, and consulting engineer to resolve the open items offline before returning with a clean resolution.

After the prior meeting's adjournment over an unfinished resolution, the applicant's team met with the town planner and consulting engineer to close out open items (revised tree count of 62 town-regulated trees, confirmed steep-slope disturbance figures, easement and access issues resolved). The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended.

cases.name: 868 North Broadway

trajectory.status: public hearing opened and adjourned to November 13, 2023

timeline.status: public hearing opened and adjourned to November 13, 2023
timeline.summary: Site plan re-approval for completion of an existing under-construction building (a new 4,300 sq ft retail building plus retaining walls). The applicant requested to open and adjourn the hearing; with no public comment, the board granted the adjournment.

Continuation of the site plan re-approval hearing adjourned from October 12 for the under-construction retail building and retaining walls. The board closed the public hearing and adopted the resolution as amended.

cases.name: 34 Creamer Road
cases.applicant: Represented by Ralph

trajectory.status: discussion only; routed to Conservation Board and ARB before scheduling a public hearing

timeline.status: discussion only; routed to Conservation Board and ARB before scheduling a public hearing
timeline.summary: Amendment to a 2018-approved spec-house site plan to add a pool for an interested buyer, shrinking the house footprint to accommodate it near a wetland buffer. Staff and the applicant's engineer confirmed disturbance within the buffer is slightly less than the prior approval with no wetland disturbance either time; some architectural elevation details needed revision for the ARB. The board had no major concerns and directed the applicant to obtain conservation board and ARB input before a hearing is scheduled.

Public hearing on an amended site plan, wetland permit and tree removal for a single-family residence with driveway and pool in a wetland buffer, previously approved in 2018. A neighbor asked about remaining tree removal and screening; the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended, adding a long-term monitoring/access note on the site plan.

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road - barn expansion / equine facility
cases.address: 14 Middle Patent Road (Lot 95.03-1-42), R4A zoning district
cases.applicationType: site plan and special use permit
cases.applicant: Represented by "Dan" with engineer Mr. Rina and property manager Brendan McKenney

trajectory.status: approved (negative declaration adopted; positive recommendation sent to Town Board)

timeline.status: approved (negative declaration adopted; positive recommendation sent to Town Board)
timeline.summary: Companion application to 263 Bedford Banksville Road for a similarly large horse farm (professional/Olympic-level riders, no lessons or shows, family-operated), seeking the board's negative declaration and a positive recommendation to the Town Board for the special permit allowing additional horses. The board adopted a negative declaration and voted to send a positive recommendation to the Town Board; the applicant will return December 11 for site plan/special permit review of the barn and stable improvements themselves.

Follow-up site plan/special-use-permit hearing for accessory structures over 800 sq ft - a 1,314 sq ft addition to the existing barn and a new 10-stall barn - on a 43.32-acre horse farm where the town board had already approved a special permit increasing the horse count from 10 to 26 and issued a negative SEQRA declaration. With no public comment and no substantive board objection, the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended to add conditions for a grading/erosion-control/stormwater plan with calculations and health department approval of a septic modification (the septic tank sits under the barn addition), plus a corrected conservation board memo date and a typo fix.

cases.name: Harris, 9 Sterling Road
cases.applicant: Property owner Mr. Harris

trajectory.status: referred to ZBA for a coverage/setback variance

timeline.status: referred to ZBA for a coverage/setback variance
timeline.summary: A years-in-the-making pool, patio, and pool-equipment addition requiring resolution of a right-of-way/property-line dispute the applicant disputed (staff advised him to verify the surveyed line rather than assume it was wrong) and a coverage variance. The board voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the needed variance.
The applicant was not ready and will return, likely at the next meeting; no substantive discussion occurred.

cases.name: 14 Tall Woods Road in-ground pool and wetland permit
cases.applicant: Property owner (in attendance) and representative

trajectory.status: discussion only; public hearing to be scheduled for January

timeline.status: discussion only; public hearing to be scheduled for January
timeline.summary: A straightforward request to rebuild a failing retaining wall in-kind (same materials, new wrought-iron railing) because half of the existing wall was collapsing and posed a hazard; the wall exceeds six feet, requiring planning board review rather than just a building permit. Staff walked the owner through the neighbor-notification and public-hearing process (certified mail via the assessor's office, posted sign). No board concerns were raised.

Continued public hearing on an in-ground swimming pool with stormwater mitigation and a pool draw-down/irrigation storage system in an R-2A wetland-buffer area; after discussion of a rain garden, roof-runoff rerouting and relocating pool equipment indoors, the board closed the hearing and adopted the draft resolution.

cases.name: 11 Whipperwill Lane (single-family home / lane improvements)
cases.applicant: Ralph Alfonzetti (applicant/engineer), rep. by attorney Corey Selm of Zarin & Steinmetz

timeline.summary: Applicant's team (attorney Corey Salomon and engineer Ralph) presented a switch to the smaller 5,800 sq ft home, private-road widening within the right-of-way, an emergency-vehicle turnaround, and commitments negotiated with neighbors; the board pressed for an engineered survey of the road improvements and a detailed landscape plan before approval, then adjourned the reopened public hearing.

Public hearing on the revised plan addressing four prior items (lane improvements, relocated turnaround, tree removal, private agreement with neighbors); board closed the hearing and approved the site development plan and tree-removal permit as amended to add a no-parking restriction on the turnaround and relocation of two trees.

cases.name: The Bristol at 90 Business Park Drive - Armonk Fire Department non-emergency call agreement
cases.applicant: HSR / Bristol at Armonk (attorney Nick Capadora; Amy Silver-Maguire, COO, Ultimate Care)

timeline.summary: The applicant sought to replace the 2012 site-plan condition requiring a 24-hour on-site EMT (which they say conflicts with New York State law) with a detailed emergency-care policy aimed at eliminating non-emergency calls to the Armonk Fire Department; the board directed staff and counsel to draft an amended site-plan resolution with an accountability mechanism, to return for a public hearing.

The board adopted an amended resolution plus an emergency-care policy and flowchart establishing a procedure to reduce non-emergency calls to the Armonk Fire Department, with the fire department to report back to the planning board biennially for accountability.

cases.name: 8 Cold Drive
cases.applicant: Nizar Masu (attorney Corey Salomon, Zarin & Steinmetz; wetland expert Steve Moreno; landscape architect Richard Quigley)

timeline.summary: The homeowners asked to amend a 2021 approval to swap the pool and sport-court locations, which would disturb a small (~900 sq ft) marginal wetland/drainage pocket, remove about 26 trees, and cut into steep slopes, offset by a proposed 2.5:1 mitigation wetland, a rain garden, and robust reforestation; the board voiced real concern about disturbing a wetland for a recreational amenity and referred the wetland question to the Conservation Board with 'no promises.'

The same attorney reported on 8 Cold Drive, noting the applicant pulled the clearing and grading permit for the sport court and anticipates constructing it in spring. The board granted the requested extension of time without objection.

cases.name: 126 Lafayette Avenue (NC Auto Repair)
cases.applicant: DNV/DNC Auto Repair

timeline.summary: A rooftop-solar site plan surfaced that the building's current auto-service use was never approved by the Planning Board (it had been approved as a tree-service base of operations); the board asked the applicant to demonstrate conformance with the town code's auto-repair/body-shop requirements so a legal site plan can be granted before permitting the rooftop solar.

Public hearing on a site plan to legitimize the existing auto-repair use, add a 48-panel rooftop solar system and a three-bay rear addition, and remove a deteriorated Butler building and cargo trailer. No public appeared. Discussion covered the low-profile roof-mounted panels (nine inches above the roofline), the absence of a parapet wall (the adjacent Bell & Tony building screens it), and stormwater: the engineer noted no existing runoff treatment and required capture/treatment of roof-drain and paved-area runoff to the town engineer's satisfaction. The board opened and closed the hearing and adopted the draft resolution the same night, approving the application with the stormwater condition.

cases.name: 41 Mead Road public hearing

timeline.summary: Public hearing on an amended site plan, wetland and tree removal permit to remediate a heavily disturbed wetland site where a prior owner built an unpermitted second story (increasing bedrooms beyond septic approval) triggering a stop-work order. The board could not close the hearing pending ARB approval and DEC/health permits, but voted to have the planner convey to the building inspector that it would not object to relief allowing at-risk interior four-bedroom work; item carried to July.
The scheduled public hearing was rolled over to the next meeting and not heard.

cases.name: 3 Cedar Hill Road
cases.address: 3 Cedar Hill Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Homeowner (house addition and new front porch)

timeline.summary: A corner lot fronting on the scenic East Middle Patent Road requires Planning Board site plan approval for a first- and second-floor addition; the board discussed screening/visibility and a wetland delineation update and directed the applicant to the ARB before returning for a public hearing and resolution.

Public hearing for a house addition and new front porch on a corner lot that, because it fronts scenic East Middle Patent Road, carries two front-yard setbacks and thus came to the Planning Board rather than the RPRC. The chair explained the procedural quirk; the planner confirmed no variances were needed and that the project is wetland-compliant with verified flags and ARB approval already obtained. No public spoke. The board opened the hearing, closed it and granted the resolution in a single sequence.

cases.name: 26 Carolyn Place
cases.applicant: San Car Residence (Ralph Oppenzetti / architect Lutto Delio)

timeline.summary: The board discussed the proposed rear-yard pool and cabana with removal of illegally placed fill and legalization of existing house issues, then debated whether the gross-land-coverage overage requires a variance and voted to refer the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals, deferring a public hearing until any variance is resolved.

This application had its public hearing previously closed, but action was pending the applicant's ARB review. With ARB complete and a fill issue resolved (the applicant is removing the fill) plus a revised plan addressing town-engineer comments, the board proceeded. There were no outstanding board concerns. The board approved the site plan and tree-removal permit.

cases.name: John McNada site plan (shopping center, North Broadway)
cases.applicant: John Magnotta (represented by Mr. Dagostino; engineer Dave Toriano, PE)

timeline.summary: A field-change/as-built request to bless deviations from the approved plan (reconfigured/compact parking, relocated landscaping, revised lighting, an uninstalled light pole); the board, led by James Jensen's objections, was unwilling to simply rubber-stamp after-the-fact work and directed the applicant to return with an improved landscaping plan to break up the 'sea of asphalt.'

The applicant's team presented additional landscaping to soften the rear parking/blacktop area and screen the lot from North Broadway, noting the retaining-wall area was largely unplantable; the board approved the field change, to be memorialized by a resolution in the file.

cases.name: 47 High Street - demolition and new house (John Nickett, builder)
cases.applicant: John Nickitch (rep. Jim Atticarico, Cronin Engineering)

timeline.summary: The board reviewed the new-home site plan with a driveway off Cobbler's Lane; the driveway falls short of the required 200-foot sight line (about 140 ft) due to the crest, so a ZBA variance is likely, and neighbors raised traffic-safety concerns.

Reopened public hearing on demolishing the existing house and building a new one with a driveway relocated onto Cobblers Lane; numerous neighbors opposed the Cobblers driveway over traffic/visibility safety, but the applicant demonstrated ~201 ft of sight distance (meeting the 200 ft minimum) and the board adopted the resolution as amended (added a 50 ft septic separation and pretreatment fabric conditions) over Michael Pollack's dissent.

cases.name: 111 Lafayette Avenue - US mail logistics truck parking/warehouse
cases.applicant: Property owner operating a postal mail-hauling business

timeline.summary: Preliminary discussion of converting the property into the main office/operations base for a bulk-mail hauling business; the board needed floor plans, truck-parking layout, storage and access details and directed the applicant to meet with the town planner and engineer before proceeding.

Public hearing on a site plan to allow overnight commercial truck parking accessory to a warehouse/office building; the board worked through the parking table (9 office spaces required, 15 truck spaces, 24 provided), closed the hearing, and approved the resolution as amended to add conditions for a replacement fence and code-compliant lighting, plus floor plans to support the parking count.

cases.name: Summer Club extension of time
cases.applicant: Summer Club subdivision applicant

timeline.summary: The board supported the applicant's request to remove 72 interior trees early (before building permits) for marketing/staging of the first phase of townhouses, with stump grinding and wood-chip stabilization, and separately granted a 90-day extension of time for the final subdivision plat while health-department (sewage, water withdrawal/system) approvals are pending.
The board granted an extension of time for the Summer Club approval, a procedural item with little discussion.

cases.name: 76 Byron Ridge Road
cases.address: 76 Byron Ridge Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Lizzero

timeline.summary: Referred from the RPRC, this expansion of an existing lakeside house sits partly in a state-regulated wetland buffer; the engineer described the septic (a county no-objection letter was sought), stormwater Cultec chambers and a rain garden, a wetland mitigation/planting plan, and a reworked driveway with screening, and the board referred the application to the Conservation Board while asking that all resolution conditions be addressed promptly.

The applicant proposed an addition to an existing three-bedroom single-family house with a new driveway/curb, a rain garden for stormwater, and an extensive wetland-buffer mitigation planting plan (proposing ~16,475 sq ft of mitigation against a required ~12,838). No new bedrooms and no direct wetland impacts other than a path to Byram/Barbers Lake. The Byram Ridge Lake Homeowners Association representative and the Conservation Board both supported the plan, which they said greatly improves existing invasive-choked conditions. Construction runs fall 2026 through roughly 2029-2031 within the town's noise ordinance hours, with minimal projected traffic (about three peak-hour trucks per direction). The Conservation Board reported it had done a site walk and given a positive recommendation, and the town planner noted a thorough submission with no significant concerns. The applicant reported substantial concessions since the last review — fill needs cut 60% (from 5,300 to 2,100 cubic yards, using a box culvert to preserve natural water flow instead of geofoam), steep-slope impacts reduced 41%, a 2:1 tree mitigation ratio (67 removed, 97 replacements) and extensive new plantings, and Conservation Board and ARB positive recommendations already secured. Board members (particularly Jim Jensen, with the Town Attorney) pressed hard on an alternative that would avoid moving the lot line and steep-slope disturbance entirely — granting an easement to keep the existing driveway location while still permitting the house addition — arguing the lot-line-change code exists precisely to prevent this kind of future-development-driven encroachment. With one board seat vacant/absent, the chair directed staff to prepare draft resolutions for both approval and denial and adjourned the hearing (keeping it open) to the next meeting once a full board is present.

timeline.summary: Applicant is remediating a town stop-work-order violation after unpermitted fill work (sourced from a DEP site plus additional non-conforming material) washed out during a storm and impacted the neighboring DEP reservoir. Proposed fix: regrade the slope to a gentler angle, install erosion-control matting, hydroseed, and replant roughly 12 trees for the ~8 lost. A key dispute emerged over whether a drainage swale on the site — piped and extended without permits by the prior contractor — is a regulated wetland/intermittent watercourse (as the town engineer's office maintains, citing a 2009 designation reflected in the 2017 filed subdivision plat) or merely a drainage ditch exempt from wetland regulation (the applicant's position). The board directed a joint Planning/Conservation Board site walk, referral to the Conservation Board, and NYC DEP input (estimated 6-month timeline) before final approval, while permitting continued temporary slope stabilization (hydroseed/erosion matting) despite the still-active stop-work order.

timeline.summary: The Town Board referred a draft local law creating a new special use permit allowing day camps (long precedented at Breezemont as a legal nonconforming use since 1932) to modernize their facilities. The board debated a proposed density cap of 1,000 campers (or 60 per acre, whichever is lower) against the camp's roughly 15-acre site, weighed a remote/off-site staff parking plan (roughly 100 of ~400 staff currently park on the front lawn) as a reasonable way to relieve chronic on-site parking overflow, and spent significant time on whether off-season special events (weddings, corporate outings, fundraisers) should be approved administratively by the Town Planner as the draft proposed, or instead require case-by-case Planning Board approval — Lawrence Ruisi argued for keeping that decision with the Planning Board rather than delegating it, while acknowledging the camp itself said it did not intend to actively pursue such events, merely to retain the option. The board declined to finalize its referral, asking for the parcels' precise combined acreage (to know whether 60-per-acre or the 1,000-camper cap would actually govern) and for an update on the camp's parking discussions with nearby churches before revisiting in two weeks.

timeline.summary: The town's own project to acquire a parcel from Verizon and redevelop it as a net 43-space public parking area behind Main Street (phase one of a larger, more ambitious concept for the whole Kent Place lot), constrained by a DEC class-C stream, an adjacent locally regulated wetland/buffer, and a 100-year floodplain. The applicant's environmental consultant flagged that while wetland disturbance is offset roughly one-to-one by on-site mitigation, wetland-buffer disturbance mitigation is less than half of what's typically required, arguing invasive-species removal and the parking area's community benefit should count toward that shortfall - a determination left to the board and conservation board. The board voted to refer the project to the ZBA for a building-coverage variance and confirmed it would serve as lead agency under an uncoordinated SEQRA review. Discussion broadened into whether the town could use a future parking district (potentially funded via CPA money, given individual Main Street landowners' reluctance to self-fund repaving/improvements) and conditions on future change-of-use approvals to advance area-wide parking solutions, building on an earlier board practice of conditioning some approvals on joining a prospective parking district. Staff clarified an outstanding street-naming/tax-map discrepancy (the road is legally named Daphne Lane) would be corrected administratively. The applicant was directed to obtain ARB approval and then return for a public hearing.

cases.name: Airport Campus, 113 King Street
cases.address: 113 King Street (tax lots 118.02-1-1; 113.04-1-13, -14, -20), RMFA/RMFCH zoning districts
cases.applicant: Represented by Chris Fisher (Cuddy & Feder) on behalf of the applicant team, with engineering by John Meyer Consulting
cases.lastStatus: public hearing adjourned (not closed); continuing coordination with staff

trajectory.status: public hearing adjourned (not closed); continuing coordination with staff

timeline.status: public hearing adjourned (not closed); continuing coordination with staff
timeline.summary: Extended review of the 125-unit attached-townhome and 58-unit restricted-apartment redevelopment on the former airport office campus. The bulk of discussion concerned airport noise: the applicant's acoustic consultant characterized noise impacts as "insignificant" using FAA average (DNL) noise-contour methodology targeting a 45 dBA interior standard, which board members (particularly James Jensen, a former resident near a different airport flight path) found the word choice misleading and pushed the applicant to instead design to the loudest single-event noise level using standard architectural sound-dampening details, similar to what neighboring Fairfax County, Virginia requires near Dulles Airport; the applicant agreed to take the request under advisement without committing. Additional items covered included fencing/privacy screening between adjacent unit decks (a detail was provided at the meeting), sound attenuation between units, three requested roadway design waivers (reduced cul-de-sac radii, narrower 24-28 ft road widths, and a steeper road grade at one intersection, each mitigated by a posted 20 mph speed limit) which the town engineer's office found acceptable, a school-bus turnaround near a shared DEP driveway, and a request for a historical recreation-fee matrix. The board also indicated future individual unit landscaping approvals could be delegated to the RPRC rather than returning to the full board each time. The hearing was adjourned (not closed) for the applicant to respond to outstanding items.

cases.name: 70 Lafayette Avenue - change of use (studio)
cases.applicant: Represented by Corey (attorney) for "QK Associates" (ASR spelling uncertain)

timeline.summary: Change of use of 4,100 sq ft of warehouse space to studio/office space for video and photography, with no physical site changes. The applicant had already obtained an off-street-parking variance from the ZBA. With no public comment, the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution.

cases.name: Majidi Subdivision, 21 Whippoorwill Road
cases.applicant: Property owner represented by an engineer ("Joe," firm name unclear in ASR)

timeline.summary: Two-lot subdivision hearing where the town engineer flagged outstanding stormwater calculations (design needed to be updated from a 25-year to a 100-year storm standard, with supporting soil testing not yet witnessed by the town) and inadequate sight distance for the new lot's driveway on a sharp, accident-prone curve; the applicant proposed shifting the driveway roughly 18 feet to improve sight lines while preserving more of an existing stone wall. Two neighbors spoke: Pamela Morgan raised concerns about historic drainage/flooding problems, protecting large trees' root systems, and an existing spite fence near the shared driveway; former owner Meg Bruno, who originally subdivided the parcel, described the curve as the site of numerous serious accidents over the years and stressed the driveway relocation as a genuine safety issue. The board kept the public hearing open (rather than closing it) so neighbors can weigh in again once revised plans and soil-test results are submitted.

cases.name: Silver Lake Realty Company, 600/606 North Broadway

cases.name: Summer Club golf course maintenance facility

cases.name: 86 Old Byram Lake Road (new single-family home)
cases.applicant: Ralph (applicant's engineer/representative)

cases.name: 263 Bedford-Banksville Road (extension of time)

timeline.summary: The applicant, holding a prior special permit and site plan approval for a residence with pool, pool house, and personal equestrian accessory structures, requested and was granted a one-year extension of time to obtain permits and begin construction.

cases.name: Leisure Farm Drive

timeline.summary: Introduced for discussion but the substantive dialogue falls in a gap in the ASR transcript; later references indicate it involved a clearing-and-grading limit line similar to the Dellwood Farm Way pool item.
