cases.name: 15 / 22 (Gabriel Court apartments site plan)
cases.applicant: Joseph Crockle (architect); David Gessel (engineer)

timeline.summary: Reopened and closed the public hearing and adopted the site plan resolution after the applicant revised driveway and parking slopes off Gabriel Court to meet code for entrance, ADA and conventional parking; an outstanding lighting-illumination plan condition remains prior to signing.

cases.name: Forge Legewood single-family house (expired approval restart)

timeline.summary: A previously approved new single-family house whose resolution had expired; the applicant was told not to attend, and the board agreed to schedule a new public hearing and re-approve, discussing new practice of addressing conditions before signing and revisiting the phased planting/tree-replacement plan in the wetland buffer.

cases.name: 298 Bedford Banksville Road - accessory apartment special use permit

timeline.summary: Public hearing on a special use permit to legalize a detached accessory apartment in a structure previously approved as an office; the required ZBA variance had been obtained, the board found the resolution concise, and it approved the special use permit subject to a water test and showing required parking.

cases.name: 4 Alpine Drive - utility burial waiver request
cases.applicant: Dave Cicarni

timeline.summary: The applicant sought relief from Town Code 355-17 requiring new utility service to be placed underground, wanting instead to run overhead wires from a pole he had already erected across the street; despite sympathy for his practical and cost arguments, the board found no basis (no hardship, no precedent) to waive the statute and the town engineer remained firm that the service must go underground.

cases.name: 200 Business Park Drive - outdoor storage of construction trailers
cases.applicant: PTSD Northeast

timeline.summary: With the applicant absent, the board discussed a request by a healthcare-construction firm to store 40-yard containers/trailers behind a professional office building; citing extensive prior outdoor-storage concerns in that area, members were strongly disinclined to allow containers and suggested the applicant instead propose an enclosed structure meeting setbacks, parking, and FAR.

cases.name: Shapiro residence sport courts, 8 Rolling Drive
cases.applicant: represented by Cory Salomon (Zarin & Steinman), Paul Sci-Sack (JMC), architect Matt Barenz, lighting expert Steven Ballow

timeline.summary: Continued discussion of proposed tennis, padel and turf sport courts plus an activity building on a 17+ acre property, with ARB, conservation and zoning board sign-offs in hand. The central issue was court lighting; the applicant's lighting expert described dark-sky, house-side-shielded fixtures with no light trespass past 50 feet, and the board asked for a method to verify performance after installation before setting a public hearing next month.

cases.name: Airport campus project extensions
cases.applicant: represented by Max Millie (Cuddy & Feder)

timeline.summary: The board granted a standard 90-day subdivision extension and a one-year site plan approval extension for the airport campus project while staff finishes reviewing the filed subdivision and site plans for signature.

cases.name: Mail-truck parking application (industrial district)
cases.applicant: owner of multiple town properties (currently 176 Virginia)

timeline.summary: The applicant, who bought an industrial-district office/warehouse, wants to park mail trucks in the rear and reconfigure parking; the board referred the application to the ZBA (for the truck turning-radius variance and cars backing onto the street) and directed a concurrent town board track, with a planning board hearing to follow.

cases.name: Oamic Ingredients amended site plan, 6 Leviola Court
cases.applicant: Oamic Ingredients (Nella Morad)

timeline.summary: The board held and closed the public hearing on an amended site plan renewing/finalizing a previously approved 2022 resolution for a flavor-and-fragrance chemical warehouse and distribution use; after confirming no changes to approved chemicals or quantities, it adopted a negative declaration and the resolution.

cases.name: Bracemont estate, 8 Roseann Drive
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by Zarin & Steinmetz / Paul, Ira Granberg, Stephen Ballow lighting expert)

timeline.summary: Continued public hearing on a site plan with special use, tree removal and wetlands permits for an activity building, tennis and padel courts with fencing and lighting, and an accessory apartment; the board was largely unsupportive of the court lighting, heard strong neighbor objections about noise and light, and kept the public hearing open pending more landscaping and cleanup of the resolution.

cases.name: Autobody shop solar and rear addition, 28 Lock
cases.applicant: Autobody shop owner

timeline.summary: The board referred the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals for use-setback variances, since existing repair bays sit nearer than the 25-foot minimum to a residential lot line; a rooftop solar amendment and a three-bay rear addition would return to the planning board afterward, with a possible spray-booth permit condition.

cases.name: Sankar residence, 26 Carillon Place
cases.applicant: Sankar

timeline.summary: Public hearing on legalizing unpermitted fill, tree removal and deck construction, plus relocating the pool and adding a cabana closer to the house; the board closed the public hearing but declined to adopt the resolution until outstanding conditions (C&D removal plan, stormwater, erosion control) are satisfied.

cases.name: 167 Miamis River Road (Miamis River Gorge headquarters)
cases.applicant: Miamis River Gorge (rep. Ralph Mastromonaco)

timeline.summary: Site plan to give the Gorge organization more operating space with modest parking improvements and a generator on a scenic road; the board referred front/rear yard setback variances to the ZBA, with a special-use permit for the residence/offices to be handled at the Town Board.

cases.name: One Stillwater Place restoration (wetland violation)
cases.applicant: Property owner (both sides represented)

timeline.summary: Review of a wetland-disturbance violation affecting both the applicant's property and an adjacent (Nannis/Manus) property; submitted plans only show impacts on the neighbor's parcel, so the board is awaiting revised plans and a mitigation plan for the applicant's own property before referring the matter to the Conservation Board.

cases.name: Shapiro residence, 8 Rocking Horse Road
cases.applicant: Shapiro

timeline.summary: The public hearing was reopened and closed; the board adopted the resolution as amended, approving the site with wetland mitigation plantings but explicitly declining to approve the tennis/sport court lighting as disruptive to neighbors, and refined conditions on SWPPP permit number, planting installation before CO, and five-year maintenance.

cases.name: Gasson special use permit (additional horses)
cases.applicant: Gasson

timeline.summary: With no applicant present, the board kept the special use permit for additional horses in front of it after the building inspector's site visit found numerous code items; the applicant must bring the property back into compliance before the board would recommend approval to the town board.

cases.name: Westchester County Airport residential development presentation (Nick Hartman)
cases.applicant: Nick Hartman, Chair, Westchester County Airport Advisory Board

timeline.summary: Guest Nick Hartman presented a draft report on the environmental and safety risks of dense residential development near the airport; the board discussed the tension between the county's opposition to such development and the local housing shortage, noting most of the affected land is in Rye Brook while Arrowwood-area development is nearby.

cases.name: Goldman pool within wetland buffer
cases.applicant: Goldman (property owner)

timeline.summary: Discussion of a pool located entirely within a wetland buffer around a piped water course; the applicant reported receiving a conservation-board permit and completing mitigation planting. The board wants the conservation-board memo (not yet received/distributed) before proceeding, and directed the applicant to notice and hold a public hearing, likely with a resolution ready at that meeting.

cases.name: Sauro residence remodel with accessory apartment, 8 Lions Road
cases.applicant: Steven Sauro (planning-board member, recused), engineer Ralph presenting

timeline.summary: Remodel of an existing four-bedroom home to add an accessory apartment above the garage (five bedrooms total on an existing five-bedroom septic, ~two acres), which requires a special use permit. No wetlands or steep slopes; main hurdle is Board of Health well/septic no-objection approval, with stormwater subsurface infiltration and some front-lot tree removal near the septic. Next step is ARB approval, then a public hearing.

cases.name: 75 Hickory Kingdom Road - request to retain original curb cut
cases.applicant: Applicant not named (represented via staff)

timeline.summary: The applicant, having built a new curb cut and driveway (approved through the RPRC and Conservation Board because it crossed a wetland buffer to fix unsafe sight lines), now asked to keep the original unsafe curb cut for emergency use. The board reached a consensus against allowing it, noting the new driveway was justified only by the old one's unsafety, but a public hearing/neighbor notification is required before a formal denial. A board member recused himself citing a relationship with the applicant.

cases.name: Overhead vs. underground electric service policy (4 Alpine / 21 Wood Wool Road)
cases.applicant: N/A (policy discussion; 4 Alpine applicant to be brought back)

timeline.summary: General discussion clarifying town code on electric service in areas of existing overhead lines: burying service to the house is required, but a single utility pole at the property line for overhead service is discretionary, not mandatory. A board member acknowledged his prior stricter interpretation was incorrect; the board decided to put 4 Alpine back on the agenda and have the applicant return rather than amend the application on its own.

cases.name: Sauro residence addition, pool and accessory apartment (8 Clients Road)
cases.applicant: Steven Sauro (owner; represented by engineer Ralph and Jennifer)

timeline.summary: Public hearing on a house addition, pool and accessory apartment over the garage; the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended, conditioned on Board of Health approval and moving the water biological analysis to before CO.

cases.name: Alpine Drive residence - utility service relief
cases.applicant: Dave (homeowner building a new house on Alpine Drive)

timeline.summary: The applicant returned seeking relief from a prior condition requiring underground utility service, showing that essentially every comparable home in the neighborhood has overhead service; the board reconsidered its earlier determination and voted to allow the overhead wire across the street to a proposed pole with underground service from that pole to the house.

cases.name: Four Ledgewood

timeline.summary: The board revisited a draft resolution for Four Ledgewood, originally approved in 2023 but lapsed amid health-department and other issues and recently re-approved. The applicant had returned with a tightened resolution that let the board remove a number of prior conditions. The chair expressed reservations about the underlying concept ('I'm not sure I love it') but the board approved the draft resolution.

cases.name: 76 Fireman's Road
cases.applicant: Alan Piltch, LP Engineering (addition to existing three-bedroom house)

timeline.summary: The engineer updated the board on a ~941 sq ft addition to an existing three-bedroom house that requires wetland review. The project cleared the Conservation Board on June 24 with a satisfactory mitigation plan, a joint DEC permit application was filed, and DEC was set to verify the wetland boundary that Friday. The county health department will issue its 'no objection' for the existing septic only after DEC acts. With stormwater testing and a sight-line analysis still outstanding, the board agreed the plan looks good and set a public hearing for the next meeting (two weeks out). Conservation liaison Vincent DeAnno stressed that mitigation conditions (contingency plan, five-year buffer plan, cost estimate, and full mapping of invasive species) must be locked in and not slip through the cracks.

cases.name: 11 New Kings Street (Park Place)
cases.address: 11 New Kings Street, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: 11 New Kings Street; attorney William Noll (Cuddy & Feder)

timeline.summary: Applicant requested a two-year extension of site plan approval for the Park Place automated parking structure near the airport, the eighth such extension. Counsel reported building permit review is underway with construction plans filed and no changes to design or circumstances. Carthy asked whether it would return again or be built; counsel expected it well underway within two years. The board granted the extension.

cases.name: 135 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: Applicant represented by Corey (engineer)

timeline.summary: Request for a site plan waiver for a change of use in a ~23,000 sq ft office building, converting 3,000 sq ft from general office to dental office. Corey noted parking requirements are lower for the new use, so demand actually decreases. Carthy asked planner Adam Kaufman if he had concerns and he had none. The board granted the waiver.

cases.name: 124 Old Mianus Road
cases.address: 124 Old Mianus Road, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Applicant represented by Corey (engineer)

timeline.summary: Extension of time request. Corey reported additional comments received from the town engineer's office and the health department are being addressed, expecting to turn them around within about a week and a half. Carthy noted one item to review with planner Adam Kaufman offline. The board granted the extension.

cases.name: 18 Bedford-Banksville Road (propane exchange)
cases.applicant: Retail propane-sales operator (outdoor propane exchange cage)

timeline.summary: The board reviewed a special use permit for selling propane in an outdoor cage, which had gone to the town board and was awaiting the Planning Board's recommendation. Discussion focused on the fire department's questions about propane tank size and code compliance (to be handled by the building department under NYS building/fire code) and the fact that the submitted plan was a hand-drawn sketch lacking bollards. The board moved to recommend the town board proceed with the special use permit, subject to installation of bollards (or equivalent protective planters) and whatever else the building department and fire code require.

cases.name: 6 Maple Avenue

timeline.summary: An administrative change-of-use on the second floor with adequate existing parking. Staff had determined the applicant did not need to formally appear, and the board treated it as a routine site-plan waiver. The board adopted the resolution with no substantive concerns.

cases.name: 1/11 Round Hill (driveway field change)
cases.applicant: (existing subdivision lot)

timeline.summary: The town engineer presented a minor field change shifting a driveway slightly back into the site to create a high point at elevation 90 and better tie in a bridge, with no additional disturbance and remaining within the easement. The Board opened and approved the field change by motion.

cases.name: 10 & 20 Round Hill Way
cases.address: 10 & 20 Round Hill Way, North Castle, NY

timeline.summary: The board opened and closed a public hearing on the 10 and 20 Round Hill Way site plans, steep slope permits and tree removal permits, then adopted draft resolutions for each lot. This was essentially a re-approval: the applications had been approved before as part of a subdivision and two site plans, but due to a miscommunication the site-plan resolutions expired and the plans were never signed, so they had to be re-submitted with prior field changes incorporated. A board member questioned how Lot 5 gets access, confirming a common driveway serves the lots off Round Hill via an easement reflected in the resolution. The board was satisfied and adopted both resolutions.

cases.name: Orchard Hill Subdivision (existing house access)

timeline.summary: The board reviewed a straightforward change to the access configuration for the existing house within the Orchard Hill five-lot subdivision, where the current lot is bifurcated by a driveway serving a back lot. Two of the new houses have been added and two rear lots remain to come before the board. The item will proceed to a public hearing with neighbor notification by first-class mail and proof of mailing. A member cautioned that because the house is shifting slightly, the 250-foot neighbor notification list should be regenerated rather than reusing old labels.

cases.name: 62 Nethermont Avenue
cases.address: 62 Nethermont Avenue, North White Plains, NY
cases.applicant: Owners Lindsay & Dmitry (architect Rocco Delano; applicant's father Jim New sold them the lot)

timeline.summary: The applicant proposed a new ~4,865 sq ft single-family residence, positioned six feet off the south side line to preserve a future subdividable building lot. Neighbors raised concerns about rock excavation/hammering near a ~100-year-old adjoining home, house size/neighborhood character, and tree removal, while other neighbors and the applicant's father spoke strongly in support. The board debated at length whether to require protection beyond the standard chipping permit given the hammering's proximity to the neighbor. It ultimately closed the hearing and granted the resolution as amended, adding conditions that a seismic monitor be placed on the neighbor's (Pinella/'Davis') foundation and that the applicant pre-drill (line drilling) to reduce vibration.

cases.name: 850 North Broadway
cases.applicant: Property owner (not present)

timeline.summary: Work was done on the back of the building without a permit and now needs to be legalized, along with several site plan issues. With the applicant absent, the planner explained that a basic site plan (addressing refuse, parking, lighting, and safety requirements, similar to the 4 KSL Court approach) will be needed before the board can approve a site plan. No action taken.

cases.name: 7 Hollow Road
cases.applicant: Ralph (project engineer) for a new single-family residence

timeline.summary: Application for a new single-family residence on a 2.5-acre vacant lot within an approved subdivision, connecting to sewer with a proposed well and front/rear stormwater mitigation. The board opened the public hearing but Carthy noted the landscape plan was missing from the package and declined to close the hearing. A neighbor at 6 Hollow Place had submitted a letter raising tree-removal and screening concerns. The hearing was adjourned to a future meeting, to be reopened once the landscape plan is submitted and ARB approval is obtained.

cases.name: 3 Israel Townsend Hill (32 Orchard Drive subdivision)
cases.address: 3 Israel Townsend Hill, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Andrew Vaccarello, Federal Engineering, for the property owner

timeline.summary: Site improvements for an existing single-family dwelling that will remain, including a new driveway, septic system, and well replacing former systems; 17 trees proposed for removal consistent with the prior subdivision approval. The applicant flagged a lot-acreage typo (about 4.46 acres) in the draft resolution and asked to drop a landscaping condition given the heavily vegetated lot. Larry probed plantings near the septic close to the property line and confirmed a tree buffer would remain to the adjacent lot. The board closed the hearing and approved the site development plan and tree-removal/tree council permit.

cases.name: 26 Hurlingham Drive (field change)
cases.applicant: Property owner / project representative (name not stated)

timeline.summary: A field change on a previously approved plan (dating to around 2021) to reconfigure the driveway serving the caretaker's cottage and main house, eliminating a looping drive in favor of a direct approach. The board found the redesign an improvement and had no substantive comments. One item noted was a correction to the property address in the resolution. The board approved the field change.

cases.name: EV Charging Local Law (Level 3) Referral
cases.applicant: Town Board (referral of a proposed local law)

timeline.summary: A town-board referral on a proposed local law to permit currently-prohibited Level 3 EV charging, with an open question of whether Level 3 spaces should count toward off-street parking (a draft cap of no more than 20%). Carthy argued the board should encourage the town to reduce barriers and count the charging spaces within the parking requirement rather than requiring them in excess. Steven Sauro repeatedly cautioned about unintended consequences, including the town becoming a highway 'road stop' and businesses using chargers as a profit loophole. After an extended debate, the board declined to add a substantive recommendation and voted to send the referral back to the town board as written.

cases.name: Citibank signage
cases.applicant: Applicant/sign contractor (from Long Island / Lindenhurst)

timeline.summary: Applicant sought to replace existing directional freestanding signs (36 by 20) exceeding the one-square-foot directional allowance. The board explained it cannot grant that exception and referred the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals for the variance; if granted, the planning board could then approve the site plan. Building-mounted signs are ARB jurisdiction. The board voted to refer.

cases.name: Short-Term Rental Law (town board referral)
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Town Board)
cases.lastStatus: reviewed and returned to Town Board without formal comment

trajectory.status: reviewed and returned to Town Board without formal comment

timeline.status: reviewed and returned to Town Board without formal comment
timeline.summary: The Town Board referred its proposed short-term-rental law (a zoning-chapter amendment) to the Planning Board for input. The board discussed the framework at length: primary-residence requirement, the 30-day threshold, operating permits and building-department inspections, occupancy tax, quiet hours, and the provision barring a short-term rental on the same lot as an accessory dwelling unit (ADU). Views split on whether the law is too cumbersome (risking noncompliance) versus appropriately detailed for enforceability, but there was broad agreement its practical effect is to discourage short-term rentals. The board reached consensus to send it back to the Town Board with no substantive comment.

cases.name: Extensions of time (40 High Street; Summer Club; 298 Banksville Road)
cases.address: 40 High Street; Summer Club; 298 Banksville Road
cases.applicant: Various (Summer Club represented via Jeff Mendel)

timeline.summary: The board granted routine extensions of time: 40 High Street (subdivision, still awaiting the Health Department); the Summer Club (Board of Health approved the sewage treatment plan; applicant now working on water submissions, project still alive); and 298 Banksville Road (an accessory-apartment special use permit, first extension).

cases.name: Extensions of time (batch: 23 Bedford-Banksville; 130 Old Orchard/Middle Patent; 3 North Castle Dr; 215 Business Park Dr; 113 King St)
cases.address: 23 Bedford Banksville Road; 130 Old Orchard/Middle Patent Road; 3 North Castle Drive (Eagle Ridge); 215 Business Park Drive; 113 King Street (former MBIA senior building)
cases.applicant: Various (Anthony; Matt Barrens for Cory; Ali Fassner, Cuddy & Feder for 113 King St)

timeline.summary: The board reordered the agenda to take five extension-of-time requests first so waiting applicants could leave early. Each applicant gave a short status update (health-department septic approvals, DEC permits, cost estimates with Kellard's office, sub-tenant timing, IDA application). All five extensions were moved, seconded and granted with no substantive opposition. For 113 King Street the chair clarified the request concerned only the senior building.

cases.name: Church sidewalk / special use permit referral
cases.applicant: Church (came in for a new sidewalk / handicapped-access walkway)

timeline.summary: A church that applied for a new handicapped-access sidewalk was found to lack a special use permit for its operation, so it was referred to the Town Board, which in turn triggered a required referral back to the Planning Board. The board discussed that a positive recommendation would let the Town Board issue the special use permit and then allow the Planning Board to approve the sidewalk site plan. The board voted a positive recommendation back to the Town Board.

cases.name: OMAAC Extension of Time
cases.applicant: OMAAC

timeline.summary: Request for an extension of time. The submission explained that preliminary documents, required reviews, and coordination were completed with several remaining items still in progress needing additional time. The board saw no objection and approved the extension.

cases.name: 49 Roundhouse Road (Bedford Greenwich Animal Hospital)
cases.applicant: Bedford Greenwich Animal Hospital

timeline.summary: The applicant told staff they read the review memo and are working on it, and did not appear. The board opted to carry the item to the next meeting when they return with an amended submission addressing the comments. No substantive discussion occurred.

cases.name: 6 Massaro Court (formerly 54 Curtis)
cases.applicant: Michael Stein, Hudson Engineering
cases.lastStatus: public hearing closed; approved with conditions (as amended)

trajectory.status: public hearing closed; approved with conditions (as amended)

timeline.status: public hearing closed; approved with conditions (as amended)
timeline.summary: This was the final lot of a three-lot subdivision (two prior lots approved in January), seeking site plan and steep-slope approval to build a two-family dwelling with retaining walls, substantial grading, and a comprehensive stormwater system. Discussion focused on a condition (condition 6) requiring the grading plan be revised to eliminate a seven-foot exposed basement to the town engineer's satisfaction, and on a retaining wall shown 'by others' sitting on the property line. Michael Pollack, citing a similar issue in his own professional practice, suggested making explicit that maintenance of the wall is this property owner's obligation to avoid future disputes. The board closed the public hearing (no public spoke) and granted the resolution as amended per Pollack's suggestion.

cases.name: 22 School Street

timeline.summary: The item was laid over to a future meeting with essentially no discussion beyond noting it would carry to the next meeting.

cases.name: Shapiro residence, 8 Rosen Drive
cases.address: 8 Rosen Drive (ASR renders the street name inconsistently across meetings - heard here as "Rose and Drive"; prior meetings rendered it as Rosanne/Rolling/Rocking Horse Drive)
cases.applicant: Shapiro (owner); represented by Paul Saisek of JMC

timeline.summary: Follow-up field-change request on a previously approved site plan/special permit for tennis court and Padel court improvements. The applicant sought to shift nine evergreen screening trees closer to the property line and replace trees along the tennis court's eastern side with clumped river birch, after having removed proposed tennis-court lighting in response to earlier neighbor objections. The conservation board representative confirmed the change did not encroach on the approved wetlands mitigation area and that the revised landscaping plan actually added 53 trees and 77 shrubs net versus the original approval. The board approved the field change unanimously.

evidence.case: Summit Club — Temporary Golf Clubhouse Facilities (2021-2022 Seasons)
evidence.evidence: Pressed the applicant on why Health Department sanitary-approval filings had been delayed until so close to the planned spring opening, and drove the ARB-jurisdiction question to the Town Attorney for a definitive answer.

evidence.case: 16 Quaker Meeting House Road — Clearing & Grading Limit Line Amendment
evidence.stance: supportive of a full public hearing
evidence.evidence: Agreed that, given likely neighbor interest in the recorded clearing/grading restriction, the board should proceed with a formal published-notice public hearing rather than mailed notification alone.

evidence.case: 8 Cole Drive & 24 Davis Drive — Lot Line Change, House Addition & Driveway Relocation
evidence.evidence: Directed Town Planner Adam Kaufman to prepare both a supportive and a non-supportive draft resolution, telling the applicant candidly that "this vote could go either way," and adjourned rather than force a vote with a member absent.

evidence.case: 50 East Middle Patent Road — Two-Lot Subdivision
evidence.evidence: Acknowledged Larry Ruisi's concern as valid while noting the board wasn't substantively holding up the applicant, and worked out that the item would return to the next agenda once cleaned up with staff.

evidence.case: OAMIC Ingredients, 6 Labriola Court — Chemical Storage Classification Amendment
evidence.evidence: Pressed the applicant on what portion of the warehouse's storage would convert to the higher-flammability classification, and later voiced surprise/concern ("this is news to me") on hearing it could effectively be the whole facility, saying he wanted the town's consultants to authenticate that.

evidence.case: 3 Deer Ridge Lane — On-Site Rock Crushing
evidence.evidence: Framed the benefit of crushing rock on site (avoiding truck trips and reuse of a natural resource) for the board and helped negotiate a neighbor-letter/no-objection approach instead of a full notification hearing.

evidence.case: One Gion Lane - new single-family home
evidence.stance: Presiding; steered board to approve the resolution as amended
evidence.evidence: Framed the two options and made the motion to approve the resolution as amended with a more deer-resistant planting plan.

evidence.case: One Kent Place - Maury (legalization of sheds/coolers/patios)
evidence.stance: Presided; moved to close the hearing and adopt the resolution
evidence.evidence: Made the motions to open, close, and adopt the resolution after confirming JMC had no issues.

evidence.case: Buff's Flower Garden - nursery special permit amendment
evidence.stance: Cautiously open but wants operational detail, safety and a work session before recommending
evidence.evidence: Said the board needs to report operational aspects to the town board and proposed a work session with the conservation board to work it out.

evidence.case: 7 New King Street
evidence.stance: Supportive; thinks it silly the applicant must argue the use and wants the zoning cleaned up
evidence.evidence: Said the board should straighten out the IND-AA district to include warehouse use and that having to consider it is a little silly.

evidence.case: 428-436 Main Street
evidence.stance: Facilitated a path forward using the 1996 appraisal as a benchmark for the use mix
evidence.evidence: Concluded the board has something to work with and a benchmark, and directed the applicant to submit a use schedule then and now.

evidence.case: 20 Manus River Road - house renovation, pool and cabana
evidence.stance: Supportive; advised evaluating the retaining wall's structural integrity now
evidence.evidence: Suggested having a structural engineer look at the back wall while the work is being done, in the owner's best interest.

evidence.case: Summit Club (former Brentwood Country Club) - residential component
evidence.stance: Fairly satisfied with the residential layout; wants water and AFFH resolved before hearing
evidence.evidence: Said he's fairly satisfied with the building layout and roads and framed getting the water plan finalized before opening the public hearing.

evidence.case: Buck's Flower Garden, 65 Bedford Banksville Road — Retail Nursery/Farm Stand
evidence.stance: supportive but cautious about future intensity
evidence.evidence: Led the comprehensive-plan-consistency analysis comparing the site to Choice Nursery, and pressed the town planner on how to codify the proposed "very minor" retail use so a future change in ownership couldn't intensify it without planning board review ("law of unintended consequences").

evidence.case: 23 Bedford Banksville Road — Contractor's Yard to Stone/Masonry Yard Conversion
evidence.evidence: Repeatedly pressed the Town Attorney and applicant on the "procedural predicament" of approving anything premised on a grandfathered use the building inspector has not certified, and asked what protects the town if the promised three-year sunset doesn't happen.

evidence.case: 47 Windmill Road — Residential Addition & Front-Yard Motor Court
evidence.stance: skeptical; urged the applicant to redesign to avoid variances rather than seek them
evidence.evidence: As Chair, said he felt the plan as presented 'is not respecting the spirit of the zoning laws' and that granting these variances risked the town looking like it 'rubber stamps' everything; urged the applicant to first try to fit within the 50-foot front setback before applying for a variance.

evidence.case: Summit Club — Residential/Golf Community Site Plan
evidence.stance: generally supportive of progress, but strategic about hearing timing
evidence.evidence: As Chair (directly addressed as 'Chris' by the Town Attorney), argued the board should wait for the Town Board's water informational meeting before opening its own public hearing to avoid a drawn-out series of reopened hearings, and pressed engineers for specifics on the water tank's elevation and dimensions.

evidence.case: 20 Miamis River Road — Renovation, Addition, Pool & Tree Removal
evidence.evidence: Asked about Board of Health/septic bedroom-count risk and about the unusually steep-looking one-foot-interval grading plan, confirming both were non-issues before moving to close the hearing.

evidence.case: 655 Bedford Road — Two-Lot Subdivision with Conservation Easement
evidence.stance: supportive, called it 'an exceptional contribution' to preserved open space
evidence.evidence: Said he was comfortable sending the matter to the ZBA and viewed the large conservation easement over the remainder of a 28-acre parcel favorably, while asking staff to confirm what further environmental information might be relevant.

evidence.case: 176 Virginia Road — Mister Properties Inc. Mail-Truck Parking Buildings
evidence.stance: reluctantly supportive; framed forcing a redesign as unfair given the prior approval
evidence.evidence: As Chair, said it 'strikes me' the board was changing terms mid-process on an applicant who had already been approved once, before guiding the board to close the hearing and readopt.

evidence.case: 35 Edgar Road — Pool, Cabana & Shed Removal (Wetland Buffer)
evidence.stance: skeptical of buffer impact and septic-relocation avoidance, wants more diligence
evidence.evidence: Questioned whether the mitigation approach truly respects the town's wetland-buffer protections given that 'everyone steals part of their wetland buffer' over time, and pressed on whether partially relocating septic lines could avoid the variance altogether; also raised general concern about whether the proposal 'gives any kind of respect to our zoning laws.'

evidence.case: Summit Club — Residential/Golf Community Site Plan
evidence.stance: facilitated consensus, favored timing oversight during rather than after state/county review
evidence.evidence: As Chair, worked through the timing logic with the applicant's engineer and attorney and ultimately called the vote recommending the Town Board consider a third-party water-plan oversight consultant.

evidence.case: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road — Madonna Subdivision
evidence.stance: wanted an explanation before rubber-stamping a third extension
evidence.evidence: Noted this was already a third extension without explanation and asked why, prompting the applicant's representative to clarify the conditions were being actively worked through.

evidence.case: Eagle Ridge (3 North Castle Drive / clubhouse)

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Planning Board reopened and closed the public hearing for a single-family residence at 34 Creamer Road, adopting a resolution amended to address roadway/construction-safety conditions raised by neighbors. The board continued (adjourned without closing) the public hearing for an automated parking garage at 11 New King Street pending resolution of state DOT traffic-mitigation requirements. The board received an initial, no-action presentation on a proposed rezoning and 43-unit multifamily development at 45 Bedford Road (Mariani property), referred from the Town Board, and raised significant traffic and density concerns. The board also discussed a lot-line realignment at Wampus Mills/143 Old Mount Kisco Road (scheduling a public hearing), an informal parking/tree-removal fix at 12 Maple Avenue necessitated by new CVS sidewalk construction, a tree-removal/landscape plan with a public hearing set for August 6, and granted two extensions of time.
meetings.durationNote: Individual board members are rarely named in this un-diarized 2018 recording; only two first names surfaced via direct address ("Michael" and "Steve"), and the presiding chair is never named. Town staff present and named include Town Planner Adam Kaufman, Town Attorney Roland (Baroni), and Planning Board Secretary Val(erie).

cases.name: 34 Creamer Road — Single-Family Residence

Neighbors (Jim Dempsey, a Ms. Sanders) raised concerns about wetland-buffer disturbance/flagging accuracy, stormwater discharge, and especially driveway sight-distance safety on a blind hill, plus a request to protect possible historic remnants near the adjacent landmarked Creamer property. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended to add a condition requiring the applicant to obtain a highway department curb-cut permit and an adequate work plan (flagmen, signage) for work in the right-of-way prior to a building permit.
cases.publicComment: Two neighbors (Jim Dempsey of 38 Creamer Road and a neighbor named Sanders across the street) spoke at length with concerns about wetland delineation accuracy and, especially, the safety of the new driveway entrance on a fast, blind hill during and after construction. A third resident (Ed Woodard) asked that due diligence be paid to possible historic/archaeological remnants given the site's proximity to the historic Creamer House.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the board had looked at the sight line from the driveway and shared the neighbor's concern, pointing out that the resolution already contains a condition requiring the applicant to demonstrate compliance with the required 200-foot sight distance.

The applicant reported completed Conservation Board (with a ~$136,000 wetland-bank contribution), ARB, and Town Board special-permit approvals, but said the state DOT had not yet approved the required traffic-mitigation plan from the environmental review, with a DOT meeting scheduled for August 9. The board (citing its lead-agency responsibility) declined to close the hearing so the public could weigh in once DOT's position on mitigation is known, while allowing the applicant to keep refining site-plan details (including a reversed, left-side vehicle/bus circulation pattern at the entrance) in the interim.

cases.status: referred (informational presentation only, no board action)

Board members pressed hard on projected traffic generation, expressing skepticism that ITE trip-generation data (about 30 cars/hour) could be lower than existing nursery-business traffic given the site's proximity to school traffic patterns; the applicant team committed to a forthcoming traffic study. meetings.meetingSummary: This nearly five-hour session opened as a special 6 p.m. joint work session between the Planning Board and the Architectural Review Board for an early-stage design review of the Summit Club (formerly Brynwood Country Club) residential component — 73 condominium units in seven buildings plus an amenities building and tennis courts — with no board action taken. The Planning Board then continued alone into a full regular agenda: adopting a resolution for a Burech accessory-apartment application, approving (with a sound-attenuation condition) generators at 5 North Greenwich Road, referring a 375 Main Street Shell gas station renovation to the ZBA over an outdoor-display/sign dispute, referring a residential driveway-relocation/fill application (owner referred to as "Nazar"/"Nizzar") to the Conservation Board pending further work on natural fill material and wetland-crossing design, referring a 100 Business Park Drive warehouse expansion to the ZBA (adopting a SEQRA negative declaration first), and tabling a contentious 124 Old Mount Kisco Road fire-rebuild/two-lot subdivision request pending further board deliberation on a deed-restricted square-footage compromise.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided. Planning board members Steve Sauro, Jim Jensen, and Michael Pollack were present from the start; Larry Ruisi joined roughly an hour in (confirmed later seconding a motion). ARB members Susan Geppin, Angela Monaco, Chris Tuzo, and John Scolato participated for the joint Summit Club portion only and are not Planning Board members. This file's automated speaker-attribution pass was only partially reliable for this meeting — long stretches (especially the Summit Club presentation and the 100 Business Park Drive discussion) are labeled 'Unattributed' or given filler-word pseudo-names (e.g., 'Okay', 'Yeah', 'Well'), so most individual board-member positions below are limited to passages with an explicit, real-name direct-address cue.

cases.name: Summit Club (Brynwood Country Club) — Residential Site Plan & Design Review
cases.address: Brynwood/Summit Club, Bedford Road (Route 22), Armonk, NY
cases.applicationType: site plan / wetlands / steep slope / tree removal permit (joint ARB design work session)
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners LLC (represented by attorney Mark Winegarten, principal Jeff Mendel, architects Rich Granoff and Ken Anderson of Granoff Architects, and engineer Paul Cisak of JMC)
cases.status: informational joint work session — no board action
cases.summary: Following roughly a decade of process (2011 zoning text amendment creating a golf course community overlay district, 2016-2020 approvals for the golf course and subdivision into a 130-acre golf parcel and 26-acre residential parcel), the applicant presented the residential component's design directly to a joint Planning Board/ARB session: 73 luxury one-floor-living condominium units across seven buildings (six along the golf course, one set higher to the east), an amenities building (bar/grill, pool, fitness center, spa) doubling as an initial sales center, and four tennis courts set back roughly 100 feet from Bedford Road. Discussion covered building height relative to road grade, unit parking (two indoor spaces plus a golf-cart space per unit), massing/staggering to manage perceived height and buffer views from Route 22, and general architectural character (modern theme, described by the applicant as unusual for the town but intended to appeal to an empty-nester/second-home buyer market). The chair confirmed the boards were largely finished offering initial comments and that the applicant would continue refining the plan with staff (Town Planner Adam Kaufman and Town Engineer John Kellard) ahead of a future submission; no vote was taken.

cases.name: 375 Main Street — Gas Station Renovation

cases.status: referred to Zoning Board of Appeals
cases.summary: Continuing review of a redevelopment of the existing Shell gas station, with the board generally satisfied with the building/canopy/fueling-area design as revised since prior comments. The principal dispute was a newly-added outdoor retail display (windshield fluid, firewood, etc.) proposed along the building's prominent Main Street glass facade — several board members felt it would visually clutter an otherwise attractive facade and questioned why it needed to sit there rather than a less prominent location, floating alternatives (indenting the building envelope, widening the sidewalk). Because outdoor display requires a Town Board special permit, the board opted to send its comments/concerns to the Town Board via referral rather than force a redesign, while also addressing an oversized freestanding/monument sign (36 sq. ft. proposed vs. ~25 sq. ft. permitted, ARB-approved contingent on a ZBA variance) and street-lighting/paver consistency along Main Street. The board voted to send the applicant to the ZBA for the outstanding variances, with a revised plan expected back in about two weeks.

Seconded the chair's motion to refer the applicant to the ZBA.

cases.name: Residential Driveway Relocation & Fill (Off Davis Road area)
cases.address: Address unclear in ASR transcript (referenced as near "Davis" road/drive)
cases.applicationType: site plan / wetlands permit (driveway relocation, fill)
cases.applicant: Property owner referred to as "Nazar"/"Nizzar" (surname garbled in ASR, variously heard as "Musu"/"Armus-Sue"), represented by attorney Corey Salomon and engineer Peter/Pete Gregory
cases.status: referred to Conservation Board (not yet approved)
cases.summary: Follow-up to a January 13 site walk on a driveway relocation requiring imported fill (either natural material or manufactured geofoam/cellular fill blocks) to cross a ravine/water course; an alternative backyard-expansion layout suggested at the site walk was rejected by the applicant's team as more impactful (more fill, more retaining walls) than the original plan. The board pushed to minimize truck trips and wetland-buffer disturbance by exploring natural fill sourced on-site (potentially combined with excavation from a separately-planned playroom/gymnasium addition) rather than importing geofoam, and one member floated designing small bridge-like structures over the water course (echoing an existing pair of crossings) to reduce both fill volume and water-course impact. The applicant pressed for the board's support before investing further engineering effort; the board declined to commit and instead voted to refer the matter to the Conservation Board for further review, cautioning the applicant that, as with any application, the ultimate outcome remains undecided until a vote.

Repeatedly pressed (as acknowledged by the chair, "you've brought it up a couple of times") for the applicant to use natural fill sourced from the site rather than importing manufactured geofoam, while acknowledging his own concern about truck trips.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive — Warehouse Expansion
cases.applicant: Applicant represented by engineer Paul Seisach/Cisak and associate Paul Dumont of JMC, with floodplain consultant Leonard Jackson
cases.status: referred to Zoning Board of Appeals; SEQRA negative declaration adopted
cases.summary: The applicant reported securing a Town Board floodplain-code variance eliminating the need for compensatory flood storage construction, and reworked site grading to reduce a previously flood-prone driveway low point from four-to-five feet of flooding to one foot in a 100-year storm. Outstanding issues discussed included a front-facing truck loading area (retained to mirror an existing building's logistics and set back/offset from the street, with the board debating but not requiring an enclosing roof structure to screen it), whether continued outdoor storage would be permitted with the new warehouse, and the need for a still-unsought ZBA front-yard variance. The board formally adopted a SEQRA negative declaration (having previously coordinated lead agency status) and voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the front-yard variance, with a public hearing and draft resolution to follow once that variance is resolved. ARB approval was confirmed already in hand from earlier in the year.

cases.name: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road — Fire-Damaged Nonconforming Lot Subdivision
cases.address: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road, Armonk, NY
cases.applicant: Frank Madonna (represented by attorney Corey Salomon and engineer Ralph Alfanzetti)
cases.status: tabled — carried to a future meeting
cases.summary: The applicant, owner of a 0.4-acre lot improved with two long-standing pre-existing-nonconforming single-family houses (one built circa 1850, the other 1924), sought a two-lot subdivision after the newer house was 50-75% destroyed by a July 2020 fire, rather than simply rebuilding the fire-damaged nonconforming structure as-of-right. The applicant argued the property already reads as two lots in keeping with the street's character (which the applicant said is 80-90% similarly nonconforming) and offered a rear easement from an adjacent parcel to help meet lot-area requirements, plus a proposed deed restriction capping each new house's square footage to keep new construction modest. Town Planner Adam Kaufman's memo opposed the subdivision path (citing roughly nine required variances) and favored the code's existing as-of-right nonconforming-rebuild option instead. Board members were sympathetic to the applicant's situation but wary of setting a precedent for subdividing lots with this degree of non-compliance, and wanted more time to evaluate a square-footage-capped compromise; the board tabled the matter to a future meeting and asked the applicant to stake the proposed lot corners so members could drive by and visualize the layout beforehand.

cases.name: 164 East Middle Patent Road — Second-Story Addition & Septic Replacement
cases.address: 164 East Middle Patent Road, Armonk, NY
cases.applicant: Property owner (self-represented; architect referenced but connectivity-impaired during presentation)
cases.summary: Public hearing on a second-story addition to an existing single-family home on a scenic road, including a new septic field proposed partly within the wetland buffer. Neighbors (via emailed comments read into the record, including one from Todd Noonan/Stacy Albany citing standing water photographed at the proposed septic location and concerns about downstream well contamination) objected strongly, arguing the site was unsuitable and that fill placed over wetland soils elsewhere in town (the "Choy Nursery" precedent) had caused similar sites to become unbuildable. The town engineer defended the plan as a net reduction in impervious cover (eliminating the stormwater-mitigation trigger) and noted septic suitability is ultimately the Westchester County Health Department's jurisdiction, not the planning board's; the Conservation Board had already reviewed and approved the wetland mitigation/planting plan in February. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended to add a Health Department approval condition (inadvertently omitted from the draft) and a mitigation-planting maintenance/monitoring bond in response to neighbor concerns about plant survivability.
cases.publicComment: Neighbors Todd Noonan and Stacy Albany (156 East Middle Patent Road) raised strong concerns via email and live testimony about septic-field placement in what they photographed as standing wetland/water, potential contamination of their downstream drinking well, and skepticism that mitigation plantings could offset the impact; a separate neighbor (Christopher Robbins, 167 East Middle Patent Road) wrote in support of the project.

memberPositions.evidence: Flagged that the Health Department approval condition was missing from the draft resolution and proposed adding a mitigation-planting maintenance/monitoring bond given neighbor concerns about plant survivability; made the motion to adopt the resolution as amended.
Seconded Jim Jensen's motion to adopt the amended resolution.

cases.name: Summit Club — Temporary Golf Clubhouse Facilities (2021-2022 Seasons)

cases.summary: Public hearing on a special permit for temporary golf-season facilities (limited operation for up to 300 members, a repurposed construction trailer serving as clubhouse/pro shop/offices, a bathroom trailer, a prefabricated wooden bar structure, and a food truck) while the permanent residential/amenity buildings remain in process, for the 2021 and 2022 golf seasons. Board members pressed on Health Department approval timelines for food service and septic/sanitary operations (with the applicant citing a 21-day notice requirement) and scrutinized draft-resolution conditions, including a noise-chapter compliance reference. A related procedural dispute arose over whether the trailers required formal ARB review or could be waived to the building inspector's discretion; the Town Attorney advised the ARB has independent jurisdiction the planning board cannot waive on its own, so the board directed the applicant to work with the building inspector or seek an ARB slot. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended (striking an as-built-survey condition given the facilities' temporary nature).

cases.name: 3 Deer Ridge Lane — On-Site Rock Crushing
cases.address: 3 Deer Ridge Lane, North Castle, NY
cases.applicant: Applicant represented by Paul and Andy (contractor/site representatives)
cases.summary: Following roughly 15-20 days of on-site rock hammering that left a large rock pile, the applicant sought approval to rent a crusher/screener to process the rock into gravel for reuse on site (driveway, dry wells, septic work) rather than trucking it away and importing new gravel, estimated at 300-650 cubic yards and about 2-4 days of crushing. The board weighed whether a formal neighbor-notification hearing was warranted versus the applicant's informal outreach to the four households on the street, and ultimately opted for direct approval with conditions rather than notification, given the crusher was assessed as quieter than the prior rock-hammering already conducted without objection. Conservation Board liaison George Repel raised (and the board resolved) a question about whether crushed rock needed contamination testing before reuse, distinguishing it from soil-contamination precedents. The board approved the application on a motion by Steve Sauro, seconded by Michael Pollack, with conditions limiting work to 9:00 a.m.-4:30 p.m., no weekends, and a maximum 10-day duration.

memberPositions.evidence: Framed the benefit of crushing rock on site (avoiding truck trips and reuse of a natural resource) for the board and helped negotiate a neighbor-letter/no-objection approach instead of a full notification hearing.
Questioned the applicant on duration and truck-trip savings, said he liked that the process saved roughly 40 truckloads, and made the motion to approve with the 9-4:30, no-weekends conditions.
Said the only downside of a neighbor notification would be the process delay, and seconded the approval motion.

Flagged a discrepancy between two memo estimates of crushed material volume (650 vs. 300 yards) and asked about hours/duration and dust-control equipment before supporting conditions on hours and weekend restrictions.

meetings.meetingSummary: A long, full-agenda North Castle Planning Board meeting held by Zoom covering eight items: a new single-family home site plan at One Gion Lane (approved with conditions), a tree-removal/landscaping permit at 100 Hunter Drive (approved), an amended site plan/wetlands legalization at One Kent Place (approved), and several early-stage matters referred or held for further work: Buff's Flower Garden nursery special-permit amendment, a warehouse expansion at 7 New King Street, a parking-variance interpretation at 428-436 Main Street, a scenic-road house renovation with pool at 20 Manus River Road, and the Summit Club (former Brentwood Country Club) residential-component site plan. Recurring board themes were process/quality-control of draft resolutions, screening and deer-resistant plantings, wetlands/stormwater, parking, and special-permit/zoning questions.

cases.name: One Gion Lane - new single-family home
cases.applicant: Elliot / LEA (engineer for owner)
cases.summary: Neighbor-notification meeting on a proposed ~3,800 sf home (5,900 sf including garage/decks) on a constrained R2A lot; neighbors raised driveway headlights, privacy, screening and stormwater concerns. After a long board debate about the large number of open items on the draft resolution and how much should be delegated administratively, the board closed the notification meeting and approved the resolution as amended, requiring a more deer-resistant screening plan in place of arborvitae.

Emailed neighbors (Castellucci, others) asked about visibility from Gene Curry, stormwater runoff, erosion and wetlands; staff said runoff is directed away and there are no wetland impacts.

meetings.meetingSummary: In a special Valentine's Day session, the North Castle Planning Board (Chairman Christopher Carthy, Steve Sauro, Michael Pollack, and Jim Jensen) opened, closed, and approved a special use permit for a two-story garage at 115 Round Hill Road, then referred the tangled 120/121 Lafayette Avenue solar-panel/site-plan-legalization matter to the Zoning Board of Appeals for parking and driveway-backout variances. The board debriefed a joint site walk on the Buck's Flower Garden retail-nursery proposal at 65 Bedford Banksville Road (comprehensive-plan consistency, retail-use scope, and lead-agency status) and on a proposed contractor's-yard-to-stone/masonry-yard conversion at 23 Bedford Banksville Road (grandfathered-use and sunset-timeline concerns). It also confirmed the 73 North Broadway restaurant/taproom application would proceed to a March 14 public hearing following the ZBA's approval of its parking variance.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided with Steve Sauro, Michael Pollack, and Jim Jensen present and individually polled throughout; the chair opened the meeting by noting two (unnamed) planning board members had been injured in weather-related falls that week and wished them well, without naming them or otherwise indicating whether they were present. Larry Ruisi is not mentioned in this transcript.

The board confirmed the structure sits about 144 feet back from the front-yard setback line, is screened by existing trees, required no tree removal, and drew no public comment. The town engineer confirmed prior stormwater review was satisfactory. The board closed the hearing and unanimously adopted the draft resolution the same night.

Followed up on Michael Pollack's height question and asked how the garage related to the street/landscaping visibility from the road.

cases.name: 120 & 121 Lafayette Avenue — Site Plan Legalization / Solar Panels

The board, at the chair's and Steve Sauro's urging, opted not to hold up the applicant further and instead voted to refer both properties to the ZBA with a positive recommendation for variances covering the number of on-street parking spaces (10 spaces referenced for 120 Lafayette, cross-referenced to a license for spaces at 123 Lafayette) and backing out onto Lafayette Avenue, while directing Town Planner Adam Kaufman to work directly with the property owner/team to reconcile outstanding site-plan documentation before the matter returns for final site plan approval.

cases.name: Buck's Flower Garden, 65 Bedford Banksville Road — Retail Nursery/Farm Stand
cases.applicationType: site plan / special use permit referral (Town Board)
cases.applicant: Buck's Flower Garden (property owner referenced only as "she"; represented by Dan and engineer Joe)
cases.status: in progress — lead agency established, application returning for a joint work session with the Conservation Board
cases.summary: Following a joint Town Board/Planning Board site walk, the board debated whether comprehensive-plan language written for the nearby, never-developed Choice Nursery parcel (requiring any future development to respect environmental constraints and the area's low-scale rural character) should apply equally to this similar Banksville parcel, and agreed it should. The board and Town Planner Adam Kaufman agreed the proposed retail component (a small farm-stand/vendor table, plus horses, chickens, and an educational visit program) was less intensive than initially feared, but the chair pressed for the retail scope and location to be codified (size, height, siting away from the wholesale nursery/growing area) in the Town Board's special-permit conditions so a future change of ownership couldn't expand it without returning to the planning board. The board discussed relocating the farm-stand parking near an existing clearing to separate visitor and commercial-nursery traffic, flagged an expired prior sign approval needing to be resolved, and voted to formally act as SEQRA lead agency, with the application to return for a joint work session with the Conservation Board (tentatively set for March 14) to address wetland-buffer disturbance and pesticide/fertilizer use.

memberPositions.stance: supportive but cautious about future intensity
memberPositions.evidence: Led the comprehensive-plan-consistency analysis comparing the site to Choice Nursery, and pressed the town planner on how to codify the proposed "very minor" retail use so a future change in ownership couldn't intensify it without planning board review ("law of unintended consequences").
Agreed with applying the Choice Nursery comprehensive-plan logic to this property when polled by the chair.

The board discussed how the traffic study and ZBA parking/circulation commitments would be incorporated into the site-plan resolution, revisited (without resolving) whether to remove a no-left-turn sign at the driveway exit to help patrons head north on Route 22 versus keeping commercial trucks out of the residential street (deferred to public comment), and confirmed the applicant was ready to notice a public hearing for March 14, 2022 pending final ARB approval running on a similar timeline.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked how the traffic study findings and ZBA variance commitments (parking maneuvering/off-site leased spaces) would be specifically summarized and referenced in the site-plan resolution.

cases.name: 23 Bedford Banksville Road — Contractor's Yard to Stone/Masonry Yard Conversion
cases.applicationType: site plan / special exception use permit (Town Board)
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by attorney Anthony and site planner Peter)
cases.status: in progress — no board action; applicant directed to pursue building-inspector grandfathered-use determination and/or a direct Town Board application
cases.summary: Following a site walk, the applicant proposed renovating the front office/storage building (limited by Board of Health to 15-16 occupants) and consolidating a roughly 2.5-acre rear area currently housing five to six contractor tenants (landscaping, excavating, paving, etc.) into a smaller (~0.8-acre), fenced, landscaped high-end stone/masonry retail yard pulled back from the wetland buffer, proposing to sunset the existing contractor uses over up to three years while claiming a 1960s-era legal grandfathered use. Board members and the Town Attorney (Roland) raised sharp procedural doubts: without building-inspector documentation establishing the grandfathered use, the board has no legal basis to approve a sunset/replacement plan, and the applicant acknowledged he could not yet locate the 1960s zoning ordinance to support the claim; a fallback path (a new Town Board special-permit application for the stone-yard use, running in parallel via a SEQRA process for which the planning board is lead agency) was discussed as an alternative. The board asked for the wetland/buffer line to be more clearly superimposed on the site plan for the Town Board's benefit and raised an unresolved septic-capacity question (the 16-occupant Board of Health cap covers the whole lot, including any new stone building) but took no formal action.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly pressed the Town Attorney and applicant on the "procedural predicament" of approving anything premised on a grandfathered use the building inspector has not certified, and asked what protects the town if the promised three-year sunset doesn't happen.
Called the proposed reduction in the rear yard's footprint and intensity a "significant improvement" at first glance, while acknowledging it would take considerable time to finalize.
Suggested superimposing the wetland-buffer line onto the proposed site plan (a before/after view) to help the Town Board evaluate the reduction in disturbed area.
Questioned how adding a separate stone-yard building would affect the Board of Health's 16-person occupancy limit tied to the site's constrained septic capacity in the wetland.

cases.name: Proposed Local Law — Town Board Special Use Permit for Commercial Recreation Centers in Industrial Districts
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle
cases.status: referral comments deferred to next meeting
cases.summary: The Town Board referred a draft local law that would reclassify commercial recreation centers in industrial (PLI) districts from an as-of-right/site-plan use to one requiring a Town Board special use permit, prompted by concern over potential traffic/use-intensity impacts. A board member had independently researched broader American Planning Association definitions of 'recreation, commercial indoor/outdoor' and suggested the town board's narrow activity list (gyms, batting cages, ice rinks, etc.) be expanded so applicants better understand what would be entertained; the board appeared to reach informal consensus favoring the broader definition and the added standard requiring access to a major collector road. Because the Chair was absent, the board opted to wait until his return before formally transmitting its recommendation.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of a broader recreation-use definition
memberPositions.evidence: Presented APA-sourced broader definitions of commercial indoor/outdoor recreation and suggested the town board consider expanding its narrow activity list to better guide applicants; confirmed as Jensen's work when the same amendment was carried forward and explicitly attributed to 'Jim' at the 2022-03-14 meeting.

cases.name: 873 North Broadway — Restaurant & Accessory Brewing Adaptive Reuse
cases.applicant: Zach Goldstein (represented by attorney Daniel Patrick, Cody & Fader; engineer Rich Williams)
cases.status: public hearing closed; decision pending (applicant still awaiting ABC/liquor authority approval)
cases.summary: Adaptive reuse of a ~3,435 sq ft commercial building into a 45-seat fine-dining restaurant with a small accessory brewing operation, offsite parking arrangements, and an 18-seat rear outdoor dining area; the applicant had already obtained a ZBA parking variance for 26 spaces. The owner of the adjacent non-conforming two-family residential rental (877 North Broadway) vehemently objected, citing traffic, noise, parking spillover onto tenant amenity, and incompatibility of a brewery/restaurant use next to a pre-1923 residence. After extended negotiation over outdoor-seating hours, screening/fencing/planters behind the patio, and location of outdoor dining (front vs. rear), the board and applicant agreed to last outdoor seating at 8 p.m. Monday-Thursday and 9 p.m. Friday-Sunday, no live music, and evergreen/planter screening; the public hearing was then closed but a vote was deferred because the applicant had not yet secured required ABC (liquor authority) approval.
cases.publicComment: Gail Cryovich, owner of the adjacent 877 North Broadway two-family rental house (built 1923, predates the commercial zoning), vehemently objected: she argued a brewery/restaurant clientele is incompatible with her tenants, that cutting off the front entrance pushes all traffic past her house to the rear lot, that 10-15 staff plus customer parking would overwhelm available spaces, that late-night hours (10-11 p.m.) would drive away renters, and that outdoor dining should be sited in front (facing Route 22) rather than behind her property; she disputed that a formal traffic study addressed Route 22 volume.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the restaurant, advocated for later/more flexible outdoor-dining hours
memberPositions.evidence: Sauro pushed back on an 8 p.m. cutoff as too restrictive ('give the restaurant a little more leeway... eight or nine o'clock is more reasonable'), worked through fencing/planter screening options with the applicant's engineer, and ultimately proposed the Monday-Thursday 8 p.m. / weekend 9 p.m. compromise that the board adopted.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical that the offered concessions meaningfully relieve the neighbor
memberPositions.evidence: Pollack questioned whether restricting outdoor dining actually 'provides relief to the residential use next door,' argued a 9 p.m. last-seating time on weekdays still leaves diners finishing at 10:30-11 p.m. with cleanup noise continuing, and pressed for an earlier 8 p.m. weekday cutoff to better protect the neighbor.

memberPositions.stance: generally supportive, engaged on rear-patio screening
memberPositions.evidence: Jensen worked through the rear-patio gate/fence layout with the applicant to identify screening opportunities toward the neighbor and said he agreed with ('liked') Sauro's compromise on outdoor-dining hours.

cases.name: Proposed Local Law — Town Board Special Use Permit for Commercial Recreation Centers in Industrial Districts
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle

meetings.meetingSummary: A packed agenda with the full board present (Chair Christopher Carthy, Steven Sauro, James Jensen, Lawrence Ruisi, Michael Pollack): the board closed and approved two carried-over matters (Pleasant Grooming's dog area and the 873 North Broadway restaurant/brewery resolution), reviewed two new residential additions raising accessory-structure and motor-court/wetland-buffer issues, granted three routine extensions of time, worked through a long and contentious Town Board referral on legalizing a Bedford-Banksville contractors yard as a masonry sales business (ultimately recommending against a 'sunset' compliance provision), gave a positive recommendation on converting the RMF senior-housing floating zone to a mapped district, approved a site-plan waiver for a bagel shop replacing a dry cleaner, approved a stormwater field-design change at 94 Business Park Drive, and closed with an informal push to re-engage NYSDOT on Route 22 corridor improvements.

cases.name: 873 North Broadway — Restaurant & Accessory Brewing Adaptive Reuse
cases.applicant: Zach Goldstein (represented by attorney Daniel Patrick, Cody & Fader; engineer Rich Williams)
cases.summary: The board finalized and adopted the site plan resolution. Key negotiated points: because the required NYSDOT highway work permit/easement (a multi-year Attorney General review process) could delay the sidewalk/frontage work well past occupancy, the board substituted a performance bond (new bond in the new owner's name, amount set by the Town Engineer, work completed within one year of DOT permit issuance) for a strict pre-CO completion requirement, with proof of a submitted DOT application required before CO issuance; condition 12 was revised to track whatever on-site inspection frequency DOT's permit actually requires; a prior no-left-turn restriction onto Washington Place was removed at the applicant's request (already reflected on the site plan); and the outdoor dining hours were locked in at last seating 8 p.m. Monday-Thursday and 9 p.m. Friday-Sunday, with a landscaping/planter screening commitment toward the rear-yard neighbor.

memberPositions.stance: wanted assurance the DOT process itself would actually be pursued, not just deferred
memberPositions.evidence: Flagged that a flat six-month completion window after DOT approval didn't address the risk the applicant might never actually initiate the DOT review, prompting the board to add a condition requiring proof of a submitted DOT application before CO issuance.

cases.name: 10 Crema Road — Residential Addition & Accessory Cottage Special Use Permit
cases.applicationType: site plan / special use permit (accessory apartment)
cases.applicant: Keith Rosenthal (represented by engineer Thomas Carrigan, Sike Design Consultants)
cases.status: under review; applicant directed to flag wetlands and coordinate with building inspector
cases.summary: Proposed addition and driveway expansion to a residence with an existing pre-1984 guest cottage/accessory apartment (confirmed legal via a 1986 board resolution and 1988 CO). The board's central concern was whether the cottage's proposed expansion (bumping out and adding floor area, ~1,238 to ~1,530 sq ft, while staying under the 22-foot height cap and 25% coverage limit) could still be permitted without a ZBA variance, since modifications to a pre-1984 grandfathered accessory structure occupy a legal gray area the building inspector had informally flagged as problematic; the board separated the underlying special use permit (grantable regardless) from the proposed modifications (which may need zoning input) and asked the applicant to delineate on-site wetlands before scheduling a site walk.

cases.name: 47 Windmill Road — Residential Addition & Front-Yard Motor Court
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by engineer Thomas Carrigan and architect Dan Simone)
cases.status: negative referral leaning; applicant asked to redesign to avoid variances
cases.summary: Proposed addition, driveway/motor-court expansion, and tiered retaining walls near a rear-yard wetland/pond required front-yard setback variances for the motor court (which the town's motor-court law was specifically written to prevent so close to the road), plus a gross-land-coverage variance and floodplain/wetland permits. The Chair told the applicant the plan did not respect 'the spirit of the zoning laws' and urged a redesign within code (e.g., a smaller apron or a second curb cut rather than a full motor court) before returning; the applicant's team explained the real need was simply drop-off access at the front door given the site's constrained, wedge-shaped topography between the road and the lake. A joint site walk was scheduled.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical; urged the applicant to redesign to avoid variances rather than seek them
memberPositions.evidence: As Chair, said he felt the plan as presented 'is not respecting the spirit of the zoning laws' and that granting these variances risked the town looking like it 'rubber stamps' everything; urged the applicant to first try to fit within the 50-foot front setback before applying for a variance.

cases.name: 23 Bedford-Banksville Road — GB District Masonry Sales / Contractors Yard Legalization Referral
cases.applicationType: local law (zoning text amendment) & town board special use permit referral
cases.applicant: Property owner/contractor (represented by Tony Veneziano)
cases.status: negative recommendation on the proposed sunset provision; board asked for more information before further action
cases.summary: The Town Board sought feedback on (1) a zoning text amendment to permit masonry/stone sales in the town's only GB district and (2) a special use permit to legalize an existing, long-illegal contractors yard on the same site, under a proposed multi-year 'sunset' framework where the illegal yard would gradually be replaced by a conforming masonry business. After extensive discussion of wetland-buffer impacts, whether the use might already be covered under the existing 'building materials storage and sales' permitted use, and enforcement risk, the board declined to support a sunset arrangement — reasoning that a performance bond adequate to guarantee cleanup would likely be prohibitively expensive/impractical given unknown soil contamination risk, and that approving a site plan around a currently-illegal use set a bad precedent — and instead recommended the applicant present a plan showing only permitted uses, with existing violations cleaned up before site plan approval. The board directed staff to check with the building inspector on the 'building materials' classification question and report back.

memberPositions.stance: opposed reviewing the zoning text change in isolation; pushed to minimize wetland-buffer impact
memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly objected to a 'piecemeal' approach — approving the GB text change without seeing the whole site plan — and argued the proposed post-sunset masonry building and access could be relocated further from the wetland buffer than shown.

memberPositions.stance: opposed the sunset provision on enforcement/liability grounds
memberPositions.evidence: Pressed on what mechanism would actually compel compliance if the applicant ran out of money mid-sunset, and ultimately argued the town risked becoming 'complicit' in an illegal use with too much downside risk and no good way to unwind it.

cases.name: RMF Senior/Multi-Family Housing — Floating Zone to Mapped District Conversion Referral
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle
cases.summary: The Town Attorney explained the Town Board wants to convert the RMF senior/multi-family housing zone from a 'floating' zone (which, per state model-code guidance citing North Castle itself as an example, legally obligates the Town Board to bring any rezoning petition to a final yes/no vote, exposing 'no' votes to litigation risk) to a traditional mapped district, giving the Town Board discretion to simply return a petition it doesn't want to consider. After extended clarifying discussion (including confusion over whether this affected the whole town or only specific parcels like Eagle Ridge and the Long Ridge Road/128 site), the board voted unanimously to recommend the change.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, wants the business to succeed
