cases.name: 94 Business Park Drive — Stormwater Design Field Change
cases.applicationType: field change to approved construction plans (stormwater)
cases.applicant: 94 Business Park Drive applicant
cases.summary: New York State DEC required additional stormwater treatment/a landscaped 'rain garden' along the northern parking-lot property line because regrading work didn't meet the redevelopment exemption; separately, the applicant value-engineered the roof-runoff storage from 60-inch storage pipes to StormTech chamber units (same storage volume, different material) due to cost/availability. Because construction was still early, the board treated this as a re-signed construction-plan revision rather than a minor field change and approved it after the Town Engineer explained why an infiltration design wasn't feasible (insufficient separation to the water table) and that irrigation reuse of the detained water wasn't practical given the short (multi-day) retention time.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked the Town Engineer to explain how StormTech storage units differ functionally from pipe conveyance, and separately asked whether detained stormwater could be reused for irrigation.

cases.name: Route 22 Corridor Improvements — Renewed NYSDOT Outreach
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (Planning Board initiative)
cases.status: Town Planner directed to re-contact NYSDOT and report back
cases.summary: Prompted by news of increased state infrastructure funding, the board discussed reviving its stalled, pre-COVID push (rooted in the comprehensive plan's prioritization of Route 22 corridor safety and streetscape improvements) to get NYSDOT and state funding authorities to fund engineering/construction; DOT had previously said it lacked funds and state funding contacts had shown little interest pre-COVID. cases.name: Summit Club — Residential/Golf Community Site Plan
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners LLC / Jeff Mendel (represented by attorney Mark Weingarten; architects Ken Anderson (Grandoff) and Paul Sisak (JMC))
cases.status: pre-hearing design review continuing; public hearing to be sequenced after a Town Board informational session on the water contribution agreement
cases.summary: The applicant presented revised plans: the large clubhouse was deferred to a later phase in favor of a smaller phase-one pool house/amenities building, an 18-hole putting green was removed from the wetland buffer, and details of the new sewage treatment plant (STP) building and water treatment/storage tank complex (105,000-135,000+ gallon tank, ~30-35 ft tall, at grade) were reviewed, including the required 72-hour well pump test now underway. A significant point of board concern was the plan's designated on-site locations for AFFH units, which the applicant's attorney candidly confirmed as a fallback ('Plan B') if an off-site AFFH location isn't secured — a scenario the applicant is unwilling to pursue further (including buying another parcel) without town approval first. The board also asked the applicant to prepare a rock-excavation/blasting plan referencing a prior North Way Plains precedent. After discussion, the board and Town Attorney agreed to hold off opening the public hearing until after a Town Board work session informs residents about the amended water contribution agreement, to avoid repeatedly reopening the hearing.

memberPositions.stance: generally supportive of progress, but strategic about hearing timing
memberPositions.evidence: As Chair (directly addressed as 'Chris' by the Town Attorney), argued the board should wait for the Town Board's water informational meeting before opening its own public hearing to avoid a drawn-out series of reopened hearings, and pressed engineers for specifics on the water tank's elevation and dimensions.

memberPositions.stance: concerned about AFFH placement risk and market-rate pricing exposure
memberPositions.evidence: Pressed the applicant on what happens if the off-site AFFH location falls through mid-construction, calling it a potential 'roadblock,' and separately questioned whether AFFH units count toward the phase-one market-rate price-per-square-foot commitment (confirmed by the Town Attorney that AFFH units are excluded from that calculation).

cases.name: 655 Bedford Road — Two-Lot Subdivision with Conservation Easement
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by Tony Veneziano and engineer Ralph Fonzetti; contractor Vann DiZemo Construction) for Deborah James (daughter of the neighboring Mittelman family)
cases.status: lead agency intent declared; referral to ZBA to follow once a SEQRA negative declaration issues
cases.summary: A 28-acre R2A lot with one existing (non-conforming, undocumented) house would be split into two lots — the new lot for a house for the owners' daughter, accessed via a 50-foot easement rather than direct road frontage — with a conservation easement placed over the remainder. Because the new lot lacks frontage, the applicant will need either a ZBA frontage-variance or a Town Board open-development-area designation; the applicant and board planner agreed the ZBA route was preferable. Since SEQRA review can't segment a phased subdivision, the board must evaluate potential impacts as if up to six lots (the applicant's larger, unused development-rights study) could eventually be created, even though only two lots are actually proposed; the applicant will submit an impacts matrix. The board declared its intent to be lead agency (required before a negative declaration can issue and before the ZBA can act) and will refer the frontage variance to the ZBA once ready, noting Conservation Board interest given the parcel's size and no proposed wetland disturbance.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, called it 'an exceptional contribution' to preserved open space
memberPositions.evidence: Said he was comfortable sending the matter to the ZBA and viewed the large conservation easement over the remainder of a 28-acre parcel favorably, while asking staff to confirm what further environmental information might be relevant.

cases.name: 94 Business Park Drive — Indoor/Outdoor Container (POD) Storage Expansion
cases.applicant: Tony Vaziano (representing a national portable-storage company, PODS-affiliated, with 'Daniel' as company operations representative)
cases.status: under design review; public hearing to be scheduled alongside continued information requests

The board requested photos and site-utilization data from the company's existing Valley Cottage facility, a closer look at the approved landscaping plan (requested by a board member), and directed the applicant to submit outstanding information while scheduling the public hearing in parallel to avoid delay.

cases.name: 35 Edgar Road — Pool, Cabana & Shed Removal (Wetland Buffer)
cases.applicationType: site plan / wetland permit (pending ZBA variances)
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by attorney Leo Napier; landscape architect John Conte and civil engineer son John Conte, Conte & Conte)
cases.status: board requested additional neighborhood/lot-line documentation; applicant to return in two weeks before any ZBA referral
cases.summary: On an undersized, triangular ~1-1.5 acre lot in a two-acre zone, the applicant proposes removing a shed and building a pool, cabana with grill/counter and outdoor shower in the rear corner, requiring setback (and possibly coverage) variances because the existing septic field occupies the central yard. No wetlands were found on site (confirmed by the town's consultant), but nearly the entire buildable area falls within a 100-foot buffer of an adjacent watercourse, so the applicant proposed over 2:1 plant-material mitigation. Board members pushed back on whether the hardship justified variances given the buffer impact, questioned whether the septic field could instead be partially relocated to bring the pool closer to the house (engineers said soil/ledge conditions and current stricter Health Department separation regulations make that difficult), and asked for better mapping of a nearby vacant Connecticut-adjacent parcel's development potential to confirm no future neighboring house would be affected. Because the ZBA referral is a 'gating' issue for the applicant (who wants to avoid further engineering cost before knowing if variances are viable), the board opted to hold the item two more weeks for additional data rather than send it to the ZBA immediately.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of buffer impact and septic-relocation avoidance, wants more diligence
memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether the mitigation approach truly respects the town's wetland-buffer protections given that 'everyone steals part of their wetland buffer' over time, and pressed on whether partially relocating septic lines could avoid the variance altogether; also raised general concern about whether the proposal 'gives any kind of respect to our zoning laws.'

memberPositions.stance: wants Conservation Board input before proceeding
memberPositions.evidence: When asked if he wanted to add anything, said he'd like to get Conservation Board input on the application.

memberPositions.stance: raised wetland-buffer respect as a threshold concern
memberPositions.evidence: Referenced later in discussion as having raised the point about whether the project 'respect[s] the wetland buffer.'

The Town Attorney advised the applicant bears the risk of jurisdictional complications if the shed remains partly in Connecticut (requiring separate Greenwich approval) and recommended simply relocating it fully onto the New York parcel to avoid inter-jurisdictional entanglement; the applicant indicated willingness to do so. The board deferred further action pending documentation on the excavation tenant's storage needs and the parking reconciliation.

cases.name: Summit Club — Residential/Golf Community Site Plan
cases.applicant: Summit Club Partners LLC / Jeff Mendel (represented by attorney Mark Weingarten)
cases.status: public hearing to be scheduled (targeting late June/early July); Town Board asked to consider third-party water-plan oversight
cases.summary: With Town Board support secured to proceed, the board debated whether the town should hire an independent consultant to validate the applicant's private water-system plan (bedrock aquifer wells feeding an off-site wastewater discharge to a tributary of the Byram River) concurrently with, rather than after, state DEC and county Board of Health review — reasoning that revisiting an already-state/county-approved plan late would be unworkable. The applicant's team argued existing state/county review was sufficient and that the Town Board had already declined to require a third-party consultant; the board nonetheless voted to recommend the Town Board consider hiring an oversight professional to review the water plan concurrently with state/county review. The board agreed to schedule the public hearing for its next-available (June 27 or following) meeting.

memberPositions.stance: strongly favors independent town oversight of the water plan
memberPositions.evidence: Laid out in detail why this project's water system differs from a typical single-well design (community wells in a bedrock/fractured aquifer, off-site wastewater discharge to a river tributary) and argued the 2015 findings statement itself anticipated town oversight and an operating plan, driving the board's eventual recommendation.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of getting independent validation before, not after, state/county sign-off
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the town 'only [has] one chance to get it right' and that consequences of an error would be severe, pushing for oversight to occur in the review pipeline rather than after state/county approval.

memberPositions.stance: questioned whether this was properly a planning board matter
memberPositions.evidence: Observed that the water district acceptance and oversight decision seemed like a Town Board matter unless the Town Board specifically asked the Planning Board to weigh in.

memberPositions.stance: facilitated consensus, favored timing oversight during rather than after state/county review
memberPositions.evidence: As Chair, worked through the timing logic with the applicant's engineer and attorney and ultimately called the vote recommending the Town Board consider a third-party water-plan oversight consultant.

cases.name: 825 North Broadway — Gas Station Tank & Store Rehabilitation
cases.applicant: Gas station owner (represented by engineer Jim Gibbons, Gibbons Engineering)
cases.status: under review; applicant to consult with client on circulation/canopy changes and return
cases.summary: Proposal to replace aging underground storage tanks and rehabilitate the convenience store interior within the existing footprint. The board's primary concern was vehicle circulation — the single aisle between pump islands is too narrow for two-way travel — prompting discussion of removing a pump near the store, relocating a utility pole, or shifting the oversized canopy to create proper travel lanes; the board also suggested the applicant consider aesthetic upgrades (the canopy was called disproportionately large) and repair of badly deteriorated sidewalks, and noted stormwater quality improvements (not otherwise required) were welcome, given the significant investment already planned. Board recommended the applicant coordinate design details with staff and, if exterior changes result, with the Architectural Review Board.

cases.name: 21 Netherwood Avenue — Single-Family Home
cases.applicant: Dino and Michelle DeLaRentes (represented by attorney Noel Wolfson; engineer Elliot Sinoor; landscape architect Walter Nestler)
cases.status: under review; applicant to prepare revised plan incorporating wall/grading comments before returning for public hearing
cases.summary: After multiple prior board appearances (Jan/Nov 2021) and an April 2022 ZBA site-distance variance grant, the applicant presented a revised plan lowering the basement floor to reduce retaining-wall height and fill volume, and preserving a cluster of rear-yard trees via a riprap slope. The Town Planner objected that a riprap slope would be highly visible to the adjacent neighbor and recommended a boulder wall with planting pockets instead for a more naturalistic look; the Town Engineer separately identified opportunities to eliminate additional retaining walls/regrading on the north side (potentially saving two more large trees) by using a single taller wall rather than a lower continuous wall, which the board indicated it would support even above the standard 6-foot cap given the tree-preservation benefit. The applicant confirmed no rock hammering/chipping is anticipated. Board agreed to a public hearing at the meeting after next (~June 27).

cases.name: 11 Bedford-Banksville Road — Brothers Green Nursery/Contractors Yard Legalization
cases.applicationType: site plan / special use permit referral
cases.applicant: Brothers Green Nursery (owner since 2007, operating since 1982; represented by attorney Corey Salvo and engineer Andrew Kuzmich)
cases.status: planning board declared intent to be lead agency for SEQRA; site walk scheduled before further action
cases.summary: A residential building-permit application inadvertently surfaced the fact that this long-operating landscaping/nursery business (split-zoned CBB/GB, ~3.7 acres, mostly wetland/buffer) has never had site plan approval; the Town Board referred the special-use-permit legalization to this board. The central issue was classification: staff's read was that the operation (equipment storage, vehicle parking, multiple topsoil/aggregate stockpiles) looks more like a contractor's yard than a permitted nursery use, complicating approval in the CBB zone; discussion explored splitting uses geographically (nursery/office in the CBB front, limited contractor-type storage in the small GB rear portion) or possibly asking the Town Board to consider adjusting the GB zoning line, though the board was skeptical of a property-specific rezoning appearing to be spot zoning. The applicant emphasized the operation is materially different from (smaller-scale than) a true contractor's yard like a nearby comparison site. The board declared intent to be SEQRA lead agency and scheduled a joint site walk before further deliberation.

memberPositions.stance: seconded the lead-agency motion, engaged on the SEQRA process
memberPositions.evidence: Seconded the motion declaring the planning board's intent to be SEQRA lead agency for the application.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge — 3 North Castle Drive Two-Lot Subdivision (Hotel & 72 Townhouses)
cases.applicant: Madonna / Josh Weissman (represented by attorney Corey Salvo; engineer Ralph Alfonsetta; contract vendee Toll Brothers represented by Kevin Moses)
cases.status: subdivision application submitted; applicant asked to produce an alternative townhouse layout and 3D visualizations before further review
cases.summary: Application to subdivide a ~32-acre parcel (previously the subject of a 4-year Town Board rezoning/EIS process and a $1.5 million community benefits agreement) into a 10.6-acre hotel lot (115-key hotel) and a 21.8-acre, 72-unit townhouse lot, essentially unchanged from the plan the board gave a positive recommendation on in April 2021. The Town Planner and Chair pushed back hard on the townhouse layout — straight, tightly-spaced 'stadium seating' rows of paired units running down the slope from the IBM property line toward the hotel — calling it poor site planning driven purely by fitting 72 units within Town-Board-imposed constraints (30-ft unit separation, no more than two units per block); the applicant's team countered that the 72-unit count and those spacing constraints were locked in through the Town Board's finding statement and that any unit reduction would jeopardize project economics and potentially the community benefits payment. After a pointed back-and-forth about whether 'good site planning' could ever justify fewer than 72 units, the board asked the applicant to produce at least one genuine alternative layout and 3D renderings/elevations (rather than a flat 2D plan) to better evaluate the design, and separately flagged the unresolved question of how residents would safely cross Route 22 to reach the adjacent community park, noting NYSDOT has been unresponsive to the applicant directly and wants to deal only with the town.

memberPositions.stance: strongly critical of the townhouse layout's design quality, insisted on seeing genuine alternatives
memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly pressed the applicant's team on why a better, less 'stadium seating' layout couldn't be produced, said the current plan was 'marginal at best' in its design, and directly disputed the applicant's suggestion that any board pushback threatened the community benefits agreement or amounted to an improper attempt to reduce density.
Suggested the applicant provide 3D renderings/elevations rather than a flat 2D plan to better convey how the tiered townhouse layout would actually read on the ground.
Asked whether the substantial open space at the rear of the site (highest elevation) was a required IBM buffer setback, confirming it was a mandated 55-foot buffer with screening.

memberPositions.stance: focused on pedestrian access to Route 22 and the adjacent community park
memberPositions.evidence: Pressed on whether/how residents would be able to cross Route 22 to reach the community park, floated a Park Avenue-style median refuge concept, and asked who would be responsible for building and maintaining any connecting sidewalk given a deed restriction currently prohibiting a direct trail connection.

cases.name: 35 Edgar Road — Pool, Cabana & Shed Removal (Wetland Buffer)
cases.applicationType: site plan / wetland permit (pending ZBA variances)
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by attorney Leo Napier and engineering/landscape team)

cases.summary: Applicant, absent this meeting, is seeking a positive planning board referral to the ZBA for four variances (two side yard, one rear yard, one gross land coverage exceeding the limit by 152 sq ft) needed to build a pool/cabana on a substandard, oddly-shaped 0.6-acre lot where the existing septic system leaves no conforming location. memberPositions.evidence: Said each variance situation is different and, based on the pool's practical invisibility to neighbors, stated he personally would be okay with a positive referral to the ZBA.

memberPositions.stance: wants to see the site before making a recommendation

cases.applicant: PODS Enterprises (represented by Tony Vinesiano)
cases.status: public hearing continued (tabled pending revised application)
cases.summary: Continuation of a public hearing on an amended site plan to allow outdoor storage of up to 108-180 storage containers behind an existing warehouse building. The board pressed on inconsistent container counts between the application, staff report, and a draft resolution (108 vs. 180 vs. 858 interior units), questioned whether removing all 16 required loading docks would shift all pod loading/unloading activity outdoors, and raised noise, visual/leakage, and 'material supply yard' use concerns. The hearing was kept open with the applicant directed to return with clarified logistics, a defined storage volume/footprint, and screening details.
cases.publicComment: Adjacent property owner Ed Lashes (owner of 80/84 Business Park Drive) strongly objected, citing noise, visual impact, container 'leakage' beyond approved areas at a comparable facility in Valley Cottage, and questioned the applicant's math on container counts; he also relayed written objections from another park owner, Michael Ferrari, who suggested the FAR/rear-yard impacts warranted a variance application instead. Dean Brown, director of business development for the adjacent Bristol assisted-living community, objected to the entire pods concept, describing anticipated noise (beeping, truck traffic) disrupting senior residents' quality of life.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed for the storage capacity to be quantified by volume/'cube' footprint on the site plan rather than a raw container count, so a resolution condition could be enforceable.

Questioned how inventory could be moved without staging activity outside the building given the aisle-less stacked layout, and pushed back on the applicant's characterization that operations would remain low-impact once all 16 loading docks were eliminated.

cases.name: 12 Library Court — Holderness & Bourn Amended Site Plan
cases.applicant: Holderness & Bourne (golf apparel), represented by Thomas McDermott
cases.status: referred to Zoning Board of Appeals (pending applicant submission)
cases.summary: Applicant sought an amended site plan to consolidate a golf-apparel brand's warehouse/office/embroidery operations at an existing two-story warehouse and office building. Board discussion centered on whether reclassifying part of the warehouse to a manufacturing (embroidery) use would increase required off-street parking beyond what's provided, likely necessitating a ZBA parking variance. The board authorized planner Adam to review the applicant's updated square-footage breakdown before formally referring the specific variance to the ZBA.

The board discussed stormwater/percolation testing, road/driveway geometry, and confirmed the resolution would describe but not approve the six-lot alternative. The applicant reported a pending July 7 ZBA application for a front-yard/access variance needed before returning for a formal subdivision public hearing.

cases.name: 82 Round Hill Road — Field Change Approval
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Ralph Alfonzetti / Steve Lopez, landscape architect)

cases.name: 84 Round Hill Road — Wetland Buffer Violation / Mitigation
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Ralph Alfonzetti / Steve Lopez, landscape architect)
cases.summary: Discussion of a NYS DEC wetland-buffer clearing violation at the rear of the property (excess site clearance converted to lawn), for which the applicant had already obtained a DEC mitigation approval using a native red fescue planting plan. Because the local RPRC wetland buffer letter postdated the DEC's certified wetland line and mitigation approval, the board directed the applicant to bring the mitigation plan to the town Conservation Board for its own sign-off before further action; unrelated retaining walls built without prior approval were also noted as already addressed via a prior RPRC review.

cases.name: 47 Windmill Road — Home Addition & Retaining Walls
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Tom Parrigan and project engineer 'Dan Simmon')
cases.summary: Extensive design workshop on a revised plan for a house addition, garage, and tiered retaining walls near a lake/wetland buffer and steep slopes. The planner found the plan still 'aggressive,' flagging that a proposed motor court and second curb cut sited within the wetland buffer are not permitted by code. The board negotiated design mitigations (natural boulder walls instead of faced walls, pulling the garage back a bay, softening the rear wall curve, green-screening exposed foundations) and directed the applicant to engage the Conservation Board and return with a finalized plan and landscaping/mitigation details; the applicant confirmed the reduced plan would fall under the gross land coverage threshold, avoiding a ZBA referral.

staffInput.summary: Led technical review across nearly every agenda item — outdoor storage logistics at 94 Business Park Drive, parking calculations at 12 Library Court, subdivision/stormwater review at 655 Bedford Road, and wetland-buffer/steep-slope mitigation design at Round Hill Road and Windmill Road.
Presented engineering detail on the 655 Bedford Road subdivision stormwater/road plan and the Round Hill Road wetland mitigation and field changes.

The town engineer flagged a required 100-foot well-separation correction and a 36-inch chamber-separation issue, which the applicant agreed to address by using shallower infiltration chambers; overall disturbance was not being increased.

The planner recommended, and the board agreed, to conduct a site visit with the area staked out before deciding whether a formal neighbor-notification meeting is needed.

cases.name: 6 Library Court — WAMIC Ingredients Warehouse Storage Amendment
cases.applicant: WAMIC Ingredients
cases.summary: Applicant sought to amend the type and quantity of chemicals approved for storage in its warehouse. The town's environmental consultant, HES, reviewed the applicant's Midwest-prepared materials report and a May 24 site visit and found the storage plan compliant with OSHA/fire code with no threat to health or environment. Board member Michael Pollack raised a 'scope creep' concern that some newly-proposed chemicals fall into materially different, higher risk categories than originally approved, questioning whether the board should set a firmer benchmark; the board agreed to invite the HES consultant to the public hearing to answer questions directly rather than resolve it that night.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he was 'torn between whether this is scope creep,' noting some newly-proposed chemicals fall into risk categories two steps removed from what was originally approved, and asked whether the board should set a benchmark for how much storage composition can change.

cases.summary: Following a joint site walk with conservation, planning, and Town Board staff, the applicant revised its combined nursery and contractor's-yard special permit application: relocating contractor equipment into the correct zoning section, adding an 18-inch protective berm (reduced from an engineer's suggested 3-foot berm) along the wetland/stream side, and adding a stormwater gravel bed sized to the 1.5-inch water-quality storm standard. The board debated how specifically to designate outdoor equipment-storage areas on the plan and whether the (long-standing but never-approved) site plan needed Architectural Review Board referral, concluding ARB referral was discretionary and not warranted for legalizing existing conditions. The applicant is amending its Town Board special-permit application (for July 13) and submitting to the Conservation Board for a retroactive wetlands permit.

cases.name: 94 Business Park Drive — PODS Outdoor Container Storage
cases.applicationType: amended site plan / outdoor storage permit
cases.applicant: PODS Enterprises (represented by Tony Vinesiano)
cases.summary: Reopened hearing at which the applicant presented an acoustical expert's testimony (projecting 30-35 dB noise levels across the street) and clarified operational details, but sustained, detailed opposition from adjacent owner Ed Lashes and a nearby business-park property representative (citing lack of tax benefit, precedent for outdoor storage along the whole park, and loss of enjoyment for Bristol assisted-living residents) dominated the hearing. The board pressed hard on whether the site plan, as originally approved, actually permits any outdoor forklift/loading activity at all (concluding it does not — only interior loading docks were approved) and directed the applicant to consider redesigning loading so trucks are effectively 'parallel parked' against the building (functioning like a loading dock) rather than staging pods outdoors, eliminating the outdoor-operation objection. The hearing was adjourned without a vote.
cases.publicComment: Strong, organized opposition from Ed Lashes (adjacent owner) and a neighbor identified as Michael/Mike (relaying father-in-law Al Mayola's objection), who argued the town gets no tax benefit from outdoor storage, that it would set a precedent enabling outdoor storage along the entire business park, and that it threatens the quality of life of Bristol assisted-living residents. The applicant's attorney rebutted with acoustical testimony and argued the use is consistent with the zoning.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed to clarify that the originally-approved site plan showed only interior loading docks with no ramps, and that forklifts driving outside to load trucks was never a permitted use under the existing approval.

cases.name: 17 Old Orchard Street — St. Christopher's Slope Stabilization & Wetland Violation
cases.applicant: St. Christopher's (represented by Thomas Gibbons, LKV Engineering)
cases.status: ongoing; referred to Conservation Board, NYC DEP input needed (~6 months)
cases.summary: Applicant is remediating a town stop-work-order violation after unpermitted fill work (sourced from a DEP site plus additional non-conforming material) washed out during a storm and impacted the neighboring DEP reservoir. Proposed fix: regrade the slope to a gentler angle, install erosion-control matting, hydroseed, and replant roughly 12 trees for the ~8 lost. A key dispute emerged over whether a drainage swale on the site — piped and extended without permits by the prior contractor — is a regulated wetland/intermittent watercourse (as the town engineer's office maintains, citing a 2009 designation reflected in the 2017 filed subdivision plat) or merely a drainage ditch exempt from wetland regulation (the applicant's position). The board directed a joint Planning/Conservation Board site walk, referral to the Conservation Board, and NYC DEP input (estimated 6-month timeline) before final approval, while permitting continued temporary slope stabilization (hydroseed/erosion matting) despite the still-active stop-work order.

cases.name: 9 Barnard Road — Unpermitted Retaining Wall & Stormwater Discharge Dispute
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by project engineer)
cases.status: tabled; new site walk to be scheduled, immediate drainage fix directed
cases.summary: Long-running (over a year, since April 2021) dispute over a roughly 9-foot retaining wall built without a permit at the property line, now proposed to remain as-is on the strength of a post-hoc engineer certification, plus a PVC drainage pipe discharging driveway runoff directly onto the adjacent neighbor's property. The neighbor testified to repeated basement flooding and objected strongly to legitimizing the unpermitted wall via landscaping mitigation alone. A board member (likely Michael Pollack) challenged the board for treating the illegally-built wall as a fixed 'given' rather than asking what proper planning would have produced from scratch; the chair agreed the board needed to revisit the matter in the field rather than continue accepting the status quo, citing the year-long delay's ongoing harm to the neighbor. The board directed the applicant to plug/disconnect the offending point-discharge pipe immediately (ahead of the rainy season) while scheduling a fresh site visit to reconsider the wall itself.
cases.publicComment: The adjacent neighbor testified that a PVC pipe installed at the property line has repeatedly flooded her yard and basement since the property's regrading/wall construction, and objected to the wall (which she measured near 9-12 feet from her vantage point) being allowed to remain based on a retroactive engineering sign-off rather than proper permitted construction.

memberPositions.evidence: Challenged the board's framing, arguing it was treating an unpermitted, illegally-built wall as a fixed condition to work around rather than asking what proper planning would have required from scratch, calling the situation 'ugly' and unresolved after more than a year.

Agreed the board needed to revisit the site and get control of the timeline, noting a year had passed with nothing resolved 'to the benefit of one property owner to the detriment of another,' and directed immediate action on the discharge pipe.

The board and planner agreed the site should go to the Conservation Board and get a board site walk before any ZBA variance referral, since the practical hardship (isolated lot, existing house location) appeared strong but the buffer/wetland question needed Conservation Board input first.

meetings.meetingSummary: The October 13, 2022 North Castle Planning Board meeting (held Thursday instead of the usual Monday because of the Columbus Day holiday) covered six items: an extended, contentious debate over elevated nickel levels in unpermitted imported fill at 26 Chestnut Ridge Road and how to remediate/disclose it; a major referral push for the Eagle Ridge hotel/townhome project (approving a 4-story, 124-key hotel and referring it to the ZBA, Town Board, and Conservation Board); a positive recommendation to expand a special use permit at 263 Bedford Banksville Road from 2 to 20 horses after extensive applicant-neighbor negotiation; brief informal site-plan discussions for a 78 Lafayette Avenue warehouse expansion and a house/pool rebuild at Ledgewood; and direction on wetland mitigation for a fill-violation/slope-erosion case whose street address the ASR could not capture clearly. 33 Woodland Road was adjourned to a future meeting.
meetings.durationNote: Present: Chairman Christopher Carthy, Steven Sauro, James Jensen, Lawrence Ruisi; Town Planner Adam Kauffman; Town Engineer John Kellard; Conservation Board liaison John Crapa. Michael Pollack and Thomas Crispi did not appear to attend this meeting.

cases.name: 26 Chestnut Ridge Road — Fill Import Violation & Soil Remediation
cases.applicant: Anthony Marino (owner), represented by JMC Engineering
cases.status: under review — proceeding to neighbor notification
cases.summary: The applicant imported roughly 1,500 yards of fill without a permit, which was later found to slightly exceed the unrestricted-use residential soil cleanup objective for nickel (a memo error had initially misidentified the metal as lead). The applicant's environmental consultant recommended leaving the fill in place under a demarcation layer with a clean topsoil cap (originally proposed at 6 inches, versus a state standard the board understood to be up to 18 inches) rather than exporting it, since levels remained well under the restricted-use and groundwater-protection thresholds. The board debated at length whether a deed covenant/disclosure was needed to protect future buyers and whether the six-inch cap was adequate, ultimately voting to proceed to neighbor notification while leaving the exact cap depth and covenant mechanism to be finalized with a revised consultant memo.
cases.publicComment: The applicant's attorney/engineer and owner Anthony Marino argued that the town's own engineer would have approved the same soil for import had a permit been sought in advance, and objected to the shifting demarcation recommendation; the Chairman countered that the analysis showed the soil would in fact have been rejected as originally submitted and that a future-buyer disclosure was fair.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly pressed the environmental consultant on the actual purpose of the demarcation layer, used an extended 'apple tree' analogy to argue a future buyer deserves disclosure, and ultimately steered the board toward neighbor notification while flagging that a deed covenant should accompany any demarcation layer.
Said accepting the demarcation layer felt like 'holding your nose,' but called it necessary, and favored attaching the finding to the deed so future owners are notified.

Raised concerns about nearby drinking-water wells and the last-minute correction from lead to nickel, questioning whether the board had the expertise or standing to independently evaluate the consultant's revised recommendation.

memberPositions.stance: concerned, wants a larger clean-soil buffer
memberPositions.evidence: Argued a six-inch cap seemed inadequate compared to the two-foot standard he understood applied, and pushed for the finding to be flagged for future buyers via covenant rather than left undisclosed.

cases.summary: The applicant returned with a revised landscape plan (500+ new, largely native trees, dark-sky-compliant lighting, and an internal trail network) developed with input from Toll Brothers as the eventual builder. The board discussed increasing the hotel from 3 to 4 stories (staying within the existing 45-foot height limit) and from 115 to 124 keys, both requested because hotel operators would not commit to a 3-story building; the board voted positive recommendations to the Town Board on both changes and a positive referral to the ZBA for the story variance. A proposed pedestrian sidewalk connection across Route 22 into town was discussed and judged impractical without NYSDOT participation. The board referred the project to the Conservation Board but held the ARB referral until building elevations and a cross-section (to assess view impacts from the hotel roofline) are submitted.

memberPositions.evidence: Made and carried the motions for positive recommendations to the Town Board on the 4-story/124-key changes and the positive referral to the ZBA.

Pushed for a sidewalk/pedestrian-scale lighting solution tying the project to the comprehensive plan's 'sense of place' goals, but ultimately accepted that a Route 22 crossing was not feasible without DOT buy-in.
Requested a cross-section showing the hotel's height relative to grade before final sign-off, noting the flyover video understated the height difference.

cases.name: 263 Bedford Banksville Road — Equestrian Special Use Permit
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by J. Fane & Associates
cases.status: positive recommendation to Town Board; referred to ARB and Conservation Board; board declared itself SEQRA lead agency
cases.summary: The applicant negotiated extensively with neighbors before and after filing, agreeing to conditions including capping the horse count at 20 (with room to accommodate up to 23 including foals), maintaining strictly residential (non-commercial) equestrian use with no rentals or shows, a 150-foot landscape buffer, and a mechanism binding future property owners to the same conditions on transfer of title. A neighbor spoke strongly in favor, describing the roughly 70-acre property's role as a wildlife corridor connecting the Mianus River to Butler Sanctuary. The board voted a positive recommendation to the Town Board on the special use permit change, referred the applicant to the ARB and Conservation Board, and declared itself lead agency for SEQRA review.
cases.publicComment: A neighbor of over 40 years (Tim Madison, 256 Bedford Banksville Road) spoke enthusiastically in favor, describing the property's ecological and community value and full neighborhood support after extensive collaboration with the applicant.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion for a positive recommendation to the Town Board on increasing the permitted horse count.
Praised the extensive applicant-neighbor collaboration and moved the application through referrals without objection.

cases.name: 30 Palmer Avenue — Paddy Parking Space, Retaining Wall & Curb Cut
cases.applicationType: site plan / retaining wall / curb cut
cases.applicant: Mr. and Mrs. Paddy, represented by Blanchard & Wilson
cases.summary: After a multi-year process that shrank the proposal from three parking spaces to one and went through a ZBA variance for site-distance and lot-coverage deficiencies, the board closed the public hearing and adopted a site plan resolution for a single 33-foot parallel off-street parking space, a roughly four-foot retaining wall, and a second curb cut on Grove Street. A neighboring property owner argued the underlying 2018 traffic/site-distance study was outdated given new no-parking signage and occupied nearby homes, and that a 33-foot parallel space was oversized compared to a 14x22-foot perpendicular alternative; the applicant's attorney countered that the site-distance issue was already adjudicated by the ZBA and was outside the planning board's jurisdiction. The board added conditions requiring the existing screening fence along the southern border to remain, limiting use to a single motor vehicle with no structures or outdoor storage in the parking area, and referring future disputes over the fence to the board rather than allowing it to be removed unilaterally.
cases.publicComment: Neighboring property owner Ken Kauffman objected at length, citing an outdated 2018 traffic study, the oversized parallel parking space, and light/shading impacts from the wall and screening plants. A written letter from non-attending neighbor Nora Manuel also opposed the project as harmful to neighborhood character; the applicant countered with seven prior letters of neighbor support.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, deferential to prior ZBA findings
memberPositions.evidence: Agreed with the Town Attorney that the ZBA's site-distance determination was final and outside the planning board's jurisdiction to relitigate, and moved the resolution to adoption with added conditions.

Proposed shrinking the parking space by roughly four feet (from 33 to about 29 feet) to bring it closer to standard side-yard setbacks in deference to the neighbor's proximity concerns, though the applicant argued the reduction would compromise safe ingress/egress.

Read the public hearing notice, asked about headlight glare mitigation from prior meetings, and helped negotiate resolution language requiring the fence to remain and limiting the space to a single motor vehicle with no outdoor storage.
Noted that a shorter, perpendicular pull-in space would be impractical to maneuver and that the larger parallel space made sense despite its size.

cases.name: 23 Bedford-Banksville Road — Multi-Tenant Building Site Plan & Wetlands Permit
cases.applicant: Represented by attorney Tony Veneziano and engineer Peter Gregory (DTS Providence)
cases.status: continued — resolution not ready for adoption; public hearing adjourned to a future meeting
cases.summary: The applicant is working to occupy a 15,500-square-foot multi-tenant office/storage building and establish a building-materials storage and sales yard at the rear, while relocating several existing tenants operating out of a former contractor's yard under court-supervised stipulations. Roughly 1.78 acres of wetland and wetland buffer previously used as a contractor's yard would be restored and re-naturalized. The board directed the applicant to the ARB for exterior repainting/roof work, discussed waiving construction of up to 50% of required parking as 'land banked' green space (with a requirement that any currently-paved land-banked area be ripped out and re-vegetated rather than left as unstriped asphalt), and noted Westchester County Health Department septic constraints capping occupancy at 16 people. The resolution remains open with many unresolved conditions.

memberPositions.stance: engaged, wants a genuine parking lot or genuine open space
memberPositions.evidence: Pushed back on ambiguous 'land banking' of existing paved area, insisting that if it isn't going to be built out as parking it must actually be removed and vegetated rather than left as a half-finished lot.
Asked whether customer traffic to the 16-person building would affect the parking calculation.

cases.name: 94 Business Park Drive — Loading Ramp Widening (Field Change)
cases.applicant: Property owner Jeff Mandelbaum, represented by attorney Anthony Veneziano and engineer Dan Chanel (Dynamic Engineering)
cases.status: not approved as proposed — public hearing reopened and re-adjourned; applicant directed to return with a revised, enclosed-loading solution
cases.summary: The applicant sought to widen two rear loading ramps from 16 to 20 feet, framed as a safety improvement for forklifts in winter conditions, but neighboring property owners (adjacent to an assisted-living facility) argued the real purpose was to enable outdoor loading/unloading of PODS storage containers by a prospective tenant, which the board had already precluded via a no-outdoor-storage condition in a prior hearing. After extensive debate over whether outdoor loading/unloading was an as-of-right accessory use of a PLI-zoned warehouse absent an explicit site-plan restriction, the board declined to approve the wider ramps as presented, citing the inability to police how frequently they would be used, and adjourned the hearing again so the applicant could return with a design (e.g., a fully enclosed drive-through loading configuration, as used at a prior Stop & Shop application) that keeps all loading and forklift activity inside the building.
cases.publicComment: Neighboring property owners Michael Ferraro and the Lashon family (130 Business Park Drive) strongly opposed the ramp widening, arguing it would functionally permit outdoor PODS loading/unloading next to an assisted-living facility, raising noise concerns, and objecting that the reopened hearing had not been separately re-noticed to affected neighbors.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to the ramp widening as proposed
memberPositions.evidence: Told the applicant's representative directly that the intention to use the ramps for loading/unloading was now clear on the record, and that the board could not, in fairness to the neighbors, permit an activity it could not meaningfully police; proposed an enclosed drive-through design (enter one ramp, unload inside, exit the other) as the only path forward he could support.
Named the underlying dispute as 'the elephant in the room' — whether the board would allow an operation whose primary activity is loading/unloading trucks outside the warehouse.

Questioned why the ramps were originally built if not to be used for occasional loading/unloading, but ultimately agreed the frequency of use could not be meaningfully restricted or policed once permitted.

Analyzed the PLI zoning code's off-street loading provisions with the Town Attorney to argue that outdoor loading/unloading is not an automatic as-of-right use absent explicit authorization on the site plan.

cases.name: Madonna Senior Housing — Utility Meter Pit (Field Change)
cases.applicant: Madonna property (senior housing project)
cases.summary: The board approved a minor field change to install a 5-by-10-foot concrete utility meter-pit structure in the grass area of the senior housing project, an item the applicant wanted board sign-off on before ordering the structure given its cost.

themes.note: Central to the 94 Business Park Drive PODS ramp dispute and referenced repeatedly across the meeting.
30 Palmer Avenue parking space size versus neighbor safety concerns.
Both the Palmer Avenue and Business Park Drive hearings featured pointed neighbor objections and complaints about hearing notice.
23 Bedford-Banksville Road contractor's-yard restoration and stipulated tenant departures.

staffInput.summary: Clarified procedural questions across multiple applications, including PLI zoning code interpretation for outdoor loading areas, whether a field change versus an amended site plan required renoticing, and parking land-banking rules at 23 Bedford-Banksville Road.

Advised that the board retained the authority to condition or decline the 94 Business Park Drive ramp widening regardless of the applicant's preference, and that outdoor loading/unloading is not automatically permitted as of right merely because loading ramps exist on a site plan.

meetings.attributionNote: All five board members were named directly at multiple points in this meeting (Chris, Michael, Steve, Jim, Larry), giving higher-confidence attribution than in less-attended meetings; a few brief procedural remarks could not be attributed to a specific member and were omitted.

meetings.meetingSummary: A special (non-public) work session with two applicants. First, the Manelbaum family and PODS walked the board through the storage operation and two loading/unloading layouts for a proposed PODS facility at 94 Business Park, addressing board and adjoining-neighbor concerns about noise, forklift back-up alarms, diesel exhaust, screening and visible pods; the board felt progress was made and asked for an interior staging/capacity plan. Second, the Summer Club golf-course-community residential development on Route 22 discussed outstanding water, sewer, affordable-housing (AFFH), phasing and recreation-fee issues, with the board pressing the applicant to reconcile the town water/sewer director's comments before approval and declining to close the public hearing anytime soon.

cases.name: PODS storage facility - 94 Business Park
cases.applicant: Manelbaum family / PODS
cases.summary: Work session in which the applicant's team and a PODS representative explained the operation and proposed two options (pass-through loading on the far south side vs. rear loading with a sound wall) to keep noise and loading away from the adjacent assisted-living facility. The board asked for a schematic showing interior staging and capacity and felt the meeting made progress.
cases.publicComment: Two adjoining neighbors spoke: Michael (assisted-living owner) said he was quite satisfied, felt a sound wall was unnecessary, and suggested plantings to screen the side loading; Aaron (original park developer) objected to loading appearing on the south side facing Business Park Drive and worried empty pods parked overnight would be visible, noting other neighbors also have concerns.

memberPositions.stance: Constructive; wants interior staging demonstrated before moving forward
memberPositions.evidence: Framed the outstanding issues as outdoor storage and loading/unloading and repeatedly asked the applicant to provide a schematic showing the interior staging area, straight drive aisles and building capacity so pods aren't unloaded outside.

memberPositions.stance: Wants to understand sound propagation and guaranteed interior staging
memberPositions.evidence: Asked to hear how sound would carry the length of the building before deciding whether a sound wall was worth exploring, and confirmed the interior-staging requirement was understood 'loud and clear.'

cases.name: Summer Club golf-course-community residential development (Route 22)
cases.applicant: Summer Club (golf-course community; represented by attorney Janet and engineers JMC/WSP)
cases.summary: Work session on the residential component (6 buildings, ~73 units plus amenities) of a golf-course-community floating zone. The board and town staff catalogued outstanding items - water system design, wastewater/SCADA, conservation easement, AFFH units and phasing, over-55 restriction, recreation fees, and a newly added golf maintenance building - and pressed the applicant to reconcile the town water/sewer director's comments before approval. The board made clear the public hearing (continuing Nov 14) would not close soon.

memberPositions.stance: Wants minimal conditions but key technical issues resolved before approval
memberPositions.evidence: Pushed to group conditions and get the applicant and town water/sewer director 'on the same page,' stressed that Sal's approval must precede (not be a condition of) approval, and repeatedly raised the need to tie the golf amenities to the residential build so the zoning doesn't fail.

memberPositions.stance: Insists the water/sewer items be substantially resolved before approval
memberPositions.evidence: Said 'we've got to get them, especially on the water stuff... we've got to get the bulk of these,' and argued that splitting the residential from the golf club compromises the town's position and that a baseline must be agreed.

themes.note: Town director Sal raised serious unaddressed comments (fire lines, dead-end main, SCADA/mag meters); applicant had not revised plans, a key blocker.
Two site layouts, forklift back-up alarms, sound wall and diesel exhaust discussed; board and adjacent neighbor generally receptive.
Applicant wanted many items as conditions to close the hearing fast; board wanted a shorter condition list and issues resolved up front.
Board worried that building condos before the golf clubhouse/amenities could cause the golf-course-community zoning to fail; needs a mechanism to guarantee amenities.
Concern that pods not be stored/staged or parked outside where visible; plantings proposed for the south side.
Agreement in principle exists via recorded covenant but exact unit locations and phase treatment still need to be shown on plans.

meetings.meetingSummary: A long, dense November 14, 2022 North Castle Planning Board meeting (four members present) covered eight items: an approved special use permit for an accessory apartment at 66 North Greenwich Road; a positive referral to the Town Board for a new golf-course maintenance building tied to the Summit Club (formerly Brentwood) special use permit; extensive continued design discussion on the Eagle Ridge hotel/townhome project (internal sidewalks, a hillside meadow, unit sizing, amenities-building placement) culminating in an ARB referral and a scheduled December public hearing; an initial wetlands-constrained subdivision review for 40 High Street; a contentious outdoor-storage and truck-circulation debate on a 100 Business Park Drive warehouse/self-storage redevelopment, explicitly framed by the board as a chance to correct a prior 'mistake' of tolerating uncontrolled outdoor storage; a sharp legal dispute at 428-436 Main Street over whether a 1996 parking variance covers current retail tenants absent any site plan, which the board could not resolve and punted to the Town Attorney and Building Inspector; approval to move a wetlands-buffer legalization (retaining walls, fence, driveway extension, pergola) toward a public hearing, handled by acting chair Steven Sauro after Chairman Carthy recused himself; and an approved site plan waiver for a retail-to-nail-salon change of use at 111 Bedford Road (Eli Plaza). 26 Chestnut Ridge Road was held off the agenda.
meetings.durationNote: Present: Chairman Christopher Carthy, Steven Sauro, James Jensen, Lawrence Ruisi. Michael Pollack was absent ('we have a four-person board tonight'); Chairman Carthy recused himself from the final wetlands-legalization item, with Steven Sauro presiding in his place. Town Planner Adam Kauffman, Town Attorney Roland Baroni (by phone/Zoom), and Town Engineer John Kellard participated throughout.

cases.name: 66 North Greenwich Road — Accessory Apartment Special Use Permit
cases.applicant: Adam Barnett
cases.summary: The applicant sought to reinstate legal accessory-apartment status for a longstanding cottage on his property (status lapses on any change of title), with no new construction proposed. After a neighbor's confusion was resolved by clarifying which of several nearby structures was involved, the board closed the public hearing and adopted the special use permit resolution without objection.
cases.publicComment: A neighbor initially raised concerns based on confusion about which structure was involved; after the applicant clarified the property's layout and history, no objection remained.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion to close the public hearing and to adopt the resolution granting the special use permit.

cases.name: Summit Club (formerly Brentwood) — Golf Course Maintenance Building
cases.applicationType: special use permit amendment / site plan referral
cases.applicant: Represented by Janet Keras (Del Bello, Donnellan) and architect Ken Anderson
cases.status: positive recommendation to Town Board to amend the special use permit
cases.summary: The applicant presented a new roughly 6,000-square-foot, two-story golf-course maintenance building to replace the existing facility, which sits in the way of active construction on the residential component and cannot practically coexist with ongoing golf operations. Because tying the maintenance building to the golf course's special use permit (rather than the residential site plan) requires Town Board action, the board voted a positive recommendation referring the special use permit amendment to the Town Board.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked clarifying questions about site access and truck deliveries to the new building, then supported the referral motion.
Made the motion for a positive recommendation to the Town Board on the special use permit amendment for the new maintenance building.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge — Hotel & Townhome Site Plan
cases.applicant: Toll Brothers (Eagle Ridge project), represented by Zarin & Steinmetz
cases.status: referred to ARB; public hearing scheduled for December (submission deadline November 28)
cases.summary: The board reviewed cross-sections showing the hotel's relationship to the townhouse rows, extensively debated whether to require internal sidewalks (ultimately asking the applicant to study a one-sided, curb-adjacent 4-foot sidewalk that would push the back-to-back townhouse yards roughly seven feet closer together and closer to 12-foot retaining walls) versus land-banking a future connector sidewalk toward Business Park Drive that the board acknowledged wasn't practical to build now given a dangerous Route 22 crossing. The board also discussed relocating the amenities building toward the site's interior, screening a hillside meadow near the hotel parking lot with native evergreens (e.g., red cedar) rather than converting it entirely, and pushed back on a Town Planner comment that the two-bedroom townhouse units were oversized, accepting the applicant's argument that the unit size matched market demand for 55+ housing. The board agreed to refer the project to the ARB and to schedule a public hearing for the December 12 meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed hardest for internal sidewalks so residents could walk between homes, citing a comparable Chase development in Mount Kisco, and pressed for screening/landscaping detail at multiple points including the meadow and amenities-building placement.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of a Route 22 sidewalk connection, open to internal walks
memberPositions.evidence: Questioned the practicality of a sidewalk to Route 22 given residents would likely jaywalk at the bottom of the hill instead, but engaged constructively on the internal one-sided sidewalk design.

Directed the discussion toward scheduling the public hearing after acknowledging the applicant would study a one-sided sidewalk option, and pressed the applicant's landscape architect on staged bloom/erosion performance of the proposed hillside meadow.

cases.name: 40 High Street — Two-Lot Subdivision
cases.applicant: Represented by David Cooper (Zarin & Steinmetz) for prior owners retaining subdivision rights
cases.status: initial review — referred for wetlands flagging before Conservation Board referral
cases.summary: The prior owners of a 5.8-acre parcel, who retained subdivision rights when they sold the existing house and lot to the current owner, proposed splitting off a 3.4-acre undeveloped lot. The board found the submitted plans inadequate (missing wetland boundary and buffer delineation) and directed the applicant to have a wetland scientist flag and survey the wetlands and confirm septic area location before the application could meaningfully proceed to the Conservation Board, cautioning that the buffer alone might leave little room for development.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the submitted plan was too incomplete to evaluate and warned that if the buildable area is entirely within the wetland buffer, the wetlands permit might not be grantable regardless of the application.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive — Warehouse & Self-Storage Redevelopment
cases.applicationType: site plan / subdivision, with ZBA variance referral
cases.applicant: WMG Acquisitions, represented by David Cooper (Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.status: continued — to return to the Planning Board in December before a January ZBA referral for FAR and parking variances
cases.summary: The applicant presented a revised plan flipping the proposed warehouse and self-storage uses to separate their circulation, plus added screening for loading docks and outdoor storage areas. The bulk of the discussion concerned the existing Jantile stone-fabrication tenant's history of expanding outdoor storage well beyond what was previously approved; the board explicitly cast this application as an opportunity to correct that prior 'mistake' by requiring all loading/unloading and storage to occur within building footprints and enforceable striped limits, while acknowledging the tenant's stated need for some outdoor staging. The board also flagged an incomplete site plan that omits overnight commercial-vehicle parking (which would worsen an already roughly 50-space parking shortfall) and unresolved truck-turning movements around the new building, directing the applicant to resolve both before returning in December ahead of a January ZBA referral for FAR and parking variances.

memberPositions.stance: firm that outdoor storage/loading must be enclosed and enforceable
memberPositions.evidence: Stated directly that the site has fallen visually out of step with the rest of the business park and that the board should not repeat its prior mistake of allowing outdoor storage to be abused, insisting operations be demonstrated within the building footprint.

memberPositions.stance: concerned about enforceability and truck circulation
memberPositions.evidence: Observed on a personal site visit that existing outdoor storage already extends roughly a third of the way into the footprint of the proposed new warehouse, and pressed on whether trucks could physically maneuver around the new building.

memberPositions.stance: focused on plan completeness and parking accuracy
memberPositions.evidence: Flagged that large planters shown on the plan block driveway areas inconsistent with how the site is actually used, and pressed for the plan to show real overnight truck parking so the parking variance request is accurate.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the applicant's redesign, credited with the use-flip idea
memberPositions.evidence: Was credited by the board and applicant's team for suggesting the warehouse/self-storage flip that separated the two uses' circulation, and found the loading-dock screening adequate.

cases.name: 428-436 Main Street — Retail Site Plan / Parking Variance Jurisdictional Dispute
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by attorney (surname transcribed as 'Hollis')
cases.status: unresolved — Town Attorney to confer with the Building Inspector; public hearing tentatively targeted for January
cases.summary: The applicant's attorney argued at length that a 1996 zoning board variance finding 'no parking on premises' runs with the land and covers the building's long history of successive retail tenants (a prospective baseball-card shop was the immediate trigger), such that the Building Inspector's refusal to issue permits absent a formal site plan was legally improper (citing Esposito Builders v. Kauffman and related case law). The Town Attorney countered that the planning board lacks authority to overrule the Building Inspector's zoning interpretation and that any challenge belongs before the ZBA. The board could not resolve the underlying legal dispute, declined to recommend a temporary certificate of occupancy over the Town Attorney's objection, and asked the Town Attorney to discuss the matter directly with the Building Inspector, tentatively targeting a January public hearing on a formal site plan if the dispute isn't resolved first.

memberPositions.evidence: Acknowledged the practical unfairness of treating a prospective card shop differently from a decades-long history of retail tenants, but deferred to the Town Attorney that the board could not itself override the Building Inspector's determination, and asked the Town Attorney to intervene informally to help the applicant get a temporary CO.
Asked whether the board could make a positive recommendation to the ZBA for an interpretation, trying to identify a concrete next step for the applicant.

cases.name: Wetlands Buffer Legalization — Retaining Walls, Fence, Driveway Extension & Pergola (address not stated)
cases.applicant: Not clearly stated in the recording
cases.status: advancing toward public hearing, scheduled for December 12
cases.summary: Chairman Carthy recused himself from this application (reason not stated) and Steven Sauro presided in his place. The applicant sought after-the-fact legalization of a retaining wall, front-yard fence, driveway extension, and pergola built in a wetlands buffer without proper approval; the Conservation Board had already made a positive recommendation on a DEC-approved mitigation plan. The board directed staff to schedule a public hearing for December 12 and to prepare an approval resolution.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided in the Chairman's absence, confirmed the Conservation Board's positive recommendation was sufficient to proceed, and directed staff to schedule the public hearing and prepare a resolution.

cases.name: 111 Bedford Road (Eli Plaza) — Retail-to-Nail-Salon Change of Use
cases.applicationType: change of use / site plan waiver
cases.applicant: Tenant proposing a nail salon at Eli Plaza
cases.summary: The Building Inspector advised that converting an existing retail space to a nail salon (a personal-service use) carries the same off-street parking requirement as the prior retail use, so there is no parking impact. The board granted a site plan waiver for the change of use by motion.

themes.note: Central to the 100 Business Park Drive Jantile dispute, explicitly framed as correcting a prior board 'mistake'.
Extended Eagle Ridge debate over internal sidewalks versus a Route 22 connector.
40 High Street subdivision and the recused-chair legalization case.
428-436 Main Street's sharp disagreement over Building Inspector authority versus a decades-old variance.

staffInput.summary: Guided referral sequencing on the Summit Club maintenance building and Eagle Ridge applications, raised concerns about townhouse unit size and amenities-building placement at Eagle Ridge, flagged incomplete wetland delineation at 40 High Street, and pressed for a complete truck-parking picture at 100 Business Park Drive; also disputed the applicant's variance interpretation at 428-436 Main Street.

Advised (via Zoom, with initial audio difficulties) that the planning board lacks authority to overrule the Building Inspector's zoning interpretation at 428-436 Main Street and that jurisdiction lies with the ZBA or a court; also addressed the Eagle Ridge community-benefit funding question and the enforceability of outdoor-storage lease conditions at 100 Business Park Drive.
Advised on sidewalk width/clearance requirements at Eagle Ridge, weighed in on truck-turning feasibility at 100 Business Park Drive, and reviewed wetland/septic siting questions at 40 High Street.

meetings.attributionNote: Only four of five board members attended (Michael Pollack absent), and Chairman Carthy recused himself from the final wetlands-legalization item without stating a reason, so attribution for that case rests on Steven Sauro as presiding member. Two case addresses (the Summit Club maintenance building and the final wetlands-legalization item) were not clearly stated in the ASR audio and are left blank.

meetings.meetingSummary: A packed November 28, 2022 North Castle Planning Board meeting handled two public hearings and roughly a dozen other items. The board adjourned the 26 Chestnut Ridge Road fill-violation hearing again, asking the applicant to prepare two grading alternatives for a full board's review; closed the 94 Business Park Drive PODS hearing and adopted a heavily negotiated resolution restricting outdoor loading, staging, container storage, and dumpster use; advanced several after-the-fact violation legalizations (33 Woodland Road pool, 360 Main Street gas station/convenience store, 4 Tripp Lane fill and tree removal) with continued information-gathering; made positive referrals to the Town Board (731 North Broadway apartment conversion, 101 Old Hickory Way paper-road sale) and to the ZBA (33 Woodland Road); voiced sharp frustration with a still-unresolved tenant-occupancy parking/coverage application and with the pace of the 4 Tripp Lane violation remediation, prompting board member Christopher Carthy to raise a broader policy question about incentivizing timely correction of zoning violations; and granted several routine subdivision-approval time extensions.
meetings.durationNote: Board attendance appears to have started short-handed — a resolution vote on 26 Chestnut Ridge Road was deliberately deferred because the board was 'short two board members' — but a later unanimous 5-0 vote on the 731 North Broadway referral indicates the full board (Christopher Carthy, Michael Pollack, Steven Sauro, James Jensen, Lawrence Ruisi) was present later in the meeting. Town Planner Adam Kauffman, Town Attorney Roland Baroni, Town Engineer John Kellard, and consulting geologist Bill Canavan participated throughout.

cases.name: 26 Chestnut Ridge Road — Fill Import Violation & Soil Remediation
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by JMC Engineering (Rick Bolander)
cases.status: continued — public hearing adjourned again pending two alternative grading plans and a full board
cases.summary: The applicant's engineer revealed that simply capping the contaminated (nickel-elevated) fill in place with 24 inches of clean soil, as previously discussed, would not work with existing site grading without spreading the fill outward roughly 10-15% beyond the current disturbance area. The town's geologist, Bill Canavan, reaffirmed that DEC had endorsed a 24-inch cap and demarcation layer as adequate and that nickel at the levels found poses no meaningful health or groundwater risk, while the Town Attorney cautioned that a deed covenant might be unwarranted overkill given the soil scientist's findings. The board asked the applicant to prepare two alternatives — spreading the fill farther out with a wider cap, versus regrading to keep the disturbance within the previously discussed limits — and adjourned to allow a full complement of the board to weigh in.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed for clarity on how the grading would actually work if the fill were left in place versus spread out, and suggested the board wait for a full complement of members to have both alternatives before deciding.

cases.name: 94 Business Park Drive — Loading Ramp Widening (Field Change)
cases.applicant: Property owner Jeff Mandelbaum, represented by attorney Anthony Veneziano; PODS as prospective tenant
cases.status: approved — public hearing closed and resolution adopted as amended
cases.summary: The applicant returned with a significantly revised approach: PODS containers would be driven through the building on a ramp rather than loaded outdoors, with a small designated area on the building's south side (acting as a sound barrier toward sensitive receptors) reserved only for multi-container trailer trucks. A PODS representative walked the board through how internal staging would work even with the warehouse full, without ever needing to store or stage containers outdoors. After extensive line-by-line resolution editing — clarifying that all staging must occur indoors while only loading/unloading of multi-pod trucks may occur in the designated exterior area, prohibiting container storage anywhere outside the building, limiting overnight truck parking to a depicted rear area, restricting use to a single (southern) dumpster to protect neighbors from early-morning noise, and requiring additional street-facing landscaping/evergreen screening — the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended.
cases.publicComment: Neighbors Michael Ferraro and Ed Lashon acknowledged the applicant's significant concessions and thanked the Mandelbaum family, while pressing for stronger, more explicit language prohibiting all outdoor container storage, taller/denser screening trees on the south property line, softening the building's street-facing facade with additional trees, and eliminating the northern dumpster location closest to the neighboring Bristol property.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed to tighten resolution language so that staging is explicitly required indoors while only designated-area loading/unloading is allowed outdoors, closing a loophole in the draft language.
Walked through the PODS staging scenario in detail with the applicant's team to confirm no outdoor staging would ever be needed, then moved the resolution to adoption as amended.

cases.name: 33 Woodland Road — Pool in Wetland Buffer / Front-Yard Area Variance
cases.applicationType: site plan / area variance / wetlands permit
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by Dean (project representative)
cases.status: referred to ZBA with a positive recommendation; awaiting Conservation Board resolution
cases.summary: A proposed pool sits entirely within a wetland buffer and, due to the lot's awkward shape, effectively falls in the front yard, exceeding the maximum area allowed there and requiring a ZBA area variance. With the Conservation Board review already underway (a formal recommendation was expected but not yet in hand), the board referred the applicant to the ZBA with a positive recommendation so that process could proceed in parallel, planning to schedule its own public hearing once the ZBA variance and Conservation Board paperwork are complete.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion to refer the application to the ZBA with a positive recommendation.

cases.name: 360 Main Street — Gas Station/Convenience Store Legalization
cases.applicant: Zaidan Realty, represented by Corey Salamone (Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.status: continued — public hearing to be opened and adjourned once outstanding lease/structure questions are resolved
cases.summary: Following a notice of violation, the applicant is legalizing existing site conditions (propane tanks, air pumps, refuse area, tow-truck overnight parking) at a gas station/convenience store, plus adding three rear storage containers, after abandoning an earlier plan to expand the convenience store. A key complication is that part of the parking area sits on town-owned land under a decades-old lease to the site's mechanic tenant, whose lease payments are seriously delinquent and must be brought current before the lease can be assigned to the new owner and the planning board can proceed; the board also asked whether an oil storage tank needs to be shown as a structure. The board indicated it is close to being able to open and hold (or adjourn) a public hearing once these items are clarified.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked detailed questions about the lease term, renewal structure, and whether rent adjustments were tied to CPI, working through the town-land parking arrangement with the Town Attorney.

cases.name: 731 North Broadway (Bedrock Plaza) — Office-to-Apartment Conversion
cases.applicationType: change of use / special permit referral
cases.applicant: Property owner (Bedrock Plaza)
cases.status: approved — positive recommendation to Town Board, 5-0
cases.summary: The applicant sought to convert two second-floor office suites to two additional apartments (bringing the total to four second-floor apartments) in a building already operating under a substantial 2005 parking variance. Because apartment use requires less parking than office use under the code, the conversion actually reduces the property's parking deficiency (from an 18-space shortfall to roughly an 11-space shortfall) even though it adds units, and more than one apartment in a commercial building requires Town Board special-permit approval. The board voted unanimously (5-0) to refer the application to the Town Board with a positive recommendation.

cases.name: 4 Tripp Lane — Unpermitted Fill & Tree Removal Legalization
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by Rick (engineer)
cases.status: continued — awaiting soil testing report, wetland connectivity analysis, and Conservation Board referral
cases.summary: The applicant is attempting to legalize roughly 2,600 cubic yards of unpermitted fill and the removal of an estimated 171 trees. Soil testing found elevated lead, copper, and pesticide residues (DDE/dieldrin), for which the town's geologist recommended a similar demarcation-and-cap approach as at 26 Chestnut Ridge Road, though board members noted this site appears more contaminated and the disturbance far larger. The board also questioned whether the fill disturbed a wetland connection between neighboring properties, requiring further investigation before a Conservation Board referral. Frustrated that the violation dated back roughly two years with slow progress, Christopher Carthy raised a broader concern — beyond this board's authority — that the town lacks a system to incentivize applicants to correct zoning violations promptly rather than benefiting from delay, and asked staff to relay that concern to the Town Board liaison.

memberPositions.stance: frustrated with delay, seeking policy fix
memberPositions.evidence: Pointedly asked how the board can create incentives for applicants to correct unpermitted work more quickly, noting the memos on this matter date back to 2020 and that the board is still in the information-gathering stage two years later, and asked staff to communicate the board's frustration to the Town Board.

cases.name: 101 Old Hickory Way — Town Paper-Road Parcel Sale Referral
cases.applicant: Samantha Marina Vic (adjacent property owner)
cases.status: positive recommendation to Town Board (no planning objection to the sale)
