cases.summary: A resident with only a shared, poorly-maintained private-road access sought the board's opinion on the Town Board's proposed sale of an unimproved paper-road parcel (obtained by tax foreclosure) connecting her driveway to Pine Ridge, which is subject to a retained emergency-access easement regardless of ownership. After discussing a possible wetland/stream crossing and conservation easement on the parcel needing a survey, and confirming the sale itself would not worsen conditions (since the Highway Department had already closed the connection), the board recommended no planning objection to the sale, leaving any future driveway/road improvement plans to be reviewed separately by the board and Town Engineer.

cases.name: 10 New King Street — Landscape Equipment Storage Area Expansion
cases.applicant: Navara Landscaping (tenant), represented by Martin Deano (H2M architects/engineers)
cases.status: continued — board to conduct a site walk before further review
cases.summary: A landscaping company already permitted to store equipment as a use customarily incident to its office tenancy sought to expand its fenced storage area further into an adjacent overflow parking lot. Board members expressed concern that the landscape business appeared to be overtaking what was originally approved as an office use, questioned the poor physical condition of the existing overflow lot, and were uncertain whether the expansion was reasonable without seeing the site firsthand; the board opted to schedule a site walk and have the applicant return with more information rather than decide that night.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he did not feel he knew enough to make an intelligent decision and suggested a site walk before proceeding further.

cases.name: 901 North Broadway — Church Site Plan, Special Permit & Coverage/Parking Variances
cases.applicant: Building owner's architect (Mr. Fleming), for a prospective tenant described as a church
cases.status: continued — applicant's fifth appearance without complete information; to resubmit before returning
cases.summary: In what board members called the applicant's fifth appearance on this matter, the board remained unable to move forward because the landlord's architect had not supplied complete floor plans and an accurate parking calculation using code-defined use categories (submitted materials used an undefined 'business use' category instead of 'office use'). The board needs the building/lot coverage figures to refer the matter to the ZBA for a variance and needs the corrected parking chart to confirm the roughly 100 required spaces are actually available, including whether some spaces near an adjacent gas station are properly available for the office building's exclusive use under the town's shared-parking rule. Board members expressed visible frustration at the repeated, incomplete submissions and offered to meet directly with the architect to walk through exactly what is needed.

memberPositions.evidence: Walked through the parking-chart discrepancies use-by-use with the applicant's representative, noted the plan is 'mostly right but not 100 percent,' and offered to hold a dedicated working meeting to resolve it.

themes.note: Resolved at 94 Business Park Drive; still unresolved at 10 New King Street and looming at 4 Tripp Lane.
Central to 731 North Broadway, 360 Main Street, and the unresolved 901 North Broadway church application.
33 Woodland Road, 4 Tripp Lane, and 101 Old Hickory Way all touch wetland or conservation-easement questions.

staffInput.summary: Guided nearly every application on the agenda, including flagging that the 26 Chestnut Ridge Road grading fix would increase the disturbance area, walking through the parking-variance math for 731 North Broadway, explaining the town-land lease complication at 360 Main Street, and repeatedly pressing for a complete, code-compliant parking chart from the unresolved tenant-occupancy applicant.

Explained DEC's endorsement of a 24-inch clean-soil cap over a demarcation layer at 26 Chestnut Ridge Road and recommended a similar approach at 4 Tripp Lane, characterizing nickel and the other detected constituents as common, low-mobility soil metals not posing a meaningful groundwater or health risk at the concentrations found.

Advised that a deed covenant may be unwarranted overkill at 26 Chestnut Ridge Road given the geologist's findings, addressed the town-land lease and easement questions at 360 Main Street and 101 Old Hickory Way, and confirmed enforcement of zoning violations rests with the Building Inspector and courts rather than the planning board.
Weighed in on grading and drainage feasibility questions across several site plans and on the paper-road survey/emergency-access questions at 101 Old Hickory Way.

meetings.attributionNote: The board appears to have started this meeting short two members before reaching a full 5-0 vote later on, and several procedural exchanges could not be confidently attributed to a specific named member. The 901 North Broadway church application's address was not stated in this meeting's ASR audio and was confirmed from the December 12, 2022 meeting's transcript instead.

meetings.meetingSummary: The December 12, 2022 North Castle Planning Board meeting opened with Chairman Carthy announcing a procedural change (bringing town professionals up before applicants). The board effectively decided to deny the fill permit at 26 Chestnut Ridge Road and require removal of the imported soil rather than accept a covenant or demarcation-layer compromise, after the applicant's engineer showed neither in-place capping option could be graded without expanding the disturbed area; approved a wetlands-violation resolution at 84 Round Hill Road with Chairman Carthy recused; continued an extensive, unresolved sidewalk/fire-code/unit-size debate on the Eagle Ridge project; cleared the long-stalled 901 North Broadway church site plan onto the Town Board and ZBA; advanced a landscape-storage-yard expansion at 10 New King Street to the ZBA; sent a deficient retaining-wall application at 5 [Melon] Avenue back for proper survey data; narrowly referred the contentious 100 Business Park Drive warehouse/self-storage project to the ZBA without a board recommendation (3-1, after a first attempt to attach a positive recommendation failed to pass) amid sharp disagreement over a roughly 50% FAR variance; and reviewed a new Bedford-Banksville Road lot-merger/guest-house project that will need multiple ZBA variances, to return with revised plans in January.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy, Michael Pollack, James Jensen, and Steven Sauro were active for most of the meeting; Lawrence Ruisi arrived late/was briefly absent (a motion on 100 Business Park Drive was explicitly held to wait for his return). Chairman Carthy recused himself from the 84 Round Hill Road application, with Steven Sauro presiding in his place. Town Planner Adam Kauffman, Town Attorney Roland Baroni, Town Engineer John Kellard, and Conservation Board representative George Drapho participated.

cases.name: 26 Chestnut Ridge Road — Fill Import Violation & Soil Remediation
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by JMC Engineering (Rick Bolander)
cases.status: board directed staff to prepare a resolution denying the fill permit and requiring removal of the imported soil; public hearing adjourned to January 23
cases.summary: The applicant's engineer confirmed that capping the fill in place with two feet of clean soil is not gradeable without either expanding the disturbed area by about 15% or removing roughly 1,000 cubic yards of the existing restricted-use soil — there is no option that avoids one or the other. After private legal counsel, the board concluded it could not in good conscience allow the soil to remain without a deed covenant, but also did not want to burden the property with a covenant given the soil scientist's view that the nickel levels were not seriously hazardous; a brief discussion of commissioning new, independent (town-selected and town-paid) soil testing was raised but judged likely to be expensive and to lead back to the same conclusion. The board settled on directing staff to prepare a resolution denying the fill permit and requiring the improperly imported soil be removed, effectively restoring the site to its pre-violation condition, after which the applicant could file a new fill permit application with a clean grading plan.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to leaving the fill in place without a covenant, favors denial
memberPositions.evidence: Stated the board could not move forward without a covenant, said he disliked that option too, and proposed denying the fill permit and requiring removal as the cleanest resolution, inviting other board members' input.

memberPositions.stance: agrees removal is the most direct fix
memberPositions.evidence: Argued that every remaining option (covenant, no covenant) has real downsides, and that removing the improperly imported soil most directly and effectively addresses the underlying problem without disadvantaging a future purchaser.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of removal, skeptical of retesting as an alternative
memberPositions.evidence: Questioned how retesting could change objective facts already established by a proper sampling protocol, and endorsed removal, prepared by staff for a resolution, as the more decisive path.
Engaged in the discussion of retesting costs and logistics, ultimately concurring that removal without a covenant was the simplest and cleanest path forward.

cases.name: 84 Round Hill Road — Wetland Buffer Disturbance Without a Permit
cases.applicant: Property owner
cases.summary: Following a positive Conservation Board recommendation on a mitigation plan for unpermitted wetland-buffer disturbance, the board closed the public hearing and adopted an approval resolution, resolving disputes over draft conditions by keeping a required 85% plant-survival standard (over the applicant's request to drop it, per a New York State DEC-derived local practice explained by Conservation Board representative George Drapho), dropping an ambiguous 'reserves the right to encore local laws' clause as apparent language error, and adding an explicit annual access easement for town inspection consistent with the five-year monitoring plan.

memberPositions.evidence: Presided in Chairman Carthy's recusal, worked through each resolution condition with the applicant's attorney and the Conservation Board representative, and moved to close the hearing and adopt the resolution as amended.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge — Hotel & Townhome Site Plan
cases.applicant: Toll Brothers (Eagle Ridge project), represented by Zarin & Steinmetz
cases.status: public hearing kept open, no date certain — applicant to revise and resubmit
cases.summary: The board pressed hard on whether to require internal sidewalks along at least one side of each street, learning that doing so would push townhouse backyards roughly four feet closer to already-tall retaining walls and that the end-user (Toll Brothers) opposed sidewalks as an HOA maintenance burden with little real use; the applicant also revealed that a New York State fire code update may require 26-foot-wide roadway sections near fire hydrants (versus the planned 24 feet), which would compound the sidewalk-driven space crunch on the dead-end road. Michael Pollack and James Jensen argued walkability was effectively promised during the environmental review and findings-statement process for this age-restricted community and pushed back on the applicant's claim it was merely 'encouraged'; Steven Sauro was reluctant to force a decision without seeing a fully engineered alternative. The board also discussed relocating the pool/amenities building to a more central, less roadside location (leaving the choice to the applicant) and confirmed the applicant had separately obtained a ZBA variance for the fourth hotel story and a Town Board hearing on the amended findings statement. No sidewalk decision was reached; the hearing was kept open pending revised plans.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued that in a senior community without sidewalks, residents have no way to visit neighbors except by walking in the road, and pressed the applicant on whether unit floor plans could be tightened to make room without simply prioritizing yard size over walkability.

memberPositions.stance: sidewalk advocate, ties to prior environmental review commitments
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the environmental review and findings statement treated sidewalks as part of the project's design commitments, not merely a menu option the applicant could now decline.

memberPositions.stance: undecided, wants to see engineering detail
memberPositions.evidence: Said he was not ready to take a firm position on sidewalks and preferred to consider the design holistically alongside the fire-code road-width issue rather than in isolation.

cases.name: 901 North Broadway — Church Site Plan, Special Permit & Coverage/Parking Variances
cases.applicationType: site plan / special permit / variance referral
cases.applicant: Building owner's architect (Mr. Fleming), for a prospective church tenant
cases.status: advancing — Town Board referral to ZBA for building/lot coverage variance this week; special permit to follow
cases.summary: After repeated incomplete submissions across several prior meetings, the applicant finally supplied sufficient floor plans and a corrected, code-compliant parking calculation, allowing the board to combine its special permit and site plan review. The board agreed to waive one of two required loading spaces and approved a mechanism allowing a rear triangle of parking currently leased to an adjacent gas station to instead serve the office building (since sufficient parking exists elsewhere in the lot to cover the leased area). The Town Board was slated to refer the matter to the ZBA for a building/lot coverage variance the same week, after which the Town Board could issue the special permit and the planning board could hold its hearing and adopt a resolution.

cases.name: 10 New King Street — Landscape Equipment Storage Area Expansion
cases.applicationType: site plan amendment / fence height variance
cases.applicant: Navara Landscaping (tenant), represented by Martin Deano (H2M architects/engineers)
cases.status: referred to ZBA with a positive recommendation for the 8-foot fence variance; contingent on continued tenancy
cases.summary: After a site visit, the board revisited concerns that a landscaping tenant's storage yard had expanded well beyond the vehicle-parking use originally approved years earlier, now including stockpiles, equipment, and a stump grinder in an unpaved, poorly maintained overflow lot. James Jensen pressed on whether this was drifting into an inappropriate 'contractor's yard,' but ultimately the board found the roughly 1,000-square-foot expansion nominal and appropriate given the site's industrial, airport-adjacent location, asked for a few evergreens to soften the area, and voted to refer the application to the ZBA with a positive recommendation for the required 8-foot fence height variance, with the resolution to make clear the use expires if Navara's tenancy ends.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed on whether the expanding use amounted to a contractor's yard beyond the original vehicle-parking approval, ultimately accepting it as a modest expansion tied to continued tenancy.

cases.name: 5 [Melon] Avenue — Retaining Wall Height / Topography Verification
cases.applicant: Not named in the recording
cases.status: sent back for updated survey — plan deemed deficient
cases.summary: Referred from the RPRC over concern that proposed retaining walls may exceed the six-foot threshold requiring planning board approval, the applicant resubmitted the same plan reviewed by the RPRC without updated, source-verified topography. The board found the submission deficient, directing the applicant to have a licensed surveyor produce updated topographic data before the application can be meaningfully reviewed, and noted the item may not have belonged on the agenda given possibly unpaid application fees.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the plan was deficient because its topography source was unknown and unverified, and directed the applicant to obtain a proper survey before returning.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive — Warehouse & Self-Storage Redevelopment
cases.applicationType: site plan / ZBA variance referral (FAR, parking)
cases.applicant: WMG Acquisitions, represented by Corey Salamone (Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.status: referred to ZBA without a board recommendation, 3-1 (a prior motion for a positive recommendation failed for lack of majority support)
cases.summary: The board debated at length whether to support roughly a 50% FAR variance (0.30 to 0.43) driven by a proposed three-level self-storage component, alongside a 57-space parking variance. Current tenant Jantile's owner testified that all loading/unloading occurs at interior loading docks and none outdoors, and that any additional storage needs would go into the new building rather than expand outdoor storage; Steven Sauro supported keeping outdoor storage within previously approved limits, while Michael Pollack argued forcefully that granting such a large FAR variance for converted interior volume set a troubling precedent ('opens the floodgates') that any warehouse tenant could exploit, and Christopher Carthy voiced similar concerns about departing from the district's 0.3 FAR policy judgment. A motion for a positive ZBA recommendation failed to pass; the board then, after waiting for Lawrence Ruisi to return, passed a motion (3-1) to refer the application to the ZBA without any recommendation, leaving the variance merits for the ZBA to weigh independently.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to the FAR variance as precedent-setting
memberPositions.evidence: Argued that converting warehouse ceiling volume into a nearly 50% FAR increase via self-storage floors sets a template any similarly-built warehouse tenant could invoke, calling it 'opportunistic' rather than sound planning, and voted against a positive referral.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of the FAR variance, deferential to ZBA process
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the 0.3 FAR was a deliberate legislative policy choice for the district that a case-by-case variance risks undermining, while acknowledging the ZBA has the statutory role to weigh the balancing test.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the applicant's outdoor storage plan and use
memberPositions.evidence: Said he had been consistent throughout in supporting outdoor storage within the previously approved footprint, noting the new building and existing fencing effectively pen the tenant in from expanding further.

memberPositions.stance: engaged, ultimately reassured on outdoor storage
memberPositions.evidence: Asked the current tenant to explain on the record exactly how material moves through the site, and found it 'helpful' to learn that no trucks are loaded or unloaded outdoors, only via interior loading docks.

cases.name: Bedford-Banksville Road — Guest House/Garage Expansion & Lot-Merger Variances
cases.address: Bedford-Banksville Road (exact house number unclear in recording)
cases.applicationType: site plan / variance referral (FAR, lot coverage)
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by Peter Hollis (Hollis, Laidlaw & Simon)
cases.status: initial review — applicant to revise plans and return January 23
cases.summary: The applicant owns two non-contiguous lots (a developed 6.02-acre parcel and a substantially vacant 4.35-acre parcel) and proposes to deed-restrict the vacant parcel against further development in exchange for greater density on the developed parcel — replacing a deteriorated guest house and garage with a new guest house, garage, expanded pool, and pool house clustered near the existing main house and barn, preserving the pastoral roadside viewshed of the vacant lot. The project will require FAR and lot-coverage variances from the ZBA; the board pressed the applicant to eliminate a proposed connector structure between the main house and guest house (which would otherwise count toward building coverage) and to formalize in a deed restriction that the two lots cannot be sold or transferred separately, so the undeveloped parcel cannot fall into disrepair under a future owner. The applicant will revise plans and return January 23 before a ZBA referral.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, wants deed restriction to bind the lots together
memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the deed restriction could ensure the developed and undeveloped lots could never be sold or transferred separately, so the vacant lot could not fall into disrepair under a different future owner.

themes.note: Sharp board division at 100 Business Park Drive; also central to the Bedford-Banksville Road lot-merger case.
26 Chestnut Ridge Road moved toward denial and required soil removal.
Extended, unresolved Eagle Ridge debate intersecting with a fire-code road-width requirement.
84 Round Hill Road approved smoothly after Conservation Board sign-off.

staffInput.summary: Advocated strongly for sidewalks at Eagle Ridge as consistent with the findings statement and comprehensive plan, guided the 901 North Broadway church application to a workable parking/coverage resolution, flagged the deficient topography at 5 Melon Avenue, and framed the FAR/parking variance issues for 100 Business Park Drive.

Advised in executive session on the 26 Chestnut Ridge Road covenant question, clarified that outdoor-storage conditions cannot automatically trigger planning board re-review upon a violation (enforcement remains a judicial matter), and worked through the deed-restriction mechanics tying the two Bedford-Banksville Road lots together.

Confirmed there is no practical way to add two feet of clean fill at 26 Chestnut Ridge Road without either removing existing soil or expanding the disturbance area, and reviewed truck-turning and fire-access documentation at 100 Business Park Drive.

Explained the Conservation Board's rationale for stricter local wetland standards (including an 85% plant-survival requirement) taking precedence over less-stringent DEC guidance at 84 Round Hill Road.

meetings.attributionNote: Board members were named frequently and directly throughout this meeting (Chris, Michael, Jim, Steve, Larry), including on a closely divided FAR-variance vote, giving high-confidence attribution for most positions. Two case addresses (901 North Broadway, now confirmed from context, and a Bedford-Banksville Road house number) required cross-referencing prior/later meeting context or remain partly uncertain.

meetings.meetingSummary: The first North Castle Planning Board meeting of 2023 opened with tributes to retiring longtime secretary Valerie Desamone. The board closed the 360 Main Street gas station legalization hearing and referred it to the ZBA for two setback variances while asking staff to explore modest state-right-of-way landscaping; held its decisive debate on internal sidewalks at Eagle Ridge, with a 3-2 board lean (Sauro, Ruisi, Carthy against; Pollack and Jensen wanting more analysis) toward accepting 26-foot-wide roads without sidewalks; approved a rock-crushing permit at 45 Herrlingham Drive with dust-control conditions; opened review of a new single-family house at [1613] Old Orchard Street entirely within a wetland buffer, with a strong push from the landscape architect to use the project to eradicate an invasive-species monoculture; continued the 78 Lafayette Avenue warehouse expansion toward ARB referral; reviewed a conceptual three-lot reconfiguration on a 2009-approved subdivision; made several recommendations to the Town Board on Summit Club golf course special-permit matters (temporary permit extension, public golf during construction, maintenance building siting); and recommended Town Board adoption of a two-year extension to an affordable-housing completion deadline for a separate project.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present: Chairman Christopher Carthy, Steven Sauro, James Jensen, Michael Pollack, Lawrence Ruisi. Town Planner Adam Kauffman and Town Attorney Roland Baroni participated throughout; a Town Engineer referred to as 'Joe' (apparently a personnel change from John Kellard) also participated. This was outgoing planning board secretary Valerie Desamone's final meeting.

cases.name: 360 Main Street — Gas Station/Convenience Store Legalization
cases.applicant: Zaidan Realty, represented by Corey Salamone (Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.status: public hearing closed; referred to ZBA for two setback variances
cases.summary: The applicant is legalizing existing gas station conditions (storage sheds, oil storage, dumpster, vacuum, propane exchange, air pumps) and needs ZBA variances for an oil tank set only 4.3 feet from a 30-foot setback line and a gas pump 9.1 feet from a required roughly 15-foot setback. The board spent considerable time discussing whether a prominent Route 128 median/landscape island (in the state right-of-way) could be improved aesthetically beyond its current cobblestone treatment, concluding any planting would need DOT approval and asking staff to bring back a previously-proposed landscape plan for reference at a future meeting. The board closed the public hearing and referred the applicant to the ZBA for the two variances.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed the board to consider modest plantings to beautify the prominent Route 128 island, while acknowledging DOT approval and maintenance responsibility (likely falling to the gas station) were open questions.
Suggested planters or an evergreen hedge rather than trees, noting DOT was unlikely to want anything requiring active maintenance in the right-of-way.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge — Hotel & Townhome Site Plan
cases.applicant: Toll Brothers (Eagle Ridge project), represented by Corey Salamone (Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.status: board gave direction to proceed without internal sidewalks (26-foot roads instead); public hearing adjourned pending final plans
cases.summary: In the meeting's central and most extended debate, the applicant argued that internal sidewalks are incompatible with the site's tight townhouse layout and topography — requiring roughly seven feet of additional width per road that would push units closer to already-tall retaining walls — and offered 26-foot-wide roads (versus a 24-foot minimum) throughout as a walkability compromise instead of sidewalks. The board reviewed a Westchester County Planning Board advisory memo (which raised age-restriction and regional-connectivity concerns the board found largely outside its jurisdiction, since those parameters were fixed by the Town Board's zoning and findings statement) and debated at length whether the project's environmental findings statement effectively committed the applicant to sidewalks, with Michael Pollack and James Jensen arguing the board had never been shown a quantified trade-off (e.g., smaller units freeing room for sidewalks) while Steven Sauro, Lawrence Ruisi, and Chairman Carthy concluded sidewalks were impractical here and that requiring them risked killing project viability. The Chairman summarized a 3-2 board lean toward moving forward without sidewalks and directed the applicant to finalize plans on that basis; the hearing was adjourned without a date certain.

memberPositions.evidence: Concluded after hearing all arguments that the community could function without sidewalks and would likely produce a better overall product without them, while acknowledging the decision was a difficult one, and summarized the board's 3-2 lean to send the applicant forward on that basis.

Argued that a sidewalk on only one side of the street would leave half the homes without direct access anyway, questioned added HOA maintenance, insurance/liability, and irrigation costs, and concluded the 26-foot road width itself provided a walkability benefit (room for two cars to pass, including one parked curbside).

memberPositions.stance: against requiring sidewalks, cites project viability
memberPositions.evidence: Drew on his development experience to warn that forcing further compression of the site (to fit sidewalks) risks project economics reaching 'the point of no return' where the applicant walks away, and cited a nearby sidewalk-free development (The Enclave) as a successful precedent.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of dropping sidewalks without quantified trade-off analysis
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the board's job is good planning, not developer economics, and repeatedly asked to see the FAR-versus-open-space trade-off quantified (e.g., how much room compressing unit dimensions by a foot or two would free up) before accepting that sidewalks are infeasible.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical, ties sidewalks to findings-statement commitments
memberPositions.evidence: Read from the project's findings statement language explicitly describing sidewalks connecting the townhouse community to the hotel and pointed out the county's letter had flagged the same features as having fallen out of the current plan.

cases.name: 45 Herrlingham Drive — Rock Crushing Permit
cases.applicant: Whitehall Home Development Corporation, represented by Phil Van Galder
cases.summary: The applicant sought approval to bring a mobile crusher onto a large Conyers Farm estate lot (accessed entirely through Connecticut, with minimal North Castle road impact) to process on-site blasted rock rather than trucking 150-200 truckloads off-site, at the request of the Conyers Farm HOA. The board's main concern was dust control for the single nearby (Connecticut-side) neighbor; the applicant described a water-fed crushing system and a sound-barrier berm, and the board approved the permit conditioned on weekday 9am-4pm hours and an automatic stop-work requirement if the machine's water/dust-suppression system fails.

memberPositions.stance: supportive with a firm dust-control condition
memberPositions.evidence: Recalled a prior application where a neighbor was reduced to tears by dust, praised the town engineer's memo on the issue, and proposed the condition that crushing must stop if the machine's irrigation/dust-suppression system malfunctions.

Ran an online sound-attenuation calculation showing crusher noise would still reach roughly 93 decibels at the nearest home 110 feet away, prompting discussion of the applicant's planned sound-barrier berm.

cases.name: Old Orchard Street — Single-Family House Entirely in Wetland Buffer
cases.applicant: Represented by Ralph (project engineer) and landscape architect Steve Lopez
cases.status: referred to Conservation Board pending a landscape mitigation plan
cases.summary: A proposed roughly 4,000-square-foot, four-bedroom house on a constrained, oddly-shaped one-acre lot sits 100% within a wetland buffer, though it does not disturb the wetland itself. Landscape architect Steve Lopez urged the board to see the project as an opportunity to eradicate an aggressive invasive-species monoculture currently covering the site and replace it with a diverse, roughly two-dozen-species native planting plan that would restore biodiversity, characterizing the current condition as an ecological 'desert.' The board also flagged that the driveway's proposed sightlines cross onto a neighboring property, requiring either a redesigned driveway or a negotiated easement. The board referred the application to the Conservation Board even before receiving the landscape plan, with the understanding it will return for further review.

memberPositions.stance: neutral, wants to see the buildable constraints firsthand
memberPositions.evidence: Said the board would walk the site with the Conservation Board and asked whether the house size could be scaled down to reduce buffer disturbance, while acknowledging a smaller single-family house is difficult to make marketable.

cases.name: 78 Lafayette Avenue — Warehouse Building Expansion
cases.applicant: Represented by project engineer Ralph
cases.status: continued — floor plans/elevations submitted; heading to ARB
cases.summary: With elevations now submitted, the board focused on a tight roughly 12-13-foot secondary driveway pinch point, retaining walls up to about 40 feet high requiring temporary construction easements onto a neighbor's property (with the neighbor's informal consent), and screening for the wall facing residential properties below — questioning whether Norway spruce trees are appropriate or safe to maintain on such a steep drop and suggesting lower shrubs instead. The board indicated it was comfortable sending the application to the ARB once floor plans and elevations are finalized.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether large evergreens could realistically be planted or maintained atop a 40-foot retaining wall drop and suggested the landscape plan needed more refinement, possibly using shrubs instead of trees.

cases.name: 246 Sorel Court — Three-Lot Subdivision Reconfiguration (Concept Plan)
cases.applicant: Represented by Michael Stein (Hudson Engineering)
cases.status: conceptual review — applicant to select a preferred layout and resubmit
cases.summary: Revisiting a 2009-approved three-lot, two-family-home subdivision, the applicant presented two conceptual alternatives to reallocate lot area more evenly among the three lots (rather than one large rear lot and two smaller front lots) to better match neighborhood character and reduce steep-slope disturbance. The board found both concepts had merit, suggested reorienting the rear two units to face each other at less crowding along the shared driveway, and left it to the applicant to select a preferred alternative and resubmit for formal review.

memberPositions.evidence: Suggested reorienting the two rear units so their driveways and entries related to each other more comfortably rather than facing straight in, which the applicant agreed to explore.

cases.name: Summit Club — Golf Course Special Use Permit (Temporary Extension, Public Golf, Maintenance Facility)
cases.applicant: Represented by Mark Weingarten (Del Bello, Donnellan) and Jeff Mandelbaum
cases.status: positive recommendations to Town Board on two of three requests; permanent special use permit deferred pending more information
cases.summary: Responding to a Town Board referral, the board recommended a six-month extension of the golf course's expired temporary special use permit and endorsed a request to allow public (non-member) golf bookings during the residential construction period to help the club's finances, while asking the Town Board to have counsel review the specific zoning code amendment language needed. The board also endorsed, in concept, locating a new maintenance and storage building on the golf course lot (relocating it out of the path of residential construction) as part of the eventual special use permit, but declined to recommend the permanent special use permit itself, since Town Planner Kauffman's memo still had open questions about club operations, membership caps, and chemical storage that the applicant agreed to address promptly.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motions recommending the temporary permit extension and the public-golf-during-construction request to the Town Board.
Supported the concept of public golf during construction but asked that the specific zoning code amendment language be reviewed by Town Board counsel before final adoption.

cases.name: Former Lumberyard Site — AFFH Completion Deadline Extension (Local Law Referral)
cases.applicant: Not named in the recording (referred by Town Board)
cases.status: positive recommendation to Town Board as referred (extension to December 31, 2024)
cases.summary: The board reviewed a Town Board referral to extend, from an earlier date to December 31, 2024, the deadline by which the applicant must complete 75% of a residential project to qualify for a reduced (10% instead of 20%) affordable-housing set-aside, after delays largely attributed to a prolonged Westchester County Health Department approval process outside the applicant's control. Roland Baroni cautioned that tying such deadlines to a fixed calendar date rather than a verifiable construction start date functions as a disincentive-laden penalty structure he generally avoids, though he did not object to it here. The board recommended the Town Board adopt the local law exactly as referred, declining to extend it further to 2025 since the applicant had not formally requested that.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the referral as written
memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed the board should only act on the specific extension the Town Board referred (to 2024) rather than speculating about a further extension the applicant had not formally requested.

themes.note: The Eagle Ridge sidewalk debate dominated this meeting and produced a rare 3-2 split board direction.
Old Orchard Street's entirely-in-buffer house, framed as a biodiversity restoration opportunity.
360 Main Street's oil tank and gas pump setback variances.
Summit Club special use permit referrals covering temporary extension, public golf, and maintenance facility siting.
45 Herrlingham Drive rock-crushing permit conditions.

staffInput.summary: Advocated strongly for sidewalks at Eagle Ridge based on the comprehensive plan's complete-streets policy even while acknowledging the board settled on a compromise; guided the Summit Club and AFFH local-law referrals; and reviewed the 360 Main Street and Old Orchard Street applications for site plan and wetlands issues.

Advised on the Summit Club public-golf zoning amendment language and voiced general reservations (not specific objections) about the AFFH deadline-extension penalty structure lacking a verifiable construction start-date trigger.

Reviewed dust-control and stormwater/drainage issues at 45 Herrlingham Drive and 78 Lafayette Avenue, and weighed in on the Old Orchard Street wetland buffer constraints and the 246 Sorel Court subdivision concept.

meetings.attributionNote: All five board members were named directly and extensively throughout this meeting, especially during the closely-argued Eagle Ridge sidewalk debate, giving high-confidence attribution. Two case addresses (Old Orchard Street's house number and the Summit Club/AFFH referral properties) were not stated precisely in the ASR audio.

meetings.meetingSummary: The January 30, 2023 North Castle Planning Board meeting referred a Bedford-Banksville Road guest-house/lot-merger project to the ZBA for eight variances after a detailed discussion of how non-contiguous lots generate more required relief than combined lots would; continued review of a 25 North Broadway gas station renovation, pushing for better on-site circulation, facade improvements, and a detailed landscaping/lighting plan; conducted an extensive first review of a proposed new town special-permit law allowing day camps (driven by Breezemont Day Camp's need to modernize), debating a 1,000-camper density cap, remote staff parking, and whether off-season special events should require case-by-case planning board approval, ultimately holding the Town Board referral for two weeks pending more information; continued the long-running 4 Tripp Lane fill/tree-removal violation, planning a joint site visit to trace a wetland connection to a neighboring parcel and asking the town's soil consultant to revisit an inconsistent demarcation-layer memo; approved a rock-crushing/demolition-debris-reuse permit at 45 Bedford Road (Mariani property) with erosion-control and dust-suppression conditions; advanced a minor patio-cover application at 188 King Street (Citigroup conference facility) toward a public hearing; and worked through a tense discussion of a non-compliant outdoor dining terrace proposal at 720 North Broadway, concluding the applicant must first obtain ZBA variances for deficient parking-aisle widths before the planning board can approve a conforming site plan.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy, James Jensen, and Lawrence Ruisi were the most active board members this meeting; Michael Pollack and Steven Sauro's participation is less clearly attributable in the ASR audio. Town Planner Adam Kauffman, Town Attorney Roland Baroni, and Town Engineer John (Kellard or successor) participated throughout.

cases.name: Bedford-Banksville Road — Guest House/Garage Expansion & Lot-Merger Variances
cases.address: Bedford-Banksville Road (exact house number unclear in recording)
cases.applicant: Property owner, represented by Peter Hollis (Hollis, Laidlaw & Simon) and architect Ken Anderson
cases.status: referred to ZBA for eight variances
cases.summary: The applicant is transferring development potential from a non-contiguous four-acre vacant parcel (to be deed-restricted against further development) onto the developed six-acre parcel, requiring eight ZBA variances for coverage and height. Chairman Carthy pressed the architect on how many fewer variances would be needed if the two lots were legally contiguous, drawing out the mathematical point that combining two separately-calculated allowances (X and X) yields more total permitted coverage than treating the combined area as one lot (X+Y) — an argument the applicant plans to make to the ZBA. The board also confirmed a pre-existing garden shed on the vacant parcel would be treated as a legal nonconforming structure from the 1993 subdivision rather than requiring a separate use variance, and noted that removing a previously-discussed connector between the main house and guest house to reduce coverage inadvertently made the detached garage exceed height/size limits, adding to the variance count. The board voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA.

memberPositions.evidence: Worked through the mathematics of how non-contiguous lots generate more combined allowable coverage than a merged lot would, helping the applicant frame its ZBA argument, and moved the referral.

cases.name: 25 North Broadway — Gas Station Pump & Facade Renovation
cases.applicant: Not named in the recording (represented by project engineer)
cases.status: continued — applicant to revise plans addressing circulation, canopy, facade, landscaping, and lighting
cases.summary: The applicant proposed new gas pumps and eliminating one of two pumps positioned against the convenience store building, but the board found the resulting on-site circulation still too tight — a car at the remaining building-adjacent pump could trap other vehicles from reaching the convenience store or exiting. The Town Engineer suggested shifting the site's south exit further south to fit a third pump in-line and improve circulation, which the applicant agreed to explore alongside a request from the board for a canopy trim-back to the building edge, sidewalk/drainage repairs, a detailed landscaping plan for the Route 22 median island, a lighting plan, and consideration of facade improvements (e.g., a gable roofline) to modernize the building's appearance.

memberPositions.stance: pushing for a substantially improved plan
memberPositions.evidence: Told the applicant directly that the submitted plan was not as impressive as the board wanted and that the site's one shot to get it right should include facade and lighting improvements beyond the minimum.

memberPositions.stance: concerned about circulation being 'engineered in' as a blockage
memberPositions.evidence: Observed that with parking on one side and only one way in, a car at the building-adjacent pump effectively traps vehicles until it clears, and asked whether removing that pump would help business by freeing convenience-store access.

cases.name: Day Camp Special Use Permit Local Law (Breezemont Day Camp)
cases.applicationType: local law referral (Town Board) / special use permit framework
cases.applicant: Breezemont Day Camp, represented by planner John Kirkpatrick and camp manager Walter Colosic
cases.status: referral to Town Board held for two weeks pending additional information (exact site acreage, outcome of a shuttle-bus meeting with local churches)
cases.summary: The Town Board referred a draft local law creating a new special use permit allowing day camps (long precedented at Breezemont as a legal nonconforming use since 1932) to modernize their facilities. The board debated a proposed density cap of 1,000 campers (or 60 per acre, whichever is lower) against the camp's roughly 15-acre site, weighed a remote/off-site staff parking plan (roughly 100 of ~400 staff currently park on the front lawn) as a reasonable way to relieve chronic on-site parking overflow, and spent significant time on whether off-season special events (weddings, corporate outings, fundraisers) should be approved administratively by the Town Planner as the draft proposed, or instead require case-by-case Planning Board approval — Lawrence Ruisi argued for keeping that decision with the Planning Board rather than delegating it, while acknowledging the camp itself said it did not intend to actively pursue such events, merely to retain the option. The board declined to finalize its referral, asking for the parcels' precise combined acreage (to know whether 60-per-acre or the 1,000-camper cap would actually govern) and for an update on the camp's parking discussions with nearby churches before revisiting in two weeks.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the camp, wants planning board discretion over events
memberPositions.evidence: Argued that off-season special events should come back to the planning board for case-by-case approval rather than being handled administratively, to allow the board to weigh neighbor impact for each request.

memberPositions.stance: supportive but cautious about scope creep
memberPositions.evidence: Noted the proposed law adds uses (special events) never previously part of the camp's century-old nonconforming use, extending the neighborhood's exposure to noise and traffic beyond the traditional 8-12 week summer season.

memberPositions.stance: generally supportive, wants complete information first
memberPositions.evidence: Asked repeatedly for the exact combined parcel acreage before the board could evaluate whether the proposed 60-per-acre standard would actually let the camp reach 1,000 campers, and opted to hold the referral until that and the parking-shuttle discussions were resolved.

cases.name: 4 Tripp Lane — Unpermitted Fill & Tree Removal Legalization
cases.applicant: Property owner (Anna Pereira), represented by Rick Bolander (JMC)
cases.status: continued — joint site visit planned; consultant to revisit demarcation-layer recommendation before next meeting
cases.summary: The applicant's engineer presented an initial 2:1 wetland/tree mitigation plan based on wetland flagging from a neighboring parcel (2 Tripp Lane), but town consultants questioned whether a natural drainage swale historically connected wetlands between 2 Tripp and 6 Tripp Lane before the fill was placed, requiring further investigation (including site access through the 6 Tripp Lane neighbor). The board pushed back on the soil consultant's existing memo recommending only a 6-inch clean-soil cap over lead- and pesticide-contaminated fill, recalling that a comparable 26 Chestnut Ridge Road case ultimately required a much thicker cap (up to 24 inches); Christopher Carthy also questioned whether the town should be independently administering DEC-style soil remediation standards at all, but was told DEC declines to get involved in individual-lot matters, leaving enforcement with the town. The board asked the consultant (Bill Canavan) to attend the next meeting to clarify the memo and directed further coordination on the wetland connectivity question before deciding on the fill permit.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of the existing consultant memo
memberPositions.evidence: Said the consultant's memo 'doesn't sit well' with him given the contradictory precedent from a comparable case and asked that the consultant re-examine and clarify the recommended cap thickness before the board relies on it.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road (Mariani Property) — Demolition Debris Crushing Permit
cases.applicant: Represented by John Sbrudy (contractor)
cases.summary: Ahead of redeveloping the site, the applicant sought to crush existing building foundations and concrete features in place (separating out rebar) to backfill basement voids and create a level, structurally engineered pad rather than hauling material off-site, with a nearby crusher location chosen for being relatively removed from residential receptors. Board members probed whether importing fill to supplement the crushed material and whether stockpiling near the site's two water courses would require additional safeguards, and whether reusing on-site debris constituted a landfill/construction-demolition-debris situation requiring separate permitting (staff did not believe so, since material stays on-site). The board approved the permit with added conditions requiring a sediment/erosion control plan reviewed by the Town Engineer, a defined limited-disturbance work-area boundary, a stop-work condition if the dust-suppression system fails, and a daily street-sweeping requirement.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed on erosion control near the site's water courses and on debris-tracking risk, resulting in the added sediment-control and street-sweeping conditions.

cases.name: 188 King Street (Citigroup Conference Facility) — Patio Cover
cases.applicant: Represented by project architect and project manager Kelly McRae
cases.summary: The applicant proposed covering an existing non-enclosable patio with a fixed operable awning as part of minor interior renovations; because the structure cannot be enclosed, the board agreed it does not trigger additional floor-area or parking review, provided the applicant documents that non-enclosure capability in writing. The board directed staff to schedule a public hearing and prepare a resolution.

cases.name: 720 North Broadway (Diner) — Outdoor Dining Terrace & Non-Conforming Site Plan
cases.applicant: Represented by project architect
cases.status: unresolved — applicant directed to seek ZBA variances (parking-aisle width, front-yard parking) before a conforming site plan can be approved
cases.summary: The applicant proposed a raised outdoor dining terrace occupying two existing parking spaces, replacing lost parking spaces the site has extra capacity to absorb; the terrace's design would sit at only about 13-18 feet from the property line where the code calls for a 25-foot two-way drive aisle, and the board raised safety concerns about vehicles backing into the raised terrace, suggesting a narrower terrace and bollards. Discussion revealed the site's underlying site plan (from a prior renovation cycle) was never actually brought into full code compliance for aisle widths and front-yard parking, prompting a tense exchange when the applicant's representative pushed back forcefully against reopening those issues; the Town Planner and Town Attorney concluded the board cannot approve any change without the whole site plan being brought into compliance, meaning the applicant must first obtain ZBA variances for the deficient aisle widths and front parking before returning for planning board and ultimately ARB approval.

memberPositions.stance: cautious about safety, sympathetic to a broader fix
memberPositions.evidence: Raised the concern that a raised terrace only 13-18 feet from parked cars invites vehicles backing into it, suggested narrowing it or adding bollards, and asked whether the applicant might consider a fuller, code-compliant site plan revision.

memberPositions.stance: wants a clear procedural path spelled out
memberPositions.evidence: Walked through the ZBA-first, planning-board-second, ARB-third sequence with staff so he could explain the process clearly to the applicant afterward.

themes.note: Central to both the Bedford-Banksville Road lot-merger case and the 720 North Broadway diner terrace dispute.
New special-permit framework debated at length for Breezemont, covering density, parking, and special events.
4 Tripp Lane's continued, unresolved remediation questions echo the 26 Chestnut Ridge Road precedent.
25 North Broadway gas station and 720 North Broadway diner both centered on drive-aisle and circulation deficiencies.
45 Bedford Road crushing permit approved with environmental safeguard conditions.

staffInput.summary: Framed the day-camp special permit law's key policy questions (density, parking, special events) for Town Board referral, guided the 25 North Broadway and 720 North Broadway site circulation discussions, and confirmed the 188 King Street patio cover does not trigger additional FAR/parking review.

Advised that the planning board cannot approve a piecemeal change to a non-compliant site plan at 720 North Broadway without bringing the whole plan into compliance via ZBA variances, and weighed in on the day-camp special events/non-conforming-use expansion question.

Suggested circulation fixes at 25 North Broadway (relocating the exit to fit a third pump), reviewed erosion-control and dust-suppression conditions at 45 Bedford Road, and coordinated the wetland-connectivity investigation at 4 Tripp Lane.

meetings.attributionNote: Christopher Carthy, James Jensen, and Lawrence Ruisi were named and quoted extensively; Michael Pollack and Steven Sauro's individual contributions this meeting were harder to isolate from the ASR audio and are underrepresented in member positions as a result. Several case addresses (Bedford-Banksville Road's house number, the Breezemont/day-camp law) were not stated precisely.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Planning Board's February 13, 2023 meeting covered a full agenda including a church change-of-use approval, extended discussion of the Summit Club's permanent special use permit referral to the Town Board, a contentious debate over contaminated fill left on a Trip Lane property, an outdoor display referral for a Main Street gas station, a town-wide day-camp zoning text amendment, a historic barn/accessory-apartment rebuild on Creamer Road, and two smaller residential accessory-apartment matters. The Board commended member Steve Sauro for his long service (since 2009) at the meeting's opening.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided. Members Steve Sauro, Michael Pollack (recused himself from the final Creamer Road-adjacent matter due to personal familiarity with an applicant), and Larry Ruisi participated actively; a member referred to as "Jim" (James Jensen) also participated. Thomas Crispi was not heard from and appears to have been absent. Town Planner (Adam), Town Attorney (Roland/"Rowan" Baroni), Town Engineer (John Kellard/Kellogg), and environmental consultant Bill Cannivan provided staff input throughout.

cases.name: 901 North Broadway — Church Change of Use / Amended Site Plan
cases.applicant: Church applicant (represented by applicant's principal)
cases.summary: Amended site plan to change 390 square feet of existing office space to church use, and to memorialize existing gas-station-related parking on the parcel. The Board raised process concerns about approving the change of use and legalizing pre-existing parking arrangements in the same resolution, but concluded the parking counts had been analyzed and were resolved. Public hearing was closed and the draft resolution approved unanimously.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke for or against the application.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether the board was "putting the cart before the horse" by legalizing gas-station parking in the same resolution as the church change-of-use, but accepted staff's explanation that the parking analysis had been completed.
Chaired the hearing, confirmed the applicant's town board special permit was already obtained, and moved the matter to a vote after questions were resolved.

cases.name: The Summit Club — Permanent Special Use Permit for Golf Course/Residential Club Operation
cases.applicant: The Summit Club (represented by Mark Winegarden; principal Jeff Mandel)
cases.summary: Reopened public hearing on a permanent special use permit for club operations (membership caps, golf outings, social events, day camp for members' children, guest cottages, surface water sampling). The Board extensively negotiated operational parameters — a 500-member cap, member-sponsored golf outings, undefined "social events" left uncodified at the applicant's request, and a 100-child day camp — before voting to positively refer the permit to the Town Board, which holds final approval authority.
cases.publicComment: No public comment recorded beyond board and applicant discussion.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed repeatedly on whether the 500-member cap could enable the applicant to "mismanage" the golf course, and pushed for codifying what qualifies as a "social event" to prevent large uncontrolled gatherings like weddings; ultimately deferred to consensus that occupancy/fire code would constrain events.
Facilitated negotiation of the parameters, moved the golf outing and day-camp provisions along, and made the motion to positively refer the permit to the Town Board.
Endorsed the day-camp provision as "a good feature" that brings younger families into the club and called it typical of similar clubs.

cases.name: Trip Lane — Unpermitted Fill / Contaminated Soil Remediation
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Rick Bolander, JMC; homeowner Anna Pereira)
cases.summary: Continued discussion of unpermitted fill (up to seven feet in places) brought onto the property without required testing, resulting in numerous building department violations and removal of 171 trees plus construction of retaining walls and a basketball court. Soil sampling found lead and pesticide (DDD/DDE) concentrations exceeding the state's unrestricted-use soil cleanup objective, though within restricted-use limits. The Board firmly rejected the option of allowing the fill to remain under a demarcation layer/covenant, citing concerns about setting a dangerous precedent, and directed the applicant to return with a revised site plan proposing removal of the fill; no resolution was adopted at this meeting.
cases.publicComment: Homeowner Anna Pereira spoke, disputing characterization of all material as contaminated fill and questioning whether pre-existing soil was tested separately from imported topsoil.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to leaving fill in place
memberPositions.evidence: Pushed hard on where the line is between acceptable and unacceptable soil exceedances, and argued the town should hold to unrestricted-use standards rather than allow restricted-use soil to remain under a cap, warning it "seems odd" to legalize illegally-imported fill.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to leaving fill in place
memberPositions.evidence: Raised repeated technical questions about how the board's site-plan jurisdiction interacts with the building department's fill-permit authority, and pressed on how the town would verify removed vs. remaining fill without retesting.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to leaving fill in place / cautious
memberPositions.evidence: Recounted the Board's prior position (from the similar Chestnut Ridge Road matter) that it would not accept a covenant-based remedy, and confirmed the Board's consensus that the applicant must remove the fill rather than cap it.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to leaving fill in place
memberPositions.evidence: Stated agreement that the material exceeds unrestricted-use standards and that he is "opposed to a covenant," saying he would not allow a successor owner to discover contaminated soil years later.

cases.name: 360 Main Street — Gas Station Outdoor Display/Sales Special Permit Referral
cases.applicant: Gas station property owner (represented by counsel and Samantha Urban, La Bella)
cases.summary: Referral from the Town Board for the Board's input on a special permit to allow outdoor display and sales at a gas station, consistent with a similar approval previously granted across the street. After resolving a sidewalk-width/pedestrian-access question with the Town Engineer, the Board voted to make a positive recommendation to the Town Board to adopt the outdoor display special permit.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised concerns about whether adequate sidewalk width would remain for pedestrian passage near the pumps, noting he "didn't love" the similar prior approval across the street, but ultimately voted in favor.
Said he had "no problem" with the outdoor display given it mirrored the prior cross-street approval.

cases.name: Day Camp Special Use Permit — Zoning Text Amendment
cases.applicant: Camp owner Gordon Josie (represented by attorney John Kirkpatrick and Walter Calalcic)
cases.summary: Town-wide zoning text amendment to establish day camps as a permitted use, referred from the Town Board. The applicant revised the density formula from 60 to 65 campers per acre to reach the intended 1,000-camper cap, eliminated a proposed "events" provision, and committed to no front-yard parking. Board members noted the standard would also apply to other qualifying parcels (e.g., a golf club converting to a day camp) and considered but ultimately declined to further restrict eligible road frontage. The Board voted to recommend the Town Board adopt the special use permit text.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether the standard applied only to this property and pointed out it would also apply to the Summit Club if its golf use were ever eliminated, prompting clarification from counsel.
Accepted the 65-camper-per-acre change and indicated no objection to moving the text amendment forward.

cases.name: 38 Creamer Road — Accessory Structure Rebuild (Historic Barn)
cases.applicationType: special use permit (referral to Zoning Board of Appeals)
cases.applicant: Property owners (represented by attorney Taylor Palmer, Cuddy & Feder; contractor Pallotta/THP Consulting)
cases.summary: A roughly 300-year-old barn containing an existing accessory apartment was substantially rebuilt under a valid building and floodplain permit, but the building inspector determined the extent of replacement made it "new construction," triggering the need for a variance (since detached accessory structures built after 1984 require ZBA relief) and a new special use permit. The Board found the applicant's presentation thorough, praised the preservation effort, and voted to refer the matter to the Zoning Board of Appeals for the necessary variances, without a positive or negative recommendation.

memberPositions.evidence: Recalled the application from years earlier and called the preservation effort "admirable," commending the applicant's thorough submission.
Called the presentation "very thorough" and made the motion to refer the matter to the ZBA for adjudication of the variances.
Asked what the town's position would be if a similarly deteriorated structure simply collapsed, probing the building-new-vs-renovation distinction.

cases.name: Single-Family Residence — RPRC Referral (Screening & Setback Review)
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by design professional "Wally")
cases.summary: A new single-family residence referred to the Planning Board from the Residential Project Review Committee (RPRC) for review of driveway/property-line screening adequacy and the proposed house's alignment relative to neighboring homes. The Board requested revised plans clearly showing property lines, proposed setbacks, and the driveway, and did not take a final vote at this meeting.

cases.name: 9 Call Drive — Accessory Apartment Special Use Permit
cases.applicant: Homeowner (self-represented)
cases.summary: Applicant sought a special use permit for a pre-existing accessory apartment in a structure dating to roughly the 1920s, in a matter that had been pending for over a year while the applicant determined (with the Town) that no zoning variance was needed. The Board asked for additional documentation on the apartment's size relative to the 25% code limit and agreed to schedule a public hearing once that information is submitted.

themes.note: Multiple special-permit referrals to the Town Board (Summit Club, gas station display, day camp text amendment, Creamer Road).
Trip Lane fill violation dominated a large portion of the meeting, echoing a prior Chestnut Ridge Road case.
Three separate accessory apartment/structure matters (Creamer Road, RPRC referral, 9 Call Drive).

staffInput.summary: Presented staff memos and recommendations across nearly every agenda item, including the Trip Lane fill options, Summit Club permit parameters, and variance requirements for Creamer Road.
Advised on jurisdictional questions between the Planning Board and building department regarding fill permits, and on procedural/organizational matters for the Summit Club permit.
Provided engineering input on the Trip Lane grading plan and the 360 Main Street sidewalk width issue.

Explained DEC soil cleanup objective classifications (unrestricted vs. restricted use) and defended his recommendation that demarcated fill could remain, while acknowledging the Board's authority to hold a higher standard.

meetings.attributionNote: This transcript is un-diarized ASR; member identification relies on first names spoken aloud (Christopher=Carthy, Steve=Sauro, Larry=Ruisi, Michael=Pollack, Jim=Jensen) and role cues. Thomas Crispi was not audibly identified and appears absent. A brief board-member recusal on the final Creamer Road-adjacent case could not be attributed to a specific member with confidence and was left out of memberPositions.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Planning Board closed out two prior site plan resolutions (10 New King Street landscaping/parking, 188 King Street awning), formally adopted the resolution removing contaminated fill from the Trip Lane property discussed at the February 13 meeting, and advanced several matters in progress: a new addition/accessory-structure application at 19 Jackson, a contentious wetland/septic case at 9 Sterling Road North, a retaining-wall project at 47 Windmill Road nearing public hearing, and a horse-facility expansion at 263 Bedford Banksville Road for which the Board adopted a SEQRA negative declaration and referred the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals. Two subdivision extension-of-time resolutions were also granted.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided, with members Steve Sauro, Larry Ruisi, and "Jim" (James Jensen) actively participating. Michael Pollack and Thomas Crispi were not clearly heard by name and may have been absent. Town Planner (Adam), Town Attorney Roland Baroni, and Town Engineer John Kellard/Kellogg provided staff input.

cases.name: 10 New King Street — Landscaping & Parking Lot Revisions
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by architect/engineer)
cases.summary: Final revisions to a landscaping plan, parking lot repaving, and an equipment enclosure expansion. The applicant confirmed acceptance of prior performance conditions (pavement repair, relocated sand storage). The Board closed the public hearing and adopted the draft resolution without amendment.
cases.publicComment: No notice neighbors appeared.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed with the applicant that prior performance conditions regarding pavement repair and sand storage relocation had been addressed before recommending closing the hearing.

cases.name: 188 King Street — Rear Awning Installation
cases.applicant: Commercial property owner (not present; discussed via applicant's prior communication with staff)
cases.summary: Simple commercial application to add an awning over an existing rear patio. The applicant did not attend due to weather but had discussed the matter with staff beforehand. The Board proceeded with the noticed public hearing, closed it, and adopted the resolution.

cases.name: Trip Lane — Unpermitted Fill / Contaminated Soil Remediation
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Rick Bolander, JMC)
cases.summary: Follow-up from the February 13 meeting: the applicant submitted a revised site plan showing removal of the contaminated fill and a proposed patio. The Board added a condition requiring town inspection during fill removal and discussed whether replacement topsoil could itself trigger a new fill permit. The public hearing was closed and the amended resolution was adopted.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed for the town-inspection condition to be added to the resolution and asked pointed questions about whether importing new topsoil during restoration could itself require a separate fill permit.
Told the applicant's representative he believed "the planning board did everything it could" to work with the applicant, and moved to close the hearing and adopt the amended resolution.

cases.name: 19 Jackson — House Addition and Accessory Structures
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by owner's rep Philippe Manuel)
cases.summary: Proposal for a one-story bedroom addition plus three accessory structures (a pool house, storage building, and exercise room, reduced from an original 800 sq ft each to two at 800 and one at 750 sq ft) and a reduced pool deck. The Board questioned the visual massing/scale of three large accessory buildings clustered near the pool and discussed floor-area-ratio calculations, but found the plan generally acceptable pending referrals. The applicant was directed to the Conservation Board (stormwater/buffer) and Architectural Review Board before returning for a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the three roughly 800-square-foot accessory structures looked "way too big" relative to the pool and human scale, and suggested the applicant reconsider spacing or landscaping between them, while acknowledging it was ultimately the homeowner's call.
Asked technical questions about floor-area-ratio allocation between the main house and accessory structures, and whether connecting the buildings by a breezeway would change their classification.

cases.name: 9 Sterling Road North — Wetlands Permit / Pool & Septic Revision
cases.applicant: Homeowner Mr. Harris (with landscape architect Andrew Monaco of Yost Landscape Architecture)
cases.summary: Long-running, contentious application (four prior Conservation Board denials over roughly two and a half years) for a revised pool/septic/stormwater plan with a new wetland mitigation plan and functional analysis. The Town's wetland consultant found the applicant's functional analysis adequate but noted the mitigation plan had not yet been reviewed, and flagged a discrepancy between the Westchester County Health Department-approved septic plan and the infiltration area shown on the current site plan. The Board directed the visibly frustrated applicant back to the Conservation Board with the completed functional analysis and mitigation plan, working concurrently with the Health Department to resolve the septic/infiltration discrepancy; no vote was taken.
cases.publicComment: Applicant Mr. Harris spoke at length expressing frustration with repeated Conservation Board denials, describing significant cost and time invested over multiple revisions.

memberPositions.evidence: Acknowledged the applicant's frustration but insisted the revised plan, functional analysis, and mitigation plan first go back to the Conservation Board given no precedent for the Planning Board approving a wetlands permit over a negative Conservation Board recommendation, urging the applicant to bring his landscape architect to present the mitigation plan.

cases.name: 47 Windmill Road — House Addition & Retaining Walls
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by design/engineering team)
cases.summary: Continued review of a house addition with tiered retaining walls (roughly six and a half feet at the highest point, tapering to zero) facing Long Pond, following a positive Conservation Board recommendation. The Board discussed visibility of the exposed garage foundation from a neighboring property and from across the pond, concluding a large tree canopy and rock outcropping would largely screen the walls, which will be finished in natural rubble stone rather than mortared masonry. The Board directed the applicant to schedule a public hearing with a draft resolution.

memberPositions.stance: supportive with attention to visual impact
memberPositions.evidence: Raised the wall-height/visual-impact concern relative to the adjacent neighbor and asked about landscaping visibility from the pond side, ultimately satisfied by the applicant's explanation of tree canopy and rock outcropping screening.
Recalled the Board's prior site visits to assess the wall design and complimented the redesigned single-tier wall solution, saying "you did a nice job here."

cases.name: 263 Bedford Banksville Road — Equestrian Facility Expansion
cases.applicationType: site plan / special permit (referral to ZBA and Town Board)
cases.applicant: Property owner Kaczorowski (represented by attorney J. Fane; architect and engineering team)
cases.summary: Revised horse-facility expansion (indoor riding arena, ten-stall stable, garage with grooms' quarters) that eliminated a caretaker's cottage, reduced the main house from roughly 10,000 to 7,500 square feet, and reduced CEA disturbance, following positive referrals from the Architectural Review Board and Conservation Board. Existing paddocks and buildings require variances for wetland-buffer setbacks and double agricultural setback requirements from residential neighbors, and accessory structures now exceed the 25% floor-area limit due to the smaller main house. The Board adopted a SEQRA negative declaration and voted to refer the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals for the necessary variances before proceeding to the Town Board for the special permit.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed the applicant's attorney on whether a smaller, code-conforming paddock was feasible before agreeing the variance route made sense, then made the motion to adopt the negative declaration and refer the applicant to the ZBA.

Asked for clarification on whether the property's Critical Environmental Area designation (due to proximity to a nearby sanctuary) applied to the review, disagreeing with a summary suggesting it did not.

cases.name: Subdivision Extension of Time — Old Mount Kisco Road Area (4th Extension)
cases.applicant: Subdivision applicant (represented by Mr. McKenna)
cases.summary: Fourth extension of time granted for an approved subdivision, with the applicant paying the standard extension fee (up to $1,000/year) while finalizing outstanding items; the Board raised no substantive objection. (Note: the property name is garbled in the ASR transcript as "124-year-old Monteusco Road" and could not be confirmed precisely.)

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion to grant the fourth extension of time after confirming the applicant was paying the associated fee.

cases.name: Subdivision Extension of Time — Second Matter
cases.applicant: Subdivision applicant
cases.summary: A second, separate subdivision extension-of-time resolution was granted in brief with no discussion of substance. (Subdivision name is garbled in the ASR transcript and could not be confirmed.)

themes.note: Featured heavily in the Sterling Road North, Jackson, and Bedford Banksville Road cases.
Several matters (10 New King St, 188 King St, Trip Lane) reached final resolution this meeting.
Bedford Banksville Road horse facility referred for multiple variances.
Sterling Road North applicant voiced strong frustration with the multi-year Conservation Board process.

staffInput.summary: Presented memos across the agenda, flagged the landscaping buffer question at Trip Lane, and raised the CEA/critical environmental area consideration at 263 Bedford Banksville Road.
Advised on SEQRA negative declaration procedure and ZBA-referral sequencing for the 263 Bedford Banksville Road horse facility.

Evaluated the 9 Sterling Road North functional analysis as adequate but flagged the unreviewed mitigation plan and a septic/infiltration discrepancy with the Westchester County Health Department approval.
Identified the setback conflict between the proposed stormwater infiltration area and the septic system at 9 Sterling Road North.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR transcript; member identification relies on first names/nicknames (Christopher=Carthy, Steve=Sauro, Larry=Ruisi, Jim=Jensen). Michael Pollack and Thomas Crispi were not clearly heard and may have been absent. Two subdivision extension-of-time matters have ASR-garbled property names ("124-year-old Monteusco Road" and "hit-noke subdivision") that could not be confidently transcribed to real addresses.

meetings.meetingSummary: A very long meeting (over three hours) covering eight substantive matters: a contentious continuation of the 23 Bedford Banksville Road warehouse/office conversion (adjourned amid skepticism the applicant could satisfy zoning), an advisory letter to the Town Board on the dense 113 King Street senior/multifamily rezoning, a heated procedural dispute over wetland buffers at 3 Maple Way, a straightforward 35 Starkey Road accessory apartment moving toward a hearing, a sharply critical review of an unpermitted, oversized retaining wall at 9 Barnard Road that board members said damaged a neighbor's property and would never have been approved as built, an after-the-fact tree-removal violation resolution at 100 Business Park Drive (adopted 4-1), a Town Board referral on the Eagle Ridge rezoning (townhomes replacing a previously proposed hotel, endorsed by letter), and an extension of time for 215 Business Park Drive.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided, with members Steve Sauro, Larry Ruisi, Michael Pollack, and "Jim" (James Jensen) all actively participating throughout. Michael Pollack recused himself from the 3 Maple Way matter. Thomas Crispi was not clearly heard by name. Town Planner (Adam), Town Attorney Roland Baroni, and Town Engineer Joe/John Kellard provided staff input.

cases.name: 23 Bedford Banksville Road — Warehouse/Office Legalization
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by Tony Vinesiano and engineer Peter Gregory)
cases.summary: Continuation of a public hearing to legalize an existing warehouse/office building split between CBB and GB zoning districts, following removal of prior tenants' outdoor storage and receipt of ARB and Conservation Board approvals. The applicant needed to demonstrate that a large rear storage/warehouse use was legally accessory to office use (not the reverse) to avoid a use variance or rezoning, but had not yet provided that analysis; the Board found the draft resolution presented far too many open items to consider approval and adjourned the hearing, suggesting the applicant may need to pursue a Town Board rezoning instead.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked the applicant's representative directly why he expected approval that evening "when you're so far away from even satisfying" the site plan requirements, and noted the draft resolution's conditions ran three pages long with major items still unresolved.

cases.name: 113 King Street — Senior/Multifamily Rezoning Referral
cases.applicant: Developer (represented by attorney "Anthony")
