cases.summary: Advisory referral from the Town Board on a proposal to rezone a roughly 38-acre site (includes converting a 100,000-sq-ft office building to RMF-SCH senior housing and rezoning the remainder to RMFA multifamily) for approximately 125 units including 18 affordable units, tied to a related tax-grievance settlement and a town water-infrastructure agreement. The Board discussed traffic circulation, school bus access, FAA/airport-approach height considerations, and amenity adequacy, and voted to send a revised advisory letter to the Town Board raising density/economics balance, traffic-consultant review, noise mitigation, and infrastructure cost-sharing clarity, while explicitly leaving the ultimate density decision to the Town Board.

memberPositions.evidence: Argued the site is packed tightly with little room for anything else, and pushed for the letter to explicitly recommend the Town Board seriously consider reducing density, also questioning whether the affordable units would end up smaller than the market-rate units.

Reframed the density issue as a value judgment for the Town Board to balance against project economics, drafted the compromise sentence for the letter, and separately flagged that the letter's infrastructure-cost language needed to clarify that cost allocation between the applicant and town was still undetermined.

Requested that a sentence about traffic consultant review of internal circulation and King Street turning patterns be added to the memo, and noted the Board's role as an involved agency under the pending Town Board SEQRA process.

cases.name: 3 Maple Way — Site Plan Revision / Wetland Buffer Dispute
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by architect Wally Tuscano)
cases.summary: Continued site plan review involving parking-area revisions and screening between neighboring properties, complicated by a dispute over whether an off-site wetland/watercourse buffer on an adjacent parcel (also owned by the applicant) extends onto the subject property, and by the applicant's frustration that the Town Engineer's comment memo was only posted online rather than directly emailed. The Board directed the applicant's wetland consultant (Beth Evans) to coordinate directly with the Town's wetland consultant (Dave Sessions) to reconcile the buffer question, and to resubmit missing plan sheets, before scheduling a public hearing. Michael Pollack recused himself from this matter.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly redirected the applicant's disputes with staff back to a practical path forward, recommending the applicant's and town's wetland consultants speak directly to reconcile the buffer question rather than continue arguing at the dais.

cases.name: 35 Starkey Road — Accessory Apartment
cases.applicant: Homeowner Mike Grimaldi
cases.summary: Application for an accessory apartment in the older portion of a century-old house (renovated as part of an in-progress, already-approved addition) to accommodate the homeowner's aging in-laws. The Board resolved minor floor-area and parking-space clarifications (three spaces required, two in the garage) and directed the applicant to schedule a public hearing with a draft resolution to follow.

cases.name: 9 Barnard Road — Unpermitted Retaining Wall & Fill
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by engineer/surveyor "Elliot" and landscape architect Walter Nestler)
cases.summary: Long-running violation case (wall built 5-8 years ago without required permits, now up to roughly 7.5 feet tall) with a newly introduced HES soil report finding non-residential-level contaminants and recommending a demarcation layer and additional fill — a remedy the applicant's soil consultant sharply disputed as using the wrong DEC standard. Board members voiced strong, consistent criticism that the resulting wall severely and permanently harmed the neighboring property's quality of life, sunlight, drainage, and value, and stated they would never have approved the wall as built. No vote was taken; the Board directed the applicant to prepare a cut-and-fill topography comparison and coordinate a site meeting between the Town Engineer, HES, and the applicant's team before returning.
cases.publicComment: A neighbor's letter and photographs describing property damage were introduced; a representative described as present on the neighbor's behalf indicated a desire to speak but was asked to let the board finish first.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the wall's impact on the neighbor's quality of life, sunlight, drainage, and property/market value was "dramatic" and "drastic," and stated that had the board reviewed this before construction it would likely have required a smaller, terraced wall set back from the property line.

Called the situation "confiscatory," saying the applicant enhanced his own property's market value "to your detriment" of the neighbor without permits, and stated he would not have approved this trade-off had the application come before the board in the proper sequence.
Said Michael and Larry "summed it up really well" and that he too would have doubts this application would have been approved had it come before the board first, rather than after construction.

Pressed on the inconsistency between the town consultant's contamination findings and the applicant's soil scientist's rebuttal, and said the board could not rely on secondhand accounts of that dispute, suggesting the town's consultant be brought in directly.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive — After-the-Fact Tree Removal Violation
cases.applicant: Basis Acquisitions (represented by attorney Corey Salamo, Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.summary: Applicant sought after-the-fact approval for removal of 38 town-regulated trees beyond the roughly 200-plus previously approved, attributed to a large silver maple falling the wrong way during construction and damaging surrounding trees, which the applicant said prompted a broader (uncoordinated) cleanup. A mitigation plan proposing 87 new trees, mostly evergreen screening, was presented informally. After debate over whether to condition approval on an already-accepted mitigation plan versus a future one, the Board adopted a SEQRA negative declaration and an amended resolution removing the tree-removal violation, requiring that any future mitigation plan and bonding amount be reviewed and approved by the Planning Board (not staff). The vote passed 4-1.

memberPositions.evidence: Proposed that approval be conditioned on an acceptable mitigation plan to be worked out as the larger site plan progresses, rather than locking in the specific plan presented that night, given the plan might not fit later site changes.

memberPositions.stance: insisted on Planning Board (not staff) review
memberPositions.evidence: Stated firmly that any future mitigation plan must be reviewed and approved by the full Planning Board, not delegated to staff, and asked pointed questions about whether the tree removal was truly an accident or a broader disregard for the permit.
Cast the lone dissenting vote (4-1), stating he was sympathetic to concerns that the board had not had adequate opportunity to consider the rushed application.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge — Rezoning Referral (Townhomes, Hotel Removed)
cases.applicant: Toll Brothers (represented by attorney Corey Salamo, Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.summary: Town Board referral on an amended rezoning petition to reclassify the full roughly 32-acre site (previously split between OB-H hotel zoning and RMF-SCH age-restricted senior zoning) to RMFA multifamily, proposing 83 fee-simple townhouse units (market-rate plus affordable) with a clubhouse, pool, and trails, entirely eliminating the previously controversial hotel component. Board members welcomed the hotel's removal but raised concerns about amenity adequacy for a now car-dependent, potentially family-oriented (not age-restricted) community, and about whether the layout still leveraged the site's topography for views as an earlier iteration had. The Board voted unanimously to send a letter endorsing removal of the hotel and an all-residential, non-age-restricted concept with a maximum unit cap, while reserving site plan-level issues (internal circulation, sidewalks, unit design) for later review.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he was glad the hotel was gone but flagged that three-bedroom units could bring young families who would rely entirely on cars (no realistic walk to town), and pressed on whether additional amenities beyond the clubhouse/pool were warranted.

Questioned whether the revised plan, no longer age-restricted or including a hotel, still conformed to the comprehensive plan's housing-diversity and affordability goals, ultimately accepting the applicant's response that it did.

Pushed back on colleagues' skepticism about unit spacing/economics, noting the plan already represents roughly 48,000 fewer square feet of development and no 45-foot building compared to the hotel concept, and ultimately made the motion to send the endorsement letter.

cases.name: 215 Business Park Drive (former CarQuest Building) — Extension of Time
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by Corey Salamo)
cases.summary: Routine extension of time granted for the previously approved site plan at the former CarQuest building, with no substantive discussion.

themes.note: Three separate matters (23 Bedford Banksville Rd, 9 Barnard Rd, 100 Business Park Dr) involved after-the-fact approval of unpermitted construction or removal, with sharply differing board reactions.
113 King Street and Eagle Ridge were both Town Board referrals on major rezoning/density questions.
3 Maple Way and 9 Barnard Road both involved contested wetland/soil consultant findings.
9 Barnard Road dominated by strong, unanimous board concern about harm to an adjacent property owner.

staffInput.summary: Presented memos throughout, flagged the office/warehouse use classification issue at 23 Bedford Banksville Road, and summarized comprehensive plan consistency for Eagle Ridge.
Advised on procedure for the 100 Business Park Drive negative declaration/resolution amendment and helped draft compromise language for the Eagle Ridge referral letter.
Reviewed drainage, wall stability, and cut-and-fill topography questions at 9 Barnard Road and engineering comments at 3 Maple Way.

Recommended a demarcation layer and 24 inches of additional fill at 9 Barnard Road based on non-residential-level soil contaminants; his methodology was directly disputed by the applicant's soil consultant.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR transcript; member identification relies on first names (Christopher=Carthy, Steve=Sauro, Larry=Ruisi, Michael=Pollack, Jim=Jensen). Thomas Crispi was not clearly identified by name and may have been absent. This was an unusually long (over 3-hour) meeting; several exchanges were rapid, overlapping, or garbled in the ASR and are summarized at the level of overall position rather than verbatim quotation.

meetings.meetingSummary: A lighter agenda covering four items: the Board closed the public hearing on the 47 Windmill Road addition/retaining-wall application, pending a trimmed-down resolution; heard an enthusiastic presentation on restoring the long-ruined Signal Hill Country Club mansion at 601 Bedford Road into a single-family home; reviewed a proposed rooftop solar array at the Westchester Reform Temple (845 North Broadway, the former North White Plains Elementary School) and scheduled a board site visit before setting a hearing; and advanced a subdivision lot-line change at 246 Massaro/North White Plains Road toward a public hearing.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided, with members Steve Sauro, Michael Pollack, and James Jensen ("Jim") participating. Larry Ruisi and Thomas Crispi were not clearly heard by name and may have been absent. Town Planner Adam and Town Engineer Joe provided staff input.

cases.name: 47 Windmill Road — House Addition & Retaining Walls
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Dan Simone, Simone Design Group)
cases.summary: Continuation following prior conservation and ARB approvals; the applicant requested the draft resolution's extensive conditions be trimmed since they left too much open-ended follow-up to the Town Engineer. The Board closed the public hearing (no members of the public appeared) and directed staff to prepare a streamlined resolution for adoption at the next meeting.
cases.publicComment: None; no notice neighbors appeared.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he would be amenable to closing the hearing and adopting the resolution with remaining plan details checked off administratively by the planning department and town engineer, since there were no outstanding issues of substance.

cases.name: 601 Bedford Road — Signal Hill Country Club Ruins Restoration
cases.applicationType: site plan / special use permit (referral to ZBA and ARB)
cases.applicant: Nick Waller (property owner)
cases.summary: Proposal to rebuild the fire-gutted 1959 ruins of the former Signal Hill Country Club mansion (stone exterior walls intact since the fire) into a single-family home for the applicant's extended family, converting the existing smaller cottage (currently his residence) to an accessory structure requiring a special permit. The roughly 18,000+ square foot restoration will need variances (likely rear-yard setback for a water tank buffer) but relies on existing nonconforming coverage predating current zoning. The applicant plans a taller roofline/cupola partly to screen a neighboring water tower, coordinated informally with adjacent neighbors. The Board found the concept appealing and directed the applicant to the Zoning Board of Appeals and Architectural Review Board.

memberPositions.evidence: Called it "an interesting application," noted the property had sat as ruins since the 1950s, and said the town was "fortunate to have somebody addressing this again."
Asked pointed technical questions about variance needs (floor area, coverage, rear setback relative to the water tank) and access/driveway plans off Evergreen Row.

cases.name: 845 North Broadway — Rooftop Solar Array (Westchester Reform Temple)
cases.applicant: Westchester Reform Temple (represented by Jamie Glover, Green Hybrid Energy Solutions)
cases.summary: Proposal for an 86 kW community-solar rooftop array at the former North White Plains Elementary School, now the Westchester Reform Temple, with panels set roughly 9.5 inches off the roof deck behind a parapet wall to minimize street visibility. A resident's letter raised concern about visibility from elevated homes on Nethermont and Roberta Place looking down onto the roof; the applicant clarified that only one lower-roof array (of four) would be partially visible from those homes, at a shallow 5-degree tilt. The Board discussed temporary safety railing color/permanence and requested a board site visit to view the roof before scheduling the public hearing.
cases.publicComment: A written comment from a neighbor and former student, Nora Kanzi Manuel, expressed general support for the building's upkeep but asked the Board to consider visibility from elevated homes overlooking the roof.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, advocating for neighbor visibility review
memberPositions.evidence: Pushed back on framing that panels were simply "not visible from the street," noting homes above the building look down onto the roof, and offered to join a board site visit to evaluate the view firsthand before the hearing.
Asked about parapet height on the lower array building and whether temporary yellow safety railings might become permanent, requesting that be clarified on the site plan.

Said he saw nothing that would motivate him against the panels, noting they likely look better than the existing rooftop chillers and HVAC equipment, while agreeing a site visit was worthwhile out of respect for the neighbor's concerns.

cases.name: 246 Massaro / North White Plains Road — Subdivision Lot Line Change
cases.address: 246 Massaro Road / North White Plains Road
cases.applicant: Subdivision applicant
cases.summary: Routine follow-up on a previously discussed lot-line change and home reorientation (to reduce homes facing each other directly); the Board had asked for a note retaining Planning Board site-plan jurisdiction over future house construction. With the reoriented plan submitted, the Board found no reason to delay and directed staff to schedule the public hearing concurrently with continued minor engineering comments on rear-lot layout to be resolved at the site plan stage.

themes.note: Both 601 Bedford Road (historic ruins) and 845 North Broadway (former school building, now temple) involve preserving and reusing older structures.
Solar array proposal drew generally supportive but detail-conscious board review.

staffInput.summary: Coordinated next steps across all four applications, including ZBA/ARB referral guidance for 601 Bedford Road and site-visit logistics for the solar array.
Provided minor comments on the reoriented lot layout at 246 Massaro Road, agreeing they need not delay the public hearing.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR transcript; member identification relies on first names (Christopher=Carthy, Steve=Sauro, Michael=Pollack, Jim=Jensen). Larry Ruisi and Thomas Crispi were not clearly heard by name this meeting and may have been absent.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Board closed the public hearing on the 3 Maple Way pool/addition project pending final engineering sign-off, reviewed (with some pointed frustration from Larry Ruisi about slow-moving open items) a near-final resolution for 47 Windmill Road, spent the bulk of the meeting working through wall-height and landscaping alternatives for the long-running 9 Barnard Road retaining wall violation in a notably more constructive tone than prior sessions, heard a preliminary presentation on a proposed seven-lot subdivision at 32 Orchard Drive (the former Danziger estate, including an abandoned cemetery parcel), and granted a routine extension of time for 100 Business Park Drive.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided, with members Larry Ruisi, Michael Pollack, and James Jensen ("Jim") participating throughout. Steve Sauro and Thomas Crispi were not clearly heard by name. Town Planner Adam, Town Engineer John/Joe Kellard, and Town Attorney Roland Baroni provided staff input.

cases.name: 3 Maple Way — Site Plan Revision / Wetland Buffer Dispute
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by design/engineering team; engineer Michael Campbell)
cases.summary: Public hearing held on the pool/addition project first reviewed in March; remaining items were narrow engineering and pool-code technicalities (pool fence height compliance, drainage treatment, septic relocation confirming no wetland permit needed). No neighbors spoke at the hearing. The Board closed the hearing and directed the applicant to resolve the remaining engineering checklist items with the Town Engineer so the resolution could be kept brief rather than adopted with numerous open conditions.
cases.publicComment: No neighbors appeared to speak.

cases.name: 47 Windmill Road — House Addition & Retaining Walls
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Dan Simone, Simone Design Group)
cases.summary: Review of the updated draft resolution; the applicant asked to soften language regarding the existing septic expansion area given the system's age. Larry Ruisi pressed pointedly on why numerous straightforward open items (gross land coverage, floor area, elevations) remained unresolved after months of review despite the applicant's belief they had already been submitted, questioning whether a miscommunication with staff was to blame. The Board declined to adopt the resolution as-is and directed the applicant to close out the remaining items before the next meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned why simple, non-complex items ("that's arithmetic") remained unresolved after extended review, and pushed to understand whether the applicant's team or town staff had failed to close the loop, ultimately recommending the applicant ensure answers are documented so the resolution appears brief when it returns.
Acknowledged Larry's point was fair but noted the board had no issue adopting the resolution with conditions in place, framing the delay as reducing risk rather than distrust of the engineer.

cases.name: 9 Barnard Road — Unpermitted Retaining Wall & Fill
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by engineer "Elliot")
cases.summary: The applicant presented three alternative wall-reduction concepts (a new lower wall filled/terraced in front of the existing 7.8-foot wall; a shorter modified section preserving certain trees; and a no-new-wall grading/boulder option preserving existing vegetation), all keeping the existing wall largely intact while reducing its effective height to roughly six feet through combinations of new walls, fill, and plantings. After extensive back-and-forth on each option's tradeoffs (proximity to the neighbor, tree preservation, material selection), the Board gave the applicant conceptual direction — favoring moving the wall closer to the soil stockpile, preserving a substantial landscape buffer, reconsidering wall material (skepticism toward a "Unilock" modular option in favor of natural stone), and reviewing whether certain pine trees should come out to enable better landscaping — while still awaiting official fill-quantity data needed for HES to set a soil testing protocol. The exchange ended cordially, a marked shift from the sharply critical March 27 session.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed to have the board articulate concrete consensus direction before sending the applicant away again, proposing the wall be relocated closer to the stockpile with the tiered wall closer to the existing wall and a preserved landscape buffer.
Probed whether regrading the driveway/lawn area could reduce runoff toward the neighbor given the new stormwater capture system only addressed roof runoff from the house, not the driveway.

Pushed back on the proposed modular block ("Unilock") wall material in favor of natural stone, but closed the discussion by telling the applicant's engineer "you did a good job tonight," a notably warmer tone than the prior meeting.

cases.name: 32 Orchard Drive — Seven-Lot Subdivision (Former Danziger Estate)
cases.applicant: Property owner (represented by engineer Dan[ny] RCA, CRC Engineering)
cases.summary: First presentation of a preliminary seven-lot subdivision on a roughly 13-acre estate with an existing single-family home, tennis courts, a barn, and an abandoned, unowned cemetery parcel requiring preserved public access. The applicant is exploring extending town water and possibly sewer service, and proposed rock-face cuts rather than retaining walls where feasible given road grading. Staff flagged that zoning-conforming lot yield (whether the site supports seven, six, or fewer lots) still needs to be established through slope, wetland, and net-lot-area analysis, and that clearing/grading limits should account for amenities beyond the houses themselves. The Board deferred declaring SEQRA lead agency until the zoning metrics are clarified in a future submission.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised the question of preserving public access to the on-site abandoned cemetery and asked directly whether the engineer's comment about subdivision difficulty implied a smaller lot count might be more realistic.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive — Site Plan Extension of Time
cases.applicant: Property owner (Basis Acquisitions)
cases.summary: Routine extension of time granted for the approved site plan at 100 Business Park Drive, with no discussion of substance.

themes.note: 9 Barnard Road dominated the meeting; tone was noticeably more collaborative than the prior session.
Both 3 Maple Way and 47 Windmill Road involved narrowing down long lists of open conditions.
32 Orchard Drive's zoning-conforming lot count remains an open question.

staffInput.summary: Coordinated engineering sign-off tracking across 3 Maple Way and 47 Windmill Road, and outlined subdivision review requirements for 32 Orchard Drive.
Reviewed wall design alternatives and road-grade/utility feasibility questions for 9 Barnard Road and 32 Orchard Drive.
Advised on cemetery public-access easement requirements and water/sewer extension process for 32 Orchard Drive.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR transcript; member identification relies on first names (Christopher=Carthy, Larry=Ruisi, Michael=Pollack, Jim=Jensen). Steve Sauro and Thomas Crispi were not clearly heard by name this meeting and may have been absent.

meetings.meetingSummary: A productive meeting that closed out several long-pending matters: an extension of time for 375 Main Street, approval of an amended single-family residence at 8 East Lane (part of the East Lane subdivision, with neighbor questions about utility pole relocation and road-widening timing), a lot-line reconfiguration at 2 Massaro Court, approval of the 845 North Broadway rooftop solar array (Westchester Jewish Community Services) after a supportive public hearing, approval of an accessory apartment at 34 Starkey Road, a preliminary look at a new landscaping/pool project at 33 Baybury Road, approval of an as-built field-change resolution for Frank Madonna's senior housing development, and final approval of the long-running 47 Windmill Road site plan/wetland/tree-removal permit.
meetings.durationNote: Chairman Christopher Carthy presided, with members Larry Ruisi, Michael Pollack, and Steve Sauro participating; Larry Ruisi and Michael Pollack read public hearing notices. James Jensen and Thomas Crispi were not clearly identified by name (the ASR speaker attribution for this meeting was best-effort/partial per the source file's own note). Town Planner Adam and Town Attorney Roland Baroni provided staff input.

cases.name: 375 Main Street — Extension of Time
cases.applicant: Property owner
cases.summary: Routine extension of time granted; the applicant was reportedly ready to begin construction within days.

cases.name: 8 East Lane — Amended Single-Family Residence
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Nicholas Gabri, Bibbo Associates)
cases.summary: Amended site plan slightly reducing the previously approved house footprint and rear patio, with no changes to bedroom count, drainage, curb cut, or driveway location. The application is tied to the broader East Lane subdivision, which includes widening East Lane to town road standards, creating a cul-de-sac, and relocating/undergrounding several utility poles. Neighbors raised questions about construction timing and utility coordination; a minor notice-paperwork date discrepancy was resolved when the mailed notice was confirmed correct. The Board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution, adding a condition for an updated landscaping plan near the pool to be reviewed administratively by staff.
cases.publicComment: Neighboring property owners asked detailed questions about utility pole relocation timing, road right-of-way limits, and construction start scheduling; staff/applicant committed to keeping affected neighbors updated.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the draft resolution was long and somewhat arcane but did not object to its substance.

cases.name: 2 Massaro Court — Lot Line Change
cases.applicant: Subdivision applicant
cases.summary: Reconfiguration of a previously approved three-lot subdivision (in a two-family zoning district) to increase spacing between houses, with no new building lots created. The Board retained site plan jurisdiction over future house construction on each lot. The Board closed the hearing and adopted a negative declaration, preliminary resolution, and final resolution.

cases.name: 845 North Broadway — Rooftop Solar Array (Westchester Jewish Community Services)
cases.applicant: Westchester Jewish Community Services (represented by Jamie Glover, Green Hybrid Energy Solutions)
cases.summary: Public hearing on the 86 kW rooftop solar array first reviewed in April, following a board site visit. The applicant detailed panel height (4 to 8.9 inches above roof grade), a 10-year operation and maintenance commitment to the nonprofit (double the standard term, offered given the applicant's own adjacent building and neighborly relationship), and grant funding covering the full project cost while saving the nonprofit roughly $25,000/year. A neighbor and local historian spoke supportively while reiterating that some panels would be visible from elevated homes; Michael Pollack asked about screening exposed mounting hardware, which the applicant addressed by showing cross-sections confirming minimal visible hardware. The Board closed the hearing and adopted a negative declaration and resolution.
cases.publicComment: Nora Kanzi Manuel, a neighbor and Conservation Board member speaking personally, thanked the applicant and the nonprofit for maintaining the historic building and reiterated (without objecting) that the panels would be visible from some elevated homes.

memberPositions.evidence: Followed up on his April site-visit observations, asking whether perimeter mounting hardware could be screened, and was satisfied by the applicant's cross-section showing minimal visible hardware from the affected homes.

cases.name: 34 Starkey Road — Accessory Apartment
cases.applicant: Homeowner Michael Grimaldi
cases.summary: Public hearing on the accessory apartment first reviewed in March, with final clarification of floor-area calculations (928 sq ft ADU within a 3,712 sq ft total) and delineated parking. No new construction was involved, only interior conversion of already-approved addition space. The Board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution.

cases.name: 33 Baybury Road — Pool & Landscaping Project
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by landscape designer Keegan O'Neill, Miranda Brooks Landscape Design)
cases.summary: New application (redesigned with significantly less impact than an earlier, more aggressive RPRC-reviewed version) for a pool, spa, reinforced-concrete retaining walls, elimination of one of two existing driveways, and extensive landscaping including minor tree removal below the tree-permit threshold. The main open question was whether the pool/spa area should use tiered retaining walls versus a single larger wall; the Board opted to schedule a site walk before proceeding to neighbor notification and a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Called the property "a gorgeous home" and the plan "amazing," while agreeing a site walk was warranted to help decide the retaining wall configuration.

cases.name: Madonna Senior Housing — As-Built Field Change
cases.applicant: Frank Madonna
cases.summary: Resolution recognizing several as-built deviations from the approved site plan for a senior housing development, including a required utility meter pit, a Con Edison electric service change, redesigned retaining walls (repurposing excavated stone for aesthetic facing), reduced entry-pillar placement, removal of a teardrop courtyard/gate feature (cited safety concerns given the roadway's approach speed and curve), and a flattened, drivable center parking island. The applicant reported strong sales interest (two units under contract at what would be the town's highest per-square-foot sale price). The Board approved the resolution with no objections.

memberPositions.evidence: Agreed the removed entry gate was an improvement given the roadway's approach speed and dangerous curve, seconding the applicant's safety rationale.

cases.name: 47 Windmill Road — House Addition & Retaining Walls
cases.applicant: Homeowner (represented by Dan Simone, Simone Design Group)
cases.summary: Final resolution adoption for the site plan, steep-slope wetland permit, and tree removal permit, after the Board's earlier insistence on trimming the resolution's conditions was satisfied. Very few conditions remained. The Board approved the resolution unanimously, closing out an application reviewed across multiple meetings since February.

themes.note: Several multi-meeting applications (47 Windmill Road, 34 Starkey Road, 845 North Broadway) reached final approval this meeting.
8 East Lane tied to broader road-widening and utility undergrounding work.

staffInput.summary: Coordinated resolution finalization across nearly every agenda item and confirmed public notice compliance for 8 East Lane.
Confirmed the significance of the public hearing notice date discrepancy for 8 East Lane before the Board proceeded.

meetings.attributionNote: This transcript carries a prior best-effort ASR speaker-attribution pass, but the large majority of lines remain labeled Unattributed; identifiable cues were limited to procedural chair statements and a few named individuals (Larry, Adam, Michael). Member positions in this file are drawn only from clearly attributable statements; many substantive exchanges could not be confidently assigned to a specific board member and were folded into case summaries instead.

meetings.meetingSummary: A full-agenda North Castle Planning Board meeting covering a reapproval subdivision, an accessory-apartment/tree-removal application, an amended gas-station site plan, and several substantial discussion items: a self-storage/warehouse-to-recreation (pickleball) use question at 100 Business Park Drive headed to the ZBA, an extended review of the 45 Bedford Road ("Gateway to Armonk") multifamily special-use-permit referral with heavy discussion of community benefits, garage enclosure/FAR, and fair-and-affordable housing, and two contentious imported-fill/retaining-wall legalization cases (9 Barnard Road and 4 Tripp Lane) where the board firmly rejected soil-covenant/demarcation solutions in favor of requiring soil export or redesign. The meeting closed with an unrelated resident's stormwater/drainage grievance raised during general comment.
meetings.durationNote: Christopher Carthy (Chair) presided; Lawrence Ruisi, Michael Pollack and James Jensen were active and clearly identified; Steven Sauro and Thomas Crispi were not clearly identifiable by name in this transcript. Town Planner Adam, a Town Engineer referred to as "John," and outside counsel Roland (Town Attorney) supported the board; the board went into executive session briefly on the 9 Barnard Road matter.

cases.name: 655 Bedford Road — Mittman Two-Lot Subdivision (Reapproval)
cases.applicant: Mittman (owner); represented by Anthony (engineer)
cases.summary: Reapproval of a previously-approved-but-expired two-lot subdivision preserving most of the estate parcel as open space with one new building lot; the county could not sign the final plat because the resolution had lapsed. No neighbors appeared. The board closed the public hearing and re-adopted the negative declaration, preliminary resolution, and final resolution unchanged in substance.
cases.publicComment: No neighbors or members of the public appeared or commented.

memberPositions.evidence: Made and seconded the motions to close the hearing and adopt the negative declaration, preliminary, and final resolutions with no objections raised.

cases.name: 42 Sarl Street — Accessory Apartment & Tree Removal
cases.applicant: Cory Sammons (attorney) for the owner
cases.summary: Applicant sought to convert an existing 1,600 sf art studio in an accessory structure into an accessory apartment (having obtained a ZBA waiver of the two-year ownership requirement) along with removal of 33 dead or dangerous trees. Board members had only minor questions (undefined apartment size, resolution wording nits) and no public opposition appeared. The board closed the hearing and adopted the draft resolution as amended.
cases.publicComment: One notice neighbor was present but raised no objection; no other public comment.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the accessory apartment size had been defined and noted resolution wording nits ("depicts" should be singular, etc.) before voting to approve.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive — Self-Storage/Warehouse & Recreation Facility (Pickleball)
cases.applicant: Paul Seisach (CHA/PC) and Christopher Mitchell (KSTW Architecture) for the owner
cases.summary: Applicant presented a revised plan reducing the requested FAR variance from .13 to .07 and eliminating the previously-needed 57-83 space parking variance by adding parking (317 spaces total) through a reconfigured self-storage/warehouse building plus an 11-court pickleball/recreation facility with locker rooms and a mezzanine party space. Board members pressed hard on whether the original variance justification ("benign," low-traffic self-storage/warehouse use) still holds given the recreation use's much higher intensity, on pedestrian safety from parking to the facility, and on what happens if the use later converts to office. With a ZBA hearing set for June 1, the board concluded it had no further substantive input before that hearing and let the applicant proceed to the ZBA.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; this was a board discussion item, not a public hearing.

memberPositions.stance: concerned about precedent and use-intensity mismatch with the original variance justification
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the original excess-FAR justification was predicated on self-storage being a low-intensity/benign use, and questioned whether swapping in a high-intensity 11-court recreation facility "sets a precedent" for other Business Park Drive variance requests.

memberPositions.stance: cautious, wanted more time to study the revised plan
memberPositions.evidence: As chair, said he'd rather take time to look at the new plan before any decision and pressed on how patrons would walk safely from parking to the recreation entrance past warehouse/loading truck traffic.

memberPositions.stance: neutral/procedural, noted discussion isn't binding on the ZBA
memberPositions.evidence: Observed the board spent time discussing a plan that had already been superseded and that the board's comments "aren't necessarily pertinent to the ZBA's discussion."

cases.name: 360 Main Street — Amended Site Plan (Legalization / Outdoor Display)
cases.applicant: Cory Sammons (attorney) for the gas station/realty owner
cases.summary: Amended site plan to legalize existing conditions and add a four-foot sidewalk matching a town-board-approved outdoor display/special permit plan, after the applicant had already secured ZBA setback variances (oil tank, gas pump) and a town board special permit for outdoor display and sales. The board asked about the sidewalk's effect on pump access and confirmed additional landscaping (wood barrels, plantings) as previously requested, then adopted the draft resolution.
cases.publicComment: No public comment recorded.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed the plan matched what the town board approved for the outdoor display area and pressed on whether the additional 4-foot sidewalk narrowed pump access before voting to approve.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road — Gateway to Armonk (Multifamily Special Use Permit / Site Plan)
cases.applicationType: special use permit / site plan (referral to Town Board)
cases.applicant: JD Summa / Kings Capitol (formerly "Mariani Gardens"); Ron Hoyna (Design Development Architects)
cases.status: referred (town board holds public hearing June 14)
cases.summary: Extensive review of a revised 34-unit townhouse concept (down from 43) ahead of the Town Board's June 14 special-use-permit hearing, with the applicant reorienting buildings to eliminate a loop road along Maple, splitting four-unit buildings into pairs to look like single-family homes, and citing a roughly $1-1.25 million cumulative community benefit agreement (CBA) with the town. The board pushed hard on front/back orientation so backyards wouldn't face Maple Avenue at the town's "gateway," screening while preserving the church view, whether open (uncounted-FAR) carport parking versus town-board-requested fully enclosed garages would require a new FAR variance or a code amendment, a 10% fair-and-affordable housing component, traffic/turning-lane and fire-truck circulation concerns, and a requested pedestrian crosswalk to the shopping center. The board agreed to send the Town Board a recommendation rather than requiring new renderings first, given the June 12/14 deadlines.
cases.publicComment: No general public comment; this was an applicant/board working session ahead of a Town Board referral.

memberPositions.stance: engaged and constructive but pushing for gateway-appropriate aesthetics
memberPositions.evidence: Argued repeatedly that as "a major gateway to the town," the project should not present a wall of backyards/screening to Maple Avenue, and pressed for reoriented fronts facing the interior with softened rear treatment.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical about the CBA/density tradeoff and enclosed-garage/FAR issue; wants the fair-and-affordable and density questions addressed head-on
memberPositions.evidence: Asked directly whether the project would have a 10% or 20% fair-and-affordable component and where those units would sit, drawing an extended comparison to a prior 18-unit project he had developed decades earlier on a nearly identical parcel.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of the shifting plans and process
memberPositions.evidence: Noted frustration that the board spent time discussing a plan version that had already changed again by the time of the meeting.
Raised wanting a physical (not just painted) crosswalk connecting the site to the adjacent shopping center to get people safely into the site.

cases.name: 9 Barnard Road — Retaining Wall Legalization / Imported Fill
cases.applicant: represented by Elliot (engineer) and Andrew Bradnik (counsel)
cases.status: tabled — additional soil testing and revised cross-section plans required
cases.summary: Continuation of a contentious matter to legalize an unpermitted retaining wall and roughly 650 cubic yards of imported fill near a property line; a neighbor (Corey, representing the abutting owner) objected strongly that the applicant's newest "double wall" proposal did not address the board's prior direction to set walls back from the property line and that the wall remained overbearing. After extended technical debate on wall heights/setbacks, septic and drainage implications, and site history (with a neighbor asserting fill was trucked in as early as 2000), the board recessed into executive session with counsel and, on returning, directed the applicant to develop a soil-testing protocol with HES and prepare two alternative wall/cross-section plans (a stepped/lowered-wall option and a set-back-new-wall option) for a future meeting.
cases.publicComment: A neighbor's representative (Corey) argued the applicant had not addressed the board's prior direction and that the wall remained overbearing to the abutting homeowner; another neighbor stated fill had been observed being trucked onto the property as early as the early 2000s, undercutting the applicant's 2008-aerial-photo fill estimate.

memberPositions.stance: frustrated with the pace of the review, pushed for the board to make critical decisions and give firm direction
memberPositions.evidence: Said the board would "go around and around" without making critical decisions, called for an executive session with counsel, and on return laid out the two specific plan options the applicant must bring back along with a soil-testing protocol.

memberPositions.stance: concerned about soil/septic conditions underlying the wall design
memberPositions.evidence: Questioned how much of the wall design was predicated on untested soil conditions and whether fill sat atop the septic area.

cases.name: 4 Tripp Lane — Imported Contaminated Fill Legalization
cases.applicant: Rick Bolander (JMC, site engineer)
cases.status: denied proposed remedy — board directed export of contaminated fill and a revised site plan
cases.summary: Follow-up soil testing (with HES present) confirmed that native, undisturbed soil on the property tested clean while the previously imported fill (roughly 2,600+ cubic yards) had elevated impurities. The applicant proposed capping two feet of contaminated fill with a demarcation layer and clean topsoil under a deed covenant; the board rejected this outright, stating North Castle does not want contamination covenants or demarcation layers running with deeds, and directed the applicant to export the contaminated fill and return with a revised site plan reflecting the removal (with a wetlands consultant review also needed given an altered watercourse).
cases.publicComment: No outside public comment; discussion was between the board and the applicant's engineer.

memberPositions.stance: firmly opposed to the covenant/demarcation approach as a matter of town policy
memberPositions.evidence: Stated flatly that the board would not support importing fill over a demarcation layer with a deed covenant, saying "we don't want North Castle to be a town where people... got to be careful... there isn't a covenant on their property for contaminated soil," and directed export of the fill instead.

cases.name: 3 Maple Way — Single-Family Home Site Plan (Draft Resolution)
cases.applicant: represented by project engineer (unnamed in transcript)
cases.summary: Board reviewed and adopted a draft resolution for a single-family home, working through a minor driveway grading/drainage issue (a long, nearly flat 150-foot driveway needing pitch to avoid ponding and ice) that engineering staff indicated would only require a fractional grading adjustment and would not require the board to revisit the approval if changes stayed minor. Christopher Carthy recused himself from this application and did not participate.
cases.publicComment: No public comment recorded.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, flagged a technical grading detail for the applicant's benefit
memberPositions.evidence: Raised that the flat driveway wouldn't shed water and asked whether the home's base elevation needed a slight lift to create adequate pitch, noting it was meant to help the applicant avoid future problems.

themes.note: Central to 100 Business Park Drive (variance eliminated via added spaces, precedent concerns) and to garage-enclosure/FAR debate at 45 Bedford Road.
Central to the 45 Bedford Road special-use-permit discussion (CBA of $1M+) and referenced by name in board deliberation.
Two separate legalization cases (9 Barnard Road, 4 Tripp Lane) with firm board pushback on covenant/demarcation solutions.
Repeated framing of 45 Bedford Road and, implicitly, 100 Business Park Drive as town 'gateway' properties requiring higher design scrutiny.
Raised in the 3 Maple Way driveway grading discussion and in a resident's closing-comment grievance about upstream development runoff.

staffInput.summary: Introduced and framed nearly every application; on 45 Bedford Road suggested breaking four-unit buildings into pairs for a single-family-home aesthetic and coordinated site-plan mechanics; on 100 Business Park Drive walked through the FAR/parking variance history.
Provided technical input on drainage, fire-truck circulation, and soil/fill matters across several site-plan items.
Advised the board during the executive session on the 9 Barnard Road matter and on procedural questions.

meetings.attributionNote: This transcript is un-diarized ASR; speaker turns were attributed primarily via role cues (Chair leading procedural motions, named individuals reading public-hearing notices) and direct address. Steven Sauro and Thomas Crispi were not clearly identifiable by name anywhere in this meeting's audio-derived text, so no positions are attributed to them here.

meetings.meetingSummary: The board reconvened its continued review of the 45 Bedford Road "Gateway to Armonk" multifamily special use permit, declining to give the Town Board a same-night recommendation on a plan it had not yet formally reviewed despite applicant pressure ahead of a Wednesday Town Board hearing. The board then approved a wetlands/tree-removal legalization at 2 Tripp Lane, worked through several discussion-stage items (11 New King Street outdoor vehicle/contractor-yard use, the Summit Club residential component's maintenance-building relocation and infrastructure sequencing, the Eagle Ridge 88-unit rezoning referral with community-benefit-agreement questions, and a new mixed-use retail/apartment building at 15 Old Route 22 near Gavi restaurant), and closed by granting two routine extensions of time (124 Old Mount Kisco Road, 13 Hidden Oak Road).
meetings.durationNote: Christopher Carthy (Chair) presided. Lawrence Ruisi, Michael Pollack, and James Jensen were clearly identified; Steven Sauro was referenced by name once ("Steve, if you'd like to digest it") indicating attendance. Thomas Crispi was not clearly identifiable by name. Town Planner Adam and Town Attorney Roland supported the board throughout.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road — Gateway to Armonk (Multifamily Special Use Permit / Site Plan)
cases.applicationType: special use permit / site plan (referral to Town Board)
cases.applicant: JD Summa / Kings Capitol; Tony Viniziano
cases.status: referred / deferred — board declined to vote on a recommendation this meeting
cases.summary: Applicant presented a revised layout (loop road along Maple eliminated, buildings split into two-four-two unit groupings, all units facing one direction) and pushed for a same-night board recommendation ahead of a Wednesday Town Board special-permit hearing. Several board members, led by Lawrence Ruisi, objected strongly to reviewing a just-submitted plan "on the fly" and setting a precedent for rushed reviews, while also debating whether enclosed garages (versus open carports) would require a zoning text amendment or an area variance given FAR limits. The board ultimately asked the applicant to formally submit plans and return in two weeks rather than issuing an immediate recommendation, over the applicant's objection about deadline pressure.
cases.publicComment: No general public comment; session was a working discussion with the applicant team.

memberPositions.stance: opposed to rushing a recommendation without full plan review
memberPositions.evidence: Argued that giving a recommendation based on a plan seen for the first time that evening "undermin[es] the purpose of the planning board" and would set a dangerous precedent for every future applicant.

memberPositions.stance: sought a middle path, ultimately sided with a two-week continuance
memberPositions.evidence: As chair, framed the choice for the board ("review the site plan on the fly tonight... or ask the applicant to come back in two weeks") and closed by asking the applicant to formally submit and return in two weeks despite the applicant's Wednesday Town Board deadline.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical of the applicant's un-broken-up building massing, wanted the FAR/garage-enclosure path clarified
memberPositions.evidence: Said he did not agree with the applicant's choice not to break the buildings into two-unit sections and pressed on whether enclosing garages would need a ZBA variance versus a town-board zone text amendment.

cases.name: 2 Tripp Lane — Site Plan / Wetlands Permit / Tree Removal Legalization
cases.applicant: Ralph (project engineer); Phil (property owner)
cases.summary: Legalization of tree removal within a wetland buffer and an unpermitted patio/driveway extension; an earlier fill-permit question was resolved when a town engineer located a legitimate historical permit. The Conservation Board had already approved a mitigation/replanting plan (13 replacement trees), and the board closed the public hearing and adopted the draft resolution, with a condition that an encroaching stone wall in the town right-of-way either be removed or the applicant obtain a town board license for it.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, asked clarifying questions about wetland mitigation and the stone wall condition
memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the wetlands mitigation area was cleared and filled or just cleared, and flagged the resolution's stone-wall/town-right-of-way condition before voting to approve.

cases.name: 11 New King Street — Accessory Outdoor Vehicle Storage / Contractor's Yard Legalization
cases.applicant: Dennis Knoskin (architect) for New King Street Associates
cases.status: discussion — hearing to be scheduled pending further review
cases.summary: Applicant sought to legalize overnight outdoor storage of an electrical contractor's service vans and a landscaping tenant's equipment on a gravel pad, framed as an accessory use to office tenants in the building. Board members debated at length whether this was truly "incidental" to permitted office use or was effectively converting the site into a contractor's/landscaping yard use not otherwise permitted in the IND-A zone, and questioned the adequacy of screening toward nearby residential lots. No formal action was taken; the matter was to be refined and scheduled for a hearing.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; discussion-stage item.

memberPositions.stance: concerned about compatibility with adjacent residential use
memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether converting office-tenant accessory space into what functions as a contractor's yard was appropriate given a residential lot directly behind the site, and noted the screening shown appeared to sit on a neighbor's property, not the applicant's.

cases.name: Summit Club (former Brentwood Country Club) — Residential Component & Golf Course Maintenance Building
cases.address: Business Park Drive / Bedford Road area (Summit Club)
cases.applicant: represented by project counsel/engineer (unnamed) and Town Attorney Roland
cases.status: advanced toward public hearing on final site plan
cases.summary: Discussion focused on relocating and downsizing a golf-course maintenance building (from a two-level design to a 5,000 sf slab-on-grade structure near the ninth hole) and on whether the residential component's final site plan approval could proceed ahead of the club's permanent special-use-permit process, since sewer/water infrastructure sits on a separate lot. Town Attorney Roland advised the board could approve the residential site plan with conditions tied to pending County Health Department and DEC sign-offs on the sewer/water systems. The board indicated it was ready to move toward scheduling a public hearing on the residential final site plan.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; discussion-stage item.

memberPositions.stance: pressed for clarity on why residential approval was tied to the golf course special use permit
memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly asked what the applicant was hoping to accomplish that evening and why residential site plan approval should be contingent on the golf course's separate special use permit process, before being satisfied that the infrastructure sits on its own lot.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge — 3 North Castle Drive (88-Unit Townhouse Rezoning Referral)
cases.applicant: Frank Madonna; Cory Sammons (Zarin & Steinmetz, counsel); Josh Weishman; Ralph Alfonsetti
cases.status: referred — town board to consider rezoning; hearing tentatively scheduled July 10
cases.summary: Applicant presented a redesigned 88-unit, fee-simple townhouse project (80 market-rate, 8 affordable) proposed for rezoning to RMFA ahead of a Town Board hearing, eliminating the prior hotel (OBH) zoning designation. Board discussion covered whether affordable units should be spread throughout the project versus concentrated near the pool/clubhouse, a large rock-processing/cut-and-fill operation (~100,000+ cubic yards) not yet fully engineered, a possible DOT-funded roadway/turn-lane improvement near Route 22, and whether the project's community benefit agreement funds (currently earmarked broadly, with $500,000 for parking/circulation) could be directed toward that roadway project. The board referred the matter to the Conservation Board and County Planning and tentatively set a July 10 public hearing pending Wednesday's Town Board rezoning action.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; discussion-stage referral item.

memberPositions.stance: generally supportive, probed community benefit agreement flexibility for infrastructure
memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the project's community benefit agreement funds could be directed toward the DOT roadway/turn-lane improvement rather than going into the general fund.

memberPositions.stance: detail-oriented on grading scope and affordable unit distribution
memberPositions.evidence: Asked about the scale of rock processing and cut-and-fill (reportedly over 100,000 cubic yards) and whether affordable units, being smaller, could be more evenly distributed rather than clustered in one location.

cases.name: 15 Old Route 22 — Mixed-Use Retail/Apartment Building (near Gavi)
cases.applicant: David Gussle (engineer); Frank Diodati; Joseph and Chris Procco (architects)
cases.status: discussion — proceeding to Architectural Review Board
cases.summary: Applicant proposed demolishing an existing 1,240 sf retail building and constructing a new 2,500 sf mixed retail/carry-out-restaurant building with two apartments above, paving an existing gravel lot with a modular retaining wall to add parking (roughly 35 existing spaces increasing to 52-55), and adding municipal sidewalk/streetscape improvements; the adjacent Gavi restaurant building itself would not be altered. Board reaction was generally positive; members asked about building elevations, retail-versus-carryout-restaurant use classification, and whether additional spaces could be fit along the street frontage. No hearing was opened; next step is the Architectural Review Board and addressing staff review comments.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; discussion-stage item, no hearing opened.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, wanted to see building elevations and street-frontage parking optimized
memberPositions.evidence: Asked to see building elevations that were missing from the initial presentation and suggested the applicant study whether four or five additional parking spaces could fit along the building's street frontage.

cases.name: 124 Old Mount Kisco Road — Extension of Time
cases.applicant: unnamed (final plat pending)
cases.summary: Routine 90-day extension of time granted while the applicant finalizes and submits its final plat map; no objections raised.
cases.publicComment: No public comment.

cases.name: 13 Hidden Oak Road — Subdivision Extension of Time
cases.applicant: unnamed
cases.summary: Routine extension of time granted for the Hidden Oak subdivision with no board objection.
cases.publicComment: No public comment.

The board's refusal to give an on-the-fly recommendation for 45 Bedford Road was the meeting's most heated exchange.
Raised in 45 Bedford Road (garage enclosure/FAR), Eagle Ridge (CBA-funded roadway/parking), and 15 Old Route 22 (added spaces).
11 New King Street's contractor's-yard-versus-accessory-use question.

meetings.attributionNote: Un-diarized ASR; attributions rely on role cues (Chair leading motions, named individuals reading hearing notices) and occasional direct address by first name. Steven Sauro is referenced once by name but has no directly attributable substantive statement in this transcript; Thomas Crispi could not be identified.

meetings.meetingSummary: A long (three-hour-plus) full-agenda meeting: the board approved a landscaping/pool site plan at 33 Bayberry Road and an accessory-apartment special use permit reissuance at 38 Creamer Road, tabled the contentious 9 Barnard Road imported-fill dispute again over a restricted-versus-unrestricted-use soil testing standard, and finally voted to send the Town Board a formal positive special-use-permit recommendation on the 45 Bedford Road "Gateway to Armonk" project with a detailed list of conditions. The board also declined to shortcut an expired site-plan/variance reinstatement at 868 North Broadway, advanced several discussion-stage items (a barn-removal/driveway project needing a wetlands permit, a legalized freestanding sign at 386 Main Street, a building redesign at 78 Lafayette Avenue), and granted an RPRC-referral appeal at 11 Whippoorwill Lane conditioned on road-access/turnaround improvements.
meetings.durationNote: Christopher Carthy (Chair), Lawrence Ruisi, Steven Sauro, and James Jensen were clearly identified and active. Michael Pollack and Thomas Crispi were not identifiable by name anywhere in this meeting's transcript, suggesting they were likely absent. Town Planner Adam and Town Attorney Roland supported the board throughout.

cases.name: 33 Bayberry Road — Landscaping, Pool, Pergola & Play Area
cases.applicant: Ralph Mastromonaco (engineer); Keegan O'Neill (Miranda Brooks Landscape Design)
cases.summary: Site plan for extensive rear-yard landscaping, a new pool with stone-veneer walls, pergola, and children's play area, with only seven trees removed and a full stormwater/erosion control and subsurface infiltration plan. A neighbor (Rachel Foreman) supported the project but raised drainage/flooding concerns from prior tree removal by a former owner and a boundary stone-wall question; the applicant's engineer explained the drainage system would not change hydrology outside the new pool area. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended (striking inapplicable wetlands-mitigation boilerplate and allowing a licensed landscape architect or designer, not only a surveyor, to certify as-built plantings).
cases.publicComment: Neighbor Rachel Foreman (29 Bayberry Road) called the plans "beautiful" but raised drainage/flooding concerns tied to prior tree removal and a boundary stone wall; neighbor John Scrum (4 Fox Run) asked whether the disturbed footprint was expanding toward his downslope property and was satisfied it was not.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, wanted construction-phase stormwater management explained for the public record
memberPositions.evidence: Asked the applicant's engineer to explain the erosion control plan and silt fencing in detail for the audience before the board closed the hearing.

cases.name: 38 Creamer Road — Accessory Apartment Special Use Permit (Reissuance)
cases.applicant: Taylor Palmer (Cuddy & Feder) for the Dempsey property owners
cases.summary: A 1996 accessory-apartment special use permit needed reissuance after extensive structural rehabilitation (including physically moving the historic building to a new foundation to save it from sinking) led the building department to deem the structure "new," also requiring and obtaining a ZBA variance. A neighbor and longtime area resident spoke in support, recounting the barn/structure's history as part of the historic Green Valley Farm. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution with minor wording amendments and an added condition for additional landscaping to the planning department's satisfaction.
cases.publicComment: A longtime area resident (Barry) spoke in support, describing the structure's history on the historic Green Valley Farm and personally recalling that it had been rented as far back as the 1980s; no opposition was voiced.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, requested a minor landscaping condition
memberPositions.evidence: Reminded the board and applicant's counsel of a prior conversation about adding a condition requiring additional landscaping to the planning department's satisfaction, which was incorporated into the amended resolution.

cases.name: 9 Barnard Road — Retaining Wall Legalization / Imported Fill
cases.applicant: Andrew Bradnik (counsel) for Joe Gentile
cases.status: tabled — dispute over soil testing protocol unresolved, continued to July 10
cases.summary: Continued dispute over whether imported fill (contested as either under or over 1,000 cubic yards) must meet the town consultant HES's more stringent "unrestricted use" soil testing standard versus the "restricted use" general-fill standard the applicant's completed testing already satisfied under DEC Part 360. The applicant's attorney argued the fill's provenance being unknown (because it was never permitted in advance) justified the town's tougher standard, while the visibly frustrated property owner argued he had already spent roughly $11,000 on testing that showed compliance and that the town had let the unpermitted wall construction proceed for years without objection. The board tabled the matter again, directing the applicant to work quickly with HES and asking that HES attend the July 10 meeting.
cases.publicComment: No outside public comment; contentious exchange was between the board, Town Attorney/consultants, and the applicant/his counsel.

memberPositions.stance: pressed for resolution but held firm that the tougher HES protocol governs given the unpermitted, unknown-provenance fill
memberPositions.evidence: Reiterated it was "very important that we move this application along" while maintaining that since the fill was imported without a permit, the town's unrestricted-use testing protocol applies until proven otherwise, and set the matter for July 10 with HES invited to attend.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road — Gateway to Armonk (Multifamily Special Use Permit / Site Plan)
cases.applicationType: special use permit / site plan (referral to Town Board)
cases.applicant: JD Summa / Kings Capitol
cases.status: referred — board voted to send Town Board a positive recommendation with conditions
cases.summary: After extensive review of the revised plan (loop road removed, units regrouped into two-four-two clusters facing away from Maple, back facades redesigned to look front-like), the board formally endorsed the design and voted to send the Town Board a special-use-permit recommendation. Conditions/asks included: pursuing enclosed garages via a ZBA variance or code text change to resolve the FAR conflict, upgraded landscaping/screening of backyard vistas along Maple, an easement for a future right-turn lane and sidewalk to the bus stop plus a crosswalk toward Armonk Square, coordinating the unit bedroom count (flagging a den/office with a full bath as a de facto bedroom against the environmental review's unit-count benchmark), and support for a roughly 3.7%-over building/lot coverage variance. James Jensen separately cautioned that unresolved floodplain/compensatory-storage engineering could force the applicant to materially alter the layout after Town Board approval, which the applicant and Town Attorney Roland agreed would be handled at site plan review.
cases.publicComment: A local resident/church-affiliated individual (Ed) raised suggestions about mirroring building layouts for a "town green" effect and asked that the ARB weigh in before the Town Board acted, which the board noted was premature at this stage.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, drove the final recommendation list
memberPositions.evidence: Recapped and made the motion to send the special use permit recommendation to the Town Board covering sidewalks/crosswalks, garage enclosure, landscaping, the right-turn-lane easement, bedroom count, and building coverage.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the redesign, wanted enclosed garages formally supported
memberPositions.evidence: Praised how the new renderings made the backs "look like the front," and pushed for the board to explicitly state it would support a variance for enclosed garages rather than leave it ambiguous.

memberPositions.stance: supportive but cautionary about unresolved engineering risk
memberPositions.evidence: Warned that unresolved floodplain/compensatory-storage design work could force the applicant to "go back and alter their plan" after a Town Board special-use-permit approval, drawing on his experience with a prior applicant on the same site.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the redesign's overall concept ("bones")
memberPositions.evidence: Said the site's "bones" seemed to work and endorsed the reunited four-unit buildings, noting he liked the open-garage compromise Anthony/JD proposed.

cases.name: 868 North Broadway — Expired Site Plan / Variance Reinstatement
cases.applicant: represented by attorney Buroni
cases.status: denied reinstatement shortcut — must reapply to ZBA for variance renewal, then return for a new hearing
cases.summary: Applicant's counsel argued the board should reinstate an expired site plan approval and associated variances without new hearings, framing the delay (a building permit sat unissued past the two-year variance clock) as unfair and citing a vested-rights theory. Town Attorney Roland advised the code's two-year variance expiration is fixed and the board cannot condition site plan approval on not-yet-renewed variances; the board agreed it lacked authority to shortcut the process and directed the applicant back to the ZBA to renew variances before returning for a reinstatement hearing.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; procedural discussion between the board, Town Attorney, and applicant's counsel.

memberPositions.stance: sympathetic to the applicant's frustration but bound by the code
memberPositions.evidence: Said he understood the applicant's frustration and that it seemed unfair for a building permit to lapse while sitting on the building inspector's desk, but concluded "we'll do what we have to do" and directed the applicant back to the ZBA.

cases.name: Barn Removal & Driveway Improvements — Two Semi-Contiguous Lots (Wetlands Permit)
cases.address: unspecified (property with an existing barn and driveway within a stream setback)
cases.applicant: represented by project engineer (Joe / "Dave")
cases.status: discussion — pending Conservation Board review; hearing tentatively targeted for August 7
cases.summary: An owner of two semi-contiguous lots proposed removing an old barn and modifying a driveway partly within a stream setback, requiring multiple ZBA variances and a wetlands permit since a report found no wetlands outside the stream banks. The board directed the applicant's wetland consultant to coordinate with the town's reviewer and go before the Conservation Board before scheduling a public hearing, tentatively targeting the August 7 meeting given publication/mailing timing.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; discussion-stage item.

cases.name: 386 Main Street — Freestanding Sign Legalization
cases.applicant: Brian Collin (Gotham Signs and Graphics)
cases.summary: Replacement of an existing post-and-panel freestanding sign that, upon review of prior approvals, was found never to have been formally approved on the site plan; the applicant sought to legalize the sign's location while a separate sign-design review proceeds before the Architectural Review Board. The board approved the freestanding sign's site-plan location, with a resolution to be prepared and filed after the vote.
cases.publicComment: No public comment.

cases.name: 78 Lafayette Avenue — Building & Site Plan Revision
cases.applicant: represented by project engineer (Alpha & ZEDI Engineering)
cases.status: discussion — proceeding to ARB, hearing tentatively targeted for early August
cases.summary: A revised plan shifted the building toward the northern property line, reducing retaining walls by letting the building itself retain the hillside. The board welcomed the changes as an opportunity to improve the building's street-facing architecture and add curbing/landscaping along Lafayette Avenue, debated whether on-street parking or a landscaped buffer was the better use of frontage space, and pressed on whether outdoor storage (construction "Conex" boxes currently on the ground) would actually be relocated indoors as represented given a prior 15-25% outdoor-storage allowance discussion. Next steps are ARB review and addressing staff comments ahead of a public hearing.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; discussion-stage item.

memberPositions.stance: supportive of the redesign, pushed for a beautification/curb-and-landscaping standard over added on-street parking
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the applicant had an opportunity to "take a step up" for Lafayette Avenue with a new curb and planting buffer, questioning whether adding street parking actually relieved parking pressure versus a beautified streetscape.

memberPositions.stance: skeptical that outdoor storage would truly move indoors as claimed
memberPositions.evidence: Noted the plan showed no outdoor storage despite large construction storage ("Conex") boxes visibly sitting on the ground during a site visit, and recalled a prior board discussion capping outdoor storage at 15-25% of the area.

cases.name: 11 Whippoorwill Lane — Appeal of RPRC Referral (New House / Pool)
cases.applicant: represented by project counsel (unnamed)
cases.status: appeal granted — remanded to RPRC for administrative review conditioned on road-access improvements
cases.summary: A new owner sought to appeal an RPRC referral to the full planning board, arguing the redesigned house (same size, location, driveway, septic, and stormwater system as a prior approved plan under the previous owner, which had not required planning board review) should be handled administratively like its predecessor. The RPRC had referred it up specifically over access-safety concerns on narrow, driveway-like Whippoorwill Lane, prompting debate over whether the new applicant should bear the cost/burden of road improvements never required of prior approvals. The board granted the appeal and sent the house portion back to the RPRC for administrative review/approval conditioned on a hammerhead turnaround and town-engineer/emergency-services sign-off on road access; the accompanying pool (which needs a retaining wall over six feet, requiring planning board review) was paused to resume once the house obtains its building permit.
cases.publicComment: No public comment; procedural argument between the board, Town Attorney, and applicant's counsel.

memberPositions.stance: sympathetic to the inconsistency concern but focused on resolving road-safety access
memberPositions.evidence: Questioned why the same access issue wasn't raised for the prior owner's nearly identical application, then made the motion granting the appeal and remanding to RPRC with the hammerhead/emergency-access condition attached.

cases.name: 14 Tallwood Road — In-Ground Pool Within Wetland Buffer
cases.applicant: Peter Gregory (DTS engineer); Connor O'Donnell (Bedford Poolscapes); Seth Tyshurst (landscape architect)
cases.status: discussion — referred toward Conservation Board and possible NYC DEP watershed permit
cases.summary: Proposed 18-by-38-foot in-ground pool with an 8-10 foot retaining wall, with nearly all of the roughly 5,600 sf of disturbance (5,200 sf) falling within a stream/wetland buffer regulated by NYC DEP given proximity to a protected watercourse. The applicant proposed exceeding required buffer mitigation (10,733 sf offered versus 10,520 sf required) via invasive removal and native plantings, plus stormwater infiltration/possible cistern reuse. Because the project sits entirely within the wetland buffer — a category the board has historically found very difficult to approve — the board directed the applicant to first pursue a DEP watershed determination and warned that a negative Conservation Board recommendation would likely be fatal to the project as designed.
cases.publicComment: No public comment.

memberPositions.stance: cautionary about the project's viability given full-buffer siting
memberPositions.evidence: Noted that in the past the board has "looked long and hard at projects that are entirely within the buffer" and found them historically very difficult to approve, and that a negative Conservation Board recommendation would make it "very difficult... to move forward with this project."

cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue — New Restaurant (Parking Variance & Community Benefits)
cases.applicant: Tony Viniziano; Stefan (developer, Remix Properties); Roxanne (chef); John Canning (Kimley-Horn, traffic engineer)
cases.status: referred — traffic study to Town's consultant, then ZBA variance hearing (targeting September 7)
cases.summary: New farm-to-table restaurant proposed for a long-vacant 1820s building adjacent to CVS in Armonk Square, expanding from roughly 900 to 3,400 sf (144 seats) with a rooftop terrace, greenhouse dining addition, and facade preservation. The code requires 48 parking spaces against only 15 on-site, so the applicant proposed valet parking plus a secured 20 Maple Avenue lot arrangement (up to 22 self-park or 32 valet-stacked spaces) and stalled informal talks for overflow use of the adjacent CVS lot, backed by the town's 2020 parking study and a cell-phone mobility study showing complementary (lunch-vs-dinner) peak demand patterns among nearby businesses. The applicant cited substantial community support (400+ responses in a local Facebook thread), 20 new jobs, increased tax assessment, and commitments to unified downtown wayfinding signage and reviving the Armonk community lunch/events tradition as community benefits. The board directed the applicant to submit to the town's traffic consultant (H2M) for a report, then proceed to the ZBA for the parking variance (targeting a September 7 ZBA hearing off an August 15 submission), holding off on ARB submission for now, and to consult the town engineer on water/sewer capacity given the use change.
cases.publicComment: No formal public hearing yet; the applicant cited over 400 supportive responses in a local community Facebook group as informal public sentiment.

memberPositions.stance: probing on the legal mechanics of shared/reciprocal parking and infrastructure capacity

meetings.meetingSummary: A packed agenda opening with a moment of remembrance for September 11th. The board approved a new house at 4 Ledgewood Place and a master-bedroom-suite/three-accessory-structure addition at 19 Jackson Road, but grew visibly frustrated with an unresolved, overly open-ended draft resolution at 1 Guion Lane and adjourned that hearing without adopting it. Several long-running matters advanced substantially: the Eagle Ridge townhouse subdivision continued design refinement, the 45 Bedford Road "Gateway to Armonk" project's garage-enclosure and building-coverage variances were finalized for ZBA referral, 23 Bedford Banksville Road's self-storage building was referred to the ZBA for a reduced (third-story-within-30-feet) height variance, and 100 Business Park Drive's pickleball/recreation special use permit received a negative declaration and a positive Town Board recommendation. New discussion-stage items included a shared-driveway house at 6 Kensico Place and a challenging four-lot subdivision with a historic cemetery access question at 32 Orchard Drive. The board noted 9 Barnard Road had been pulled from the calendar by the building inspector for continued noncompliance, and closed with a routine extension of time.
