cases.summary: Applicant reported completed ARB (model/color approval) and Conservation Board recommendations, shifted several units (81-88 and 49-52) for more separation from the entrance drive aisle and added a retaining wall creating flatter backyards, relocated a water main to avoid steep slopes, and — in response to a Conservation Board/town engineering concern about concentrating stormwater discharge onto adjacent park athletic fields sitting partly in a floodplain — agreed to pipe runoff through an upsized existing park pipe rather than using a hillside level spreader. The landscape plan now proposes over 460 new trees, tree-themed street "neighborhoods," and a roughly 1.5-acre central passive-recreation open space with rustic seating/art. Two items remained open: defining room/bedroom counts for zoning-calculation purposes, and confirming whether the built design still satisfies specific site-design commitments (pavers, stone walls, cottage gardens evoking the site's farm history) made in the DEIS.

cases.name: 45 Bedford Road — Gateway to Armonk (Multifamily Special Use Permit / Site Plan)
cases.applicant: JD Summa / Kings Capitol; Tony Viniziano; Ron Hoyna (architect)
cases.status: board voted to refer applicant to ZBA for FAR and building-coverage variances
cases.summary: Applicant finalized the garage-enclosure design the board had previously requested: fully enclosing parking garages on all five affected buildings, raising FAR from 0.40 to 0.477 and building coverage from a 20% code maximum to 23.7% (both requiring ZBA variances). In exchange, the "tucked-under-car" open-garage look is eliminated town-wide across the project, with field-stone and clapboard detailing to break up massing. The board discussed redirecting community-benefit funds (potentially $100,000+) toward a sidewalk/crosswalk connection to the county bus stop across Bedford Road, and agreed the dense evergreen screening along the shared boundary with the adjacent town-owned parcel could be relaxed now that the site is being redeveloped from a construction/storage use into a residential community (no longer needing to be hidden). The board voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the two variances, with next steps including the ARB, a Conservation Board wetland-buffer-impact review, and a targeted return by the September 28 meeting.
cases.publicComment: No general public comment; working session with the applicant team.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, drove the ZBA referral motion and screening-relaxation discussion

cases.name: 23 Bedford Banksville Road — Self-Storage Warehouse (Height/Story Variance)

meetings.meetingSummary: A meeting centered heavily on parking and zoning-district questions: a Tua Salon tenant fit-out at 395 Main Street exposed the lack of a formal parking district on the west side of Main Street, forcing a theoretical on-property parking layout and a ZBA variance referral, and a contentious car-wash zoning-text-amendment petition for 125 Business Park Drive split the board (deferred for fuller input from absent members). cases.name: 395 Main Street — Tua Salon Tenant Fit-Out (Parking Variance)
cases.applicationType: minor site plan / parking variance referral
cases.applicant: Chris Crocco (Just Crocco Architects) for owner Alie Lora
cases.status: referred to ZBA for a parking variance (approximately six spaces)
cases.summary: A hair salon (Tua Salon) fit-out in space previously occupied by lower-parking-demand retail exposed that the west side of Main Street has no formal parking district, so the applicant had to submit a theoretical layout showing the maximum parking that could physically fit on the owner's own three parcels (not counting adjacent lots under cross-access easements) to establish the real variance need. cases.publicComment: No public comment.

cases.name: 125 Business Park Drive — Car Wash Zoning Text Amendment Petition
cases.applicationType: zoning text amendment referral (Town Board petition)
cases.applicant: Cory Sammons (Zarin & Steinmetz) for Basis Industrial; Paul Sysac (JMC); Chris Mishalak (SWG Architects)
cases.status: referred back for further board discussion — no final recommendation made
cases.summary: Petition to add car washes as a permitted use in the PLI (business park) zoning district for a proposed 6,900 sf single-lane, high-end, recycled-water car wash with four vacuum stations on a vacant 3.7-acre parcel (previously approved for office/warehouse use). The board was split: one member argued a car wash is incompatible with the business park's increasingly "stately," recreation/service-oriented character (citing the adjacent pickleball/gym use across the street) and that the town deliberately limited gas-station conforming zoning to Kensico Place years ago; Michael Pollack and others argued it was a compatible, low-traffic service amenity comparable to other non-industrial uses (assisted living) already allowed in the park. Given the split and two board members' absence, the board declined to finalize its recommendation and asked to revisit the item with fuller board input before responding to the Town Board's October 12 petition hearing.
cases.publicComment: The applicant's principal noted he had informally polled friends/family in town who thought a car wash would be a welcome addition to the business park, offered as anecdotal support.

memberPositions.stance: opposed, viewing the use as incompatible with the business park's character
memberPositions.evidence: Said plainly "I don't see this as a good use in the business park... I don't see car washes as an appropriate use," citing the town's deliberate historical decision not to extend conforming gas-station zoning beyond Kensico Place as a parallel precedent for restraint.

memberPositions.stance: supportive, viewed it as a compatible service amenity
memberPositions.evidence: Argued the car wash "is an appropriate use in the business park... an amenity that the town needs" on an otherwise fallow parcel, and pushed back on the incompatibility argument by analogy to the assisted living facility already sited there.

cases.name: 4 Tripp Lane — Imported Contaminated Fill Legalization

meetings.meetingSummary: A packed, short-handed meeting (only three of five members present) covering ten items. Two contentious threads dominated: an extended, unresolved discussion of parking for the proposed 12 Maple Avenue restaurant - centered on valet parking, an off-site lease with 20 Maple Avenue, and the restaurant's economic/community benefit case for a large parking variance - and a use-variance referral for a parking-lot expansion at 5 North Greenwich Road that drew strong, organized neighborhood opposition and ultimately went to the ZBA with a negative recommendation from the board. The board also closed hearings and approved a barn relocation (1 Asheville Lane) and adopted SEQRA findings plus preliminary/final subdivision resolutions for the Eagle Ridge subdivision (3 North Castle Drive), while adjourning or continuing several other applications (868 North Broadway, 176 Virginia Road, 15 Old Route 22/Gavi restaurant, 34 Creamer Road, 10 Creamer Road) and recommending a special use permit to the Town Board for a seminary housing addition (486 Bedford Road).
meetings.durationNote: Only three of five board members were present tonight ("we've got three people here tonight... you don't have the two other opinions"): Christopher Carthy (Chair), Lawrence Ruisi, and James Jensen. Michael Pollack and Steven Sauro were absent.

cases.name: 15 Old Route 22 - Gavi restaurant improvement / mixed-use building
cases.applicant: Represented by Chris Crocco and Joseph Crocco (Crocco Architects), with Dave and Frank
cases.status: discussion only; applicant to revisit FAR calculation and site design before returning
cases.summary: Follow-up review of an expanded restaurant (Gavi) renovation plus a new mixed-use building with basement parking, two upper-floor apartments, and flexible "vanilla box" ground-floor retail space. The board questioned whether the two speculative retail spaces made sense functionally next to a restaurant, whether a fully residential building might fit the site better, and - the central issue - whether the basement parking area should be excluded from the FAR calculation; if it were, the project would need a variance from the 0.3 FAR max (currently ~0.4). The applicant agreed to revisit the FAR calculation and consider board feedback on site layout (e.g., relocating parking away from the restaurant patio) before deciding whether to proceed to the ZBA.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned why the retail space wasn't sited differently or made fully residential, and whether the applicant risked ending up with hard-to-fill vanilla-box space disconnected from the restaurant's identity.

Pressed on whether basement parking should count toward FAR and whether the whole building could instead comply with the 0.3 max, saying "I'm not as concerned as Jim is" about the retail-space question specifically.

cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue - Restaurant Site Plan
cases.applicant: Represented by Tony Viniziano, with parking/traffic consultants Stefan Martenavix and John Cummings (Kimley-Horn)
cases.status: discussion only; applicant to return to ZBA (adjourned to November 2) and Planning Board scheduling own public hearing for November 13, 2023
cases.summary: Extensive discussion of parking for the proposed 141-144 seat restaurant. The site has 15 on-site spaces against a 48-space code requirement; the applicant's plan combines valet service (providing 56 spaces total), a proposed long-term lease for 22 spaces at neighboring 20 Maple Avenue (evenings/weekends), and efforts to secure additional off-site employee parking (American Legion, other Main Street lots). The town's traffic consultant found the valet-based plan sufficient, especially given restaurant-industry data showing only ~20% of business occurs at lunch. Board members pushed back hard: skepticism that valet parking is a strong planning argument post-COVID, concern that the 20 Maple lease could unravel if that property sells (the applicant countered the lease would be structured to survive a sale/financing default), doubt about employee-parking enforcement (docking pay was raised and questioned as possibly illegal), and explicit statements that the board should not consider informal overflow parking at CVS as part of the calculus even though everyone acknowledged it would happen in practice. The applicant leaned on the project's economic/community case ($4 million investment, tax revenue, job creation, ~950 petition signatures of community support, filling a decade-vacant building) as justification for the scale of the parking ask. The board ultimately deferred to the applicant's procedural right to pursue the ZBA variance and did not send an additional recommendation, while scheduling its own site plan public hearing for November 13.
cases.publicComment: No general public spoke, though the applicant referenced roughly 950 petition signatures and Facebook-group support gathered outside the meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly challenged the valet argument as "a lot of blue sky" and said it strikes him that a 141-144 seat restaurant is being asked for on a lot with only 15 on-site spaces, while also acknowledging the applicant found a lease-based way to satisfy the code and that the investment "resonates" with him.

Said he didn't share the chair's trepidation about valet, and argued the applicant "found another way to figure out a solution to make it work" that should be respected if it satisfies the code through a durable lease.

The board adopted the SEQRA findings statement (updated primarily to reflect removal of the hotel), closed the hearing, and adopted both preliminary and final subdivision resolutions as amended to require native/drought-tolerant plantings, clarification of community/open-space acreage credit, and later confirmation that AFFH-unit patio space matches market-rate units - deferring detailed site plan issues (fuel source for heating, generator siting, patio/fence details) to individual lot site plan review.

memberPositions.evidence: Raised detailed questions about whether AFFH (affordable) units would have comparable patio space and utility/generator provisions to market-rate units, and about native/drought-tolerant landscaping, but ultimately supported adopting the findings and subdivision resolutions.
Made the motions to adopt the findings statement and the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions as amended.

cases.name: 34 Creamer Road - site plan amendment (pool addition)
cases.applicant: Represented by Ralph
cases.status: discussion only; routed to Conservation Board and ARB before scheduling a public hearing
cases.summary: Amendment to a 2018-approved spec-house site plan to add a pool for an interested buyer, shrinking the house footprint to accommodate it near a wetland buffer. Staff and the applicant's engineer confirmed disturbance within the buffer is slightly less than the prior approval with no wetland disturbance either time; some architectural elevation details needed revision for the ARB. The board had no major concerns and directed the applicant to obtain conservation board and ARB input before a hearing is scheduled.

memberPositions.evidence: Indicated no objection to proceeding and directed the applicant to the conservation board and ARB before scheduling the hearing.

cases.name: 486 Bedford Road - seminary housing addition
cases.applicant: The seminary (applicant not present)
cases.status: positive recommendation adopted, sent to Town Board
cases.summary: Referral seeking the Planning Board's input on a proposed 1,100 sq ft addition to existing seminary student housing plus a new two-bedroom dwelling unit for an incoming priest, replacing a retiring priest who will remain in his current unit. With no global planning concerns identified, the board adopted a resolution recommending the Town Board favorably consider the amended special use permit; the seminary will return to the Planning Board later for site plan approval.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion recommending the Town Board favorably consider the special use permit.

cases.name: 5 North Greenwich Road - parking lot expansion / use variance
cases.applicant: Property owner represented by attorney John Sarkone
cases.status: referred to ZBA with a negative recommendation from the Planning Board; lead agency declared
cases.summary: After the Town Board unanimously rejected a related zoning text change (opposed by a large, organized neighborhood petition), the applicant returned seeking referral to the ZBA for a use variance to extend PBO (commercial) parking-lot uses roughly 0.4-0.7 acres into an adjoining residential-zoned parcel, adding about 12 parking spaces for a physical-therapy tenant. Numerous neighbors (including Stephanie Samaritano and Kristen Mathis) testified strongly against it, citing loss of backyard privacy/green space, a large petition (~210 Armonk residents), and frustration that promised neighbor engagement hadn't happened. The town engineer had separately flagged that the proposed driveway/turning-radius layout was not optimal and that a reconfigured existing PBO-zone lot might yield only 1-2 additional spaces - far short of what's needed. The chair stated he could not recall the last use variance the board handled and argued extending PBO uses into a residential lot was bad land-use policy; the board voted to refer the application to the ZBA with a formal negative recommendation and declared itself lead agency for SEQRA coordinated review.
cases.publicComment: Multiple neighbors spoke in strong opposition, including Stephanie Samaritano (4 Byron Brook Place, citing a ~210-signature petition and lack of promised outreach) and Kristen Mathis (North Greenwich Road), both objecting to a parking lot abutting their backyards and asking why an existing upper lot couldn't instead be reconfigured.

memberPositions.evidence: Stated plainly "I don't want to permit the PBO uses in the residential" and made the motion to refer the application to the ZBA with a negative recommendation from the Planning Board.

Argued the submitted plan wasn't fully baked from an engineering standpoint (citing the town engineer's turning-radius and driveway-extension comments) and that the board hadn't seen a revised layout before being asked to refer it.

cases.name: 10 Creamer Road - accessory apartment / wetland permit
cases.applicant: Represented by Joe
cases.status: discussion only; awaiting Conservation Board memo before scheduling a hearing
cases.summary: Special use permit for an accessory apartment expansion (confirmed permissible by the building department) plus a local wetland permit, delayed by a lengthy DEC wetland-jurisdiction review that has now concluded. About 14 trees would need removal and the proposed accessory structure height (about 16+ feet) falls within the code's allowable range (up to 22 feet). No fundamental board concerns were raised; the Conservation Board's recommendation memo will trigger scheduling of the public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Indicated the board had no fundamental concerns with the proposal and confirmed the Conservation Board memo would trigger the next step.

themes.note: Dominant across 12 Maple Avenue, 15 Old Route 22, and 5 North Greenwich Road.
Strong, organized opposition at 5 North Greenwich Road.
12 Maple Avenue applicant leaned heavily on a jobs/tax-revenue/community-support case.

staffInput.summary: Confirmed paperwork order across nearly every application, walked through FAR/parking code mechanics for the Gavi restaurant and 12 Maple Avenue, and explained procedural next steps (ZBA referrals, conservation board/ARB routing) throughout the meeting.
Provided engineering critique on the 5 North Greenwich Road driveway/turning-radius layout and weighed in on drainage questions for 176 Virginia Road and the Gavi restaurant basement parking.

meetings.attributionNote: This transcript is un-diarized ASR. With only three board members present and repeatedly self-identified by role or direct address (chair, "Larry," "Jim"), attribution for procedural motions and their most distinctive remarks is reasonably confident; extended multi-way exchanges (especially the 12 Maple Avenue parking debate and the 5 North Greenwich Road back-and-forth) could not always be split cleanly between the three members and were folded into case summaries where uncertain.

meetings.meetingSummary: A full-board meeting covering seven items ranging from routine approvals to major long-range projects. The board closed and approved two site plans (176 Virginia Road's extension, and 100 Business Park Drive's pickleball/self-storage facility), gave mixed, non-binding feedback on a car-wash zoning text-change referral at 125 Business Park Drive (125 Business Park Drive), and continued substantive design discussions on three large, still-evolving projects without votes: a two-lot subdivision at 40 High Street, the Gateway townhouse project at 45 Bedford Road (concerns about a stormwater-retention "moat" along Maple Avenue), the redevelopment of the former MBIA/airport campus at 113 King Street (an initial subdivision/site-plan presentation heavy on community-benefit framing - affordable housing, tax revenue, water infrastructure, conservation easements), and legalization of unpermitted site improvements at the St. Christopher's/Jennie Clarkson campus.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present: Christopher Carthy (Chair), Michael Pollack, Steven Sauro, Lawrence Ruisi, and James Jensen.

cases.name: 176 Virginia Road - Mercedes Properties Inc.
cases.applicant: Mercedes Properties Inc.
cases.summary: Continuation from the prior meeting's inquiry into unpermitted excavation/site work; staff confirmed the building department found some violations but no active summons, and that work is proceeding through the normal permitting process. With that clarified, the board closed the hearing and approved the draft resolution.

memberPositions.evidence: Accepted staff's confirmation that no summons existed and moved to close the hearing and approve the resolution.

cases.name: 100 Business Park Drive - pickleball/self-storage facility
cases.address: 100 Business Park Drive (Lot 108.03-1-51), PLI zoning district
cases.applicant: Represented by Corey Salma (Zarin & Steinmetz), Paul Seisach (JMC), Chris Mishalick (SGW Architects), on behalf of Basis Acquisitions
cases.status: approved (negative declaration adopted; site plan, tree removal, and wetlands permit approved as amended)
cases.summary: Approval of a three-story self-storage facility, an 8,000 sq ft warehouse addition, and a 26,000 sq ft recreational facility with 11 pickleball courts on an 11-acre site with an existing 62,000 sq ft warehouse, plus legalization of an existing manufacturing space and private gym. The board confirmed a previously granted compensatory-flood-storage variance and its offsetting, permanently protected upstream parcel remained valid, and amended the resolution to add truck-maneuvering and wayfinding-signage conditions. With no water/sewer department objections and no further public comment, the board adopted a negative declaration and approved the site plan, tree removal, and wetlands permit as amended.
cases.publicComment: Two notified neighbors (Patrick McCarthy and Michael Ferrari) attended; Ferrari, representing the existing private gym tenant, asked that the resolution reflect the gym's private (non-public) status and voiced overall support for the resolution.

memberPositions.evidence: Walked carefully through the compensatory-storage variance history to confirm the offsetting parcel (now town-owned with a Westchester Land Trust conservation easement) permanently satisfies that condition, then supported approval.
Made the motions to close the hearing, adopt the negative declaration, and approve the amended site plan/tree removal/wetlands permit.

cases.name: 125 Business Park Drive - car wash zoning text amendment referral
cases.applicant: Represented by Corey Salma (Zarin & Steinmetz) on behalf of Basis Acquisitions
cases.status: referred back to Town Board with a neutral list of discussion topics (no formal positive/negative recommendation)
cases.summary: Discussion of a proposed zoning text change to permit car washes (here, a high-end single-lane tunnel wash with retail and 100%-recycled-water operations) in the PLI district, replacing a previously approved 9,300 sq ft office/warehouse building. Board members voiced significant reservations: that the use is a poor fit for the district's character, that permitting one automotive-adjacent use invites a slippery slope toward oil-change or collision-repair uses, and that a car wash would foreclose the site (the last substantially undeveloped PLI parcel in town) from other uses the comprehensive plan envisions for the corridor's evolution. A notified neighbor who disclosed a potential business interest in the venture spoke strongly in favor, calling it a valuable community amenity and noting the site's proximity to the sensitive water-supply watershed would require careful pollutant/wastewater mitigation. Rather than a formal recommendation, the board voted to forward the town planner's list of roughly eight discussion topics (compatibility, additional automotive uses, PFAS/environmental impacts, outdoor activity noise, screening, hours of operation, setbacks, and traffic intensity) to the Town Board for its consideration.
cases.publicComment: Michael Ferrari, a neighboring property owner who disclosed he was considering becoming a partner in the car wash venture, spoke in support, describing it as a valuable town amenity and addressing environmental/water-quality safeguards.

memberPositions.evidence: Questioned whether a high-volume, short-duration car wash use (potentially 30-60 cars/hour) fits the district's other uses, and worried about vacuum/activity noise near a 20-foot setback from the curb.

Argued the text change would foreclose other, comprehensive-plan-aligned uses for the last undeveloped PLI parcel and could set a precedent for further automotive uses (oil change, collision repair), framing it as "a bird in the hand" risk he was uncomfortable taking.
Cited a successful comparable car wash (Splash 'n Dash near the Hutchinson River Parkway) as a positive local precedent that doesn't typically add oil-change/mechanic uses.

cases.name: 40 High Street - two-lot subdivision
cases.applicant: Represented by Corey Salma and project engineer Peter Gregory (DTS)
cases.status: discussion only; site walk to be scheduled, public hearing to follow
cases.summary: Follow-up on a two-lot subdivision simplified by the town's determination that a stream along the High Street frontage is an unregulated drainage channel rather than a wetland. The board asked the applicant to show a more realistic future house footprint/disturbance area (rather than an undersized placeholder) so future buyers aren't constrained, to resolve stormwater discharge routing near the drainage ditch/wetland boundary to avoid triggering a wetland permit, and confirmed the New York City aqueduct easement crossing the property would not be disturbed. The board agreed to schedule a site walk ahead of a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Pushed the applicant to show a realistic house footprint and disturbance area upfront so future development on the lot isn't hamstrung by an undersized placeholder plan.

cases.name: Gateway, 45 Bedford Road
cases.applicant: Represented by an attorney (Anthony) and project engineer
cases.status: discussion only; working toward a public hearing
cases.summary: Continued site plan review of this gateway-to-town townhouse project, following resolution of an earlier floor-area-ratio issue via ZBA variance. Roughly 20 mostly stormwater-related engineering comments from the town's consultant were largely deemed resolvable, including upsizing a sewer line and floodplain-related adjustments. The dominant concern was aesthetic: a large stormwater detention area integrated along the Maple Avenue-facing frontage and behind unit patios was described by board members as resembling a dry "moat," a significant departure from the park-like open space originally envisioned, prompting suggestions of a landscaped wall to soften the appearance; a proposed $100,000 pledge from the applicant (made during the earlier town board rezoning) toward Bedford Road sidewalks/crosswalk was also discussed as needing to be finalized. No vote was taken; the applicant continues revising plans toward a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Said the site felt like it was accumulating too many constraints at once (floodplain, stormwater, cultec units) and described the resulting detention feature along Maple Avenue as looking like "a hamlet's castle... with a big dry moat out front."
Pressed on what the practical alternative to the current building layout would be, given the buildings themselves are fixed in place by prior board consensus.

cases.name: Airport Campus, 113 King Street
cases.applicant: Represented by Chris Fisher (Cuddy & Feder) on behalf of Toll Brothers and Airport Campus/Pan Am Equities
cases.status: discussion only; initial referrals (ARB, engineering) to begin
cases.summary: First Planning Board presentation of the integrated redevelopment following town board rezoning and SEQRA approval: 125 age-targeted townhomes (Toll Brothers) plus repurposing an office building into 43 age-restricted senior apartments (Airport Campus), on a site vacant for eight years amid a regional office-space glut. The applicant emphasized community-benefit elements: Byron Hill School District's support, an NRDC/Riverkeeper water-quality agreement, an expanded conservation easement (over 9 acres), extension of public water to the site (aiding a future water district), affordable-housing compliance, roughly 900 new trees and a half-mile of walking trails, and net-positive tax revenue after municipal/school costs. The board raised the still-unresolved recreation-fee calculation (a potentially large per-unit fee the applicant argued their amenity package should offset) and construction phasing between the two co-applicants; no formal action was taken, with next steps being ARB and engineering referrals.

memberPositions.evidence: Complimented the applicant's presentation and raised the recreation-fee calculation as a key open item to resolve going forward.

cases.name: St. Christopher's / Jennie Clarkson campus - legalization of site improvements
cases.applicationType: special use permit / site plan (legalization of unpermitted improvements)
cases.applicant: Represented by Tom Gibbons (LKB) and Christine Wozniak (chief administrative officer)
cases.status: discussion only; amended special use permit to be filed with Town Board concurrent with continued site plan review
cases.summary: Update on legalizing decades of unpermitted site improvements (including an additional animal-husbandry/equine facility beyond what was originally approved) at the residential treatment school campus. Since the last meeting the applicant worked with the Conservation Board and DEP on a wetland-area site plan (favorably reviewed, with minor plant-material and erosion-armoring changes incorporated) and closed out a long-dormant, no-longer-needed septic overflow pipe permit. An ADA-accessible entrance retrofit was also flagged as a minor building modification. The applicant was directed to file for an amended special use permit with the Town Board (to formally bless the animal-husbandry facility and other changes) concurrently with continued Planning Board site plan review.

memberPositions.evidence: Acknowledged the progress made through the conservation board/DEP review and confirmed the parallel next step of the Town Board special use permit amendment.

themes.note: Car wash text change drew notable reservations.
Central to the Airport Campus presentation's framing.

staffInput.summary: Framed the car-wash text-change discussion against the 2018 comprehensive plan's PLI guidance, walked the board through recreation-fee code mechanics for the Airport Campus, and coordinated conservation-board/ARB routing across several applications.

Provided detailed stormwater/engineering review across multiple applications, including truck-maneuvering comments at 100 Business Park Drive and floodplain/stormwater comments on the Gateway project.

meetings.attributionNote: This transcript is un-diarized ASR with a full five-member board present. Direct-address cues (chair, "Jim," "Michael," "Larry," "Steve") gave reasonably confident attribution for distinctive remarks, but long multi-way technical exchanges (especially on the Gateway and Airport Campus items) could not always be split cleanly between members and were folded into case summaries.

meetings.meetingSummary: A very long, full-board meeting (following a Board of Ethics training presentation) covering roughly fourteen items. The board approved several straightforward site plans and change-of-use applications (Tenny's Lane, 4 New King Street's parking/storage layout, two Main Street salon/food-service change-of-use hearings, 868 North Broadway, 209 Bedford Banksville Road, and 263 Bedford Banksville Road's major equestrian-estate redevelopment), adopted a negative declaration and sent a positive special-permit recommendation to the Town Board for the 14 Middle Patent Road horse farm, and referred several applications to the ZBA for variances or interpretations (Marquis Associates/70 Lafayette Avenue, the 32 Or Two Drive subdivision, and Harris's pool project at 9 Sterling Road). Two significant items did not conclude: the 23 Bedford Banksville Road self-storage hearing was kept open and adjourned to December given unresolved neighbor concerns, and 11 Whippoorwill Lane - a legally-nonconforming lot generating extensive neighbor objection - required the board to adjourn into executive session for advice from newly retained special counsel (the town attorney was conflicted out) before continuing to December 11.
meetings.durationNote: Full board present: Christopher Carthy (Chair), Michael Pollack, Steven Sauro, Lawrence Ruisi, and James Jensen. The meeting opened with a mandatory annual ethics training presentation from the Board of Ethics (not a planning matter).

cases.name: Tenny's Lane - new single-family residence
cases.applicant: Represented by Matthew Giranda (Bibbo Associates), applicant Jane Doone Associates
cases.summary: New five-bedroom home with pool on a vacant lot within an existing subdivision. The board pressed the applicant on a previously requested but not-yet-satisfactorily-addressed condition to add landscape screening between two adjacent driveways (to block headlight glare); the applicant agreed to expand the plantings there. With that resolved and no other significant issues, the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution.
cases.publicComment: One notified neighbor (Robert Brewster) attended with no comments.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed the applicant on why the driveway-screening comment from prior meetings hadn't been addressed in the submitted planting plan, then accepted the applicant's commitment to expand it before voting to approve.

cases.name: 4 New King Street - site plan amendment (tenant parking/storage)
cases.address: 4 New King Street (Lot 118.02-2-1), IND-A zoning district
cases.applicant: Represented by Dennis Doncenko on behalf of owner Mitch Beneroff
cases.summary: Formalized overnight parking/storage arrangements for two building tenants: an electrical contractor (PS Electric, seven marked vehicle spaces) and a landscaping company (Mariani, five vehicle spaces plus a gravel equipment-storage yard that doesn't count toward parking). A board member who visited the site questioned whether more than seven electric-company vehicles were actually parking there and suggested the applicant lock in whatever number they truly needed rather than under-commit; the applicant confirmed seven was sufficient and did not want to risk needing a ZBA parking variance. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended to reconcile the equipment list with site conditions.

memberPositions.evidence: Noted the board hadn't formally signed off on the equipment list in an earlier discussion and framed tonight's vote as doing so.

cases.name: Hot Blow Dry, 450 Main Street - change of use (hair salon)
cases.applicant: Represented by Chris Krakow (Krakow Architects)
cases.summary: Conversion of vacant retail space to a hair salon, following a previously obtained ZBA parking variance; no changes to the site plan itself. With no public comment, the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motions to close the hearing and adopt the resolution after confirming the ZBA parking variance was in hand.

cases.name: 395 Main Street - change of use (food/beverage walk-up)
cases.summary: Change of use for a 582 sq ft walk-up food/beverage space on the west side of Main Street, approved using a "land bank" parking mechanism - a theoretical plan showing full on-site compliance is approved on paper while the site continues operating under its existing shared-parking-lot arrangement. No public comment; the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motions to close the hearing and adopt the resolution using the land-bank parking approach staff explained.

cases.name: 868 North Broadway
cases.summary: Continuation of the site plan re-approval hearing adjourned from October 12 for the under-construction retail building and retaining walls. The board closed the public hearing and adopted the resolution as amended.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motion to adopt the resolution as amended.

cases.name: 209 Bedford Banksville Road - guest house, pool house, garage addition
cases.address: 209 Bedford Banksville Road (Lot 95.03-2-35), R4A zoning district
cases.applicationType: site plan and special use permit
cases.applicant: Represented by Daniel Hollis (Hollis Laird & Simon) and engineer Mr. Rina
cases.summary: Special use permit for a new guest house, pool/pool house addition, and garage on a 6.02-acre parcel, conditioned on coverage variances the ZBA had granted and a deed restriction on a non-contiguous 4.35-acre panhandle parcel (191 Bedford Banksville Road) limiting it to a pre-existing shed and horticultural garden to preserve the scenic-road view of the farmhouse. With the deed restriction still being finalized for county filing as a resolution condition, the board closed the hearing and approved.

memberPositions.evidence: Asked staff to walk through how the panhandle/deed-restriction arrangement worked before supporting approval.

cases.name: 23 Bedford Banksville Road - self-storage building
cases.address: 23 Bedford Banksville Road (Lot 102.04-1-9), GB zoning district
cases.applicant: Represented by Tony Viniziano (Greenwich Realty Group) and project engineer Peter Gregory (DTS)
cases.status: public hearing kept open, adjourned to December 11, 2023
cases.summary: A new three-story, 68,000 sq ft self-storage building (replacing a cleared contractor's yard) behind a renovated existing 15,500 sq ft multi-tenant office/storage building, following a ZBA variance for building stories. Numerous notified neighbors attended with concerns; stormwater/wetland-buffer design (capture structures under the site vs. surface basins) was still being worked out between the applicant's engineer and the town engineer, and conservation board input was still pending. The chair explicitly told neighbors the board would not close the public hearing that night, and adjourned it to December 11.
cases.publicComment: Several notified neighbors attended and were recorded as present (including individuals surnamed Rube, Pursky, and Grande); the chair kept the hearing open specifically to allow further neighbor input once stormwater/wetland design issues are resolved.

memberPositions.evidence: Told the audience directly the board would not close the hearing that night given outstanding engineering and neighbor-concern items, and adjourned to the December meeting.

cases.name: 263 Bedford Banksville Road - equestrian estate redevelopment
cases.address: 263 Bedford Banksville Road (Lot 95.03-2-56), R4A zoning district
cases.applicationType: site plan and special use permit
cases.applicant: Represented by Jay Vane (site planner/environmental consultant), owners Kyle and Chloe Gusserowski
cases.summary: Comprehensive rebuild of an equestrian estate for 20 additional horses: a new ~5,000 sq ft five-bedroom house with pool/pool house, renovated indoor riding ring, a new 10-stall barn replacing an existing stable, a new groom's quarters/barn/garage, expanded outdoor riding ring, renovated paddocks, and a new two-bedroom servants' quarters. The applicant had already secured conservation board approval, ARB approval, a ZBA variance (paddock/building coverage), and Town Board approval of the special use permit for the additional horses over a roughly two-year process. The town engineer confirmed no wetland issues and only minor technical stormwater items remained. The board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution with minor drafting corrections (dates, applicant names, a clarified "groom's quarters" designation distinct from an accessory apartment).
cases.publicComment: Three notified neighbors (Matt Sullivan, Dimitri Petlyuk, and Roger/Hamill Madris) attended but the applicant noted neighbors had been supportive throughout the process.

memberPositions.evidence: Reviewed the resolution's minor edits line by line and confirmed satisfaction before the vote.

cases.name: 11 Whippoorwill Lane - new single-family home (nonconforming lot)
cases.applicant: Represented by Corey Salma (Zarin & Steinmetz)
cases.status: discussion continued to December 11, 2023 pending special counsel's legal memo
cases.summary: Construction of a 7,300 sq ft home on a pre-existing, legally nonconforming 1.2-acre lot that has generated substantial legal complexity requiring the town to retain special counsel (the town attorney was conflicted out) and extensive neighbor comment. The board adjourned into executive session for legal advice before returning; afterward the chair explained special counsel would prepare a detailed response to the neighbor comments for the December 11 meeting and invited the applicant to present technical details (septic, stormwater, municipal water connection, a fire-hydrant service question) that evening or defer them to December.
cases.publicComment: Extensive written neighbor comments were submitted and are being reviewed by special counsel ahead of a detailed response at the December meeting.

memberPositions.evidence: Called for executive session to get the board's attorney's legal counsel on the nonconforming-lot question before proceeding, and set the matter over to December 11 for a fuller response to neighbor comments.

cases.name: Marquis Associates, 70 Lafayette Avenue - change of use (sound stage)
cases.applicationType: site plan (change of use) / ZBA parking variance referral
cases.applicant: Represented by an attorney from Zarin & Steinmetz
cases.status: referred to ZBA for a parking variance
cases.summary: Change of use from warehouse to sound stage increases the code-required parking from the site's existing 66 spaces (already 12 spaces under a prior variance) to 91, creating a 13-space shortfall. A board member questioned whether the applicant's argument that current partial vacancy masks the parking problem was sound, since occupancy is a temporary condition and code-required parking is calculated by square footage regardless of actual use intensity. The board voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the parking variance.

memberPositions.evidence: Pointed out the code calculates required parking by square footage regardless of current occupancy, questioning whether the applicant's under-occupancy argument was a sound basis for the variance the ZBA would ultimately decide.

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road - barn expansion / equine facility
cases.address: 14 Middle Patent Road, R4A zoning district
cases.applicationType: special use permit (Town Board referral) and SEQRA negative declaration
cases.applicant: Represented by "Dan" with engineer Mr. Rina and property manager Brendan McKenney
cases.status: approved (negative declaration adopted; positive recommendation sent to Town Board)
cases.summary: Companion application to 263 Bedford Banksville Road for a similarly large horse farm (professional/Olympic-level riders, no lessons or shows, family-operated), seeking the board's negative declaration and a positive recommendation to the Town Board for the special permit allowing additional horses. The board adopted a negative declaration and voted to send a positive recommendation to the Town Board; the applicant will return December 11 for site plan/special permit review of the barn and stable improvements themselves.

memberPositions.evidence: Made the motions to adopt the negative declaration and to send the applicant to the Town Board with a positive recommendation.

cases.name: 32 Or Two Drive subdivision
cases.applicant: Represented by Ralph (project engineer)
cases.status: referred to ZBA for frontage interpretation/variance; subdivision design otherwise generally acceptable
cases.summary: Two-lot subdivision where a dispute over whether the upper lot has adequate frontage requires a ZBA interpretation of the building inspector's (not yet issued) determination, and potentially an area variance under the open-development-area provisions for shared-driveway access. Separately, a roadside drainage/gutter design near a common driveway (to avoid excavating close to existing trees) needed a site meeting with the highway superintendent and town engineer to finalize. The board found the subdivision design generally acceptable pending these items and voted to refer the frontage question to the ZBA.

memberPositions.evidence: Confirmed he was comfortable moving the application forward to the ZBA referral once the driveway/drainage approach was worked out.

cases.name: Harris, 9 Sterling Road - pool and patio
cases.applicant: Property owner Mr. Harris
cases.status: referred to ZBA for a coverage/setback variance
cases.summary: A years-in-the-making pool, patio, and pool-equipment addition requiring resolution of a right-of-way/property-line dispute the applicant disputed (staff advised him to verify the surveyed line rather than assume it was wrong) and a coverage variance. The board voted to refer the applicant to the ZBA for the needed variance.

memberPositions.evidence: Walked the applicant through resolving the survey/right-of-way confusion and made the motion to send him to the ZBA for the variance.

cases.name: Two Trip Lane - imported fill remediation
cases.applicant: Represented by Michael Surin on behalf of the homeowner
cases.status: discussion only; routed to Conservation Board (wetland flow verification)
cases.summary: Update on remediating unpermitted imported fill, now understood to be concentrated along the western boundary line rather than site-wide; the applicant confirmed the fill will be removed. A wetland flow feature at the rear of the property still needs conservation board review before the application can proceed further.

cases.name: Two Massaro Court - lot-line change / preliminary subdivision extension of time
cases.summary: Routine extension of time for the preliminary subdivision plat approval on a lot-line change application, approved with no discussion.

themes.note: 23 Bedford Banksville Road and 11 Whippoorwill Lane both drew significant, unresolved neighbor engagement.

staffInput.summary: Reintroduced and framed nearly every application, explained the land-bank parking mechanism, walked through the deed-restriction and frontage-interpretation issues, and coordinated ZBA/conservation board/Town Board referrals throughout this unusually long agenda.

Provided stormwater/wetland-buffer engineering review on 23 Bedford Banksville Road, confirmed no significant open issues on 263 Bedford Banksville Road, and worked through drainage design with the applicant's engineer on the 32 Or Two Drive subdivision.

Advised on procedural questions (ZBA interpretation vs. variance pathways) and, for 11 Whippoorwill Lane, the board convened executive session for his advice given the town attorney's conflict requiring special counsel.

meetings.attributionNote: This transcript is un-diarized ASR from an unusually long, full-board meeting. Direct-address cues (chair, "Jim," "Michael," "Larry," "Steve") support reasonably confident attribution of procedural motions and distinctive remarks, but many extended technical exchanges could not be reliably split between specific members and were folded into case summaries. The meeting opened with a Board of Ethics annual training presentation, which is boilerplate and excluded from cases.

meetings.meetingSummary: A post-Thanksgiving meeting with the chairman attending remotely and unable to vote (he could only comment). The board approved the Eagle Ridge master site plan (delegating individual-lot review to the RPRC), advanced the Gateway 45 Bedford Road and 130 Business Park Drive (Cor Sports/physical therapy) applications toward the ZBA and Town Board respectively, continued design review of the 113 King Street Airport Campus project toward a January public hearing, and had an extended discussion of the town's own Kent Place/Verizon parking-lot subdivision - which surfaced a wetland-mitigation shortfall and prompted a broader policy conversation about using a future parking district and change-of-use approvals as leverage to extract community benefits (parking contributions) from Main Street/Armonk property owners.
meetings.durationNote: Christopher Carthy (Chair) participated remotely and was explicitly noted as unable to vote on any item, though he could comment. Voting members present: Michael Pollack, Steven Sauro, Lawrence Ruisi, and James Jensen.

cases.name: Eagle Ridge subdivision, 3 North Castle Drive
cases.applicant: Represented by Mr. Alfonsetti's team, with Frank Padana, Josh Weissman, and Norman Madonna
cases.summary: Approval of a master site plan for the townhome subdivision, with individual lot-level site plans (chosen from three pre-approved unit models) delegated to the RPRC rather than returning to the full board, and the future clubhouse to come back as its own separate site plan. Board members new to this style of phased, menu-based approval (as opposed to a traditional subdivision-then-individual-RPRC-review process) questioned how the mechanism would work in practice, drawing a comparison to the prior Shoemaker Lane subdivision; staff explained the site's tight lot constraints leave little room for RPRC-level deviation. The board adopted the master site plan resolution.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly questioned how RPRC review of individual lots would function given the tightly constrained, menu-based unit selection, comparing it to prior projects, but ultimately supported adopting the master site plan.

cases.name: Airport Campus, 113 King Street
cases.applicant: Represented by the applicant team (Toll Brothers / Airport Campus)
cases.status: discussion only; public hearing to be scheduled for January 2024

memberPositions.evidence: Helped work through whether a positive recommendation to the ZBA was warranted, noting the ZBA appreciates it when the board does attach one, before voting in favor.

cases.name: Kent Place / Verizon Parking Lot subdivision
cases.address: Kent Place, behind Main Street (Verizon parcel)
cases.applicationType: subdivision, site plan, and wetlands permit
cases.applicant: Town of North Castle (municipal applicant), presented by Roland and Joe
cases.status: discussion only, continuing; referred to ZBA for a building-coverage variance; Planning Board confirmed as (uncoordinated) lead agency
cases.summary: The town's own project to acquire a parcel from Verizon and redevelop it as a net 43-space public parking area behind Main Street (phase one of a larger, more ambitious concept for the whole Kent Place lot), constrained by a DEC class-C stream, an adjacent locally regulated wetland/buffer, and a 100-year floodplain. The applicant's environmental consultant flagged that while wetland disturbance is offset roughly one-to-one by on-site mitigation, wetland-buffer disturbance mitigation is less than half of what's typically required, arguing invasive-species removal and the parking area's community benefit should count toward that shortfall - a determination left to the board and conservation board. The board voted to refer the project to the ZBA for a building-coverage variance and confirmed it would serve as lead agency under an uncoordinated SEQRA review. Discussion broadened into whether the town could use a future parking district (potentially funded via CPA money, given individual Main Street landowners' reluctance to self-fund repaving/improvements) and conditions on future change-of-use approvals to advance area-wide parking solutions, building on an earlier board practice of conditioning some approvals on joining a prospective parking district. No final vote was taken on the subdivision/site plan itself; the meeting adjourned with the item unresolved.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed on how the wetland-buffer mitigation shortfall would get resolved and whether the same two-to-one mitigation or off-site mitigation-bank standard applied to other applicants should apply to the town's own project.

Raised (remotely) whether the board should be using change-of-use approval moments to advance community-benefit objectives like a parking district, referencing an earlier practice of conditioning approvals on district participation.

themes.note: Central to the Kent Place discussion's parking-district/CPA-funding conversation.

staffInput.summary: Framed the RPRC-delegation mechanism for Eagle Ridge, drafted the positive Town Board recommendation for 130 Business Park Drive, and worked through SEQRA lead-agency and referral mechanics for the Kent Place project.
Presented and answered legal/procedural questions on the Kent Place/Verizon parking lot as the town's own applicant representative, including the parking-district and CPA-funding policy discussion.

Reviewed the Kent Place site's environmental constraints (stream, wetland buffer, floodplain) and stormwater/mitigation calculations, and discussed road-radius/driveway design refinements for the Airport Campus.

meetings.meetingSummary: The Planning Board's last meeting of 2023, run with only three of five members present. The board closed out a horse-farm barn expansion (14 Middle Patent Road) and a new single-family home (6 Canato Place, amended to add a double-tiered retaining wall for a safer garage backout), but declined to close a contentious public hearing on a multi-unit project at 78 Lafayette Avenue over an unresolved 20-foot retaining wall design, incomplete plan submissions, and fencing/tree details, sending it back for one more round. Several other items (70 Lafayette Avenue change-of-use, a 14 Tall Woods Road retaining-wall repair, a Woodwell Road subdivision lot, and a Daphne Lane subdivision-lot site plan) were discussion-only items being teed up for hearings in January.
meetings.durationNote: Only three of five board members were present: Christopher Carthy (Chair), Steven Sauro, and James Jensen. Michael Pollack and Lawrence Ruisi were absent ("the left side of me looks a little blank tonight"; Jensen later remarked "I'm one of three here tonight").

cases.name: 14 Middle Patent Road - barn expansion / equine facility
cases.address: 14 Middle Patent Road (Lot 95.03-1-42), R4A zoning district
cases.applicationType: site plan and special use permit
cases.applicant: Property owner represented by Mr. Hollis (attorney) and Brendan McKenney (property manager)
cases.summary: Follow-up site plan/special-use-permit hearing for accessory structures over 800 sq ft - a 1,314 sq ft addition to the existing barn and a new 10-stall barn - on a 43.32-acre horse farm where the town board had already approved a special permit increasing the horse count from 10 to 26 and issued a negative SEQRA declaration. With no public comment and no substantive board objection, the board closed the hearing and adopted the resolution as amended to add conditions for a grading/erosion-control/stormwater plan with calculations and health department approval of a septic modification (the septic tank sits under the barn addition), plus a corrected conservation board memo date and a typo fix.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke; one neighbor (Eric Cameron) signed in but had no comments.

memberPositions.evidence: Ran the hearing, confirmed no public comment, and made the motions to close the hearing and adopt the amended resolution.

cases.name: 6 Canato Place - new single-family dwelling
cases.applicant: Owner represented by Lulu Dulale (architect), Nick of Hudson Engineering, and others
cases.summary: Public hearing on a new single-family home with a shared driveway; the neighbor with concerns had already met with planning staff and had no objections. The board's engineering consultant (John, town engineer) flagged that the proposed 26-foot garage backout area was too tight given a 10-foot drop-off and retaining wall at the end of the driveway, and pushed for widening it to roughly 30 feet with a taller, two-tiered retaining wall (about 4 feet plus 6 feet) faced with a reinforced guardrail modeled on a Merritt Parkway detail. The applicant agreed. The board closed the hearing and amended the resolution to require the wider driveway, the double-tiered wall, the guardrail detail, and an updated planting plan, then adopted it.
cases.publicComment: The one notified neighbor (sharing the common driveway) raised no objections after meeting with planning staff to review the plans in advance; no one spoke at the hearing itself.

memberPositions.evidence: Pressed the engineer on whether widening the backout area was worth the added steep-slope disturbance, ultimately endorsing the safer design and moving to amend and adopt the resolution.

cases.name: 78 Lafayette Avenue
cases.applicant: Represented by Ralph (project engineer/planner) and an architect (ASR names unclear)
cases.status: public hearing continued to January 10, 2024 (board declined to adopt resolution)
cases.summary: A reopened public hearing that the board had previously declined to close because the draft resolution carried roughly 20 unresolved conditions. The applicant's team brought updated engineering plans but, by their own admission, had not resubmitted current architectural elevations to the board (only the original ARB submission), and had not brought details of a proposed roughly 20-foot "ReadyRock" retaining wall - including a needed temporary construction easement from a neighbor, top-of-wall fencing, a guide rail to stop vehicles, drainage/regrading behind the wall, and tree-health/removal near the wall - despite these being flagged as outstanding in staff review memos. After extended, increasingly frustrated back-and-forth about which plan versions had actually been submitted, the board concluded it was not comfortable adopting a resolution with this many open technical items and continued the public hearing to the January 10, 2024 meeting, directing the applicant to meet directly with the town engineer beforehand.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke; the exchange was between the board, staff (town engineer, town planner), and the applicant's team.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly pressed on missing wall, fence, and guardrail details and outdated plan submissions, ultimately stating the board was "not comfortable coping [adopting] this resolution" and that the applicant needed to "tighten up" the plan before the next meeting; noted "I'm one of three here tonight."

Acknowledged the unusual, last-minute nature of trying to resolve so many open items in one meeting, said the board didn't want to set a precedent approving plans without critical details like vehicle-stop guardrails, and agreed to continue the hearing to January.

cases.name: 14 Tall Woods Road - retaining wall repair

cases.name: Airport Campus, 113 King Street
cases.address: 113 King Street (tax lots 118.02-1-1; 113.04-1-13, -14, -20), RMFA/RMFCH zoning districts
cases.applicant: Represented by Chris Fisher (Cuddy & Feder) on behalf of the applicant team, with engineering by John Meyer Consulting
cases.status: public hearing adjourned (not closed); continuing coordination with staff
cases.summary: Extended review of the 125-unit attached-townhome and 58-unit restricted-apartment redevelopment on the former airport office campus. The bulk of discussion concerned airport noise: the applicant's acoustic consultant characterized noise impacts as "insignificant" using FAA average (DNL) noise-contour methodology targeting a 45 dBA interior standard, which board members (particularly James Jensen, a former resident near a different airport flight path) found the word choice misleading and pushed the applicant to instead design to the loudest single-event noise level using standard architectural sound-dampening details, similar to what neighboring Fairfax County, Virginia requires near Dulles Airport; the applicant agreed to take the request under advisement without committing. Additional items covered included fencing/privacy screening between adjacent unit decks (a detail was provided at the meeting), sound attenuation between units, three requested roadway design waivers (reduced cul-de-sac radii, narrower 24-28 ft road widths, and a steeper road grade at one intersection, each mitigated by a posted 20 mph speed limit) which the town engineer's office found acceptable, a school-bus turnaround near a shared DEP driveway, and a request for a historical recreation-fee matrix. The board also indicated future individual unit landscaping approvals could be delegated to the RPRC rather than returning to the full board each time. The hearing was adjourned (not closed) for the applicant to respond to outstanding items.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke; discussion was between the board, staff, and the applicant's team.

memberPositions.evidence: Repeatedly challenged the applicant's noise consultant's use of the word "insignificant" and their reliance on average (rather than peak single-event) noise levels, referencing his own experience living near a flight path and pressing for FAA-circular-based design guidance; said the applicant's team "could give more meat" to their noise response.
Said he agreed the word "insignificant" was misleading from a layman's and board perspective and would not want that language used in any offering plan or notice.
Walked through and appeared satisfied with each of the three roadway design waivers after the applicant explained the posted 20 mph speed limit mitigation.

cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke.

cases.name: Majidi Subdivision, 21 Whippoorwill Road
cases.applicant: Property owner represented by an engineer ("Joe," firm name unclear in ASR)
cases.summary: Two-lot subdivision hearing where the town engineer flagged outstanding stormwater calculations (design needed to be updated from a 25-year to a 100-year storm standard, with supporting soil testing not yet witnessed by the town) and inadequate sight distance for the new lot's driveway on a sharp, accident-prone curve; the applicant proposed shifting the driveway roughly 18 feet to improve sight lines while preserving more of an existing stone wall. Two neighbors spoke: Pamela Morgan raised concerns about historic drainage/flooding problems, protecting large trees' root systems, and an existing spite fence near the shared driveway; former owner Meg Bruno, who originally subdivided the parcel, described the curve as the site of numerous serious accidents over the years and stressed the driveway relocation as a genuine safety issue. The board kept the public hearing open (rather than closing it) so neighbors can weigh in again once revised plans and soil-test results are submitted.
cases.publicComment: Pamela Morgan (adjacent neighbor) raised drainage, well-protection, and tree-root concerns and asked about a boundary fence; Meg Bruno (the property's former owner/original subdivider) strongly emphasized the dangerous accident history at the curve and urged the driveway be relocated for site distance.

memberPositions.evidence: Kept the public hearing open specifically so the neighbors could comment again on the amended plan, and pressed on whether soil testing would be a condition of approval or a prerequisite to it.

cases.name: 12 Maple Avenue - Restaurant Site Plan
cases.applicant: Represented by Tony (project representative, delayed arrival); property being sold to the restaurant operator by current owner Randy Caches
cases.status: discussion only; applicant directed to return and defend valet/parking plan and explore a parking district
cases.summary: Discussion-only review of a proposed 141-seat fine-dining restaurant with a kitchen addition. The site can only provide about 15 on-site spaces against a roughly 43-45 space need, which the ZBA already granted a large parking variance to cover; the plan relies on valet service, evening off-site spaces leased across the driveway at 20 Maple Avenue (assumed 100% cleared out at night), and 9 staff spaces leased at the American Legion (subject to the town's right of first refusal and not a guaranteed long-term solution). A board member voiced strong reservations: the daytime/lunch parking model (assuming only ~20% lunch occupancy) seemed unrealistic, the single shared in/out driveway allows queuing for only about 3 vehicles, and the practical reality is overflow parking into the nearby CVS lot - which the board explicitly said it has no authority to rely on or facilitate. The discussion pivoted to reviving a long-dormant idea (previously explored around when Mark Miller was practicing) of forming a formal parking district for that stretch of Maple Avenue, which under the town code would durably satisfy off-street parking requirements without relying on terminable private agreements; a prior attempt by the 12 Maple Avenue owner to organize neighboring property owners (including a resistant adjacent owner, "Trulis"/spelling uncertain) had failed for lack of participation, though a district could be imposed on non-participants representing less than 51% of assessed value. The board asked the applicant team to return prepared to defend the valet operations plan in detail and to explore parking-district feasibility with the town before scheduling a public hearing.

memberPositions.evidence: Said he had "reservations about the obliteration... of our parking regulations," questioned whether a 141-seat restaurant simply doesn't fit the space ("seven pounds of sugar in a five-pound bag"), and objected to the burden being placed on other private property owners' lots.

Raised the historical idea of a Maple Avenue parking district as a more durable solution than terminable lease agreements, and directed the applicant team to come back prepared to defend the valet plan.
Engaged on the day/night parking-synergy premise (that 20 Maple Avenue clears out for evening restaurant use) as a partially mitigating factor.

themes.note: Central to 12 Maple Avenue's restaurant parking/valet debate and the Majidi subdivision driveway sight-distance issue.
Extended airport-noise methodology debate on the 113 King Street Airport Campus.

staffInput.summary: Confirmed paperwork order across applications, drafted the positive ZBA recommendation letter, explained the mechanics and history of a potential parking district on Maple Avenue, and flagged re-noticing requirements for adjourned hearings.
Reviewed stormwater and sight-distance issues on the Majidi subdivision and weighed in on airport-campus and restaurant traffic/parking logistics.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Planning Board (Carthy chairing, with Jensen and Sauro present, Ruisi on Zoom, Pollack absent) approved the Feb 12 minutes and worked through a long agenda of subdivisions, site plans and wetland permits. Public hearings were held on the 32 Orchard Drive 5-lot subdivision (held open, hydrogeologist to be engaged), the 14 Tall Woods Road pool/wetland permit (approved), the contentious 23 Bedford Banksville Road office/storage site plan with the self-storage building now removed (held open amid heavy neighbor opposition), and the 40 High Street two-lot subdivision (approved with a negative declaration). The board also took up discussion items including the Airport Campus townhouse project nearing final approval, new-home site plans at 4 Armonk Heights and 99 Byram Ridge, wetland/golf-path work at 92 & 94 Round Hill, a mixed-use renovation at 12 Bedford Road, a special-use-permit amendment for the 448 Bedford Road nursery school, and granted several extensions of time.

memberPositions.evidence: Proposed keeping the subdivision under Planning Board jurisdiction, agreed to engage a hydrogeologist, and said 'we're going to pump the brakes' and keep the public hearing open.

cases.name: 4 Armonk Heights Road new single-family home
cases.address: 4 Armonk Heights Road (corner of Fairway and Armonk Heights Road)
cases.applicant: Angela Gavino (owner/developer)
cases.summary: Early site-plan review of a proposed ~7,000 sq ft home (with a barn removed from the plan after wetlands-consultant concerns); the board asked the applicant to reduce disturbance, consider tiered grading on steep slopes, stake out the house, and set up a Planning Board and Conservation Board site walk.
cases.publicComment: Neighbor Jennifer Nippo (32 Fairway, immediately downslope) opposed the size and hillside location of the home and described past stormwater flooding of her basement, urging a different location; the applicant said she would pipe and spread the town drainage to help mitigate the neighbor's water problem.

memberPositions.stance: Cautious/neutral; wants a site walk, staking and Conservation Board referral before proceeding
memberPositions.evidence: Said he drove by, told the applicant to stake out the house and driveway and coordinate a site walk, and to address staff memos and the Conservation Board.

cases.name: 92 & 94 Round Hill Road wetland permits (golf holes / access paths)
cases.applicant: Jerry Tortarella (Hocherman Tortorella & Wexler), attorney; Tim Allen (Bibbo Associates)
cases.summary: Introductory review of two related wetland applications: shifting/reworking golf putting greens and access paths on 92 (originally permitted administratively in 1999) and remediation of path work behind a pool on 94 that had drawn a building-department violation resolved by plea; treated as a Type II action, the board directed a site walk and referral to the Conservation Board, with a functional wetland analysis to follow.

memberPositions.stance: Neutral; wants a site walk and Conservation Board review before acting
memberPositions.evidence: Said he drove by the site and that 'this really sounds like the conservation board needs to dig in here,' agreeing to meet the applicant on-site.

cases.name: 12 Bedford Road mixed-use renovation (office + residence)
cases.applicant: John Jay Scarla Jr. (architect)
cases.summary: Review of a plan to renovate a historic structure into a law office in the front and residential duplex in the rear, remove the barn/shed, and build a rear parking lot; the board worked through driveway width, buffer/screening and clearance so delivery vehicles won't hit the building, and directed the applicant to LPC (certificate of appropriateness), ARB, and possibly the ZBA before scheduling a public hearing.

memberPositions.stance: Broadly favorable but wants driveway/parking clearance and screening resolved
memberPositions.evidence: Raised concern that a UPS/sprinter delivery truck could hit the building at the narrow rear driveway and asked whether the drive could be screened and shifted, while calling it in keeping with the neighborhood.

cases.name: 448 Bedford Road special use permit amendment (CMA Hillside nursery school)
cases.applicant: Steve Veneruso (Veneruso, Curto, Schwartz & Curto), attorney; Tom Curto/Carroll, architect
cases.summary: Introductory review of a request to amend a 1983 special use permit (which allowed two classrooms) to legalize the six classrooms the ~30-year-old nursery school actually operates, with added egress; the board explained the parallel special-permit track through the Town Board and directed the applicant to compile the outstanding items from staff comments before referral.

memberPositions.stance: Neutral/process-focused; probed for deficiencies and how oversight would work
memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether there were any major deficiencies or hurdles on staff's list that would block going to the Town Board (e.g., parking or outdoor play area), which Carthy framed as a question about keeping oversight.

cases.name: Birken property, 99 Byram Ridge Road new single-family home
cases.applicant: Alan Piltch (LPN Engineering); Taylor Seguinza, architect
cases.summary: Review of a single-family house (replacing a demolished home) on a ~1.34-acre R-1A lot with no wetlands and no variances required; after twice at the RPRC, the applicant detailed stormwater mitigation (subsurface pipe network, two rain gardens, infiltration trench) and the board directed a site walk to review five-foot retaining walls and neighbor sightlines, plus a neighbor-notification public hearing.
cases.publicComment: No public spoke, but the RPRC requested a neighbor-notification meeting given the neighborhood's long-standing stormwater concerns; a neighbor is to receive screening.

memberPositions.stance: Mildly supportive; wants a site walk on the walls/driveway and a public hearing scheduled
memberPositions.evidence: Said he remained concerned about the walls, driveway and what the neighbor would look at, directed the applicant to stake the house and walls for a site walk, and agreed to schedule the public hearing.

cases.name: Extensions of time (215 Business Park Drive, 124 Mount Kisco Road, Hidden Oaks subdivision)
cases.address: 215 Business Park Drive; 124 Mount Kisco Road; Hidden Oaks
cases.summary: The board granted routine extensions of time for 215 Business Park Drive, 124 Mount Kisco Road, and the Hidden Oaks subdivision (the latter reported nearly complete with the plat picked up for county filing).

themes.note: Central to nearly every application (Tall Woods, 40 High St, Byram Ridge, Armonk Heights, Orchard); board generally satisfied mitigation is being addressed.
Wetland permits, buffers and delineations recurred (Tall Woods, 23 Bedford Banksville, 40 High St, Round Hill, Armonk Heights).
Repeated neighbor worry about septic-vs-sewer, well drawdown and shared aquifers, especially at 32 Orchard and 40 High St; board agreed to consult a hydrogeologist for Orchard.
Slope disturbance debated at 32 Orchard, Armonk Heights and Byram Ridge; board notes regulations permit disturbance when erosion is controlled.
Repeated complaint that neighbors learned of projects late (Orchard, Banksville, Armonk Heights); board emphasized keeping items under its jurisdiction for future public hearings.
Dominated the 23 Bedford Banksville hearing where office/storage/woodworking uses may be non-conforming; board declined to approve.
Raised at 32 Orchard (66 trees, 11 over 24 inches) and Round Hill; mitigation via landscaping and conservation easements discussed.
Segmentation/lead-agency and Type II determinations discussed at 23 Bedford Banksville, 40 High St (neg dec) and Round Hill.
Airport Campus school-bus sight-line/right-turn exit on Cooney Hill Road prompted a request to consult Byram Hills transportation.
12 Bedford Road renovation requires LPC certificate of appropriateness and ARB review.

meetings.meetingSummary: The North Castle Planning Board approved the February 26 minutes and noted three applications (Harris, ~4/36 Main Street, 12 Maple Avenue) had come off the agenda. It reopened and then adjourned the public hearing for 11 Whipperwill Lane, focusing on private-road widening, an emergency-vehicle turnaround, tree loss and a promised landscape plan. It adopted the SEQRA findings statement and the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions for the Airport campus at 113 King Street (site plan withheld pending ARB approval). It introduced and referred the 10/20 Round Hill Road lot-line realignment to the ZBA (accessory-apartment variances) and Conservation Board, and worked through contaminated-fill removal, wetland/swale restoration and driveway-pier height on the Tripling Lane application, referring the piers to the ZBA.

cases.name: 11 Whipperwill Lane residential development
cases.summary: Applicant's team (attorney Corey Salomon and engineer Ralph) presented a switch to the smaller 5,800 sq ft home, private-road widening within the right-of-way, an emergency-vehicle turnaround, and commitments negotiated with neighbors; the board pressed for an engineered survey of the road improvements and a detailed landscape plan before approval, then adjourned the reopened public hearing.
cases.publicComment: No members of the public spoke; the applicant relayed neighbor requests (smaller home, added screening, limited work hours 9-6, porta-potty kept distant, no removal of additional mature trees).

memberPositions.stance: Supportive of progress but insists on an engineered survey plan of the road improvements and a robust landscape plan that satisfies neighbors before approval
memberPositions.evidence: Said the board will want an engineer's plan and urged the applicant to bring back an impressive landscape plan and keep working with the neighbors.

memberPositions.stance: Sought clarity that the road widening stays within the private right-of-way and would not require easements or tree removal
memberPositions.evidence: Asked whether the widening was in the public/right-of-way and whether easements from neighbors would be needed; a later speaker referenced 'like Jim just asked.'

cases.name: Airport campus subdivision, 113 King Street
cases.summary: The board adopted the SEQRA findings statement (consistent with the town board's) and approved the preliminary and final subdivision resolutions as amended, dated March 11, 2024; site plan approval was withheld because the applicant has not yet obtained ARB approval. Members debated the roughly 70 conditions but staff confirmed most were routine engineering items.

memberPositions.stance: Concerned about the large number of conditions in the preliminary and final resolutions
memberPositions.evidence: The town planner noted 'Jim has expressed some concerns regarding the number of conditions' in the resolutions of approval.

memberPositions.stance: Shared concern about ~70 conditions and questioned the urgency of signing off now
memberPositions.evidence: Said 'like Jim, I'm kind of concerned about ... 70 conditions ... I don't think we've ever signed off on one,' and asked where the urgency was.

memberPositions.stance: Moved the approvals and wanted the tax-certiorari discontinuance held in escrow until approvals and statutes of limitation expire
memberPositions.evidence: Continued to hold the stipulation of discontinuance in escrow pending approvals and made the motions to adopt the findings and subdivision resolutions.

cases.name: Hoberman lot-line realignment, 10 & 20 Round Hill Road (Rolling Hill subdivision)
cases.applicant: Robert and Jill Hoberman
cases.summary: Applicant team (Corey Salomon, engineer Rich Williams, architect Zachary Harwin) introduced a lot-line realignment of 2006 lots 4 and 5 creating a ~16-acre estate/family compound plus a smaller home, with no new lots; discussion centered on expanding the clearing-and-grading limit (4.7 to ~5.94 acres) to balance ~20,000 yards of cut, steep slopes, septic, and the environmentally sensitive Mianus River headwaters. The board scheduled a site walk and referred the detached accessory-apartment (ADU) variances to the ZBA and the application to the Conservation Board.
cases.publicComment: No general public spoke; the Conservation Board liaison confirmed the referral over the 10+ acre parcels was appropriate.

memberPositions.stance: Cautiously receptive but wants a site walk and respect for the prior board's environmental delineations; questioned filling sensitive areas just to balance earthwork and moved to refer ADU variances to the ZBA
memberPositions.evidence: Urged going out to see the site and suggested exporting fill might be the better environmental solution than filling areas the earlier board wanted preserved; moved to send the applicant to the ZBA.

memberPositions.stance: Engaged on the comparison of original vs. proposed clearing-and-grading limit lines and their side-to-side expansion
memberPositions.evidence: Worked through the red/blue/purple clearing-and-grading overlay, confirming where proposed limits expanded versus the original.

cases.name: Tripling Lane residence site plan / wetlands
